Forces from the Data

We read 221 US industries side by side and asked: what forces keep showing up? These are the 15 that do — each its own collection, with the real numbers as proof.
The method

The data-grounded companion to the Strategy Under a Force series. Every claim traces back to a specific industry we researched — 149 write-ups across 15 forces and five lenses.

A · The auto reordering

The auto tariff shock

25% tariffs on cars and parts in 2025 forced the auto supply chain to abandon the US and pivot toward Mexico, killing a century of manufacturing geography overnight.

In April 2025, the Trump administration slapped a 25% tariff on all imported vehicles and auto parts. It looked like one policy. What it actually did was rewrite the supply chain for an entire industry. Within months, US automakers and parts suppliers faced a choice: absorb massive costs, pass them to customers, or move everything to Mexico. Most of them chose Mexico.

What changed

The tariff hit on May 3, 2025, and it was not abstract. A 25% import duty on vehicles immediately raised the price of a car by $1,600 to $8,900 depending on where it was made. Steel and aluminum costs for domestic car makers jumped too. Ford, GM, and Stellantis absorbed $41.7 billion in collective tariff costs in the first half of 2025 alone. Stellantis reported a €2.3 billion ($2.7 billion) net loss partly because of the early tariff shock. BMW, Mercedes, and Volkswagen combined for $6 billion in losses. Customers simply didn't show up for the higher prices. EV sales, which were supposed to be the future, actually fell 4% in 2025 compared to 2024. Tesla's market share dropped from 49% in 2024 to 45% by 2026, even as the number of battery plants exploded—70 new facilities opened in 2025 alone, bringing US cell capacity to 20 GWh per year and threatening oversupply. What made all of this worse was that it happened right as the entire supply chain was supposed to transition away from gasoline engines toward electric. That transition requires retooling, new components (battery thermal management, lightweight materials, power electronics), and billions in R&D. Small parts suppliers didn't have the money to both absorb tariff losses and invest in EV tech. Some of them simply died. Auto parts supplier bankruptcies hit decade highs in 2025. First Brands, which owned Raybestos, Autolite, and FRAM, filed Chapter 11 in September 2025. Tayco and Accuride followed. About 29,000 parts manufacturing jobs disappeared in 2025 despite the fact that actual production volume stayed flat. The jobs vanished because suppliers automated harder and moved faster than ever before to Mexico.\n\nNearshoring to Mexico became the only rational move. In the first nine months of 2025 alone, new Mexican auto parts investment surged 200%. Mexico already sits inside USMCA, the trade deal that was supposed to keep manufacturing in North America. But the tariff regime created a new incentive structure: tariffs on non-FTA parts meant that Mexican-made components qualified for preferential duty treatment, while US-made parts faced retaliatory tariffs from China (10–15%) and compliance headaches with new Mexican tariffs (25–50% on non-FTA parts starting January 2026). For a supplier in Ohio or Michigan, the math became brutal. Move to Mexico, stay competitive, or go bankrupt. Stellantis announced a $13 billion US investment plan in October 2025, but the money was going into selective modernization—like a new four-cylinder engine plant in Kokomo, Indiana that will produce the GMET4 EVO starting 2026. This was not a reshoring surge. This was triage. The company was keeping just enough US capacity to say it was investing while pivoting the rest of the supply chain to Mexico.\n\nMeanwhile, the engine business was not dying—it was mutating. CAFE standards were reset in June 2025 to exclude EV credits from compliance calculations, which meant OEMs could sell more gasoline cars without penalty. But nobody wanted pure gasoline anymore. The market demanded hybrids, which jumped 10% year-on-year. So engine makers stopped making engines. They started making powertrains: gasoline blocks for legacy sedans, hybrid modules for new platforms, 48-volt mild-hybrid systems for trucks, and control electronics for everything. Engine and parts manufacturing in 2026 was a $43.8 billion market growing at 2.5% per year, which sounds stable until you realize it was half the complexity it used to be. The number of car platforms was shrinking. The number of suppliers was shrinking (from consolidation). The percentage of supply coming from Mexico was rising. By mid-2026, auto parts manufacturing in the US was a $74.9 billion market growing at 5.4% per year, but employment hadn't recovered from the 2025 collapse, and the margin profile had flipped: larger suppliers with R&D muscle were consolidating smaller players, and whoever wasn't big enough to invest in EV tech or agile enough to nearshore was getting acquired or liquidated.

The evidence

  • Auto parts manufacturing: US market size $74.9 billion in 2026, growing 5.4% annually, but employment collapsed after 2025 nearshoring wave.
  • Vehicle manufacturing: US auto industry lost $393.3 billion in 2026 (−1.0% growth), with Ford, GM, and Stellantis absorbing $41.7 billion in tariff costs in first half of 2025 alone.
  • Engine and parts manufacturing: $43.8 billion market in 2026 (2.5% growth), with 29,000 jobs lost in 2025 despite stable production, signaling rapid automation and nearshoring.
  • EV transition stalled: EV sales declined 4% in 2025 versus 2024; only 20% of new US sales were EVs or hybrids; Tesla share dropped to 45% by 2026.
  • Supply chain reordering: Mexican auto parts investment surged 200% in first nine months of 2025; Stellantis committed $13 billion to US modernization in October 2025 but shifted majority production toward Mexico under USMCA.

Who rides it

Mexico became the only rational location for North American auto supply. Any large supplier who could move manufacturing there did—whether to avoid tariffs, access USMCA duty treatment, or sidestep the Mexican retaliatory tariff regime by producing locally. Mexican facilities suddenly had cost advantage, political cover, and preferential access to the US market. Hybrids and battery thermal systems won too. Demand for hybrids jumped 10% year-on-year through 2025–2026, while pure gasoline demand stayed flat. That meant suppliers who could pivot to hybrid components and battery cooling systems (Denso, Bosch, Continental) picked up market share from legacy engine makers. Larger parts suppliers with R&D muscle and cash reserves won through consolidation. They bought up bankrupt competitors (First Brands, Tayco, Accuride) on the cheap and consolidated supply bases, which reduced their per-unit costs and made them more attractive to OEMs looking for financial stability.

Who's squeezed

Small and mid-sized US auto parts suppliers got squeezed the hardest. They couldn't absorb the tariff costs, couldn't afford EV retooling investments, and couldn't move to Mexico as easily as the big players. Decade-high bankruptcies in 2025 (First Brands, Tayco, Accuride) were the result. Traditional gasoline engine makers lost demand to hybrids and faced pressure from both tariffs and the shift toward electrification. About 29,000 parts manufacturing jobs disappeared in 2025 even though production stayed flat—automation and nearshoring killed them. Regions like the Rust Belt saw job losses concentrated in first-tier suppliers (the small shops that feed the big Tier 1 suppliers). EV startups and pure-electric platforms lost momentum too. EV sales actually fell 4% in 2025, and the industry was left with 70 new battery plants and capacity approaching oversupply by mid-2026—a classic boom-then-bust cycle where overinvestment preceded actual demand.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the supply chain gets so concentrated and so dependent on Mexico that any disruption—a pandemic, a political crisis south of the border, a labor shortage—cascades through the entire North American auto industry. Stellantis, Ford, and GM have already committed to massive Mexican investments. If Mexico's investment environment shifts, if labor costs rise, or if political instability slows shipping, the US auto industry has no fallback. The US never actually reshored. It just offshored one state to the west. That gamble works fine until it doesn't.

In one sentence

The auto tariff shock in a nutshell

Tariffs killed reshoring dreams and forced a 200% nearshoring surge to Mexico, collapsing small suppliers and consolidating the industry in nine months.

A · The auto reordering

The EV transition & legacy parts

Electrification voids some parts and creates others; suppliers must pick a side — and tariffs force the choice fast.

The auto industry is splitting. EVs don't need transmissions. Battery costs fell 8% in 2025, but federal tax credits disappeared September 30, 2025, crushing demand. Meanwhile, tariffs jumped from 2.2% to 17.0% by April 2025, and the Big Three took $65 billion in writedowns. Legacy parts suppliers are caught: nearshore now or get steamrolled.

What changed

The EV boom was never real — it was a subsidy mirage. Hybrid electric vehicle manufacturing hit $108.2 billion in 2026, up 15.7% since 2021, but that growth stopped when Congress ended federal consumer tax credits on September 30, 2025. BEV market share dropped 1.9 percentage points in the following months, falling to 5.9% by July 2026. Sales fell 4% nationally — the first annual decline after a decade of growth. The Big Three automakers (GM, Ford, Toyota) collectively took $65 billion in EV-related writedowns through early 2026. GM alone took a $6 billion charge; Ford took $19.5 billion. Both delayed EV production and pivoted aggressively to hybrids. Toyota cut 2026 BEV production by one-third. This forced the real reckoning: electrification eliminates entire categories of legacy parts.

A conventional transmission disappears in every EV. Automobile transmission manufacturing was already shrinking — the market fell from $54.7 billion in 2022 to $44.6 billion in 2026, a 2.9% decline in 2026 alone. Employment in transmission manufacturing dropped 68,000 workers during 2025. But hybrids offer a temporary reprieve: hybrid sales surged 20.5% through mid-2026, and hybrids need efficient multi-speed transmissions. This created a two-tier industry: transmission makers with hybrid expertise survive; those betting only on EVs face obsolescence. Allison Transmission, recognizing the shift, acquired Dana's off-highway business for $2.7 billion in early 2026, capturing ~$120 million in annual synergies. Smaller players didn't make it. TransAxle, a New Jersey-based drivetrain remanufacturer, shut down all 13 locations in 2025, laying off 209 workers — no bankruptcy, just a permanent exit because there was no business left to restructure.

Then tariffs became the bigger killer than electrification. The average effective US tariff rate spiked from 2.2% at end-2024 to 17.0% by April 2025, with retaliatory duties specifically targeting US steering racks and control arms from China. Automobile steering and suspension manufacturing dropped to $17.7 billion in 2025, down 3.8% that year, from a $14.1 billion baseline in 2022. The industry has 250 US companies, down from more, and margins sit at 2.6% — thin enough that a 15-point tariff increase wipes out all profit. Suppliers faced an ugly choice: absorb the cost and destroy margins, or nearshore to Mexico and Europe to avoid duties and collapse domestic volume. USMCA labor-cost compliance surged from 44% in 2024 to 67% in 2025, forcing $16/hour minimum wages in Mexican plants. By early 2026, compliance exceeded 80%, which paradoxically made reshoring of some transmission component production to the US suddenly economic compared to China tariffs — but only for firms large enough to absorb the reshoring capex.

The existential threat for suppliers is steer-by-wire. Electric power steering became standard across most compact and mid-size vehicles by 2025, replacing hydraulic systems entirely. But that's just the transition. Steer-by-wire — fully electronic steering with zero mechanical backup — reached production milestones in 2026. Mercedes-Benz deployed ZF's Steer-by-Wire system beginning 2026. Nexteer launched Motion-by-Wire innovations in September 2025, including series-production Steer-by-Wire systems with ASIL D certification on Chinese new-energy vehicles. Nexteer posted $4.6 billion in 2025 revenue and is capturing the market. ZF Friedrichshafen posted €38.8 billion in 2025 sales with a 4.5% adjusted EBIT margin. Only firms with deep pockets and global reach can afford the software, sensors, and electronics R&D to stay in the game. Tenneco recognized this and sold its Ohlins Racing suspension brand to Brembo for $405 million in January 2025 to refocus on electric steering. Smaller suppliers can't. This is not disruption — it's erasure.

The evidence

  • Hybrid electric vehicle manufacturing: $108.2 billion in 2026, up 15.7% CAGR 2021-2026, but tariffs and tax credit expiration (Sept 30, 2025) triggered first sales decline in a decade
  • Transmission manufacturing: $44.6 billion in 2026, down 2.9% year-over-year, with 68,000 jobs lost in 2025 as EVs eliminate transmission demand
  • Tariffs: average effective US tariff rate spiked from 2.2% (end-2024) to 17.0% (April 2025), forcing nearshoring decisions for steering and suspension suppliers
  • Steering and suspension manufacturing: $17.7 billion in 2025, down 3.8% that year, with 250 US companies facing 2.6% margins crushed by tariffs
  • Steer-by-wire: Mercedes-Benz deployed ZF systems beginning 2026; Nexteer launched series-production systems in September 2025, signaling end of mechanical steering columns

Who rides it

Global tier-one suppliers with scale win. Nexteer, Allison Transmission, and ZF are consolidating the market. Nexteer posted $4.6 billion in 2025 revenue capturing steer-by-wire and motion-by-wire production. Allison acquired Dana's off-highway business for $2.7 billion in early 2026 and captured ~$120 million in annual synergies. ZF secured the Mercedes Steer-by-Wire contract for 2026 onward. Suppliers with scale can nearshore to Mexico under USMCA to avoid US tariffs (USMCA compliance jumped to 80% by early 2026), invest in electric steering R&D, and bid for the next-generation steer-by-wire contracts. The hybrid boom also buys them time: hybrid sales surged 20.5% through mid-2026, and hybrids need efficient multi-speed transmissions that only established firms can mass-produce.

Who's squeezed

Smaller regional suppliers and transmission-only specialists are crushed. TransAxle, a New Jersey-based drivetrain remanufacturer, shut down all 13 locations in 2025 and laid off 209 workers. Transmission manufacturing employment fell 68,000 in 2025 alone. Suppliers betting on EVs-only strategy face obsolescence; those without hybrid product lines lost volume as BEV sales collapsed 4% nationally after tax credits ended September 30, 2025. Domestic US steering and suspension makers lose to tariffs: a 17.0% tariff rate by April 2025 forces choices between absorbing losses (impossible at 2.6% margins) or nearshoring to Mexico (which collapses domestic volume). Mid-market firms like Tenneco had to sell off entire business units (Ohlins Racing to Brembo for $405 million in January 2025) just to stay solvent and refocus on surviving capabilities.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that electrification and tariffs are moving faster than supplier adaptation. Steer-by-wire production is ramping at Mercedes (ZF), ZF-China deals, and Nexteer contracts right now in 2026. Only firms that have already invested billions in electronic steering and sensor software since 2023-2024 can bid. But the tariff regime is shifting again: if tariffs spike further or retaliation escalates, even nearshored suppliers face supply-chain whiplash. USMCA compliance costs ($16/hour minimum wages in Mexico by 2025, 80%+ compliance by early 2026) are rising. And battery costs, which fell 8% in 2025 to $108/kWh, are volatile: tariffs on lithium-ion cells are up 25%, and China still dominates 80%+ of global battery production. A supplier that invests $500M in a Mexico steering plant, bets the farm on the hybrid cycle lasting through 2028, and then sees steer-by-wire adoption accelerate, EV sales rebound on cheaper batteries, or tariffs change again — that supplier goes under. Speed matters more than strategy now.

In one sentence

The EV transition & legacy parts in a nutshell

Electrification kills whole part families while tariffs force suppliers to choose nearshoring over domestic production.

B · Heavy materials & metals

Metals Behind the Tariff Wall

Steel and aluminum tariffs ripple into every downstream builder and maker.

When Trump imposed 25% to 50% steel tariffs in early 2025 and doubled them by June, the US steel industry got a short jolt of demand and pricing power. Same story with aluminum: tariffs climbed from 25% to 50%, and prices spiked 25% year-over-year to $3,273 per ton by August 2026. But the bounce is already fading. Global oversupply is relentless, and the cost of the metals themselves—raw materials for steel up 9% to 17%, electricity for smelting now at $115+/MWh—is eating into those gains.

What changed

Steel bounced hard, then reality hit. The US steel industry hit $112.9 billion in market size in 2026, a 3.3% jump from 2025, after tariffs triggered a price spike and domestic production surge. The US became the third-largest steel producer globally in 2025. But the gains are narrowing fast. Raw material costs climbed: iron ore up 9%, coking coal up 17%, and scrap up 2% for 2025. Margin pressure is real—the gap between input costs and selling prices has tightened since spring 2025. Demand is not coming to the rescue. Construction spending grew 2.6%, but construction volume is flat. Automotive demand stays steady at 10.2M units, but steel content per vehicle keeps shrinking as EVs (now 42% of forecast output by 2031) are lighter than gas cars. Meanwhile, the world is drowning in steel. China exported a record 131 million tonnes in 2025, up 153% since 2020. The OECD warns that global excess capacity will grow from 640 to 745 million tonnes by 2028—new capacity of 139 million tonnes will arrive while demand grows only 34 million tonnes. The industry is consolidating fast because survival is hard. Cleveland-Cliffs swallowed ArcelorMittal and Stelco. Nippon Steel completed a $14.2 billion buyout of US Steel in June 2025 under government oversight. Headcount and mill count keep dropping: 196 steel establishments in 2026, down from 332 in 2022. Employees fell to 72,600 in 2026, declining 2.3% annually since 2021.\n\nAluminum tells a different, supply-constrained story. Prices surged 25% year-over-year by August 2026 to $3,273 per ton, driven by tariff protection, China's production ceiling at 45.5M tons, Russia's export collapse, and soaring EV demand for battery enclosures and body panels. The market is booming: $71.8 billion projected for 2026, up from $46.5 billion in 2022, with 6.09% CAGR projected through 2034. But growth is crippled by an electricity crisis. Primary smelting requires vast, stable power. Four US smelters produce only 683,500 tonnes per year, and just two run at full capacity, because electricity now costs $115+/MWh. Tech companies outbidding aluminum makers for renewable power has left the smelting sector half-idled. The answer is secondary (recycled) aluminum: it's energy-efficient and now dominates the sector. Eighty-five percent of US-made aluminum is recycled, up from 20-30% in the 1980s. Secondary jobs exploded—recycling employment up 20%+ since 2024. Novelis, the largest rolled-products maker, got hit hard by fires at its Oswego, NY facility from September to November 2025, disrupting shipments 5% in fiscal 2026. But the company is building back: Bay Minette, Alabama (600 kt capacity) opens in the second half of 2026. Century Aluminum restarted Mt. Holly capacity in June 2026 after a $50 million investment. The tariff wall is working for aluminum makers—prices are up, demand is up—but they are bottlenecked by power, not tariffs. The reshoring and nearshoring play here is not new mills but new recycling and downstream finishing capacity, because primary smelting will stay capped by electricity cost until power prices fall or AI competition for power eases.

The evidence

  • Iron & Steel: US steel became third-largest producer globally in 2025 after tariffs, but faces 131M tonnes of Chinese exports (up 153% since 2020) and OECD forecast of 745M tonnes global excess capacity by 2028
  • Iron & Steel: Employment down to 72,600 in 2026 (2.3% annual decline since 2021), mills consolidated from 332 in 2022 to 196 in 2026, despite 25-50% tariffs and $112.9B market size
  • Aluminum: Prices hit $3,273/ton by August 2026 (up 25% YoY) on tariff protection and EV demand, but primary smelting capped at 683,500 tonnes/year as electricity costs $115+/MWh—tech outbidding metalmakers for power
  • Aluminum: Secondary recycling now 85% of US production (up from 20-30% in 1980s), with recycling jobs up 20%+ since 2024; Novelis fires (Sept–Nov 2025) cut rolled-product shipments 5% in fiscal 2026
  • Aluminum: Market size projected $71.8B in 2026 (up from $46.5B in 2022), with 6.09% CAGR through 2034, as EV demand for battery enclosures and body panels accelerates despite global oversupply in steel

Who rides it

Recyclers and secondary aluminum processors win. Energy-efficient recycling dominates and jobs are up 20%+ since 2024. EV makers win on aluminum because tariff protection and EV demand (battery enclosures, body panels for lighter cars) send prices high but also guarantee supply—at least as long as power stays available. Integrated mills that can source scrap and run rolling/finishing lines (like Novelis, despite its fire setback) win over pure primary smelters. Foreign acquirers win: Nippon Steel bought US Steel for $14.2 billion in June 2025, and the company kept operating because the US saw no downside to Japan owning the brand, only upside in tariff rents.

Who's squeezed

Primary steel mills get squeezed. Global oversupply is immovable: 640 million tonnes of excess capacity growing to 745 million by 2028. China's 131 million tonnes of exports in 2025 (up 153% since 2020) blow through any tariff wall. US steelmakers lose headcount (down 2.3% annually since 2021) and mills (332 down to 196 in six years). Tariff-driven price gains vanish once raw materials (iron ore +9%, coking coal +17%) catch up. Downstream builders—auto, construction, appliance manufacturers—lose because they pay the tariff tax upfront and never see margins recover if they raise their selling prices. Primary aluminum smelters lose to electricity prices ($115+/MWh). Four US smelters make only 683,500 tonnes per year with two running below capacity. AI data centers outbid them for renewable power, and coal power is fading. The tariff wall protects the price, but power scarcity protects the shortage.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Global oversupply in steel is irreversible by tariff alone. The OECD warns 139 million tonnes of new capacity arrives by 2028 while global demand grows only 34 million tonnes. China's 131 million tonnes of exports in 2025 (up 153% since 2020) and China's ceiling of 45.5M tonnes of aluminum prove that no US tariff wall seals completely. The real risk is that tariffs exhaust political capital without solving the structural problem—demand isn't growing, vehicle steel content keeps dropping as EVs scale, and the world has too many steelmakers. In aluminum, the electricity crisis could persist. If power stays above $115/MWh and AI keeps outbidding metalmakers, the US never repairs primary smelting capacity. Tariffs protect price and recycled supply, but they leave primary mills and smelters crippled.

In one sentence

Metals behind the tariff wall in a nutshell

Tariffs lifted steel and aluminum prices in 2025-2026, but global oversupply in steel and an electricity crisis in aluminum smelting mean the gains are borrowed—reshoring winners are recyclers and downstream finishers, not primary producers.

B · Heavy materials & metals

The materials of everything

Tariffs and energy costs repriced basic materials—cement, chemicals, glass, rubber—making nearshore sourcing the only math that works.

When tariffs hit in early 2025, the price of everything made from basic materials spiked overnight. Chemical feedstock costs jumped 8–15%, cement got slapped with a 25% tariff in April, and synthetic rubber hit $2,387 per metric ton by Q1 2026. Manufacturers couldn't just raise prices—their customers were already reeling. So margins collapsed, consolidation accelerated, and whoever could move supply chains closer to home suddenly had an advantage worth billions.

What changed

Tariffs made feedstock cheap in the past look like a fantasy. US chemical product manufacturing generates $53.1 billion (2026), but that's growing at just 1.9% annually—a sector flatlining under pressure. When the US imposed its 10% universal tariff in early 2025, plus 20–50% targeted levies on selected countries, chemical makers faced immediate feedstock costs that rose 8–15%. Crude oil swung from $64 per barrel (2022 baseline) to $84.81 in June 2026, adding another layer of volatility that makes planning impossible. Downstream demand—automotive and construction—had already collapsed during 2024 under prior price spikes, and tariff uncertainty kept those customers afraid to commit to projects. Firms absorbed losses instead of passing them downstream because they had no choice. The response: automation and consolidation at a scale not seen in years. Global chemical M&A surged 18% in 2025. Borouge grabbed NOVA for $13.4 billion, ADNOC picked up Covestro for $14.7 billion, and Carlyle took a $7.7 billion stake in BASF's coatings business. These were not growth acquisitions—they were survival plays. Larger players retreated from commodities into specialty and high-margin segments. Smaller players got squeezed out.\n\nCement tells the same story in sharper relief because the math is concrete (literally). The US cement market is $16.94 billion (2025), but domestic production capacity is frozen at 102–105 million metric tons annually while consumption sits 105–108 million tons. That gap used to be filled by imports—25–26 million tons, nearly 21% of supply. Then the 25% cement tariff took effect in April 2025. Canadian and Mexican imports, which once accounted for 27% of the market, became price-uncompetitive overnight. Turkish and Vietnamese suppliers faced even steeper punitive duties. Import volumes fell 8% year-on-year in 2024 and stayed depressed through 2025. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act created durable demand—207,000+ miles of roadway and 11,400+ bridge projects underway—but it deployed only $500 billion of $1.2 trillion by September 2025. This floors demand but doesn't rescue margins: the industry runs a 4–5% EBIT margin, and tariffs ate straight through it. One bright spot emerged: Portland-limestone cement (Type IL) captured 97% of blended cement shipments by 2026 because it has 10% lower CO2 and all 50 states approved it by April 2024. Suddenly manufacturers had leverage on sustainability to justify higher prices, and consolidation quickened. CEMEX reported 19% EBITDA growth to $2.27 billion in Q3 2025—the first consolidated net sales increase since Q1 2024.\n\nGlass product manufacturing faced a different kind of disruption: tariffs upended financing while demand shifted. The market is $33.3 billion (2026) with 4,012 establishments, but the shocks in 2025–2026 are reshaping who survives. Tariffs on steel and aluminum hit 50% in June 2025, forcing fabricators to either pass costs downstream or absorb losses. Import restrictions on Chinese and Malaysian float glass tightened supply, but domestic producers haven't built new capacity yet because capital spending is still frozen by uncertainty. What changed is demand architecture: 89% of premium brands plan to switch from plastic to glass by end-2026. That shift is real because recycled PET now costs 20% more than virgin plastic, making glass cost-competitive for the first time in decades. This is creating new growth—container glass could grow 45% by 2035—in a historically stagnant industry. Regulatory pressure on emissions, heavy metals, and VOCs is also mounting, so smaller firms either invest in cleaner furnaces or exit. That's why NSG Group went private via Apollo restructuring in April 2026, why Apogee Enterprises acquired Kalwall for ~$115 million in July 2026, and why consolidation continues: the tariff-driven supply tightness meets the plastic-to-glass switch at exactly the moment firms need capital to upgrade emissions controls.\n\nRubber product manufacturing is the smallest market here—$23.7 billion (2026)—but it shows the clearest pain. The sector contracted 1.1% in 2026; employment declined; wages grew 4.4% in 2025 even as total sector size shrunk, meaning wage growth couldn't offset job losses. US manufacturers face 12% tariffs on rubber and plastics products (2025), and Japanese imports got hit retroactive to August 2025 at 15% baseline. Synthetic rubber prices stayed elevated at $2,387 per metric ton in Q1 2026, squeezing profit margins on commodity goods. Nearly 20% of domestic demand is now met by imports, up from historical levels. Automotive—the largest end market—weakened under consumer caution, though EV production creates specialized demand for new tire compounds and sealing systems that command premium margins. The only bright spot is that Mexico, 84% USMCA-compliant and tariff-advantaged, captured nearshore rubber production: imports from Mexico stayed competitive where Asian and Japanese suppliers got priced out. Import penetration rose overall, but geography mattered. Manufacturers report difficulty filling skilled roles; wages spiked but talent stayed scarce.

The evidence

  • Chemical manufacturing: Tariffs raised feedstock costs 8–15% in early 2025; global M&A surged 18% YoY with deals like Borouge/NOVA ($13.4B) and ADNOC/Covestro ($14.7B) consolidating into specialty segments (2025)
  • Cement: 25% tariff in April 2025 shrunk Canadian/Mexican imports from 27% to non-competitive; import volumes fell 8% in 2024, stayed depressed through 2025; CEMEX reported 19% EBITDA growth to $2.27B in Q3 2025, first sales increase since Q1 2024 (2025–2026)
  • Glass: 89% of premium brands planning plastic-to-glass switch by end-2026; recycled PET up 20% above virgin plastic, making glass cost-competitive; NSG Group went private (April 2026), Apogee acquired Kalwall for ~$115M (July 2026) amid tariff-driven consolidation (2025–2026)
  • Rubber: Synthetic rubber at $2,387/MT in Q1 2026; sector contracted 1.1% in 2026; import penetration at 20% of demand (up from baseline); US faces 12% baseline tariffs, Japanese imports 15% retroactive August 2025 (2025–2026)
  • Energy/crude volatility: Crude oil swung from $64/bbl (2022) to $84.81/bbl (June 2026), forcing chemical feedstock planners into impossible forecasts; manufacturers investing in automation and predictive maintenance to cut maintenance costs 25% and preserve margins (2022–2026)

Who rides it

Large materials producers with enough scale to consolidate and access to capital win. Borouge, ADNOC, Carlyle, CRH, and CEMEX all made major moves in 2025–2026 when smaller competitors couldn't afford to upgrade for emissions compliance or absorb tariff costs. Geographic arbitrage winners include Mexican rubber producers (84% USMCA-compliant, tariff-advantaged) and Turkish/Vietnamese cement suppliers facing lower duty rates than China and Southeast Asia. The plastic-to-glass shift rewarded glass makers who could finance new capacity and fund regulatory compliance upgrades at the exact moment tariffs made capital expensive. Companies that automated early—investing in digital twins and predictive maintenance that cut maintenance costs 25%—preserved enough margin to outbid rivals for acquisitions and talent.

Who's squeezed

Small and mid-sized chemical, cement, glass, and rubber manufacturers with low margins and no pricing power got squeezed out. Cement makers couldn't raise prices fast enough to offset 25% tariff costs and still keep construction customers. Rubber makers saw import penetration rise as tariffs pushed domestic prices above Mexican and USMCA-compliant alternatives. Glass fabricators absorbed margin cuts rather than lose customers to price-sensitive competitors. Chemical makers—especially those dependent on volatile crude oil feedstock with no specialty differentiation—either consolidated or shrank. Workers in rubber manufacturing saw wages spike 4.4% in 2025 even as total sector employment declined, meaning aggregate paychecks fell. Regions dependent on these manufacturing jobs faced continued attrition.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The largest risk is a liquidity crunch for mid-market suppliers when tariffs persist long enough to exhaust working capital. Chemical and cement makers operate on 4–7% margins; if tariff pass-through stays incomplete for more than 18–24 months, many will run out of cash before consolidation or price increases rescue them. A second risk: nearshoring capacity doesn't build fast enough to absorb tariff-driven reshoring demand. The US cement industry is already running at capacity; cement can't move easily across borders; if reshoring accelerates faster than domestic capacity grows, prices will remain pinched and project financing will seize up. A third risk: energy costs don't stabilize. Crude oil volatility makes feedstock forecasting impossible for chemical makers, and furnace energy is non-negotiable for cement, glass, and rubber production. If geopolitics drive another energy spike, these industries—which already operate at thin margins and have invested heavily in automation to preserve profitability—could face a cascade of bankruptcies among firms that bet wrong on energy futures.

In one sentence

The materials of everything in a nutshell

Tariffs repriced basic materials overnight—chemical feedstock jumped 8–15%, cement got 25% duties, synthetic rubber hit $2,387/MT—forcing consolidation at scale and shifting power to large players with capital to upgrade and nearshore faster than competitors.

C · Reshoring the factory

Reshoring advanced manufacturing

Defense mandates and tariff uncertainty pull chip fabs, 3D printers, and electrical equipment back home—but at the cost of margin and speed.

Advanced manufacturing isn't coming home because it's profitable. It's coming home because tariffs, defense mandates, and supply-chain anxiety made offshoring too risky. Semiconductors, 3D printers, and electrical equipment—the infrastructure of an AI-soaked grid—are suddenly strategic. The companies that move fastest to build US capacity are locking in government contracts and customer loyalty. Everyone else is getting squeezed.

What changed

Semiconductors became a matter of national defense. In January 2026, the US and Taiwan signed a $250 billion direct-investment agreement to push Taiwanese chip makers into US fabs. Intel is now running 18A production at its Arizona Fab 52; TSMC and Samsung are building out US capacity on the back of $52.7 billion in CHIPS Act funding spread across 18 planned factories. This is not market economics—it's forced relocation with government backing. The payoff is that any company with a US fab now has guaranteed demand from defense contractors and data centers nervous about supply shocks. The cost is real: US semiconductor manufacturing is more expensive than Taiwan or South Korea, and margins are thinner.

Computer manufacturing illustrates the gap between what reshoring looks like in theory and practice. The overall market reached $22.3 billion in 2026, up 15.3% from 2025—but this masks a collapse in consumer PCs and a surge in AI servers. Consumer PC shipments dropped 7% in Q1 2026 to 15.8 million units as DRAM costs jumped 40–70% year-to-date, with another 60% increase forecast for Q1 2026. By contrast, Dell recorded $113.5 billion in revenue in FY2026 (ending January 30) with 40% growth in infrastructure solutions and a $43 billion backlog, all from AI servers. Chinese laptop exports to the US fell 47.6% year-over-year in April 2025 after tariff threats. The problem: building consumer PCs domestically is currently uneconomic. Building AI servers for hyperscalers is the only reshoring path that closes, because the margin is there and the government demand is certain.

Electrical equipment manufacturing—transformers, switchgear, motor controls, distribution systems—faces a different kind of pressure. The market hit $81.4 billion in 2026, up 7.8% from 2025, driven by grid modernization and data-center buildout. US utilities are spending $84.9 billion on transmission and distribution in 2025 alone and laying over 26,000 miles of new power lines to connect distant renewable farms to cities. Data centers are expected to add electricity demand above 2% annually through 2026—more than twice the historical average. But profitability is collapsing. Copper prices jumped 18% in 2025, steel conduit costs rose 14%, and tariffs can add another 25% on top. A 50% tariff on copper products took effect in August 2025. Equipment lead times have doubled to over 26 weeks. The industry operates on 5.5% margins (2022), so any input cost shock translates to losses. Eaton, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and ABB are all investing heavily in US capacity—Siemens opened a new Fort Worth plant in 2025 with 480 jobs hired immediately and a target of 800—but this is defensive positioning against tariffs, not profit maximization. They're betting that sustained grid and data-center demand will eventually make the investment pay out, but in the near term they're eating costs.

3D printer manufacturing is racing for a different finish line: the defense contract. The global market hit $30.5 billion in 2025 with 20.5% growth projected to 2026. The US had 182 manufacturers and 5,569 employees in 2025, up from a $5.181 billion baseline in 2021. Metal additive manufacturing—printing rocket nozzles, turbine blades, aircraft parts—is the fastest-growing segment, projected to reach $102 billion globally by 2035 at 24% CAGR. The FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act included restrictions on foreign 3D systems for Department of Defense work, and those orders are real. Stratasys merged with Desktop Metal in 2023 to integrate polymer and metal capabilities, invested in Tritone Technologies for metal and ceramic printing in 2025, and is hunting for every aerospace and defense contract available. Entry-level machines from Chinese makers (Bambu Lab, Creality) are underpricing commodity models, but the high-margin action is in aerospace aftermarket parts and military contracts. Companies that own domestic metal-printing capacity are locking in 10–15 year defense relationships. Companies that don't are watching their industrial printer sales collapse into a low-margin commodity market.

The evidence

  • Semiconductors: US and Taiwan signed $250B direct-investment agreement (January 2026) to push chip making into US fabs; Intel now runs 18A production at Arizona Fab 52; $52.7B in CHIPS Act funding backs 18 planned factories (2025-2026).
  • Computer manufacturing: Dell hit $113.5B revenue in FY2026 with 40% growth in AI infrastructure and $43B backlog; consumer PC shipments dropped 7% in Q1 2026 as DRAM costs surged 40–70% YoY; Chinese laptop exports fell 47.6% YoY in April 2025 (2025-2026).
  • Electrical equipment: Market reached $81.4B in 2026, up 7.8% YoY; copper prices jumped 18% in 2025 and tariffs add another 25% on top; switchgear lead times doubled to 26+ weeks; Siemens Fort Worth plant (opened 2025) hired 480 with target of 800 (2025-2026).
  • 3D printing: Global market hit $30.5B in 2025 with 20.5% growth; metal additive manufacturing to reach $102B by 2035 at 24% CAGR; FY2026 NDAA restricts foreign systems for DoD work; Stratasys-Desktop Metal merger (2023) integrating polymer and metal capabilities (2025-2026).
  • Grid modernization: US utilities spending $84.9B on transmission/distribution in 2025; laying 26,000+ miles of new power lines; data-center electricity demand expected above 2% annually through 2026, more than 2x historical average (2025-2026).

Who rides it

Companies with domestic manufacturing capacity—Stratasys in 3D printing, Intel and TSMC in chips, Eaton and Siemens in electrical gear—are locking in long-term defense contracts, government subsidies, and customer loyalty from risk-averse buyers. They're paying more to build here, but they're also getting certainty: guaranteed off-take agreements, tariff protection, and priority access to government infrastructure spending. For AI-server makers like Dell, reshoring is not a cost but an asset—the supply-chain security is worth a price premium to hyperscalers. For 3D printer makers, the defense mandate is a moat: Stratasys and Desktop Metal (now merged) own metal-printing IP that Chinese competitors can't easily replicate in the timeframe that DoD contracts require. First-mover advantage in domestic capacity is worth years of operating margin loss.

Who's squeezed

Low-cost contract manufacturers and commodity-hardware makers are getting crushed. Chinese 3D-printer makers (Bambu Lab, Creality) are undercutting industrial models in consumer and low-end commercial segments, but they're locked out of defense work. Chinese laptop makers lost 47.6% of US export volume in a single year as tariffs and supply-chain anxiety pushed customers toward domestic assembly. Entry-level computer manufacturers who don't have an AI-server story or government contract are watching margins compress: consumer PC margins were already thin, and now DRAM costs have spiked 40–70%, making a profit on a $500 laptop nearly impossible. Small electrical-equipment distributors are squeezed between tariffs pushing costs up 25–40% and lead times that have doubled to 26 weeks, destroying working capital and forcing inventory hoarding. Companies without US manufacturing have to choose between absorbing tariff costs or losing customers to Eaton and Siemens, who built domestic capacity and can pass costs along to government buyers.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that reshoring is only economically viable at the high end. AI servers and defense contracts have margins fat enough to absorb higher US manufacturing costs. Consumer PCs, entry-level 3D printers, and commodity electrical gear do not. If tariffs stay high and the government doesn't continue massive subsidies (like the CHIPS Act), reshoring will hollow out to just military and luxury goods, leaving the bulk of manufacturing offshore and the US supply chain more fragmented, not less. Companies betting on reshoring are also betting that government infrastructure spending (grid, data centers, defense) stays strong through 2028 and beyond. If demand softens—if recession hits, if AI buildout slows, if political will for defense spending wanes—the massive capacity investments made in 2025-2026 become stranded assets. Lead times are already at 26 weeks; if orders dry up, backlogs evaporate overnight and factories go dark.

In one sentence

Reshoring advanced manufacturing in a nutshell

Tariffs and supply-chain security rules are forcing US manufacturers of chips, 3D printers, and electrical gear to invest domestically—and fast—even though it's more expensive and less profitable.

C · Reshoring the factory

Appliances & durable goods

A 50% tariff on imported appliances in mid-2025 crushed margins and forced US makers to nearshore fast—or absorb billions in costs.

In June 2025, the US government slapped a 50% tariff on the steel-equivalent content in imported refrigerators, washers, dryers, dishwashers, and ovens. Within months, every major appliance maker in America was bleeding. Whirlpool absorbed approximately 300 million dollars in new tariff costs. Electrolux went negative on operating margins. LG and Samsung posted losses. And the market was too weak—too promotional, too flat—to pass those costs to consumers. The appliance business, which had hummed along at 2.8% operating margins when times were good, hit rock bottom. So they pivoted: nearshoring US plants, modernizing old factories, and betting on smart appliances instead of competing on price.

What changed

Tariffs on imported appliances rewrote the economics overnight. Before June 2025, US appliance makers had outsourced heavily: 55% of domestic demand was still met by imports despite decades of trade protection. Whirlpool, Electrolux, LG, and Samsung had spread manufacturing across Mexico, China, and Southeast Asia to keep costs down. The tariff was meant to protect US makers, but the timing was brutal. The housing market was already mixed—single-family starts fell 6.9% in 2025 to 943,000 units, while multifamily jumped 17.4%—and the retail market for appliances was essentially flat, growing just 0.3% to 0.6% in 2026. When you can't raise prices and your input costs jump 50%, you absorb the hit. Whirlpool's Q4 2025 margins collapsed to 2.8%. Electrolux turned negative at -2.9%. The market was so competitive and promotional that no one could pass through the tariff cost.

Tariffs made nearshoring newly valuable—and urgent. The moment those tariff bills landed in Q4 2025, every major appliance maker announced big US investment plans. GE Appliances (the Haier subsidiary that makes everything from refrigerators to ranges) committed 3 billion dollars over five years in August 2025, including modernization of 11 US plants and expansion in Kentucky, Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, and South Carolina. Whirlpool followed with 300 million dollars for laundry manufacturing at its Clyde and Marion plants in Ohio, expecting to add 400 to 600 jobs by end-2026 and early 2027. These weren't small tweaks. They were bets that even though tariff costs were punishing in the near term, building in the US—or nearshoring to Mexico—was cheaper and faster than importing from Asia and eating the 50% hit.

The tariff also made smart appliances—AI-powered, connected to home ecosystems—newly valuable. When you're competing on price and your margins are destroyed, you pivot to higher-margin segments. Whirlpool, LG, and Samsung all shifted strategy toward connected appliances where consumers will pay premiums for convenience, energy efficiency, and smart features. This was the escape route from pure commoditization. But it also meant smaller, local manufacturers without the R&D budget to compete in smart appliances were locked out. The five major players—Haier/GE Appliances, Whirlpool, Electrolux, LG, and Samsung—controlled about 60% of the market going into 2026, and the tariff and margin crisis only concentrated power further.

By 2026, the appliance industry faced a painful choice: nearshore fast to Mexico or Southeast Asia with fresh investment, or stay in Asia and absorb tariff costs in perpetuity. For major players, nearshoring became the only path to margin recovery. For smaller manufacturers without capital for factories or supply chains, it became a squeeze play. The broad retail appliance market was 144.83 billion dollars in 2026—huge—but growth was essentially flat at 0.3% to 0.6%, leaving zero room for error. Tariffs made scale, speed, and capital decisive.

The evidence

  • Appliance Manufacturing: Whirlpool absorbed 300 million dollars in tariff costs from the June 2025 50% tariff on steel-equivalent imports, with Q4 2025 margins collapsing to 2.8%.
  • Appliance Manufacturing: Electrolux, LG, and Samsung all posted negative or razor-thin margins in Q4 2025, unable to pass tariff costs to consumers in a flat, promotional market.
  • Appliance Manufacturing: GE Appliances committed 3 billion dollars (August 2025) to modernize 11 US plants and expand in Kentucky, Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, and South Carolina.
  • Appliance Manufacturing: Whirlpool announced 300 million dollars for US laundry manufacturing (October 2025), expecting 400-600 jobs by end-2026; industry market was 144.83 billion dollars in 2026 with flat 0.3-0.6% growth.
  • Housing: Single-family starts fell 6.9% in 2025 to 943,000 units, but multifamily surged 17.4%, creating demand for compact and stackable appliance configurations.

Who rides it

Whirlpool, Electrolux, GE Appliances (Haier), and other major manufacturers with capital to invest in US plants win in the long run. The nearshoring strategy—modernizing existing US factories and building new capacity in Mexico—puts them ahead of imports. They also win by moving into smart appliances, where margins are better and tariffs matter less because consumers pay for convenience and data, not just steel. Regional winners in the US South (Kentucky, Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, South Carolina) gain jobs and factory investment. Suppliers of components for smart home systems also win.

Who's squeezed

Smaller appliance manufacturers without capital to nearshore lose access to low-cost Asian supply chains and can't compete on price anymore. The tariff and margin collapse squeeze out anyone who didn't have scale or R&D budget to move upmarket into smart appliances. Importers and distributors who counted on cheap Asian appliances to drive volume also get hurt. Consumers in the near term lose too—appliances got more expensive through the promotional squeeze (retailers absorbed costs), and the flat market meant less choice and innovation. Housing was weak in 2025 (single-family starts down 6.9%), which dampened appliance sales overall.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that nearshoring to Mexico or Southeast Asia doesn't solve the tariff problem fast enough, and US appliance makers stay trapped in margin collapse for years. The retail market grew just 0.3% to 0.6% in 2026—essentially flat. If housing demand doesn't recover (single-family starts are already down), and the market stays promotional and competitive, then even with lower costs, appliance makers won't have room to recover margins. The other risk: if tariffs on Mexico or other nearshore destinations rise later (as trade policy can do), then all the investment in new US plants and supply chains becomes stranded.

In one sentence

Appliances & durable goods in a nutshell

When tariffs hit appliances in June 2025, major manufacturers couldn't raise prices on consumers and lost 300 million dollars to Whirlpool alone—now they're racing to build back US factories.

D · Food & the retail edge

Food's tariff exposure

Tariffs and commodity shocks are reshaping meat, coffee, and soy processing—winners are those fast enough to nearshore or consolidate.

Food processing sits at the collision point of three forces that don't normally hit at once: tariffs, commodity volatility, and labor scarcity. Meat plants can't find workers to fill cutting roles even at rising wages. Coffee roasters face a 60% year-over-year spike in bean prices and tariffs that choke imports. Soybean crush margins are collapsing even as volumes hit record highs. The industry is reshaping fast—and winners are the ones moving fastest to consolidate, automate, and lock in supply.

What changed

The meat processing industry—a mature $387.7 billion (2026) sector that has barely grown in 50 years—is now squeezed from both sides at once. Beef cattle prices are up 7% to an average of $240 per cwt in 2026 as supplies tighten. But labor is the real shock: the Big Four processors (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef) can't fill meat-cutting and evisceration roles at any wage. The work is brutally physical, and immigration enforcement under Trump has tightened the labor pipeline sharply. The result is a surge in automation investment—meat processors are pouring money into cobots and AI vision systems to replace skilled butchers. Simultaneously, export markets have collapsed and recovered unpredictably. China locked out US beef in 2025, wiping out 96% of sales and leaving September 2025 exports at just 556 metric tons. A May 2026 Trump-Xi trade deal restored partial access, but US plants still struggle to meet the new quota requirements. Plant-based meat, which was the boogeyman in 2023–2024, has effectively vanished—down to 2–3% retail share as consumers rejected the taste and "lack of naturalness." What's actually reshaping the industry is consolidation and antitrust pressure: the DOJ opened investigations into the Big Four in 2025–2026, and price-fixing settlements have cost them hundreds of millions.

Coffee roasting—a $23.76–$29.03 billion (2025) industry—is caught between premiumization and commodity chaos. Consumers aged 18-40 are driving specialty demand; 66% of American adults drink coffee daily as of 2025, and ready-to-drink cold brew is growing at 7.5% annually through 2034. But input costs have turned brutal. Arabica prices hit record highs of $4.30 per pound by December 2024, up 60% year-over-year, as droughts ravaged Brazil and Vietnam—which together supply over 50% of global coffee. Brazil's 2025-26 production fell 4.4%, and Vietnam faces a 10-20% harvest decline. Then the US slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian coffee imports in mid-2025, cutting August imports 75% versus 2024. Roasters scrambled to Colombian and other origins, but that creates supply-chain fragility and quality variation. Margins are compressed—retailers take 11–19 months to pass cost increases to consumers, leaving roasters absorbing losses in 2025-26. Consolidation is the response: Royal Cup acquired Farmer Bros in March 2026 to create scale, and Nestlé and Starbucks launched a cold-coffee concentrate line together, betting that RTD and functional (mushroom, vitamin, adaptogen-infused) formats can escape commodity volatility.

Soybean processing is flooded—but not for the reason anyone expected. The EPA's renewable-diesel mandates under the RVO (Renewable Volume Obligation) have created nearly unlimited demand for soybean oil as a feedstock. This triggered a 23% capacity expansion over three years, with over $6 billion invested in new crush facilities. Crush volumes hit a record 2.54 billion bushels forecast for 2025–26. But here's the trap: crushing soybeans for oil leaves meal—a massive byproduct. The flood of cheap meal has collapsed crush margins from $2–$3 per bushel in 2023 to just $1.10–$1.50 per bushel in 2025 as four new major plants came online in North Dakota, Kansas, and elsewhere. China's 13% tariff on US soybeans (imposed 2018, still standing in 2025) has reduced US soybean exports to China by 33% versus 2024, forcing processors to rely on domestic crush instead of global markets. Soybean prices themselves swing wildly—they peaked at $12.30 per bushel in early 2024, fell to $9.55 mid-August 2024, recovered to $10.30 by end-of-2025, and sat around $11.60 by August 2026. The response is aggressive expansion: Louis Dreyfus, North Dakota Soybean Processors, and Incobrasa all broke ground on new plants in 2024. By 2025–2026, ADM, AGP, and SD Soybean Processors brought facilities online. In August 2026, ADM alone announced upgrades unlocking ~700,000 metric tons of additional annual capacity. But margins stay compressed because supply is massive and there's nowhere to sell it except into renewable diesel—which is mandated, not profitable.

The evidence

  • Meat processing: Beef cattle prices forecast to average $240 per cwt in 2026, up 7% from 2025, while the Big Four (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef) face DOJ antitrust investigations and price-fixing settlements totaling hundreds of millions in 2025–2026.
  • Coffee roasting: Arabica coffee hit $4.30/lb by December 2024 (up 60% YoY), and the US 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in August 2025 cut imports 75% YoY, forcing roasters to shift to Colombian origins and compress margins for 11–19 months until retail prices catch up.
  • Soybean processing: Crush margins fell from $2–$3/bushel in 2023 to $1.10–$1.50/bushel in 2025 as new facilities added 75 million bushels of annual capacity, yet China's 13% tariff (2018–2025) reduced US soybean exports to China by 33% versus 2024.
  • Meat automation: Global market for automation robots projected to reach $4.5B by 2033 (9.2% CAGR) as meat processors race to replace labor in de-hoofing, evisceration, and packaging roles.
  • Coffee consolidation: Royal Cup acquired Farmer Bros in March 2026 to create scaled integrated beverage platform, while Nestlé and Starbucks launched cold-coffee concentrate line to capture fast-growing RTD and functional coffee segments (7.5% CAGR through 2034).

Who rides it

Consolidators win. Royal Cup, Nestlé, and Starbucks move fast to lock in scale and differentiate into cold brew and functional formats. Big meat processors with capital for automation—even facing antitrust heat—can offset labor scarcity by replacing butchers with cobots. Soybean crushers with integrated renewable-diesel operations (ADM, AGP) can absorb margin compression because they're making fuel, not competing on meal alone. The shared pattern: whoever captures nearshore supply first, invests in automation or product innovation, and has enough scale to weather tariff swings wins. Smaller, single-format players—regional coffee roasters, independent crush mills, local meat packers—get squeezed.

Who's squeezed

Regional and independent players get hammered. Small coffee roasters can't absorb the 60% commodity spike or negotiate tariff pass-through like Nestlé can. Independent soybean crushers can't invest in the capacity expansions that ADM and Louis Dreyfus are pouring $6 billion into—they get margin-crushed as meal prices collapse. Small and mid-sized meat packers can't afford the automation surge or the compliance burden of DOJ antitrust investigations. Labor-dependent processors without capital for automation lose workers to other sectors. And retailers initially absorb losses—the 11–19 month lag before coffee price increases hit shelves means smaller roasters face 12+ months of margin compression with no relief. Import-dependent roasters betting solely on Brazilian coffee get hit hardest by tariffs.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is tariff-on-tariff cascading and supply-chain bifurcation. If the US slaps reciprocal tariffs on another major food origin—say Colombia on coffee, or Canada on grains—the industry fractures into separate supply networks (US-nearshore vs. Asia vs. EU), forcing processors to duplicate infrastructure or pick sides. China's behavior is also unpredictable: the May 2026 beef deal restored partial access, but quota enforcement is unclear, and China could lock out US beef again over geopolitical friction. The labor crunch in meat processing is real and accelerating—automation helps, but it's capital-intensive and takes 2–3 years to deploy. If immigration enforcement stays tight and wages don't rise fast enough, some plants could go idle or relocate to Mexico. Finally, commodity volatility looks structural (climate, mandates, tariffs) rather than cyclical. Coffee droughts, soybean oversupply, and renewable-diesel mandates aren't going away. Processors with thin margins (1–5% in meat and soy, 10% in coffee but compressed) can't survive repeated $0.50–$1 per unit swings.

In one sentence

Food's tariff exposure in a nutshell

Tariffs and commodity shocks are forcing meat, coffee, and soy processors to consolidate, automate, and nearshore—but independent and regional players lack the capital and scale to survive the reshuffle.

D · Food & the retail edge

The retail import shock

Tariffs on clothing and furniture hit thin margins hard, collapsing brick-and-mortar chains while fast movers pivot to online and nearshore supply.

For decades, US retail rode on a simple machine: buy cheap from overseas, mark up thin. Tariffs—especially the August 2025 end of the de-minimis exemption that had let goods under $800 slip through duty-free—turned that machine off overnight. Clothing importers and furniture stores that made 2–5% net margins suddenly faced $136 extra costs per family just in tariff passes. The result wasn't subtle: a wave of bankruptcies, store closures, and a sharp split between retailers nimble enough to go online and those stuck in physical showrooms.

What changed

Tariffs made cheap imports suddenly expensive, and cheap imports were the entire business model. Women's clothing retail had been shrinking for years—down 0.3% annually even before tariffs hit—because fast-fashion platforms like Shein and Temu were already eating the mass-market's lunch with $3 t-shirts. Tariff costs just finished the job. The 25% duty on upholstered furniture, cabinets, and vanities (imposed October 2024, held at current rate through late 2026) forced choices: absorb the cost and watch your 3% margin evaporate, or raise prices and watch customers walk. Many chose neither and just shut down. Forever 21 filed Chapter 11 in March 2025 and liquidated all 354 stores. Liberated Brands (Volcom, Billabong, Quiksilver, Roxy, RVCA, Spyder) liquidated 122 stores. American Signature filed Chapter 11 in November 2025, closing Value City Furniture. Walker Edison Furniture filed in August 2025 and sold for a fire-sale $20 million.

The tariff wave also exposed that retail's moat was geography and shelf space, not supply chain resilience. Once shelf space became a liability—because you had to stock inventory when tariffs were in flux and customs delays made restocking risky—traditional retailers lost their edge. E-commerce platforms didn't have that problem. Wayfair captured 14% of the 2025 US furniture market; online furniture channels jumped to 28% of total market share by 2025, growing 5–10% annually. DTC brands are projected to hit $51 billion in US revenue by 2026. Women's clothing online sales hit $61.8 billion in 2025, nearly matched brick-and-mortar's $66.4 billion. Employment in online women's clothing grew 5.5% annually from 2019 to 2024, while brick-and-mortar employment kept shrinking.

The winners were retailers who could move fast: premium and specialty brands that hadn't built their entire model around volume and thin margins, and platforms that had already solved the last-mile logistics puzzle. Luxury and specialty women's retailers focused on affluent customers or niche segments (plus-size, athletic, sustainable) kept growing. They could absorb or pass tariff costs because their margins weren't 2–5%; they could also afford the geographic diversification that tariffs made necessary. Wayfair, DTC furniture makers, and Shein/Temu all had already rebuilt their supply chains around speed and scale outside traditional retail footprint, so tariffs just confirmed what they already knew: the future was logistics and omnichannel, not showrooms.

The losers were mass-market chains—independent retailers, mid-market players, and anyone who'd leaned on volume-at-low-margin as their entire strategy. Store closures hit 7,323 in 2024 and roughly 6,000 in the first half of 2025 alone. Macy's announced 150 stores over three years (66 announced January 2025). Housing-market weakness made it worse: new home sales dropped 17.6% month-over-month in January 2026 and 11.3% year-on-year, draining furniture demand just when retailers needed it most. Consumers, hit by tariff costs and inflation, traded down to cheaper goods, which meant Shein's $3 shirt beat everyone's $8 shirt. The bifurcation was brutal and fast. Tariffs didn't create the problem—e-commerce and ultra-low-cost platforms did—but they accelerated it beyond any retailer's ability to adapt except the ones who'd already adapted.

The evidence

  • Women's clothing retail in the US: $66.4B market (2026) declining at -0.3% annually with 2.3-5% net margins, hit by August 2025 tariff exemption end forcing $136 per-family cost pass
  • Furniture stores squeezed by 25% tariffs on upholstered goods (Oct 2024, held through late 2026) compressing 3% margins, while Wayfair captures 14% market share and online channels reach 28% of sales
  • Forever 21 bankruptcy liquidation (March 2025, all 354 stores), Liberated Brands liquidation (Feb 2025, 122 stores), American Signature Chapter 11 (Nov 2025) show mass-market retail collapse under tariff+e-commerce pressure
  • E-commerce women's clothing reached $61.8B (2025) nearly matching brick-and-mortar's $66.4B (2026), with online employment growing 5.5% annually while physical retail employment declined
  • Furniture market bifurcation: DTC brands projected $51B US revenue by 2026, online channels growing 5-10% annually, while new home sales dropped 17.6% month-over-month (Jan 2026) crushing traditional retailers

Who rides it

Online platforms and DTC brands won by having already rebuilt supply chains for speed and omnichannel logistics. Wayfair, Shein, Temu, and premium specialty retailers could either absorb tariff costs (if margins were fat enough) or pass them along (if their customers cared more about the product than the price). E-commerce furniture is projected to hit $51 billion by 2026; online women's clothing already crossed $61.8 billion in 2025. The winners weren't faster negotiators or smarter importers—they were the ones who'd already moved their entire operation away from traditional retail footprint and low-margin volume plays.

Who's squeezed

Mass-market brick-and-mortar chains and independent retailers got crushed. Thin margins—2-5% for women's clothing, 3% for furniture—left no room for tariff costs. Retailers couldn't absorb them, consumers wouldn't tolerate higher prices, and store closures accelerated: 7,323 in 2024, another 6,000 in the first half of 2025. Forever 21, Liberated Brands, American Signature, and Macy's (announcing 150 closures) all failed to adapt fast enough. Housing weakness made it worse for furniture: new home sales dropped 17.6% month-over-month in January 2026, draining the core demand engine.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that tariffs don't come down, and supply chains don't re-diversify—they just stay stuck in transition. That leaves US retailers in limbo: too expensive to import from Asia, too slow to build out nearshore capacity in Mexico or Southeast Asia, too dependent on physical showroom real estate in a shrinking market. If tariffs stay high and housing stays weak, furniture could look like women's clothing: a hollowed-out sector where only niche premium brands and ultra-low-cost e-commerce platforms survive, and the middle class buys nothing in between.

E · The big picture

Atoms Strike Back

Trade war tariffs make foreign supply chains expensive and risky; nearshoring wins, thin-margin importers lose.

Starting in 2025, US tariffs turned the global supply chain inside out. A 25% levy on auto parts, 50% on steel, and cascading restrictions on machinery transformed the math for manufacturers. The cost of importing is now so high that nearshoring to Mexico—or building at home—is faster and cheaper than shipping from Asia. The winners are companies with capital to move, domestic makers with pricing power, and nations next door. The losers are importers living on razor-thin margins and industries locked into oversupply.

What changed

The 25% tariff on imported auto parts (effective May 2025) hit a sector already fragile from EV transition. Auto parts makers, facing both tariff walls and evaporating demand for exhaust systems and radiators as EVs take over, had only one choice: move production to Mexico. In the first nine months of 2025 alone, Mexican auto parts investment surged 200%—a reshoring in everything but name. US auto parts are bouncing (5.4% growth in 2026, market at $74.9 billion) but only because the larger customers can afford the tariff hit and force suppliers to absorb it. Smaller specialists are going bankrupt; employment fell despite stable production as factories got leaner. Bankruptcy filings among auto parts suppliers hit decade highs in 2025. This isn't a recovery; it's a consolidation.

Steel faced a different shock but the same outcome: tariffs worked, then physics won. In February-June 2025, Trump imposed 25–50% tariffs, and steel prices spiked. The US became the third-largest steel producer globally in 2025—a genuine windfall. But the margin windfall is already eroding. Raw material costs rose sharply (iron ore +9%, coking coal +17% in 2025), and demand is flat. Construction spending grew 2.6% but volume didn't move. Automotive demand is steady at 10.2M units but is losing steel content as EV adoption hits 42% of output by 2031. Global oversupply is the immovable object: China exported a record 131 million tonnes in 2025 (up 153% since 2020), and OECD projects global capacity will grow from 640 to 745 million tonnes by 2028 while demand grows only 34 million. Tariffs won one round. Market physics is winning the next one. The industry is consolidating at speed—Cleveland-Cliffs acquired ArcelorMittal and Stelco, and Nippon Steel bought US Steel for $14.2 billion in June 2025, absorbing it under government "Golden Share" oversight. Domestic capacity is now political, not just economic.

Soybean processing tells the story of reshoring meeting market reality head-on. The EPA's renewable diesel mandates created nearly unlimited demand for soybean oil, triggering a 23% capacity expansion over three years and $6 billion in new crush facility investment. Crush volumes hit a record 2.54 billion bushels forecast for 2025–26. But crushing soybeans produces meal as a byproduct—tons of it. That meal flooded the market and collapsed margins from $2–$3 per bushel in 2023 to $1.10–$1.50 in 2025 as new plants came online in North Dakota, Kansas, and elsewhere. China's 13% tariff on US soybeans (in place since 2018, unchanged) reduced US exports to China by 33% versus 2024, forcing domestic processors to rely on crush rather than global markets. Soybean prices bounced around (peaked at $12.30 in early 2024, fell to $9.55 mid-August 2024, recovered to $10.30 end-2025, around $11.60 by August 2026) but the underlying math—record volumes, crushed margins—stayed grim. ADM announced in August 2026 that it was upgrading four crush plants to unlock 700,000 metric tons of additional annual capacity, even as margins stayed compressed. This is capacity built for politics, not profit. Only the largest processors survive; consolidation is the only answer.

3D printing is the one industry where reshoring is actually profitable—because it serves defense and aerospace, where price is secondary to security. The global 3D printer market is growing 20.5% year-over-year (2025–2026) and is projected to hit $102 billion by 2035 at 24% CAGR. Metal additive manufacturing is the fastest-growing segment, driven entirely by aerospace and defense demand plus post-FY2026 NDAA restrictions forbidding foreign 3D systems for DoD contracts. Reshoring mandates and supply chain redundancy are now strategic requirements, not cost negotiations. Stratasys merged with Desktop Metal in 2023 and is integrating capabilities; HP launched high-temperature FFF systems at Formnext 2025. Margins are thin (0.8–2.8%) and Chinese competitors (Bambu Lab, Creality) are undercutting on commodity machines, but aerospace aftermarket parts are profitable and growing. This industry is winning because tariffs aligned with geopolitical demand, not just punishing imports.

The evidence

  • Auto parts: 25% tariff on imports (May 2025) drove 200% surge in Mexican investment in first nine months of 2025; US market $74.9B (2026), 5.4% growth, but bankruptcy filings hit decade highs.
  • Steel: 50% tariff (Feb-June 2025) boosted US to third-largest producer globally in 2025, but global oversupply (China 131M tonnes exports in 2025, +153% since 2020) and material costs (iron ore +9%, coking coal +17% in 2025) eroding margins; Nippon Steel $14.2B US Steel buyout (June 2025) made domestic capacity political.
  • Soybean processing: Record 2.54 billion bushels crush forecast for 2025–26 (23% capacity expansion, $6B invested) collapsed margins from $2–$3/bushel (2023) to $1.10–$1.50 (2025); China's 13% tariff reduced US exports 33% versus 2024, forcing domestic consolidation.
  • 3D printing: 20.5% YoY growth (2025–2026), metal additive projected $102B by 2035 at 24% CAGR; aerospace/defense and NDAA reshoring mandates making margins viable (0.8–2.8%) despite Chinese commodity competition.
  • Across all sectors, tariffs succeeded in making imports expensive but unleashed market forces—oversupply, margin compression, consolidation—that reshape who survives; nearshoring and military-grade reshoring win; thin-margin importers and global commodity players lose.

Who rides it

Nearshoring hubs win hardest—Mexico captured 200% of the auto parts investment wave, and adjacency to the US makes it the obvious valve for tariff-locked supply chains. Domestic makers with political access and capital scale (Cleveland-Cliffs, ADM, Stratasys, HP) absorb tariff shocks and consolidate competitors. Aerospace and defense contractors—and the industrial base they control—are the geopolitical winners; reshoring mandates turn 3D printing and advanced manufacturing into a national security play where price is irrelevant and volumes are guaranteed. Large, integrated players (Nippon Steel buying US Steel, Stratasys-Desktop Metal) lock in scale and reduce competition. Anyone making military or critical infrastructure components rides a tailwind of government contracts and reshoring mandates.

Who's squeezed

Thin-margin importers and small auto parts suppliers are crushed. A 5% margin industry (auto parts) cannot absorb a 25% tariff hit, so they either move to Mexico or file for bankruptcy—both are consolidation. Small soybean processors cannot compete with ADM, AGP, and the mega-plants coming online; margins fell 40–50% and only the largest survive. Global commodity producers and export-dependent industries (Chinese steelmakers flooding the market, Asian auto parts makers) lose access to the US and face a tariff wall that makes local competitors cost-competitive again. Mid-tier manufacturers without capital for nearshoring or reshoring get caught between tariff costs and flat demand, unable to invest in EV transition or meet defense requirements—they disappear.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that tariffs solved the import problem but unleashed commodity oversupply and margin compression that will not resolve for years. Chinese steel capacity alone (131M tonnes exports in 2025) is now fighting a 50% tariff wall, but the global excess capacity problem (640 to 745 million tonnes by 2028, per OECD) is structural—not a tariff can fix it. Soybean processing margins at $1.10–$1.50/bushel (August 2026) leave no room for error; a single crop failure, commodity price spike, or policy reversal vaporizes profit. The same is true for auto parts—tariffs bought time, but EV adoption is shrinking demand for traditional components (exhaust, radiators, engines), and bankruptcy is the exit for suppliers who cannot transition. Reshoring works when geopolitics and demand align (aerospace, defense, 3D printing), but when tariffs hit commodities and thin-margin industries, consolidation and hollowing-out are the results, not recovery.
