A · The core banks consolidate

The scale game in banking

Deposits, tech, and compliance costs push banking toward a few giants.

Banking used to be local. Your neighborhood bank held deposits, made loans, kept the spread. That's over. Today, the cost of staying in the game—compliance software, fraud detection, digital platforms, loan origination systems—is so high that only the giants and well-funded fintechs can afford to play. The result: money is flowing to scale, and everyone in the middle is getting squeezed.

What changed

The deposit game changed first. When the Federal Reserve cut rates 1.75 percentage points from September 2024 through the end of 2025, every bank suddenly faced the same math: deposit costs were sticky but shrinking, loan yields were falling, and the net interest margin—the spread banks live on—was compressed. For the big guys, that margin recovered to 3.39% by Q4 2025, the highest since 2019, because they could absorb the pressure with sheer volume. But in Q4 2025 alone, uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion as customers shopped for better rates. Big banks could afford to pay up and keep that money. Smaller banks and credit unions couldn't. Meanwhile, that middle-of-the-road crowd was stuck with $1.26 trillion in commercial real estate exposure maturing by 2027, with many loans originally at 4.3% now having to refinance at 6.2%—a brutal math problem that weakened their credit quality and ate into capital reserves. Credit unions hit 1.02% loan delinquency in Q4 2025, a 12-year high, signaling real stress in those portfolios.

Technology became the moat. The U.S. commercial banking industry grew 9.2% annually from 2021 to 2026, reaching $1.5 trillion in size by 2026, but the margin story tells the real tale: 19.7% margins in 2025 for those who could grab business. Building the digital infrastructure to compete costs tens of millions. Loan origination systems, anti-fraud AI, cybersecurity stacks, mobile platforms—you can't cheap out on any of it. Navy Federal, the world's largest credit union, crossed $203.6 billion in assets by Q1 2026 and added 826,000 members in one year by investing aggressively in digital. Meanwhile, the number of federally insured credit unions fell to 4,287 from 4,455—consolidation accelerating because the smaller players couldn't build the tech. Mergers-of-equals are the survival strategy: First Technology ($17 billion) merged into Digital Credit Union; Wings Financial ($9.5 billion) merged into Ent Credit Union; CommunityAmerica ($5.3 billion) merged into Unify Financial. Each merger is a small bank throwing in the towel because the cost of staying independent and competitive was too high.

The charter game flipped, and that opened new competition at a different scale. Industrial banks—niche lenders that used to be dominated by Sallie Mae and Comenity—faced a restructuring when the Fed cut rates 75 basis points in 2025, compressing margins even further. Interest income is 75% of ILC revenue, so every rate cut is a direct hit. But in July 2025, the FDIC formally invited new applicants for industrial bank charters, a reversal after years of de facto closure. By January 2026, Ford Motor, GM, and Stellantis had conditional approval to start their own FDIC-insured banks. Each has one year to operationalize. That's not the future—it's happening now. These automakers can embed finance directly into dealer platforms and lending apps, cutting out the middleman bank. Fintech lenders are doing the same: Q3 2025 saw unsecured personal loan originations hit a record 7.2 million, with fintech capturing 42% of that market. The old ILCs—Sallie Mae, Comenity—are watching their deposit bases shrink and their margins compress with nowhere to hide. The industry is splitting: large, capital-rich parent-owned banks win; unprofitable smaller ones are being shut down or acquired.

Compliance and cybersecurity are now non-discretionary. The NCUA listed cybersecurity and fraud as top supervisory priorities in early 2026, after credit unions suffered 539 cyber incidents in the previous 12 months. Building the people and systems to defend against that—incident response teams, compliance specialists, regulatory reporting infrastructure—is a fixed cost that scales inversely with size. A community bank with $500 million in assets and 50 employees is paying the same regulatory burden per dollar of assets as a $50 billion bank with 5,000 employees. The math is brutal. Meanwhile, credit union net income jumped 31.5% in 2025 to $18.8 billion when rates were high, but that windfall masked the real problem: most of that gain went to large players who could invest in the defenses and digital tools needed to hold onto deposits and comply with an ever-thickening rulebook. Small and mid-size credit unions took those gains as profit and deferred modernization. Now, as the Fed cuts rates and deposit costs fall, they're left exposed.

The evidence

  • Commercial Banking (U.S., 2026): $1.5 trillion market size, 9.2% annual growth, 19.7% margins—but gains concentrate at the top four banks as smaller competitors lose deposit races and technology wars.
  • Credit Unions (U.S., 2025–2026): Navy Federal broke $203.6 billion in assets by Q1 2026 and added 826,000 members in one year through digital investment, while the number of federally insured credit unions fell to 4,287 from 4,455—signaling that only scale-capable players survive.
  • Industrial Banks (U.S., 2025–2026): Ford, GM, and Stellantis won FDIC conditional approval for their own banks in January 2026; fintech lenders captured 42% of record 7.2 million unsecured personal loan originations in Q3 2025—the old charter holders (Sallie Mae, Comenity) are being displaced.
  • Rate Compression (2024–2025): Fed cut rates 1.75 percentage points from September 2024 through December 2025, compressing deposit costs and squeezing smaller lenders; uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 as customers fled to big banks offering better rates.
  • CRE Maturity Risk (2025–2027): $1.26 trillion in commercial real estate loans mature by 2027, many refinancing from 4.3% to 6.2%, straining regional and community bank capital—while big four banks have scale to absorb the stress.

Who rides it

The big four commercial banks (JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup) win outright. They have the size to absorb deposit flight, the capital to invest in technology and compliance, and the margin floor to withstand rate cuts. Navy Federal and other scale-focused credit unions win too, because they aggressively invested in digital and could attract members with better rates and faster service. And fintech lenders win because they have no legacy baggage—they built on modern stacks from the start and can undercut traditional banks on speed and friction. Ford, GM, and the new industrial banks win because they can embed finance into their own products without paying a middleman.

Who's squeezed

Regional and mid-size banks get squeezed from both sides. They can't compete with the big four on deposits (rate-setting power) or with fintechs on speed and user experience. Smaller credit unions are consolidating or failing because they can't afford the technology stack—digital platforms, AI-driven underwriting, cybersecurity, regulatory reporting—needed to keep up. The old industrial bank model (Sallie Mae, Comenity) is in structural decline as automakers and fintechs grab their charters and customers. Community banks face a maturity wall in commercial real estate exposure that bigger banks can weather but they cannot. The 2023 bank failures (SVB, Signature, First Republic) killed the mid-size consolidation wave temporarily, but they also proved that the middle is fragile. The survivors are those with enough capital and deposit stickiness to outlast rate swings and big customers' shopping sprees.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the commercial real estate maturity wall ($1.26 trillion by 2027, with many loans underwater or nearly so) triggers a wave of regional bank failures that cascades into the credit union system. Credit unions are already at a 12-year-high delinquency rate (1.02% in Q4 2025), and most of them have significant CRE exposure. If even a handful of large regional banks fail because they can't refinance their CRE books, it could spook depositors and trigger deposit flight from smaller institutions that can't absorb the shock. The second risk is concentration—if the big four keep getting bigger by absorbing deposits and smaller players keep disappearing, you end up with too-big-to-fail banks that carry systemic risk and have even less incentive to serve smaller businesses or lower-income borrowers. Neither outcome is in the public interest.

In one sentence

The scale game in banking in a nutshell

Smaller banks and credit unions can't afford the technology and regulatory infrastructure to compete, so deposits flow to the big four and fintech, leaving the middle to shrink.

A · The core banks consolidate

The rails that tax every swipe

The payment networks have become an unavoidable tax on the entire consumer economy.

Every card swipe costs the merchant something—a percentage that goes to the card network, not to the bank. That infrastructure has become a chokepoint. In 2025 and 2026, the payment rails are stronger than ever, but the game is changing: regulatory cracks are opening, alternatives are scaling, and the players who built the rails are starting to fracture.

What changed

The credit card issuing business faces contradictions that reveal the true stress on the payment system. Card issuers in the US controlled a $178.9 billion market in 2026, barely growing at 0.3% annually, and their profitability has collapsed—return on assets fell from 5.9% in 2022 to just 2.8% in 2024, even as they charged consumers 21.5% APRs on average by February 2026. They're extracting more interest from borrowers, but they're also forced to hold massive loss provisions as serious delinquency rates hit 13.1% in Q1 2026, the highest in 15 years. Total revolving credit reached $1.25 trillion, but default risk is rising faster than revenue. The top five issuers—Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, and Bank of America—now control over 50% of the market. Capital One's $35 billion acquisition of Discover, which closed in May 2025, reshaped the competitive landscape and accelerated consolidation. What this means: issuing is becoming safer for giants but riskier for everyone else.

But issuing is just one layer. The processing rails themselves—Visa, Mastercard, and a handful of processors handling the transaction flow—sit deeper in the money flow. The credit card processing and money transferring market reached $87.4 billion to $208.57 billion in 2026 (depending on how you count the global scope), growing at 11 to 20% annually, with margins holding at 21-23% in 2025. That is the real chokepoint. Merchants paid a record $198.25 billion in fees in 2025, which is a 3-4% tax on every card sale in the economy. Visa and Mastercard are still fortified, but they face genuine threats: antitrust pressure on interchange fees, the August 2025 court vacatur of the Federal Reserve's debit interchange cap (Regulation II, now stayed pending appeal in early 2026), fragmented state-level regulation, and merchant fee revolt. Meanwhile, PayPal and Stripe are consolidating. In July 2026, Stripe and Advent International jointly bid approximately $53 billion for PayPal, with Polymarket pricing an 82% acquisition probability. If that closes, it creates a mega-player that rivals Visa and Mastercard in scale and threatens the rail-owner's pricing power.

The rails also face cannibalization from the bottom. Buy now, pay later platforms captured $70 billion in transactions in 2025, stealing share from credit cards, especially from Gen Z. FICO launched FICO Score 10 BNPL and Score 10 T in 2025, incorporating BNPL payment history into credit scores for the first time, signaling that the payment rails no longer own the definition of creditworthiness. The BNPL market reached $560.1 billion in 2025, and regulation is expected in 2026 that will require BNPL providers to conduct affordability assessments and seek full authorization—making them more like credit cards but with lower margins. At the same time, fintech funding surged 23% year-over-year to $28.6 billion globally in H1 2026, with AI-enabled fintechs capturing 23% of funding in Q3 2025, the highest share since Q4 2023. Major rounds like Plaid's $575 million in April 2025 (valued at $8 billion by February 2026) show that the payment stack is being disaggregated. What made the rails valuable is the same thing that's becoming risky: they sit on the flow of money, they know everything, and they take a cut. That cut is becoming a political and regulatory target, and real-time payments are finally becoming real.

The consolidation and regulatory pressure have made one thing scarce: the margins that used to buffer payment processors. Five thousand to five thousand nine hundred establishments provide credit card processing and money transfer services as of 2025, and they employ 183,000 to 190,000 people in the US, many at $17.99 per hour entry-level. That workforce is being automated away. Labor costs, fraud losses (synthetic identity fraud alone costs $3.1 billion annually as of 2026 and is the fastest-growing financial crime, fueled by AI deepfakes), and regulatory compliance burdens are compressing margins from both ends. The businesses that survive are consolidating into regional mega-processors or becoming specialists in vertical niches. What is new is the speed of the reshaping: the Discover-Capital One deal, the PayPal-Stripe bid, the Regulation II court vacatur, the BNPL rule-making, all happened within 13 months. The rails that used to feel permanent are becoming tactical.

The evidence

  • Credit card issuing (Finance): $178.9 billion market in 2026 with margins declining to 2.8% ROA (2024), despite 21.5% average APRs, as Capital One's May 2025 Discover acquisition consolidates the top five issuers to 50%+ market control.
  • Payment processing (Finance): $87.4 billion to $208.57 billion market in 2025-2026 growing at 11-20% annually, with merchants paying record $198.25 billion in fees (2025), but Visa-Mastercard facing antitrust pressure and the Stripe-PayPal $53 billion bid (82% probability, July 2026) reshaping the competitive hierarchy.
  • BNPL platforms (Consumer Finance): Captured $70 billion in 2025 transactions, stealing from credit cards; FICO Score 10 BNPL (2025) now incorporates BNPL history into credit scores; market reached $560.1 billion in 2025.
  • Fraud costs (Finance & Technology): Synthetic identity fraud hit $3.1 billion annually by 2026, the fastest-growing financial crime fueled by AI deepfakes, forcing issuers to tighten underwriting and set aside loss provisions.
  • Regulatory fragmentation (Finance & Government): August 2025 court vacatur of Federal Reserve's debit interchange cap (Regulation II) stayed pending Eighth Circuit appeal; BNPL regulation expected 2026; states like California and New York enforcing their own rules—creating three-tier competitive chaos.

Who rides it

Visa, Mastercard, and mega-consolidators like Stripe-PayPal (if the deal closes) win. They own the rails and the data, and even as margins compress, their scale lets them absorb fraud losses and regulatory costs that smaller processors cannot. Fintech funding surged 23% to $28.6 billion globally in H1 2026, with AI-enabled fintechs capturing 23% of funding in Q3 2025—but only those building real-time payment alternatives, embedded finance, and vertical stacks with their own data moat. Issuers who can absorb delinquency (Capital One, Chase) also benefit because they can cross-sell other products. What they all have in common: they control the chokepoint, they know the customers, and they can turn that knowledge into adjacent revenue.

Who's squeezed

Regional banks, small processors, and traditional credit card middlemen get squeezed. The five thousand to five thousand nine hundred establishments providing payment processing are being automated and consolidated. Merchants are the biggest losers—they pay 3-4% in fees on every transaction (a record $198.25 billion in 2025) and have few alternatives as long as credit cards remain the dominant payment method. BNPL platforms lose too, as regulations roll in requiring affordability checks and full authorization, turning them into credit card competitors with lower margins and higher friction. Card issuers outside the top five face collapsing ROA and delinquency risks as consumers carry $1.25 trillion in revolving debt and default rates hit 15-year highs—the math doesn't work unless you're already big enough to absorb losses or ruthless enough to exit the space.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Synthetic identity fraud is accelerating (costs $3.1 billion annually as of 2026 and growing faster than any other crime) and is now fueled by AI deepfakes. Issuers and processors are locked in an underwriting arms race—they can't stop it at the scale of the payment system, only push costs downstream onto consumers (higher rates, stricter approval) or force merchants to absorb fraud-prevention burdens. If AI-generated identity documents become indistinguishable, the entire credit card issuing model—which relies on verifying identity once, then trusting the risk—breaks down. The payment rails have no way to solve this alone; it requires government identity infrastructure and coordination across banking and law enforcement that doesn't exist yet.</worry> </invoke>

A · The core banks consolidate

The Wall Street Machine

Capital markets consolidate into a few hands—and the rails, data, and custody layer replace the traditional middleman.

Wall Street isn't shrinking. In 2026, US investment banking alone is a $219.3 billion industry that's growing 7.6% a year. But it's consolidating: fewer people are doing more deals, boutique firms are eating the lunch of giants, and the real value—custody, settlement, and the plumbing—is moving from the corner office to the tech stack. The machines and the data are winning.

What changed

In 2025, the M&A machine delivered $4.9 trillion in deals—the second-highest volume on record, up 41% from 2024. Investment banking fees hit $100 billion for the year, and Morgan Stanley's IB revenue jumped 47% while JPMorgan's advisory fees were up 12%. On paper, Wall Street is booming. But behind the deal bonanzas, the industry is automating away its people and outsourcing the high-touch work. Employment fell 1.1% in 2026 even as deal flow recovered, and margins compressed from 35% in 2022 to 30-35% today. Why? Competition on execution fees (especially in equities), regulatory costs, and AI infrastructure investments all bite into profits. Meanwhile, the boutiques—Houlihan Lokey, Moelis, and smaller advisory shops—grew 18% to 28% in 2025, partly because they don't have to carry the capital-intensive trading and compliance burden of the Big Five.\n\nThe real action, though, is in custody and settlement. The custody, asset, and securities services industry is only $46.1 billion and growing at just 1.9% in 2026, but this layer—where assets are actually held and moved—is where the margin and the control live. Four dominant banks (BNY Mellon, State Street, JPMorgan, and Fidelity) now dominate this space. Global custody fees are under intense pressure, but the firms that own the rails are forcing clients to accept lower fees on the settlement side in exchange for higher fees on new services: blockchain custody, compliance AI, risk analytics. Digital assets are the wedge. Crypto custody is projected at $834 billion globally in 2026, and the OCC permitting national banks to offer crypto custody in March 2025 and approving five new digital-asset bank charters in December 2025 means the plumbing for digital wealth is becoming native to the traditional system. BNY Mellon and State Street both launched crypto custody platforms in May 2025. In July 2025, State Street became the first third-party custodian to settle tokenized debt on JPMorgan's blockchain, turning custody into a programmable layer. The SEC's Custody Rule Modernization, planned for April 2026, will require explicit provisions for crypto assets and updated identity verification for digital instruments—a compliance overhaul that costs money to implement but cements the advantage of scale.\n\nWhat's scarce now is not capital—there's plenty of capital. What's scarce is the data about who owns what, the real-time ledgers that tell you what's moving, and the rails that move it. Those are expensive to build and impossible to replicate. Bank of America cut junior investment banking staff in March 2025, and Bridgewater Associates cut 90 employees (7% of its workforce) in January 2025, both signaling that the firms no longer need human intermediaries for the routine work of moving capital around. The machine is faster and cheaper. What remains valuable is either the brand and the client relationships (for the boutiques) or the data and the plumbing (for the custodians and settlement layer). The rest gets automated, offshored, or squeezed into margin compression.

The evidence

  • Investment Banking & Securities Dealing: $219.3 billion market in 2026, with $4.9 trillion M&A volume in 2025 and boutique advisory firms (Houlihan Lokey, Moelis) growing 18-28% while Big Five rationalize headcount despite deal recovery
  • Custody & Asset Services: $46.1 billion market expanding to crypto, with State Street settling tokenized debt on blockchain in July 2025 and four dominant banks (BNY Mellon, State Street, JPMorgan, Fidelity) controlling the plumbing
  • Crypto Custody: $834 billion globally in 2026, with OCC approving five new digital-asset bank charters in December 2025 and traditional custodians (BNY, State Street) launching digital platforms in May 2025
  • Employment Rationalization: 1.1% job cuts in 2026 despite strong deal pipelines, with Bank of America cutting junior IB staff in March 2025 and Bridgewater Associates cutting 90 employees (7% of workforce) in January 2025
  • Margin Compression: Investment banking margins fell from 35% in 2022 to 30-35% in 2026, driven by competition on execution fees, regulatory costs, and AI infrastructure investment

Who rides it

The winners are the custodians, settlement layer operators, and boutique advisory firms. BNY Mellon, State Street, JPMorgan, and Fidelity now control the rails that move trillions. They can charge lower fees on routine custody but higher fees on new services (blockchain, compliance AI, risk analytics). Boutique firms like Houlihan Lokey and Moelis win because they can operate without capital-intensive trading operations, meaning higher returns on capital and no need to rationalize staff. They're lean, focused, and expensive for clients—which is exactly what works when deals are complex and margins are tight elsewhere.

Who's squeezed

Junior investment bankers and traditional regional custodians get squeezed. Banks like Bank of America cut junior staff in March 2025, and employment fell 1.1% in 2026 despite robust deal flow—the message is clear: machines do the work humans used to do. Regional custodians and smaller settlement firms can't compete on cost or scale with the Big Four, so they either get bought or starve. Bridgewater Associates cutting 7% of its workforce signaled that even top-tier private wealth firms can't support the old staffing model. The middlemen—brokers, back-office processors, compliance officers working on routine tasks—are being systematically replaced.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is concentration of power. Four banks now dominate custody and settlement—BNY Mellon, State Street, JPMorgan, and Fidelity. They control the rails that trillions of dollars flow through every day. If one of them has a technology failure, a regulatory problem, or a security breach, it cascades across the entire system. The SEC's Custody Rule Modernization planned for April 2026 will put more compliance burden on these firms, but it also cements their advantage over smaller players because they have the scale to absorb the cost. What looks like progress (blockchain custody, automated settlement) is actually consolidation of power.

In one sentence

The Wall Street machine in a nutshell

Wall Street isn't disappearing—it's consolidating: fewer people, fewer firms, and total control of the plumbing that moves capital.

B · Credit leaves the bank

Lending without a bank

Credit routes around traditional banks through brokers, fintechs, and nonbank servicers—and the middlemen are getting crushed.

Lending has left the building. Online platforms, embedded-finance companies, and nonbank lenders now move credit directly to borrowers, bypassing the loan broker entirely. The traditional bank is no longer the gatekeep—it's just one option among many, and a shrinking one at that.

What changed

For decades, a mortgage broker was the middleman between borrower and lender. You wanted a loan, you paid them a fee, they found you a bank. That model is dead. Online originations reached 45-47% market share by 2025-2026, and direct-to-consumer platforms like Rocket Mortgage have made the broker economically optional. Fewer people need intermediation when they can get a rate quote in five minutes on their phone. The loan broker industry fell 17.1% from 2021 to 2026 (from $11.5 billion to $9.1 billion), and employment in the sector has crashed 39% off its peak. Yes, margins ticked up in 2024-2025—independent mortgage banks averaged 21 basis points per loan in 2025 (up from 10 bp in 2024) and made $727 per loan in Q1 2026—but that's a survival rebound, not a growth story. The real action is happening at the extremes: either you're large enough to compete with direct lenders (United Wholesale Mortgage originated 422,120 loans worth $164.3 billion in 2025), or you're being rolled up into someone else's platform. Guild Mortgage sold to Bayview Asset Management in November 2025. Cenlar was acquired by Pennymac. There were 62 M&A deals in 2025, up from 37 the year before, mostly small independents realizing they have no succession plan and no moat.\n\nInvoice factoring tells a parallel story, with a twist. Factoring is also shrinking overall—the US market is $3 billion in 2026, down from $3.9 billion in 2022 (declining 1.9% in 2025 alone). But within that shrinking pie, two distinct bifurcations are happening. First, transportation factoring survives because trucking has structural cash-flow problems. The 2023-2024 freight recession drove spot rates below operating costs, forcing weak carriers out and driving survivors into factoring. Yet total invoice volumes still fell 5.7% year-over-year by December 2024. Interest rates were the swing factor: when rates were elevated through 2024, factoring became competitive against bank loans. But as the Federal Reserve cut rates after May 2024, that advantage evaporates. Factoring rates are now squeezing into a 1.95-4.0% range for trucking. Second, fintech and embedded-finance platforms are picking off the high-growth segments. AI-powered credit scoring and fraud detection are table-stakes now, and platforms like Lendflow bundle factoring with loans and merchant services to reach small businesses that never would have called a traditional factor. Global embedded finance is projected to hit $155.96 billion in 2026, with factoring as a core component. The industry forecast expects global invoice factoring to grow 10.5% CAGR from 2024-2034, reaching $7.75 billion, contradicting the US-only decline—meaning growth is happening everywhere but the US, and it's being captured by fintech, not traditional factors.\n\nBut the biggest story is loan servicing, where nonbanks have become the actual backbone of the mortgage market. Nonbanks now control 66% of all mortgage servicing as of early 2024, and 84% of Ginnie Mae-backed loans. This is not a niche. When Rocket Companies closed its $14.2 billion acquisition of Mr. Cooper Group in October 2025, it created a 2.1 trillion combined origination-and-servicing powerhouse with 10 million customers. The deal was explicitly about vertical integration: fusing the nation's largest lender with the nation's largest servicer to capture $500 million in annual synergies. PennyMac, another nonbank, added 740 billion in subservicing relationships when it acquired Cenlar in March 2025. H1 2025 mortgage originations hit 2.3 trillion (later revised to 2.1 trillion), driving servicing portfolio growth of 33-57% year-over-year for major nonbanks. The technology shift is accelerating the consolidation: 38% of mortgage lenders used AI/ML in 2024, jumping to 83% planning GenAI budget increases in 2026. AI now automates borrower monitoring, default prediction, payment processing, and compliance—the very jobs that once justified having dozens of regional servicers. The regulatory environment is shifting too. The CFPB finalized a streamlined servicing rule in September 2025 that eliminated the complex "complete application" framework, reducing compliance burden but raising expectations for borrower assistance. Meanwhile, regulators are recommending higher capital and liquidity standards for nonbanks, which favors the scaled players (Rocket, Mr. Cooper, Lakeview with $738 billion UPB as of July 2025) over small independent servicers.\n\nWhat's made scarce here is the independent intermediary—the small loan broker, the regional factor, the single-state servicer. What's become cheap is origination (online channels and direct banks have commoditized the rate), underwriting (AI delivers non-QM decisions in under five minutes, removing human expertise), and servicing (automation and scale). What's newly risky is being a nonbank without enough scale to absorb regulatory compliance and interest-rate swings—FDIC consent orders against BaaS sponsor banks in 2024-2025 have raised compliance costs for embedded-finance platforms. What's valuable is data (the 10 million customers Mr. Cooper gets access to via Rocket), technology (AI-powered credit scoring and compliance), and the rails themselves (if you own the platform, you own the borrowers).

The evidence

  • Loan Brokers (Finance & Insurance): Market fell 17.1% CAGR from 2021-2026 (from $11.5B to $9.1B); employment down 39% from peak; online originations captured 45-47% market share by 2025-2026, displacing intermediaries; United Wholesale Mortgage originated 422,120 loans ($164.3B) in 2025 but faced direct competition from Rocket Mortgage.
  • Invoice Factoring (Finance & Insurance): US market contracted from $3.9B (2022) to $3.0B (2026), down 1.9% in 2025 alone; transportation segment remains resilient despite freight recession (spot rates fell below operating costs in 2023-2024); invoice volumes fell 5.7% YoY by Dec 2024; embedded-finance platforms bundling factoring with loans projected global embedded finance to reach $155.96B by 2026.
  • Mortgage Servicing (Finance & Insurance): Nonbanks now control 66% of all servicing (early 2024) and 84% of Ginnie Mae-backed loans (mid-2024); Rocket-Mr. Cooper merger ($14.2B, October 2025) created 2.1 trillion combined origination-servicing platform with $500M annual synergies; H1 2025 originations hit 2.3 trillion, driving 33-57% YoY servicing portfolio growth for major nonbanks.
  • AI Adoption in Lending (2024-2026): 38% of mortgage lenders used AI/ML in 2024; 83% planned GenAI budget increases in 2026; AI now automates underwriting (non-QM decisions in under 5 minutes), borrower monitoring, default prediction, and compliance—eliminating the human expertise that once justified broker networks.
  • Regulatory Environment (2024-2025): CFPB September 2025 streamlined loss-mitigation rule eliminated complex 'complete application' framework; FDIC consent orders against BaaS sponsor banks (2024-2025) raised compliance costs for embedded-finance platforms; regulators recommending higher capital and liquidity standards for nonbanks, favoring scaled players.

Who rides it

The winners are platform companies with scale and data: Rocket Companies (merged with Mr. Cooper to get 10 million customers), PennyMac (now controlling 659 billion UPB after acquiring Cenlar), Lakeview Loan Servicing (738 billion UPB as of July 2025), and embedded-finance startups like Lendflow that bundle multiple products (loans, factoring, merchant services) into one API. They win because they own the customer relationship, control the technology stack (AI automation, real-time credit scoring), and can absorb regulatory and interest-rate swings. Online lenders win. Direct-to-consumer channels win. Anyone with a platform and 100+ million dollars in scale wins.

Who's squeezed

Regional brokers and independent servicers get squeezed into irrelevance or sold off. The 46,000-52,000 broker employees (down 39%) are consolidating into larger firms or leaving the industry. Independent factors survive only in transportation, where structural cash-flow problems keep borrowers coming, but general commercial factoring is eviscerated by cheaper bank lending and fintech platforms offering the same service embedded in a broader product. Small regional servicers can't compete on technology, compliance, or customer acquisition—they're being rolled up (Guild Mortgage to Bayview, Cenlar to PennyMac) or shuttered.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that nonbanks have become too central to mortgage origination and servicing (66% of servicing, 84% of Ginnie Mae loans) without the same regulatory backstop or capital buffers as banks. When interest rates swing or markets freeze, nonbanks don't have access to the Fed's discount window or stable deposit funding. The CFPB and regulators are tightening capital and liquidity standards, and FDIC consent orders have already raised compliance costs. If servicing liquidity crises recur—especially during forbearance periods—the scaled nonbanks could face systemic pressure that ripples through the entire mortgage market, and there's less redundancy now that the small regional players are gone.

In one sentence

Lending without a bank in a nutshell

Credit has left the bank and gone to platforms, fintechs, and scale players, leaving behind a graveyard of regional brokers, independent servicers, and traditional factors.

B · Credit leaves the bank

Who grades your credit

The credit-scoring layer is getting thinner, more AI-driven, and more concentrated.

Your creditworthiness used to be a black box. Now it's becoming a commodity—but whoever controls the score controls the gate. The credit bureaus and rating agencies that decide if you can borrow are caught between a crumbling regulatory system and AI-powered alternatives that measure you in new ways.

What changed

The US credit bureaus and rating agencies industry is worth $17.6 billion as of 2026, growing at just 2.7 percent annually since 2020, with 2025 itself seeing only 0.6 percent growth—a company walking on a treadmill. That sluggish top line hides a deeper fracture. Moody's, one of the Big Three, reported $7.7 billion in revenue in 2025 and grew operating income 17 percent year-over-year, but that performance depends on investment-banking work and derivatives pricing; the pure credit-rating business is under siege. The real disruption is coming from two directions at once. First, AI-powered alternative scoring is dismantling the traditional moat. Zest AI research showed its machine-learning model could approve 25 percent more loans while holding risk constant—a jaw-dropping efficiency gain that forces the incumbents to scramble. FICO, the gold-standard scoring firm, launched Score 11 in early 2026 explicitly to widen coverage by incorporating rent payments and cash-flow data. That move alone could bring 9 million previously credit-invisible consumers into the scoring system, diluting the scarcity value of a FICO number. Second, security is now a cost center, not a differentiator. The TransUnion breach in August 2025 exposed 4.4 million Americans' names, Social Security numbers, and birthdates. The 700Credit breach, discovered in late 2025, exposed 5.8 million more. Both incidents forced the Big Three to pour resources into cybersecurity, eroding the ~29 percent margins the industry has held stable for years. Compliance is tightening too: the SEC's proposed overhaul of rating-agency rules targets governance, analyst independence, and methodologies, and regulatory experts predict it will force hiring of compliance and technology staff that existing firms will struggle to absorb at current fee levels.

Meanwhile, the credit repair industry—the middleman layer that sits between consumer and bureau—is getting demolished. Lexington Law and CreditRepair.com, which once dominated via aggressive telemarketing, are zombies. Their parent company PGX Holdings emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2024-2025 with roughly 80 percent of operations shuttered. In August 2023, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau secured a $2.7 billion settlement against them for charging illegal upfront fees before delivering any results—a Telemarketing Sales Rule violation. That settlement came with $1.8 billion in consumer redress distributed to 4.3 million harmed consumers starting in December 2024. The old model is dead. What's replacing it is automation: modern platforms use machine learning to analyze credit reports, detect errors instantly, generate dispute letters in seconds, and predict which disputes will succeed—gutting the need for call centers and sales floors. The industry still has revenue—$5.29 to $6.6 billion in 2025, up from $4.4 billion in 2022—but employment plummeted 4.7 percent year-over-year as of 2026. About 29.6 percent of US consumers still carry subprime credit as of September 2025, so the market for repair services persists, but the jobs, the commissions, and the gatekeeping power of the repair firms are evaporating. In June 2026, the CFPB announced new rules to crack down on credit repair firms abusing complaint portals to remove legitimate negative information, closing off another escape hatch for the old business model.

The third piece—appraisers, credit counselors, and surveyors—reveals a parallel squeeze on human expertise. The US credit counseling, appraisal, and surveying industry hit $96.9 billion in 2025, up from $76.8 billion in 2022, but growth slowed to 1 percent in 2025 alone despite skyrocketing demand signals. Household debt reached $17.5 trillion by mid-2025; credit card debt alone hit $1.233 trillion. Bankruptcy filings surged 14 percent in 2025. Student loan delinquencies spiked to 7.74 percent in Q1 2025 (from under 1 percent in Q4 2024) as the pandemic pause on loan payments ended and reality resumed. Nonprofits reported onboarding 15,000 new debt-management clients in the first half of 2026—the highest half-year total since 2017. All of this should be a growth engine for appraisers and counselors, but it's not. Automated valuation models (AVMs)—software that estimates property value without a human appraiser—are eating volume. Starting October 2025, the OCC imposed federal quality-control standards on AVMs, which sounds like regulation but actually legitimized the technology by giving it a compliance framework. The mortgage market itself remains soft because interest rates stay elevated, capping appraisal volume. Appraisal utilization did begin to tighten in June-July 2026 (appraisal volume grew faster than active appraiser count for the first time since 2022), suggesting capacity constraints may eventually push pricing up—but for now, the humans are watching their workload flatten while the algorithms accelerate.

The evidence

  • Credit bureaus: Moody's (one of Big Three) reported $7.7 billion revenue in 2025 with 9% growth in analytics and 17% growth in operating income year-over-year, driven by investment-banking and derivatives work rather than pure credit rating.
  • Fintech scoring: Zest AI proved its ML model approves 25% more loans at constant risk; FICO launched Score 11 in early 2026 to expand coverage using rent and cash-flow data, targeting 9 million previously invisible consumers.
  • Credit repair: Market hit $5.29–6.6 billion in 2025 (up from $4.4B in 2022) but employment fell 4.7% YoY; Lexington Law and CreditRepair.com (80% of operations shuttered) are zombies after $2.7B CFPB settlement in August 2023.
  • Appraisals and counseling: $96.9 billion industry in 2025 (up from $76.8B in 2022) but only 1% growth in 2025 despite 14% surge in bankruptcies, 7.74% student loan delinquencies (Q1 2025), and 15,000 new debt-management clients in H1 2026 (highest since 2017).
  • Cybersecurity cost: TransUnion breach (August 2025, 4.4M exposed) and 700Credit breach (5.8M, July–October 2025) forced all three major bureaus to invest heavily in security, eroding stable ~29% margins and raising regulatory compliance burden (SEC overhaul of rating-agency rules underway).

Who rides it

The winners are scale and data. Moody's and the Big Three stay profitable by diversifying—investment banking, analytics, software platforms. TransUnion is pivoting: it acquired Monevo in April 2025 to plug instant pre-qualification into its OneTru cloud platform, capturing lead referrals and building a tech moat instead of a pure-bureau one. FICO, by launching Score 11 to incorporate rent and cash-flow data, is betting it can stay relevant by expanding its reach into populations traditional credit couldn't see. AI-powered alternative scoring platforms like Zest are winning by proving they can do better risk assessment with different data—a direct threat to incumbents but a huge win for lenders willing to adopt. On the counseling side, nonprofits are scaling to meet demand (15,000 new clients in H1 2026), and those leveraging automation for dispute letters and error detection are outpacing the old call-center model.

Who's squeezed

The squeezed are the middlemen and humans. Credit repair firms are collapsing: Lexington Law and CreditRepair.com went zombie after the CFPB settlement, and the June 2026 CFPB rules to close complaint-portal abuse shut off another escape hatch. The old telemarketing playbook is dead—80 percent of operations axed, thousands of jobs gone, employment down 4.7 percent even though total market revenue grew in dollars. Appraisers and human counselors face displacement: automated valuation models are now federally legitimized (October 2025 OCC standards), mortgage volume remains soft, and utilization is only now beginning to tighten after years of slack. Regional and independent credit bureaus—of which there were 1,280 establishments as of 2026—lack the scale or data to compete with Moody's, Equifax, and TransUnion, and they're getting squeezed out of M&A consolidation and data-sharing partnerships. Consumers also lose: every data breach (4.4M + 5.8M in 2025 alone) means their sensitive financial history is at risk, and the shift to alternative scoring data (rent, cash flow, digital payments) means no credit history is truly private anymore.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that credit scoring—the gate between you and capital—is concentrating into a smaller set of black boxes run by machine learning. Moody's, FICO, and TransUnion control the data and the models, and while regulation is coming (SEC overhaul of rating agencies, CFPB crackdowns on repair firms), it's reactive and slow. AI models are opaque: if Zest AI's model approves 25 percent more loans at constant risk, it's hard to know if that's a better model or if it's gaming incentives we haven't noticed yet. Breaches like the TransUnion (4.4M) and 700Credit (5.8M) incidents in 2025 show the bureaus can't reliably protect the data they hoard—yet lenders have no choice but to use their scores because everyone else does. The shift to alternative data (rent, cash flow) means the traditional notion of "credit invisible" people getting access is real, but it also means every digital footprint you leave is now fair game for scoring. And if AI-driven models start making lending decisions at scale, and those models are trained on historical data that encodes past discrimination, you've got a systemic amplification problem that neither regulation nor patch fixes can solve fast.

Who grades your credit in a nutshell

Credit scoring was a moat; now it's a commodity line managed by three big firms and disrupted by AI, while security breaches and regulatory pressure make it more expensive to run and everyone else gets squeezed.

C · Advice & the retail saver

Advice gets commoditized

Passive funds and robo-advisors compress fees; scale and trust win.

Money management used to be personal. A financial advisor took your call, knew your goals, and charged you accordingly. Now the machine is eating the business. Passive index funds and robo-advisors are pulling assets away from active managers while crushing the fees advisors can charge. The industry is consolidating fast—because scale is the only way to survive.

What changed

Ten years ago, active management was the norm and passive index funds were the cheap alternative. That's flipped. By 2025, passive index funds and ETFs held 55% of all mutual fund and ETF assets in the US, up from just 34% a decade earlier. At the same time, active mutual funds bled $1+ trillion in net outflows in 2025—the steepest year of an 11-year exodus. Only 38% of active fund managers beat their passive peers after fees in 2025, down from 42% the year before. Clients noticed. They left.

The fee compression is punishing. In 2024, advisors managing a $10 million portfolio charged around 75 basis points. By 2026, that fee had dropped to 66 basis points—a 12% cut in a single year. Institutional clients demand even lower rates. The portfolio management industry still generated $340 billion in revenue in 2025, but margins shrank to 32-36%, down from 36.1% in 2022. The industry has 75,000 establishments and 580,000+ employees, but the work itself is becoming commoditized: algorithm-driven advice, index tracking, and low-touch platforms can do what used to require a human.

The winner is scale. BlackRock's strategy tells the story. In December 2024, it bought HPS Investment Partners for $12 billion, expanding its private credit footprint by 40%. Three months later, in March 2025, BlackRock bought Preqin for £2.5 billion to lock in data dominance in private markets. Meanwhile, robo-advisors and hybrid advisory services—human plus algorithm—now manage $1 trillion in US assets as of 2026. Vanguard Personal Advisor alone crossed $300 billion. These are not boutique operators. They are platforms that can serve millions at once, lower their cost per client, and still make money.

The industry is consolidating at a historic pace. In 2025, there were 466 M&A deals in wealth management, up 27% from 2024. By 2029, the industry could see 1,500+ deals as scale becomes non-negotiable. Younger clients—42% of under-40 fintech users versus 11% at traditional firms—prefer robo-advisors and apps like Wealthfront and Betterment to phone calls with advisors. Gen Z and millennials now hold $3.1 trillion in equity holdings, a record as of August 2026, and they are shifting wealth toward stocks and digital platforms, not real estate or traditional advisors. The 148,000+ independent RIAs and financial planning firms that existed in 2022 are shrinking and consolidating. Those who survive will do so by adopting AI-driven prospecting, automation, and hybrid models—or by being absorbed into larger firms.

The evidence

  • Portfolio Management: Passive funds now hold 55% of US mutual fund and ETF assets by 2025, up from 34% a decade ago (2025).
  • Financial Planning: Advisors' fees fell from ~75 basis points to 66 basis points on a $10M portfolio between 2024 and 2026 (2026).
  • Robo-Advisory: Robo-advisors and hybrid advisory services manage $1 trillion in US assets, with Vanguard Personal Advisor at $300 billion (2026).
  • Wealth Management M&A: 466 M&A deals in wealth management in 2025, up 27% from 2024, with potential for 1,500+ deals by 2029 (2025).
  • Generational Shift: Gen Z and millennials hold $3.1 trillion in equity, a record, shifting wealth to digital platforms and away from traditional advisors (August 2026).

Who rides it

BlackRock and other consolidators with scale, data, and technology win. Robo-advisory platforms and fintech apps like Wealthfront and Betterment win by serving younger clients efficiently at lower cost. Any advisor or firm willing to adopt hybrid models—AI-driven prospecting, automation, and algorithm-assisted advice—survives. The winners are those who can process millions of clients with minimal human touch and still deliver results.

Who's squeezed

Independent financial advisors and boutique RIAs get squeezed. The 148,000+ independent firms and RIAs from 2022 are consolidating rapidly. A solo advisor or small team can no longer compete on price or technology. Advisors at traditional firms face pressure to adopt AI tools or risk being replaced. Regional wealth managers and mid-market players who can't reach scale disappear into acquisitions. Active fund managers who underperform passive benchmarks lose assets and shut down or merge. The fee compression means revenue per client drops every year—only scale and technology can offset that.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that advice itself becomes a loss leader. If passive funds are truly indistinguishable and robo-advisors can serve millions, then charging any advisory fee becomes harder. Firms may give up charging for advice and instead make money on execution, insurance, lending, and other ancillary services. That leaves truly independent advisors with nowhere to stand. Additionally, as older clients die and younger clients never use human advisors, the talent pipeline dries up—it becomes harder to recruit and retain advisors when the job is shrinking and the fees are declining. Regulatory changes, like the SEC's recent Regulation S-P compliance deadlines in June 2026, also raise operational costs for smaller firms that can't spread the burden across millions of clients.

C · Advice & the retail saver

Moving and Holding the Money

Brokerage, custody, and float are being reshaped by automation, scale, and the shift to digital assets—killing commissions and squeezing regional middlemen.

For decades, moving money and holding it safely were lucrative, quiet businesses. Brokers took a cut. Custodians charged fees. The float—the time your cash sat in transit—belonged to the bank. That model is breaking. AI now executes most trades. Cryptocurrency custody is forcing every major bank to build new infrastructure. Fee pressure is relentless. The businesses that win are those with scale, data, and direct access to the rails. Everyone else gets compressed.

What changed

The commodity dealing and brokerage industry in the US—the middlemen who execute trades and move money—has seen margins collapse from 14.3% in 2022 to 6.6% in 2025. That's not a temporary dip. It's structural. Pandemic-era chaos in 2020-2022 created wild volatility: crude oil crashed, agricultural futures spiked, currencies swung violently. Dealers made 31.5% more revenue in 2021 alone. But once economies stabilized in 2024-2025, that volatility evaporated. Spreads tightened. Commissions fell. Today, the US commodity industry generates $21.6 billion in annual revenue (2025), down from $24.3 billion in 2022, with only 2.2% annual growth and a negative 1.6% actual decline in 2025 itself. The human broker—the person who knew the market, could execute a big order without moving prices too much—is becoming obsolete. AI now handles 89% of world trading volume as of 2025. Machine learning algorithms execute thousands of trades per second. Hedge funds report that AI agents in commodities have cut slippage by 35%. When volatility returns, volume surges: commodity derivatives trading jumped to 12.49 billion contracts in 2025, up 17.5% from 2024, with options alone up 48%. CME Group averaged 28.1 million daily contracts across all products in 2025, up 6% year-over-year. But the money made per trade shrinks with every upgrade to the plumbing. Brent crude jumping from $72 to $118 per barrel in early Q1 2026 sustained hedging demand and trading volumes in energy derivatives, but not the explosive arbitrage spreads of 2020-2022. Geopolitical shocks—Middle East tensions, US tariffs on aluminum and steel (25% to 50% in 2025), Chinese trade tensions—keep markets unpredictable. This creates hedging opportunity. But it's opportunity split among thousands of automated traders, not concentrated in the hands of a few dozen elite brokers with exclusive market access.\n\nCustody and asset services tell a parallel story with a digital twist. This industry is larger and growing faster: $46.1 billion in 2026, up at a 3.7% CAGR since 2021. But the growth masks a concentration crisis and a forced reinvention. Four dominant banks—BNY Mellon, State Street, JPMorgan, Fidelity—control most institutional custody. Margins are still healthy at 26.9% in 2026, but fee pressure is relentless. Custody, by definition, is boring: hold the assets, keep them safe, settle transactions, file the paperwork. The money comes from volume and the float. But volume is being automated—blockchain-based settlement is getting faster. JPMorgan's blockchain-based Digital Debt Service (launched July 2025) enables institutional clients to settle tokenized debt securities with automated clearance, cutting the float to near-zero. The float, that quiet profit center, is disappearing. The industry is forced into a race to capture digital asset custody. Cryptocurrency custody was projected to reach $834 billion globally in 2026. Until March 2025, national banks couldn't legally hold crypto for clients. Then the OCC issued Interpretive Letter 1183, opening the door. By December 2025, the OCC had conditionally approved five new national trust bank charters for digital asset firms: Circle, Ripple, Paxos Trust Company, BitGo Bank & Trust, and Fidelity Digital Assets. This is a rare moment of regulatory permission—a green light to build. BNY Mellon and State Street both launched comprehensive digital asset custody platforms in May 2025. They're not waiting for the next crisis to prove digital assets matter. They're racing to embed themselves in the post-traditional custody stack.\n\nWhat changed is the definition of winning in these businesses. Scale, automation, and regulatory access to new rails matter more than relationship skill or discretionary trading talent. Approximately 8,000 commodity dealing and brokerage establishments exist in the US, employing 25,500 people (2025). That's down from higher numbers a decade ago. Consolidation is underway but not dramatic—yet. Regional commodity brokers, insurance-backed trading operations, and independent FCMs (futures commission merchants) are under pressure. They can't match the margin compression. They don't have the AI infrastructure. They can't afford the compliance build for crypto or blockchain. The custody industry has roughly 30,975 establishments (2026), which sounds diverse, but 76,500+ employees are concentrated in a handful of global giants. The SEC's Custody Rule Modernization, planned for April 2026, will mandate explicit provisions for crypto assets, new onboarding procedures, identity verification, and recordkeeping systems for digital instruments. Building these systems costs tens of millions. Smaller custodians can't afford the build alone. The result is a quiet reshuffling: smaller regional players, brokerage arms at community banks, and independent asset servicers get absorbed or marginalized. The scale players—JPMorgan, BNY Mellon, State Street, Fidelity—can amortize infrastructure investment across trillions in assets under administration. They become the only rational choice for institutional clients who need to hold crypto, tokenized securities, and traditional assets in one regulated place.

The evidence

  • Commodity dealing and brokerage: margins dropped from 14.3% (2022) to 6.6% (2025) as AI now executes 89% of global trading volume, cutting broker value and flattening per-trade economics.
  • Crypto custody: projected $834 billion globally in 2026; OCC approved five new digital asset bank charters in December 2025 and cleared national banks to offer crypto custody via Interpretive Letter 1183 in March 2025.
  • CME trading volumes: 28.1 million average daily contracts in 2025 (up 6% YoY), with commodity derivatives hitting 12.49 billion contracts (up 17.5% from 2024), but spreads tightening as AI automates execution.
  • Custody industry concentration: 30,975 establishments (2026) employ 76,500+ people but are dominated by four global giants (JPMorgan, BNY Mellon, State Street, Fidelity) preparing for blockchain-based settlement and digital asset mandates.
  • Geopolitical re-volatilization: Brent crude spiked from $72 to $118/barrel in Q1 2026; US tariffs on aluminum and steel (25-50% in 2025) created new arbitrage windows but not enough to restore 2020-2022 margin levels.

Who rides it

Banks with scale, global compliance infrastructure, and regulatory approvals for digital assets (JPMorgan, BNY Mellon, State Street, Fidelity). They can absorb the cost of crypto custody platforms, blockchain settlement systems, and SEC compliance overhauls. They become the only choice for institutions managing assets across traditional and digital rails. AI-native trading platforms and electronic exchanges like CME Group that have automated execution and built the infrastructure for high-frequency, low-margin volume trading. The rails themselves—CME Group, Nasdaq, Bloomberg—win because they own the plumbing and the data flow.

Who's squeezed

Regional commodity brokers and independent FCMs face margin compression (now 6.6%) and can't match AI capabilities, making them acquisition targets or marginalized players. Community bank asset servicers and smaller independent custodians get squeezed by regulatory complexity (SEC Custody Rule Modernization looming April 2026 mandates for crypto and blockchain) and can't afford the tens of millions required to build compliant digital asset infrastructure. Mid-market trading operations and relationships-based brokers who built careers on execution skill and market knowledge find that skill priced to near-zero by 10,000 competing algorithms.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is regulatory overshoot on digital asset custody. The OCC has approved five new digital asset bank charters (December 2025) and cleared national banks to offer crypto custody (March 2025), but the SEC's Custody Rule Modernization (planned April 2026) could impose compliance costs so severe that only the largest institutions can afford to serve this market. If the rules demand real-time blockchain auditing, continuous identity verification, or custodian-level regulatory capital buffers for digital assets, mid-market players are locked out entirely. This could starve the entire digital asset ecosystem of custody providers and push institutions to unregulated or offshore solutions, defeating the stated policy goal of bringing crypto into the regulated banking system.

In one sentence

Moving and holding the money in a nutshell

Automation and digital rails are killing traditional broker margins and float profits, concentrating both services into a handful of scale players with regulatory permission to build crypto infrastructure.

89%

D · The tensions

The regional-bank squeeze

When deposits get expensive and tech costs soar, the math turns against smaller banks — and forces them out.

Regional and community banks face a three-part squeeze in 2025-2026. The Fed's 1.75 percentage-point rate cuts from September 2024 through Q4 2025 have compressed the margins they rely on, uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 alone as depositors shop for rates, and a $1.26 trillion commercial real estate maturity wall looms by 2027. Meanwhile, the technology and compliance costs required to compete with big banks and fintechs have become fixed overhead only scale can spread across.

What changed

The commercial banking industry grew 9.2% CAGR from 2021 to 2026, reaching $1.5 trillion in revenue (2026), but that aggregate masks a brutal bifurcation. Net interest margins recovered to 3.39% by Q4 2025, the highest since 2019, but that peak is reversing. The Fed's rate cuts have compressed deposit costs for big banks with scale and network effects. Smaller banks cannot follow suit without hemorrhaging uninsured depositors. In Q4 2025 alone, uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion, a flight toward safety and better rates. For regional banks with less than $50 billion in assets, deposit shopping is existential because they lack the scale to replace them.

The commercial real estate crisis is the second pressure. Banks are holding $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure, and $1.26 trillion in CRE loans will mature by 2027. Those loans, many originated at 4.3% when rates were stable, are refinancing at 6.2%—a 190 basis-point jump that bleeds borrower equity. Delinquencies hover near decade highs, forcing regional banks into loss reserves and capital draws. Big banks can absorb these hits because CRE is one line item in a diversified portfolio. For a $10 billion regional bank with 30% of loans in CRE, the math is catastrophic.

The third squeeze is technology and regulatory spend. Credit unions hit record net income of $18.8 billion in 2025, but that tailwind is ending. Large credit unions with $500 million-plus in assets are consolidating aggressively and pouring capital into AI, cybersecurity, and digital banking. Loan delinquency hit a 12-year high of 1.02% in Q4 2025 across credit unions, constraining profitability growth. Smaller credit unions face 539 cyber incidents in the past 12 months and must invest in fraud detection or lose members to big banks and fintechs like Robinhood and Rocket Mortgage that offer seamless digital experiences and faster approvals. The cost to remain competitive has become a fixed burden that only scales across a large member base or deposit book.

The result: consolidation by force. Credit union federally insured count fell from 4,455 to 4,287 in one year (Q4 2024–Q4 2025). Navy Federal, the world's largest credit union, crossed $203.6 billion in assets and added 826,000 members in one year (6% YoY growth), while smaller players merge into larger ones. First Technology ($17B) merged into Digital Credit Union ($12.7B); Wings Financial ($9.5B) merged into Ent Credit Union ($10.3B); CommunityAmerica ($5.3B) merged into Unify Financial ($3.5B). What was once a network of local credit unions is becoming a pyramid with a few giants at the top.

The evidence

  • Commercial banking: $1.5 trillion market size (2026), 9.2% CAGR (2021-2026), but compressed margins as Fed rate cuts ease and CRE refinancing crisis looms
  • Credit unions: $149.3 billion revenue (2026), but net income growth ending as rate cuts compress margins from 3.44% peak (Q1 2026) and delinquencies hit 12-year high of 1.02% (Q4 2025)
  • Consolidation: Credit union federally insured count fell from 4,455 to 4,287 (one year), with Navy Federal adding 826,000 members at 6% growth and major mergers of equals announced (First Tech+Digital, Wings+Ent, CommunityAmerica+Unify)
  • Deposit flight: Uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 alone, showing depositors shopping rates and fleeing to larger, safer institutions
  • CRE crisis: $1.26 trillion in commercial real estate loans mature by 2027 at 6.2% versus original 4.3%, while $2.7 trillion total CRE exposure sits on bank balance sheets and delinquencies hover near decade highs

Who rides it

The big four—JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup—grow stronger in relative terms. They can absorb CRE losses because CRE is one line among diversified portfolios. They keep deposits because size and the implicit safety premium matter in a volatile environment. Navy Federal and other mega-credit-unions ($200B+ in assets) capture the consolidation windfall, adding scale, branch networks, and member bases that let them invest in AI and digital without breaking their margin math. Fintechs and embedded finance platforms capture the dissatisfied edge cases—speed and transparency matter more to small businesses and depositors tired of regional banks' slow digital tools and opaque pricing.

Who's squeezed

Regional banks ($10–50 billion in assets) face the squeeze. They can't outprice big banks for uninsured deposits. They can't diversify CRE risk fast enough. They can't invest in the tech stack required to retain younger, mobile customers. Community banks (sub-$1 billion) are disappearing into mergers or acquiescence. Smaller credit unions ($50–500 million in assets) face the same trap: tech costs and compliance burdens are fixed, scale is not. The 2023 banking failures (SVB, Signature, First Republic) proved mid-size banks could die in real time, killing confidence in the $10–50B tier. Depositors remember. The regional bank model—local lending, personal service, embedded community ties—cannot compete on either technology or deposit cost when centralized platforms offer both at scale.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is a cascading commercial real estate default wave if property values fall or interest rates spike unexpectedly. Banks are holding $2.7 trillion in CRE, and $1.26 trillion matures by 2027 at rates 190 basis points higher than original. If defaults rise sharply, regional banks will face capital crises simultaneously (deposit flight + loss reserves), triggering forced sales or FDIC seizures. Unlike the 2023 failures (which were deposit-flight events), a CRE wave would be asset-side, affecting every bank on the same clock. Large banks can absorb it; mid-size banks cannot. The second worry is that consolidation accelerates into a true credit vacuum—if regional banks fail too fast, small businesses and underserved communities lose access to lending, and credit becomes moated behind big-bank or fintech gatekeepers with their own credit scoring and underwriting biases.

Rate cuts and deposit competition are crushing net interest margins for regional banks while tech investment demands and commercial real estate risk accelerate consolidation toward the giants.

D · The tensions

Living and Dying by the Rate

When the Fed moves rates, entire lending middlemen either thrive or vanish.

A one-percent move in interest rates doesn't just shift what borrowers can afford. It rewires the entire lending supply chain — which middlemen survive, which ones get cut out, and which industries become suddenly valuable or instantly obsolete. For brokers and factors, the rate is not just a pricing input. It's whether they exist.

What changed

Mortgage brokers built their business on information advantage and access. They knew lenders that direct borrowers didn't. They got paid commissions for closing the gap. But in 2025-2026, as rates held near 6.5% and the volume pie shrank by an estimated 400,000 home sales nationally, that information advantage vaporized. Online originations now capture 45-47% of the market (2025-2026), and platforms like Rocket Mortgage took the broker out of the loop entirely. At the same time, AI underwriting — non-QM systems now issuing decisions in under five minutes — removed the human expertise brokers once charged for. The math is brutal. Independents mortgage banks earned $443 per loan in net production profit in 2025, then $727 per loan in Q1 2026, a 64% jump. But that recovery masks a collapsing transaction count. The industry shrank from $13.2 billion in 2021 to $9.1 billion in 2026, a 17.1% decline over five years. Since 2021, employment fell 39%, from roughly 76,000 people to 46,000-52,000. The fix? Consolidation. M&A deals exploded to 62 in 2025, up 68% from 37 in 2024. Bayview Asset Management bought Guild Mortgage in November 2025. Pennymac bought Cenlar's servicing platform. Small independents realized they had no succession plan and no way to compete at scale. They sold or closed.

Invoice factors face a different rate squeeze but just as unforgiving. The 2023-2024 freight recession crushed transportation carriers, eroding working capital and driving demand for factoring. But when rates spiked in 2024, factoring became competitive against bank loans — factors charged 1%-4%, banks wanted 5%-6%. Then the Fed began cutting. As rates normalized toward 2025-2026, bank loans became cheaper again. Factors lost their rate-insulated advantage. Meanwhile, the market size was already broken. US invoice factoring sits at $3.0 billion in 2026, down from $3.9 billion in 2022. Growth was negative 1.9% in 2025 and negative 4.4% compounded annually from 2020-2025. The factoring company count fell to 247 (2025), and employment dropped from 5,254 (2022) to roughly 5,000-5,200 today. Yet there's a counterintuitive twist: global embedded finance is projected to hit $155.96 billion in 2026, and factoring is embedded as a core component. Platforms like Lendflow bundle invoice factoring directly into their APIs, selling it to SMBs who never touched a factoring house. The technology is becoming table-stakes — AI/ML for credit scoring, fraud detection, and workflow automation. But the old standalone factoring firms are margin-squeezed and oversupplied. Transportation factoring survives because freight delays and cash burn are structural; it's the general commercial factoring that bleeds to platforms. And regulatory headwinds make it worse. FDIC consent orders against BaaS sponsor banks in 2024-2025 raised compliance costs, slowing fintech partnerships and raising the cost floor for embedded-finance plays.

What changed across both industries is the same: the rate environment turned a margin business into a volume trap. When rates were high, brokers and factors could charge more and still be competitive. Volume was less crucial. But as rates normalized, the only way to scale margin was to reach new customers, automate processes, and shed overhead. Big platforms can do that. Solo brokers and regional factors cannot. The spoils go to whoever can embed lending into their existing product — a fintech with a customer base, a lending marketplace with data, a carrier with an open API. The margins don't disappear; they migrate to players with scale, data, and technology. The old gatekeepers lose the gate.

The evidence

  • Mortgage brokerage: Loan broker market contracted 17.1% from 2021–2026 (2026 size $9.1 billion), with online originations capturing 45-47% by 2025-2026 and employment falling 39% to 46,000-52,000 people.
  • Mortgage consolidation: M&A activity in mortgage banking accelerated to 62 deals in 2025 vs. 37 in 2024, with major acquisitions like Bayview's purchase of Guild Mortgage (November 2025) reflecting a squeeze on independents.
  • Invoice factoring: US invoice factoring declined 4.4% CAGR from 2020-2025, ending at $3.0 billion in 2026, with the factoring company count at 247 and employment roughly 5,000-5,200 (down from 5,254 in 2022).
  • Freight recession impact: Invoice volumes fell 5.7% year-over-year by December 2024 as the 2023-2024 freight crisis eroded carrier working capital and pushed spot rates below operating costs.
  • Embedded finance shift: Global embedded finance market projects $155.96 billion in 2026, with platforms like Lendflow bundling factoring into APIs and reaching SMBs who bypassed traditional factors.

Who rides it

Big platforms with embedded lending win. Fintech APIs bundling factoring, loan matching, and underwriting reach scale that solo brokers and regional factors cannot. Online lenders like Rocket Mortgage win. They own the customer, own the data, own the rate. And the banks win — when rates normalize, direct bank lending becomes the cheapest option, and brokers have no reason to exist. Technology and data become the scarce resource; middleman relationships become the cheap commodity.

Who's squeezed

Regional loan brokers and independent factors get crushed. They lose volume to platforms and banks. Their margin shrinks as rate volatility subsides. They can't automate fast enough to stay competitive. Consolidation is their only exit — sell to a bigger firm or close. Employment evaporates. Mortgage brokerage shed 30,000 jobs in five years. Factoring companies are shrinking their payrolls quietly. The small, independent, human-driven lending business has no economic moat left.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that rate volatility actually disappears for a long period. When rates are stable and predictable, there is no reason for a broker or factor to exist at all. A borrower with perfect information (which the internet provides) and a bank with the best rate wins every time. If the Fed manages to anchor rates in a boring, low-volatility band for the next three years, the remaining factoring and brokerage capacity becomes purely redundant. That is when the final wave of consolidation and job loss hits — not a gradual squeeze, but a sudden collapse once survival mode ends and optimization begins.

Living and dying by the rate in a nutshell

Brokers and factors only survive when rate volatility gives them a margin cushion; when the Fed stabilizes rates, the middleman economics flip from viable to obsolete almost overnight.
