E · The big picture

Money Gets Unbundled

Finance splinters out of banks into rails, apps, and platforms; scale and data win, middlemen lose.

Banking is leaving the banks. What used to be a service only a bank could offer—moving money, lending, managing portfolios—is now embedded in payment apps, card networks, lending platforms, and robo-advisors. The same force that unbundled retail (Amazon), media (YouTube), and taxis (Uber) is now unbundling finance itself. The winners are platforms with scale, data, and control over the rails. The losers are regional banks, loan brokers, and traditional middlemen.

What changed

The US financial system is fragmenting into three layers. At the top, giants who control the rails or the data are consolidating power: Visa and Mastercard process $198.25 billion in merchant fees annually (2025), fortified against antitrust pressure by pivoting to data services and embedded finance. Stripe and PayPal are on the verge of merging at $53 billion (2026), a deal that signals the winner-take-most dynamic at play—only mega-players can afford the infrastructure, regulatory complexity, and talent to compete. BlackRock is buying its way into private markets dominance through acquisitions like HPS for $12 billion (2024) and Preqin for £2.5 billion (2025), because that's where the higher margins are as retail money flees high-fee active management. At the bottom, traditional banks and brokers are being squeezed from three directions at once. Commercial banks face a $1.26 trillion commercial real estate maturity wall by 2027, with loans originally at 4.3% now refinancing at 6.2%, while deposit costs stay sticky (uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 alone). Margins are compressing despite the Fed's rate cuts of 1.75 percentage points through Q4 2025—the industry's net interest margin bottomed and is only now recovering to 3.39%, the highest since 2019, but the rebound is fragile. Regional banks that can't invest $50+ million in technology and compliance simply can't survive: the 2023 bank failures (SVB, Signature, First Republic) killed the mid-size consolidation wave temporarily, but the big four are now stronger relative to community banks than ever.\n\nLoan brokers are the clearest losers. The industry collapsed 17.1% from 2021 to 2026 (from $11.5 billion to $9.1 billion), with headcount down 39% from peak. Why? Because technology made them obsolete overnight. Online lenders and direct bank channels now handle 45-47% of mortgage originations (2025-2026), and the human broker's edge—understanding the loan process, navigating complexity—is being replaced by AI underwriting systems that deliver decisions in under five minutes. United Wholesale Mortgage originated 422,120 loans ($164.3 billion) in 2025, but it competes directly against Rocket Mortgage's slick consumer app, which brokers can't match. The few brokers that are profitable (earning $727 per loan in Q1 2026) are surviving only because they've become data aggregators or volume plays for lenders, not true intermediaries. Consolidation is the only exit: 62 M&A deals in 2025 (up from 37 in 2024), with Bayview acquiring Guild Mortgage in November 2025, are firms with no succession plan selling out.\n\nThe credit card and payment processing industry ($87.4 billion in 2026) is in the middle of a radical realignment. Merchants paid $198.25 billion in fees in 2025—a 3-4% tax on every card sale—so they are actively exploring alternatives: digital wallets, stablecoins, peer-to-peer rails. Visa and Mastercard face antitrust pressure on interchange fees and debit-routing regulations (the Federal Reserve's debit cap was vacated in August 2025, now pending appeal in 2026), yet they're adapting by offering data services and real-time rails that smaller processors can't match. Fintech funding surged 23% YoY to $28.6 billion globally in H1 2026, with AI-enabled fintechs capturing 23% of Q3 2025 fintech funding, but most of these startups are either niche players (handling BNPL or embedded payroll) or acquisition targets. BNPL alone reached $560.1 billion in 2025 and is now subject to affordability assessment rules (2026), pulling retail credit away from traditional card issuers but generating its own middlemen squeeze as regulations tighten. Finally, portfolio management ($340 billion revenue in 2025) is being hollowed out by passive index funds and ETFs, which captured 55% of mutual fund and ETF assets by 2025 (up from 34% a decade ago), while active mutual funds faced $1 trillion+ in net outflows in 2025. Only 38% of active funds beat their peers after fees (2025), so the survivors are either being acquired or specializing in alternatives and private markets—where margins are higher but scale is everything. Robo-advisors and hybrid advisory now manage $1 trillion in US assets (2026), with Vanguard Personal Advisor alone managing $300 billion, pulling retail clients away from traditional advisors.

The evidence

  • Commercial banking: net interest margins compressed by Fed rate cuts (1.75 pp through Q4 2025) while $1.26 trillion in CRE matures by 2027 at refinancing spreads of 380+ basis points wider (2025-2026)
  • Payment processing: merchants paid record $198.25 billion in card fees (2025), driving fee revolt and search for alternatives like stablecoins and peer-to-peer rails
  • Portfolio management: passive index funds and ETFs captured 55% of mutual fund and ETF assets (2025), up from 34% a decade ago, forcing active managers to consolidate or specialize in higher-margin private markets
  • Loan brokerage: industry declined 17.1% CAGR (2021-2026) as online originations reached 45-47% market share (2025-2026) and AI underwriting displaced human intermediation
  • Consolidation signals: $53 billion Stripe-PayPal merger bid (July 2026), BlackRock's $12 billion HPS acquisition (2024) and £2.5 billion Preqin deal (2025), 62 mortgage broker M&A deals (2025 vs. 37 in 2024)

Who rides it

Platforms with scale and control of the rails—Visa, Mastercard, the eventual Stripe-PayPal colossus, and passive index fund managers—are winning because they own the infrastructure that everyone else must use. BlackRock's consolidation into private markets wins because it owns both the data and the distribution. Regional banks and fintech platforms that can invest heavily in compliance, AI, and consumer experience also win, but only if they have capital and customers. Everyone else is a renter paying rent to the platform owner.

Who's squeezed

Regional banks are squeezed by deposit competition, the CRE maturity wall, and inability to invest in technology. Loan brokers are the clearest victims: 39% headcount reduction since peak, 17.1% revenue decline (2021-2026), and automation displacing their core value proposition. Traditional active managers are hemorrhaging assets to passive funds and robo-advisors. Traditional card processors and smaller payment networks can't compete against Visa/Mastercard's data and rail advantages and can't afford the consolidation price. Independent mortgage originators are disappearing into larger shops or going direct-to-consumer, eliminating the broker middleman entirely.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that as finance unbundles, it rebundles around giants who control the data and the rails, creating oligopolistic chokepoints and systemic fragility. Visa and Mastercard face antitrust pressure but survive because regulators can't easily break them up without breaking commerce itself. Stripe-PayPal at $53 billion (2026) creates a player nearly as powerful as a legacy network. When the next crisis hits—a spike in loan defaults as rates stay high, a commercial real estate collapse as the CRE maturity wall hits, or a run on uninsured deposits (which surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025)—the concentration of risk in fewer, larger players could amplify rather than dampen contagion. Regional banks are weak and interconnected. Retail investors are chasing passive funds that own everything, amplifying drawdowns when markets fall. The rails are controlled by a handful of players who can deny access or raise fees whenever regulation weakens.

The AI Rewiring

AI automates the routine cognitive work — and the value moves to whoever deploys it, owns the data, or sells the judgment a machine can't.

A · Creative & knowledge work gets automated

Design & the web: the fork

AI builders made commodity website design free. Strategy and brand just became worth more.

Five years ago, hiring a web designer meant hiring an agency. Today, a founder can build a professional site in hours with no code and AI doing the heavy lifting. This didn't kill the design industry—it split it in half. The glue work, the stuff you can template and automate, is now cheap and accessible. The hard work—positioning, brand, personalization—suddenly commands 55 to 80 percent margins and is the only thing agencies are competing on.

What changed

AI website builders went from a niche to a market force in three years. The global AI-powered website builder market hit $6.3 billion in 2026 and grew 26 percent year-over-year—with Gartner estimating that AI will reshape 70 percent of design and development effort for new web apps. Sixty percent of new websites are now built partly with AI.

What changed is not that designers disappeared. It's that template-based, execution-level design work collapsed in price and got absorbed into platforms. Wix, Squarespace, Webflow, and newer entrants like Bolt and Lovable all raced to add AI assistance—turning website builders from "template + drag drop" into "natural language to deployed site." Wix's Base44 acquisition (June 2025) generated $100 million in annual revenue in a single year and hit $150 million by May 2026. The message: AI code generation for websites is real, fast, and expensive to compete against.

Meanwhile, the design services industry—$61.23 billion in the US alone in 2025—is stratifying. Top-tier agencies are surviving by selling strategy, brand positioning, and personalization. Mid-market and small firms are racing to the bottom on price and losing. Talent is bifurcating: the best designers are moving up the value chain (brand, UX strategy, accessibility compliance), and the rest are being priced out by cheaper labor globally or displaced by AI builders.

The evidence

  • Web Design Services: US market $61.23 billion in 2025 with 8.5% CAGR (2025-2030), but stratifying into high-margin strategy tier (55-80%) and shrinking commodity tier
  • AI Website Builders: $6.3 billion market in 2026 with 26% YoY growth; 60% of new websites now built partly with AI
  • Wix Base44: $150 million ARR by May 2026, just nine months after acquisition, signaling how fast AI code generation is scaling
  • Website Creation Software: growth slowing to 2% annually in a 20-year-old commodity market, with traditional builders losing share to AI-native platforms

Who rides it

Agencies that sell brand strategy and personalization are winning. They've moved upmarket and are commanding 55 to 80 percent gross margins—real money. The companies acquiring design studios (Accenture bought Yumemi in early 2025) and the platform giants (Wix, Squarespace, Webflow) are winning because they own the distribution and the AI layer. AI-native builders like Bolt are winning because they don't have a legacy template business to protect; they can be pure AI-first. And founders, small businesses, and anyone who doesn't need bespoke positioning—they're winning too. They get professional-looking sites for a tenth of what they would have paid five years ago.

Who's squeezed

Mid-market and small design agencies are getting squeezed. They competed on execution—HTML, CSS, maybe a plugin or two—and that work just got commodified. Freelance web designers in developed markets are losing pricing power because they're competing against AI builders and global freelancers on a level field. And junior designers? The apprenticeship is drying up. The work that used to teach you the craft—the repetitive templating and basic execution—is gone. There's no low-risk entry point anymore.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The accessibility regulation tailwind (European Accessibility Act enforcement started June 28, 2025, and WCAG mandates are tightening in the US) created a temporary moat for compliance-focused agencies. But that moat is already eroding. AI website builders are baking accessibility compliance into their platform defaults and charging a premium, just like the agencies do. When automation eats the next layer up—personalization, conversion optimization, A/B testing logic—there's nowhere left to hide except pure brand and strategy work. That's real and scarce. But it also means the number of people who can charge premium fees for this work stays small.

Design & the web in a nutshell

AI collapsed the price of building a website; strategy and brand just became the only design work worth buying.

A · Creative & knowledge work gets automated

Video & content: the automation squeeze

Generative video makes content cheap. Distribution and judgment become the real asset.

AI video tools (Sora, Runway, Kling) can now generate and edit footage at scale. This made video production cheaper and faster, which sounds great until you realize it eroded the value of the routine work that funded the entire industry. The scarce thing isn't content anymore—it's distribution, taste, and the rights to sell it.

What changed

Generative AI video and automated editing compression made the labor-intensive middle of video production redundant. A decade ago, every commercial, short film, or streaming show required dozens of editors, colorists, and effects artists doing months of careful work. Now a studio can generate lower-tier shots in minutes and let AI handle basic cuts and color grading. Sora and Runway didn't have to be perfect—they just had to be cheap enough that studios stopped outsourcing that work to humans.

This squeezed the post-production sector first. The video post-production market is $6.8 billion (2025), growing 5.9% annually, but that surface recovery hides the real damage: studios are now automating away 20-30% of routine editing work inside their own walls rather than paying freelancers and small shops. The Writers and Actors strikes of 2023-2024 already cut demand by halting production on 47 projects. Streaming giants like Netflix and Disney then slashed content budgets by $2-5 billion combined to chase profitability. Now the same studios are replacing the remaining work with software. Smaller editing shops are caught between shrinking job volume and per-project budgets that no longer cover their overhead.

The evidence

  • Post-production Services: US market $6.8B (2025), growing 5.9% but facing 20-30% automation of routine editing work by decade's end
  • Advertising Agencies: US market $88.7B (2026) with only 1.8% growth in 2026 and 4.7% CAGR 2021-2026, as AI automates ad copy, visuals, and strategy work previously done by human teams
  • Motion Picture & Video Employment: down 21% from 2016 to 2024 (405,400 employees); Writers and Actors strikes (May-September 2023) halted production on 47 projects; Netflix cut content spend then raised it back to $18B in 2025 while automating internal post-production
  • Agency Consolidation as Weakness: Omnicom-IPG merger ($13.5B, November 2025) created $25B revenue entity but reflects market dysfunction—clients flee to smaller shops and AI tools rather than traditional full-service model

Who rides it

AI tools let smaller, leaner creative shops compete with legacy holding companies. A 10-person production studio with Runway and a good pitch can now do work that once required a 50-person agency. Companies like Publicis (winning the Mars account) bet that specialist creatives plus AI automation outcompete the WPP model. Similarly, studios that own AI video and editing tools internally keep that margin instead of paying external shops. The winners are (1) studios with the capital to invest in in-house AI tooling, and (2) boutique agencies or production companies agile enough to build new kinds of judgment—narrative strategy, brand psychology, distribution insight—that a machine still can't do.

Who's squeezed

Traditional advertising holding companies and mid-market post-production shops. WPP's market cap fell from £24B to £3.1B in 2025, losing Coca-Cola and Mars to smaller competitors who deployed AI and cut overhead faster. Motion picture and video employment dropped 21% from 2016 to 2024; even as streaming budgets recover (Netflix now $18B in 2025), studios cut the freelancer and outsourcing budgets first. Post-production shops that did routine cutting, color, or effects work face margin compression from both angles: fewer projects from streaming consolidation, and lower budgets because studios now handle that work in-house with software.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Downstream creative atrophy. If AI handles routine editing and basic effects, fewer humans learn those skills at entry level. In a decade, the people who know how to cut film by hand or grade color competently may be rare. This creates a bottleneck: you need human judgment for the hard aesthetic calls, but you may not have a pipeline of editors trained to recognize them. The second risk is concentration: only large studios and well-funded boutiques can afford the AI tooling and still afford to pay human creatives to do the judgment work. Mid-market production shops disappear, and talent becomes dependent on a handful of big players.

In one sentence

Video & content in a nutshell

Generative video made content cheap and plentiful; the scarce asset is now distribution, taste, and human judgment—and only the shops lean enough (or big enough) to afford both AI and real creatives survive.

Words & Publishing

AI drafting makes words cheap. The money follows brand, curation, and control of the catalog.

AI can draft faster than humans now. That floods the market with cheap text. But publishing was already hollowed out by the internet—what's left is whoever owns readers' trust, the data, and the rights to sell later. The winners own the attention and the archive. The losers write for nothing.

What changed

AI made routine text production nearly free. Audiobook narration, self-published titles, backend copywriting—all got automated and cheap fast. The economics inverted: supply of words exploded, but demand did not. Self-published ISBN titles hit 3.5 million in 2025, up 39% in a single year. Half of self-published authors now use AI tools. That abundance killed gatekeeping but also killed middlemen who used to live off scarcity.

What got scarce instead: reader attention, verified information, and brand trust. The Big Five publishers shifted from acquiring *more* titles to refining their portfolio—they stopped trying to buy everything and started picking winners. Amazon still controls 71% of reader purchases; indie bookstores unexpectedly opened 422 new locations in 2025, a 24% jump, because they offer curation humans actually want. Newspapers collapsed because advertising died and digital subscriptions stayed cheap. But the New York Times added 250,000 subscribers in Q1 2025 alone by making readers pay for judgment and access.

The evidence

  • Book Publishing: self-published titles hit 3.5 million in 2025, up 38.7% YoY, with audiobook sales at $2.43 billion (2025)
  • Book Publishing: Amazon Print-on-Demand revenue jumped from 24% to 30% of PublishDrive sales in 2025, but indie bookstores opened 422 new locations (24% increase, 2025)
  • Newspapers: print advertising revenue crashed from $73.2 billion in 2000 to $407.7 million in 2024; digital advertising only $315.1 million in 2024
  • Newspapers: News Media Corporation closed 14 newspapers in August 2025; New Jersey Star-Ledger and Times of Trenton ended print editions in February 2025

Who rides it

Publishers who own a brand readers trust and pay for. The New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg—national outlets with subscriber walls that actually stick. Amazon, which controls the catalog and takes a cut of everything sold through it. Indie bookstores and niche publishers, who survived by offering curation that algorithms can't replicate. Self-published authors in romance and graphic novels, where social media drives discovery and AI tools made production affordable.

Who's squeezed

Small newspapers and local news outlets. Advertising revenue evaporated—print dropped 99% from its 2000 peak to $407.7 million in 2024. Digital ads never replaced it. Mid-market publishers without a paywall strategy or brand moat got squeezed. Freelance writers and editors who sold commodity work—copy editing, routine drafting, fact-checking structure—now compete with free models. Newspapers owned by private equity got bought and stripped of costs, like Lee Enterprises under Berkshire's refinance.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Misinformation at scale. When drafting text is free and publishing is frictionless, the signal-to-noise ratio collapses. The same AI that let indie authors flourish also floods Amazon with SEO spam and scam books. Trust gets weaponized: if readers can't tell AI-generated content from human reporting, the few outlets that *do* earn trust monopolize the market. That concentrates power and leaves everyone else invisible.

In one sentence

Words & publishing in a nutshell

AI made words cheap, so value moved to whoever owns readers' trust, controls the distribution catalog, or builds the curation that humans still crave.

Accounting & Audit: The Close Gets Hollowed

The machines are taking the grunt work, the liability is staying human, and the junior accountant has nowhere left to hide.

AI is automating the work that used to be the entry point into accounting: client bookkeeping, expense categorization, tax return assembly, even the audit sample selection. The machines are fast and accurate. But the sign-off stays human—because liability does. The result is a junior accountant squeeze that's reshaping the whole profession.

What changed

AI automation cut the time to analyze financial documents in half and now handles 80% or more of routine tax return preparation. Compliance tasks, data collection, and document review that used to burn hours of junior labor now run through AI agents—PwC's pushing end-to-end audit automation by late 2026, EY deployed 150 AI agents onto 80,000 tax staff in 2025-26, and Deloitte's Zora AI handles autonomous work.

But here's the catch: a machine can categorize an expense. A machine cannot sign the audit. Compliance judgment, the decision to flag a risky line, the call about what the auditor thinks is really going on—those stay human. So do the client relationships. The value isn't in the routine cognitive work anymore. It moved to whoever owns the technology, whoever has the data at scale, and whoever the client trusts to say yes or no.

That shift is hollowing out the middle. The Big Four are investing billions in AI—6.4 billion dollars in 2025-26 alone—and hiring people with tech skills. Mid-market and smaller firms are getting squeezed between AI tool costs and a collapsed talent pipeline. There are fewer junior roles. The roles that exist demand tech fluency that didn't used to be part of the job.

The evidence

  • Accounting Services: Tax revenue growth diverged sharply—KPMG's tax revenues grew 7.5% in 2025 while EY and Deloitte each posted ~5.5% and PwC only 1%, reflecting uneven positioning on AI-assisted offerings
  • Audit Services: PwC announced end-to-end AI automation of audits expected by Q4 2026 (April 2026 announcement); EY deployed 150 AI agents to 80,000 tax staff simultaneously (2025-2026)
  • Private Equity Consolidation: Accounting firm M&A hit record 194 transactions in 2025, up 26% YoY, with financial acquirers driving 54.8% of deals (up from 38.9% prior year), targeting 4-7x EBITDA multiples on mid-market and smaller firms
  • Talent Pipeline Collapse: CPA exam participation down 30% since 2016; 300,000+ accounting professionals exited the field; open audit roles now take 73 days to fill (41% longer than other positions); 87% of finance leaders report talent shortages

Who rides it

The Big Four win. KPMG launched a law firm in 2025 and is expanding capacity while rivals consolidated—Deloitte, EY, and KPMG all grew headcount in 2025. They own the AI, the data, the client relationships, and the ability to absorb the tech investment. Mid-market and smaller firms that own their niche and can keep clients close also hold their own—but only if they don't get rolled up into a PE consolidator chasing scale. Private equity financial buyers are betting that pooling smaller firms and running AI across them will unlock margin. They're likely right, but the fee pressure will be real.

Who's squeezed

Junior accountants get squeezed. The entry-level work that used to be rote but reliable—bookkeeping, tax prep assembly, expense categorization—is now mostly automated. The roles that remain demand coding, data literacy, or compliance expertise. For anyone who wanted to learn the craft before moving up, the path just got narrower and longer. Solo practitioners and small local firms lose because they can't afford the tech and can't compete on scale. A one-person CPA shop in a small town can still serve local clients, but the competition from AI-assisted online services and mid-market roll-ups keeps the fees compressed.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The junior accountant exodus could flip into an undersupply crisis faster than firms can retrain. CPA participation is already down 30% since 2016, and the remaining pipeline is drying up. If AI automation accelerates faster than the profession can rebrand itself as "judgment and strategy," not "data entry," the shortage will get acute. Firms can automate faster than they can hire. And if mid-market firms get rolled up by PE at a record pace (194 transactions in 2025, up 26% YoY), the consolidators might optimize the junior roles out of existence entirely, leaving fewer on-ramps for new talent to enter the field. That narrows the future talent pool even further.

Accounting & audit in a nutshell

AI hollowed out the routine work that used to be the accountant's entry point, but kept the liability human—so now the Big Four and PE roll-ups dominate while mid-market firms and junior accountants get squeezed.

Insurance claims and broking: The adjuster vanishes

AI triages claims and prices risk faster than humans; the middle layer of adjusters and brokers thins out as the work moves in-house or consolidates upward.

For decades, insurance adjusters and brokers were the connective tissue—the human judgment layer between carrier and customer. AI is automating the routine parts (claim triage, document sorting, risk quotes) so fast that the entire staffing model is breaking. In 2025-2026, the claims adjusting market shrank even as AI adoption exploded, and insurance employment collapsed.

What changed

AI made routine claims triage cheap and fast. Instead of a human adjuster reviewing a storm-damage photo and opening a file, a machine now does it in seconds, flags outliers for fraud, and routes the claim to the right endpoint. Carriers tested this in 2024 (8% deployed full-scale AI) and punched it in 2025 (34% deployed). By end-2026, 91% of insurers committed to production deployment. The speed gains are real: 50–70% cycle-time cuts, 20–50% cost drops per claim.

But the second part is what breaks the industry: once a carrier can automate straight-through processing in-house, they don't need the third-party adjuster network anymore. They just need better fraud detection and claims data. Meanwhile, climate rewired the volume pattern. Catastrophe frequency doubled (one billion-dollar event every 10 days now vs. every 82 days in the 1980s), but the composition flipped. Secondary perils—hail, flooding, wildfire—now dwarf hurricanes, creating year-round grinding volume instead of seasonal spikes. Adjusters can't hire fast enough to absorb the new shape of risk.

The evidence

  • Claims adjusting: Carrier deployment of AI claims automation jumped from 8% (full-scale) in 2024 to 34% in 2025, with 91% committed to production by end-2026 (2025-2026 carrier surveys); cycle-time cuts of 50–70% and cost reductions of 20–50% per claim (industry reports, 2025-2026).
  • Broking: Insurance employment shed 70,000 jobs in the 12 months through June 2026 despite GDP growth (BLS payroll data); 400,000 retirements projected by end-2026 across the sector (Bureau of Labor Statistics); 854 M&A transactions announced in 2025, the third-highest on record, concentrating market power among five giants (InsuranceJournal, 2025).
  • Climate pattern shift: Catastrophe frequency doubled (one billion-dollar insured event every 10 days vs. every 82 days in the 1980s); secondary perils (hail, flooding, wildfire) became costliest insured peril of the 21st century in September 2025, surpassing tropical cyclones (Aon, January 2026).
  • Market contraction: Claims adjusting market $10.8B in 2026, growing only 1.5% CAGR (2020–2025) and contracting in 2025 due to interest rates; insurance brokers and agencies $216B in 2025, growing only 0.6–2% annually vs. historical 2.6% CAGR (2025-2026 industry data).

Who rides it

Carriers and big brokers win. Carriers automate claims triage in-house, kill the third-party adjuster margin, and keep the spread. Big brokers (Gallagher, Brown & Brown, Willis Towers Watson) vacuum up mid-market rivals at record pace ($13.5B Gallagher-AssuredPartners deal in August 2025; $9.8B Brown & Brown-Accession in August 2025), consolidate tech, and capture the 14–17% margin that small players can't defend. Data and fraud-detection vendors win too—once claims are automated, the competitive edge moves to whoever spots the patterns first. Tech-first platforms (like Newfront, acquired for $1.45B by Willis in December 2025) capture value by wrapping the machine layer in better UX.

Who's squeezed

Independent adjusters and small brokers get squeezed out. The 25% of adjusters retiring by 2027 won't be replaced; carriers need fewer humans once AI can triage 50–70% faster. The 30,000 small independent brokers generating under $1.25M annually have no succession plan and no capital to buy tech. They can't compete on data or automation, so they get consolidated or disappear. The labor cliff is real: 70,000 jobs shed in 12 months (June 2025–June 2026), and the Bureau of Labor Statistics expects 400,000 retirements by end-2026. The industry is shrinking its workforce faster than it's adding new talent.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that AI automates the easy 80% of claims (routine triage, straightforward indemnity) and leaves the hard 20% (fraud, subrogation, complex liability) to humans—but there won't be humans. Adjusters are retiring at 25% by 2027; new entrants aren't filling the gap. If a catastrophic year hits (and climate models suggest secondary perils will keep events frequent), carriers will have automation infrastructure but no human surge capacity to handle edge cases. Result: claims backlog, customer rage, and pressure on carriers to lower premiums or deny coverage. The second worry is that consolidation kills optionality. Five giant brokers now control most of the middle market; smaller carriers and niche underwriters lose negotiating power and distribution access. Independents can't start new brokers because the tech cost ($5.76B agentic AI market in 2025, $7.26B in 2026) is no longer DIY.

Insurance claims & broking in a nutshell

Law & consulting

AI does the draft; the pyramid cracks.

Law firms and consulting shops built their money machine on a simple stack: juniors do the routine work at low cost, partners handle the judgment, and the firm keeps the spread. AI is automating the routine. Juniors don't disappear—but the math that justifies hiring a college graduate to write his hundredth contract memo is broken. The firms that win are the ones that capture AI's gains before their clients demand the savings.

What changed

For decades, a law firm's or consulting shop's profit came from leverage. A senior partner charged $500 an hour; a junior associate cost $30 an hour but did 80 percent of the work—drafting contracts, running comps, writing memos. The firm pocketed the spread. AI upended the ratio. A language model now drafts a contract in 10 minutes for near-zero cost. A consultant no longer has to spend three weeks gathering industry data and formatting a PowerPoint deck; an AI agent does it in a day. The work isn't gone—it's cheaper and faster. That's a disaster for the model that priced junior labor at a markup.

The law industry felt this first. Firms jacked up their rates—fees per lawyer were up 16.8% in 2025—and landed record profits. But the bedrock numbers were weak: demand grew only 1.9 percent while expenses jumped 9.1 percent. They're spending big on AI infrastructure (budgets up 10% in 2025) and still seeing no client savings. Fifty-nine percent of corporate clients say they see zero benefit. Firms are merging frantically (59 deals in 2025, at least 16 more announced for 2026) because the math requires scale now. Consulting hit the same wall harder and faster. By 2025, AI roles outnumbered entry-level consultants for the first time in the industry's modern history. Hiring of junior consultants crashed 40 percent from 2023 peaks. The federal government cut $5 billion in consulting spend in early 2025. Clients stopped accepting hourly billing and started demanding outcome-based pricing or contingency fees. Consulting margins are under siege: AI specialists earn 56 percent wage premiums, but junior consultant salaries have flatlined.

The evidence

  • Law: 59 law firm mergers in 2025 (up 18% from 2024) and at least 16 more deals announced for 2026, driven by the mismatch between demand growth (1.9%) and expense growth (9.1%) after firms spent 10% more on AI infrastructure with no measurable client ROI.
  • Consulting: Consultant hiring down 40% from 2023 peaks by 2025; federal consulting cuts of $5B in early 2025 forced layoffs at Deloitte, Accenture, and IBM as clients rejected hourly billing and demanded outcome-based pricing.
  • HR consulting: Market growth decelerated from 6.5% (2024) to 1.4% (2026) as software platforms (Rippling, Paychex, TriNet) eroded the advisory moat and AI spending jumped 50% YoY in 2025.
  • Expert networks: AlphaSense's $930M acquisition of Tegus (June 2024) triggered consolidation as AI synthesis from transcript libraries replaces pay-per-call consulting, with research project turnaround collapsing from 2-5 days to 2 hours.

Who rides it

Big firms with capital win. Scale lets you absorb AI infrastructure costs, hire enough specialists to use it well, and keep existing clients even if margins compress. The Hogan Lovells–Cadwalader merger (2026) creates a $3.6 billion firm that can negotiate AI-powered efficiency gains directly into client contracts. Accenture doubled its AI specialist headcount to 80,000 and grew AI bookings 120 percent in 2025. Firms and consultancies that own data—especially transcript libraries and past project work—win harder. AlphaSense's consolidation play works because they own Tegus's 100,000-call library; they can resell the same insights to dozens of clients at near-zero marginal cost. Niche specialists who do judgment work—a trial lawyer, a complex M&A advisor, a human-centered change management consultant—stay valuable. Partners and senior people who own client relationships keep their place. What collapses is the middle: the junior associate who was a cheap source of routine drafting, and the mid-market consultant who sold "analysis and PowerPoints."

Who's squeezed

Junior associates and entry-level consultants get squeezed hardest. Consultant hiring fell 40 percent from 2023 peaks. A law firm no longer needs five juniors to draft contracts if one AI system does it at 1 percent of the cost. Salaries for junior consultants have flatlined while AI specialists command 56 percent premiums—the firm won't pay to develop your judgment if the machine already does your current job. Mid-market law and consulting firms—the ones too small to afford top-tier AI infrastructure and too specialized to win on pure scale—get trapped. They can't compete on price; they can't compete on judgment. Clients who've been paying for leverage-arbitrage lose their discount. A corporate legal team that used to outsource everything to BigLaw because it was cheaper than hiring in-house now sees AI reduce the advisory moat and questions whether they need BigLaw at all. Firms burning cash on AI without seeing client savings (59 percent of corporate clients report no clear benefit) are running out of runway. The margins are gone and the revenue is flat.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that firms invest heavily in AI and still can't pass savings to clients fast enough to matter. Right now, law firms hiked rates 16.8 percent in 2025 while clients see zero benefit from AI. If clients keep rejecting those prices, firms face a cascade: falling demand, rising costs per unit of work, and no way to cut head count fast enough to match. The stack of mergers already announced (16+ in 2026 alone) signals firms are betting consolidation will help—but there's no guarantee it will. A $3.6 billion merged firm still has to solve the problem that AI broke the junior-leverage model; you can't make that math work just by getting bigger. The second worry: clients defect. A corporation that sees "we hired AI and cut our consulting bill in half" succeeds; they internalize the work. Law firms and consultancies have no switching cost once clients realize the routine judgment has become commoditized. The firms that survive are betting they can move upmarket to pure judgment work fast enough. But the supply of "pure judgment" clients is smaller and more price-sensitive than the supply of "routine advisory" clients was.

Law & consulting in a nutshell

AI automated the junior associate's job, broke the leverage model that financed law and consulting, and now only the biggest firms with scale and specialist judges survive.

C · Even diagnosis & advice

Medical Diagnostics

AI reads scans and labs faster and cheaper than humans; volume rises, per-read price falls, and the physician's gate remains the only moat.

AI is flooding medical diagnostics with speed and accuracy. Radiologists can screen ten times as many scans per day. Labs can process results faster and cheaper. The machinery works—but the business is getting squeezed from both ends. Imaging reimbursements have fallen two-thirds since 2003. Lab margins are stable only for the giants. And smaller players are getting pinned between machines and consolidation.

What changed

AI made routine reading cheap and fast. A machine can flag anomalies in a chest X-ray or spot cancer in a microscope slide in seconds. That automation is real: it works. But automation didn't make diagnostics more valuable—it made them more abundant. Hospitals and health systems now run their own labs instead of sending samples out. Clinics buy point-of-care testing machines. Consumers order tests online and read results at home. The gate where radiologists and pathologists sat—reading rare, valuable images for high fees—has become a funnel. More volume, lower price per read, and the human is still liable for the miss. Imaging centers face 2% growth in a 2026 market of $26.3 billion. Labs are flat at 0.9% growth from 2021–2026 in a $90.9 billion market. Both are consolidating to survive. Both are buying AI to keep up.

The evidence

  • Diagnostic imaging centers: Radiology Partners raised $720 million in fresh equity in February 2026 to reduce debt after financial distress; GE HealthCare acquired Intelerad for $2.3 billion in November 2025 to bolt on AI and cloud platforms.
  • Diagnostic labs: Quest Diagnostics raised 2026 revenue guidance to $11.95–12.05 billion and acquired Fresenius's Spectra Laboratories clinical testing assets in August 2025 to consolidate volume.
  • Dermatology: FDA approved DermaSensor, an AI skin-cancer diagnostic device for primary-care settings in January 2024. Thirty-five-plus private equity platforms are active in dermatology consolidation as of 2025, and dermatologists see 3–5% reimbursement gains 18 months post-acquisition.
  • Cardiology: Medicare slashed amyloid PET imaging by 57% and LAA closure by 27% work RVUs in the 2026 fee schedule. Six cardiology practice acquisitions were recorded in H1 2025 alone, matching the entire 2024 volume—consolidation is accelerating as cardiologist shortages worsen.

Who rides it

The big diagnostic networks and hospital systems win. Quest and LabCorp survive through scale, acquisition, and direct integration into hospitals. Imaging chains like Radiology Partners and Envision Healthcare weather the cuts by buying AI and bundling services. PE-backed dermatology platforms thrive by consolidating fragmented solos and cosmetic-aesthetics clinics; a 1–4 location group trades at 4–9x EBITDA, and the math still works for PE because AI lets them standardize workflows and staffing across acquired practices. Hospitals win outright: they now own 41.5% of outpatient imaging claims and can build in-house labs, testing, and diagnostic dashboards at lower per-unit cost. The physicians who survive are those inside large groups or hospitals with negotiating power and AI on staff. Patients win on speed and access—results come back faster, home testing is cheap, and AI is genuinely good at spotting things humans miss.

Who's squeezed

Independent radiologists and pathologists are squeezed. Radiology practices with fewer than 10 providers can't afford AI platforms ($1–5 million in software, infrastructure, and training). Freestanding diagnostic imaging centers lose market share to hospitals and are forced to consolidate or sell. Small labs can't survive Medicare's flat rates and the coming 15% annual cuts starting 2027; they're being acquired or shut down. Dermatologists in solo and small-group practices face 9% Medicare cuts in 2027 and can't compete on cosmetics alone (where the margins are 30–50% versus 10–15% for medical dermatology). They're being rolled up by PE platforms at 3–5x multiples for control. Cardiologists outside large groups or hospitals are in crisis: burnout is driving 547 early retirements annually, the cardiologist-to-patient ratio will worsen from 1:1,087 (2025) to 1:1,700 (2035), and Medicare cuts on stress tests ($91 per procedure in 2026) and imaging make small practices unviable. Radiologist residency spots went unfilled—the next generation is opting out.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Automation of routine diagnosis breaks the economics of small practices before it ever creates new value. The moat protecting physicians—legal liability and the need for human judgment on edge cases—stays intact. But the volume game is already lost to machines and consolidation. In five years, most independent diagnostic practices will be absorbed or closed. The real risk is that AI creates an illusion of cheaper diagnostics while making physicians rarer and more overworked inside large systems, and then one AI miss in a critical case creates a liability cascade that reshapes the whole ecosystem. The other risk: consolidation into a handful of national lab and imaging networks gives them pricing power over hospitals and patients, while the physician shortage means those networks can understaff and push harder on AI, cutting corners on quality for a volume play that no one can sue because the liability stays with the hospital, not the machine.

Medical diagnostics in a nutshell

C · Even diagnosis & advice

Money & advice

AI makes financial advice routine. Winners own scale, data, and the judgment machines can't yet replicate.

AI is automating financial advice and credit judgment. Passive funds are eating active management. Robo-advisors and AI credit scoring are replacing human gatekeepers. The result: margins compress for traditional advisors while winners consolidate into giant platforms or specialized boutiques.

What changed

AI made routine financial advice cheap and scalable. A robo-advisor can now manage a $10 million portfolio for 66 basis points—down from 75 basis points just two years ago. Fintech platforms like Wealthfront and Betterment won 42% of under-40 clients by offering transparent, algorithm-driven portfolios without the white-glove service. At the same time, AI credit scoring is displacing traditional models: Zest AI's system can approve 25% more loans while holding risk constant, and FICO's new Score 11 can score 9 million previously invisible consumers using rent and cash-flow data instead of credit history alone.

This killed the comfortable middle. Active mutual fund managers lost $1+ trillion in outflows in 2025 alone—the steepest year in an 11-year exodus—because only 38% of them beat their passive peer funds after fees. Traditional wealth advisors now compete on technology and scale, not on stock-picking skill. The advisory model is shifting: large firms are moving to W-2 advisor employment and technology-centric operations rather than asset aggregation. Consolidation hit 466 M&A deals in 2025, up 27% from 2024.

The evidence

  • Portfolio Management (Finance & Insurance): passive index funds and ETFs captured 55% of US mutual fund assets by 2025, while active mutual funds faced $1+ trillion in net outflows in 2025
  • Financial Advice (Finance & Insurance): wealth management M&A hit 466 deals in 2025 (up 27% from 2024), with Q1 2026 reaching 109 deals in a single quarter—highest in 8 quarters
  • Credit Scoring & Rating (Finance & Insurance): Zest AI's model approves 25% more loans while holding risk constant; FICO Score 11 (early 2026) brings 9 million previously credit-invisible consumers into the system
  • Gen Z & Millennials (Finance & Insurance): 42% of under-40 fintech users choose robo-advisors over traditional firms; Gen Z and millennials hold $3.1 trillion in equities as of August 2026, a record

Who rides it

Winners are consolidators with scale and data. BlackRock is buying data dominance (Preqin for £2.5B in March 2025; HPS Investment Partners for $12B in December 2024) and moving into illiquid alternatives—which generate over half the industry's projected revenue by 2030. Firms that own platforms and AI tooling win younger clients: fintech platforms grabbed 42% of under-40 users. Credit bureaus with proprietary alternative data (rent payment history, cash flow) and machine learning gain market share. Boutique specialists who focus on niche clients or complex strategies survive by offering judgment machines can't replicate yet—tax optimization, family office strategy, illiquid deal sourcing.

Who's squeezed

Squeezed are solo and small-firm advisors. Advisor fees fell from 75 basis points to 66 basis points in just two years as clients shop for cheaper alternatives. Active mutual fund managers are becoming extinct: only 38% of them beat passive peers after fees, and $1+ trillion flowed out in 2025 alone. Mid-size advisory firms that can't afford the technology stack or data moat are being acquired by larger consolidators. Traditional rating agencies and credit bureaus face disruption: Zest AI's model and alternative scoring systems are eating their moat by offering better loan approval rates. Cybersecurity breaches (TransUnion exposed 4.4M Americans in August 2025) have eroded consumer trust and forced defensive spending on security rather than innovation.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that AI credit scoring locks in bias at scale. Zest AI's model works because it optimizes for lender revenue and risk, not fairness. If alternative scoring systems replace traditional bureaus before regulators impose guardrails, millions of credit-invisible consumers could be scored on proxy variables (rent, cash flow, phone bills) that correlate with race or ZIP code—automating discrimination at a speed humans can't police. The SEC is moving to overhaul rating agency rules, but consumer credit regulations lag behind AI deployment. A data breach at a major credit bureau could trigger a crisis: TransUnion's 4.4M-person breach in 2025 already raised consumer awareness and forced firms to invest in security. A breach of a robo-advisor or fintech platform holding retirement accounts could trigger a run on assets.

Money & advice in a nutshell

C · Even diagnosis & advice

Education & credentials: the degree's new job

<em>AI tutors are free and good. What a college degree actually sells now is not what it used to.</em>

AI changed what you need a class for. In 2026, ChatGPT and specialized tutors can teach you calculus, coding, or compliance frameworks for free or nearly free. The colleges and certification schools that thrived by selling "here's what you need to know" are now competing on something they forgot they were selling: who you know, what doors open, and—for employers—that you passed a gate they trust.

What changed

AI made the transmission of routine knowledge cheap and on-demand. Before 2024, you needed a professor for calculus, a bootcamp for Python, a compliance course for Azure. Those gatekeepers had pricing power because knowledge transfer was expensive to scale. Now a large language model teaches you better, faster, and asks fewer embarrassing questions. The cost of producing and distributing that content approached zero overnight.

This hollowed out the middle: commodity bootcamps that promised "learn coding in 12 weeks" face free competition from AI tutorials, corporate LLMs, and open MOOCs. Entry-level IT training bootcamps shut down in waves (Epicodus 2023, SNHU 2024, 2U entire bootcamp division 2024). Generic certification prep collapsed. But the top end moved the other direction. Cybersecurity training surged because it's locked to hiring requirements and insurance discounts. Enterprise cloud certifications command premium pricing because they're not about what you know—they're about proving to your employer that you passed someone's gate. That proof, that signaling, became more valuable as the underlying knowledge became free.

The evidence

  • Colleges & Universities: US sector reached $605.1B (2026), contracting 7.5% CAGR through pandemic recovery, now stabilizing but losing international graduate students (-12%, fall 2025-2026)
  • Business Certification & IT Schools: $6.4B market (2026), bifurcating sharply—cybersecurity training at 16.6% CAGR to $6.66B (2025), cloud bootcamps 12.7% CAGR, while commodity bootcamps shut down en masse
  • Consolidation: Elon acquired Queens (2026), Russell Sage merged Albany, Ursuline joined Gannon, Villanova absorbed Cabrini and Rosemont—wave of forced small-school mergers
  • Platform consolidation: Coursera acquired Udemy (April 2026, $2.5B equity value) to control 290M learners and 95,000 instructors, consolidating online-learning oligopoly as free alternatives displace entry-level training

Who rides it

Employers and the credentialing gatekeepers. Employers win because they can now outsource technical training to free AI and hire on credentialed proof. Cybersecurity and cloud certifications command premium pricing because they're not teaching knowledge—they're pre-screening: you paid someone to test you so I don't have to. Big platforms (Coursera, Udemy, now unified) win because they control the gates: 290 million learners and 95,000 instructors funnel through one checkout. Elite universities survive because their networks never went digital and their research keeps them a brand. The accreditors win because the Trump administration is weakening regulatory barriers and streamlining approval, letting more credential players enter the market.

Who's squeezed

Small regional colleges, bootcamp operators, and anyone selling knowledge transfer as their core product. Community colleges in rural areas are growing enrollment but losing revenue per student. Mid-tier private colleges can't compete with free tutorials and consolidated platforms, so they're consolidating or closing (Siena Heights closed after 2025-26 AY, Union Institute filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy). Bootcamps that built business models on "we teach you this rare skill fast" can't underprice free and are exiting or pivoting. The junior developer and entry-level IT hire loses negotiating power when the barrier to entry evaporated—now employers want pre-screened, credentialed juniors, and the credential is expensive, making that first job harder to reach even if the knowledge is free.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The accreditation market is starting to look like a toll booth. As AI makes content cheap, the degree's residual value collapses to "I passed their test" and "I met their people." If accreditors can set arbitrary gates and employers trust them uncritically, colleges and bootcamps become subcontractors, not institutions. The Trump administration's push to weaken accreditor oversight and streamline approval could flood the market with new credential players, each claiming to test you, all collecting fees, none actually teaching anything new. Meanwhile, AI itself is getting embedded into hiring systems—so the credential might start mattering less than raw performance data. The real risk is that education becomes a pure compliance layer: mandatory testing, zero learning, all margin capture.

Education & credentials in a nutshell

AI made knowledge free, so colleges now sell networks and gates instead of education—and the gatekeepers are consolidating into oligopolies while small schools shut down.

D · The new scarcities

The deploy dividend

The wins go to whoever sits between the AI and the enterprise—not the ones being disrupted.

AI is automating the thinking work. But someone has to deploy it, train it, feed it data, and defend it from the rest. That's where the money is moving. The IT consultants charging $300–$500 an hour for AI strategy, the data centers building hyperscale farms, the vendors locking in contracts—they're capturing the lion's share of the rewiring, while the corporations that actually need AI are caught between hype and reality, and the junior knowledge workers are getting squeezed out.

What changed

AI pushed four things to become newly scarce or valuable: the power to deploy the systems, access to clean data, the skills to operate the infrastructure, and the judgment to know when an AI's answer is right. Capital poured in—the five largest hyperscalers will spend $630 billion on infrastructure in 2026, up 36% from 2025. But electric capacity became the hard constraint, not money. US data center electricity demand tripled from 23 GW in 2023 to 42 GW in 2026. Wholesale power prices near major data centers rose 267%. That scarcity rewires who wins.\n\nFor IT consulting firms, AI became a pricing lever. Narrow, high-touch services—AI strategy, cloud migration, cybersecurity—command $300–$500 per hour in 2026. But the firms discovered they could also shed junior staff faster than they could sell AI work. Accenture booked $5.9 billion in gen-AI work in FY2025; IBM landed $12.5 billion in gen-AI business. McKinsey cut 10% of its global workforce (3,000–4,000 people) in 2026 as AI productivity squeezed internal capacity needs. Clients hired consultants to *avoid* hiring consultants—a paradox that compressed margins and accelerated M&A. The industry grew to $821.2 billion in 2026, but at 2.9% CAGR since 2021—slower than cloud alone ten years before.

The evidence

  • IT Consulting (Technology & Digital): Accenture's gen-AI backlog hit $5.9 billion in FY2025; IBM's gen-AI business reached $12.5 billion in the same period, yet overall consulting market growth slowed to 2.9% CAGR 2021–2026, with margins compressed and 52,000+ tech jobs cut in Q1 2026 alone (up 40% from Q1 2025).
  • Data Processing & Hosting (Technology & Digital): Hyperscalers will spend $630 billion on infrastructure in 2026 (up 36% from 2025), with $450 billion explicitly targeting AI; wholesale power prices near major data centers rose 267% in 2025–2026, and 90% of operators report staffing constraints as the critical bottleneck.
  • Enterprise AI Adoption: McKinsey's 2025 survey found only 39% of organizations claim any EBIT impact from AI, with most reporting impacts below 5%, despite record consulting backlogs and the tripling of US data center electricity demand from 23 GW (2023) to 42 GW (2026).
  • Infrastructure M&A (2025–2026): CoreWeave secured a $200 MW lease in Charlotte from Digital Realty (March 2026); Q1 2026 data center M&A topped $21+ billion in a single quarter; Equinix closed a $15 billion joint venture to build hyperscale facilities.

Who rides it

The IT consulting firms and infrastructure vendors win—at least for now. Accenture and IBM have locked clients into multibillion-dollar AI backlogs. Specialized hosting platforms like CoreWeave are booking massive capacity commitments. Data center operators who own power-rich land or long-term electricity contracts are becoming bottleneck choke points. M&A accelerated; consolidation is concentrating the picks-and-shovels business. The rule: if you *deploy* AI or *sell* the infrastructure layer underneath, you capture value. The consultant charges $300–$500 per hour. The hyperscaler owns the margin on GPU capacity. The power supplier holds the scarcity card.

Who's squeezed

Junior and mid-level consultants, software engineers, and routine knowledge workers get squeezed hardest. Hourly rates for junior and mid-level staff ($90–$150) face automation pressure from AI-coding tools, while consulting firms cut headcount faster than they redeploy it. McKinsey cut 10% of its global workforce; tech sector shed 52,000 jobs in Q1 2026 alone. Mid-market enterprises also get pressured—they can't afford the $300–$500/hour AI strategy consultants, yet they're told they must adopt AI or fall behind. Smaller data center operators and regional hosting vendors are being consolidated or priced out by hyperscalers' buying power and access to capital and power. The real loser is the company that *buys* the AI solution, hoping for ROI—because 61% of enterprises report no meaningful EBIT impact (inverse of the 39% claiming any impact).

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Power becomes the hard limit. Hyperscalers can spend $630 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, but the US grid can't sustain 42 GW of data center demand. Wholesale power prices spiked 267% near major data centers, and capacity prices in PJM jumped 833% in a single year. If power constraints tighten further—or if electricity becomes politically contested—the entire AI deployment engine stalls. The second risk: the consulting bubble pops when clients realize 61% of AI projects deliver no measurable EBIT impact, and they stop paying $5.9B–$12.5B backlogs. Capgemini, IBM, Accenture, and others could face a sudden reckoning if enterprise confidence in AI ROI collapses. The third risk: the talent shortage never resolves. 90% of data center operators report staffing bottlenecks; demand for AI infrastructure specialists, high-voltage engineers, and cooling technicians vastly outpaces supply. That wage pressure spirals and further compresses infrastructure margins.

In one sentence

The deploy dividend in a nutshell

The deploy dividend flows to consultants, hyperscalers, and infrastructure vendors—while the enterprises buying AI solutions and the junior workers getting automated out find themselves squeezed between hype and a power-constrained grid.

D · The new scarcities

The human premium

AI is making taste, judgment, and accountability scarce — and whoever can prove a person stands behind the work is winning.

The middle of every service industry is hollowing out. On one side, AI handles the routine: the boilerplate contracts, the commodity websites, the junior consultant hours. On the other side, the premium tier — work that requires taste, judgment, or accountability — is pulling away. The gap between cheap-and-AI and personally-guaranteed is widening fast.

What changed

AI made two things scarce at once: the commodity work (now cheap; anyone with a tool can do it) and the human relationship (now rare; less of it happens). When AI handles the routine, the real value concentrates at the top and bottom — either you need genuine judgment, or you need to trust someone's name is on it. Everything in the middle gets compressed.

Clients no longer pay for hours. They pay for outcomes, or they buy the robot. That shifts who wins. Design firms with strong brands and personalization are commanding 55-80% margins. Legal work is consolidating into bigger firms that can afford the AI infrastructure and handle mega-deals. Consulting is splitting into high-end strategy (outcomes-based pricing) and algorithmic automation — entry-level consultant roles are vanishing, replaced by AI specialists paid 56% more. The judgment work is becoming a luxury product. The labor is disappearing.

The evidence

  • Web design services: AI website builders market hit $6.3B in 2026 (26% YoY growth), with 60% of new websites now built partly with AI, compressing mid-market design labor by 20-40%, while top-tier agencies earning 55-80% margins by adding strategy and personalization.
  • Law firms: US legal services posted $426.7B revenue in 2025 on rate hikes (fees per lawyer up 16.8%) despite demand growth of only 1.9%, forcing 59 mergers in 2025 (up 18% YoY) and driving tech spending up 9.7-11% annually — yet 59% of corporate clients see no clear savings from AI tools.
  • Consulting: AI roles now outnumber entry-level consultants at top firms (a reversal from 2015); Accenture cut 11,000 roles in April 2025 while doubling AI specialist headcount to 80,000; federal consulting spend dropped $5B in early 2025, forcing industry consolidation.
  • Legal market 2026: Milbank's new salary scale ($235K starting associates; $455K for 8-year associates, effective July 2026) and 16+ announced mergers signal talent pressure at the premium tier, even as mid-market firms face structural weakness on expense-demand mismatch (expenses up 9.1% vs. demand up 1.9%).

Who rides it

The winners are the branded firms that moved upmarket. Top design agencies commanding 55-80% margins by adding strategy and personalization. Large law firms merging to afford AI infrastructure and land mega-deals (Hogan Lovells-Cadwalader combination = $3.6B revenue). Consulting's Big Four keeping federal access and outcome-based pricing power. And AI specialists themselves, earning 56% wage premiums. Anyone who owns the client relationship and can say 'a person stands behind this work' is winning.

Who's squeezed

The mid-market is squeezed. Mid-tier design shops competing globally against freelancers and AI builders. Regional law firms can't afford the AI stack or the merger premium. Junior and mid-level consultants are being replaced by AI automation; their hiring is down 40% since 2023. The commodity tier of every service is getting cheaper and smaller. And in-house clients are left confused — they're paying more for outside counsel while being told the AI should save them money.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that AI investment doesn't deliver the promised ROI, but firms keep spending anyway. In law, 59% of corporate clients say they see no clear savings from AI, yet firms are hiking tech budgets 9.7-11% annually. Law firms are burning cash on technology infrastructure while demand growth is stuck at 1.9% and expenses are up 9.1%. If firms can't show measurable returns on these bets, the margin compression becomes permanent — and the talent market at the top inverts.

In one sentence

The human premium in a nutshell

AI made routine cognitive work cheap and automated, pushing value to whoever controls the client relationship, owns the data, or proves a person stands behind the judgment — and hollowing out the middle tier entirely.

D · The new scarcities

The Junior-Role Collapse

AI eats the training work, and nobody has answered who becomes the senior of tomorrow.

For fifty years, junior roles were the entry ticket. A college grad worked their way up: entry-level tax returns taught you accounting, junior associate work taught you law, junior designer work taught you how brands think. AI has automated exactly that work. And now the pipeline is broken.

What changed

AI ate the routine cognitive grind that paid junior wages. Individual tax returns that took a junior four hours now take AI thirty minutes. Contract review that took a junior a day now takes generative AI an hour. Design mockups that a junior prepared now come from an AI website builder.

The work that got automated wasn't the hard stuff. It was the stuff that taught you how to think like a professional. And it paid. A junior accountant in 2025 is cheaper to replace with software than to hire. Law firms burned through record profits in 2025 not by getting more efficient, but by squeezing associates and raising rates. Web design agencies are splitting: the top tier offering strategy commands 55-80% margins, while the commodity tier competes with AI and is vanishing.

The people who used to be squeezed upstream—the training staff who had to take on juniors—are now getting squeezed out. But the people who are hit hardest are the juniors themselves, and the future senior cohort that has no way in.

The evidence

  • Accounting: 87% of finance leaders report talent shortages; CPA exam participation down 30% since 2016; AI now handles 80%+ of individual tax returns (2025).
  • Law: US law firms posted record 2025 profits on rate hikes (fees up 16.8%), not efficiency; but 1.9% demand growth and 9.1% expense growth force consolidation.
  • Web design: AI website builder market reached $6.3B in 2026 (26% growth YoY); 60% of new websites built partly with AI; design labor compressed 20-40% (2026).
  • Consolidation across all three: Private equity is acquiring smaller accounting firms at 4-7x EBITDA; law firm mergers hit 59 deals in 2025 (up 18% from 2024); top design agencies now command 55-80% margins while commodity firms vanish (2025-2026).

Who rides it

The big firms and the software companies. Deloitte, EY, and KPMG expanded in 2025 while smaller accounting firms got rolled up. KPMG tax revenue grew 7.5% in 2025, outpacing competitors. BigLaw mergers accelerated: Hogan Lovells and Cadwalader combined to create a $3.6B revenue firm in 2026. And the design firms that pivoted to strategy and compliance—not commodity delivery—are capturing 55-80% margins. The winners are whoever owns the technology or can scale to invest in it. Smaller practices cannot compete.

Who's squeezed

The junior cohort and the firms that can't consolidate. CPA exam participation dropped 30% since 2016 because the junior role no longer teaches—and no longer pays to learn. Web design juniors are gone; they're replaced by AI builders. Law firm associates are hired at the top ($235K starting pay in July 2026) because the firm no longer wants juniors to train; it wants experienced talent to bill out at premium rates. Mid-market accounting and legal practices are caught: too small to invest in AI infrastructure, too large to compete with freelancers or AI builders on price. And the pipeline of people who could become tomorrow's partners is closing.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

No one is training the next generation of professionals. Accounting firms hiring at the top and compressing the middle. Law firms burning money on AI tools with no measurable client savings, squeezing associate headcount instead. Design shops either going high-margin or vanishing. In five years, who becomes the managing partner, the partner counsel, the principal of the design firm? You cannot jump from college to partner. You have to work up. And the work that used to do that—the junior work—is not coming back.

E · The big picture

The AI Rewiring

Routine cognitive work got cheap; judgment, data, and control got scarce and valuable.

Artificial intelligence is automating the cognitive grunt work that used to justify a salary. Web designers now compete with AI builders. Claims adjusters face machines that process cases 50-70% faster. Radiologists watch algorithms read scans. Portfolio managers discover that their decisions don't beat a $10 ETF. The pattern is everywhere: the routine got cheap, and the value migrated to whoever owns the data, deploys the system, or makes the judgment a machine still can't.

What changed

AI didn't kill these professions. It crushed the middle. Web design used to be a ladder: junior designer to senior strategist. Now it splits into two industries. The commodity tier—websites built by Wix, Shopify, and AI builders reaching $6.3 billion in 2026 with 26% yearly growth—handles 60% of new sites. The premium tier, commanding 55-80% margins, survives by selling brand strategy and personalization to clients who can pay for it. Everyone else goes away.

The same wedge splits every industry in this collection. Claims adjusters faced a dual shock: AI adoption jumped from 8% to 34% of carriers in 2025, with 91% committed to full deployment by end of 2026—cutting cycle time by 50-70% and eliminating the middle-market adjuster. Meanwhile, radiologists watch as hospitals consolidate imaging and integrate AI screening, while independent imaging centers see margins compress and struggle to afford the software they now need. Portfolio management became arithmetic: passive index funds hold 55% of US mutual fund assets as of 2025, up from 53% a year earlier and 34% a decade ago. Only 38% of active managers beat their benchmarks after fees. The math was already bad. AI made it obvious.

What got cheap: routine labor and commodity decisions. What got scarce: proprietary data, deployment infrastructure, and the judgment that can't be automated yet. What got valuable: owning the algorithm, controlling the data it trains on, and having the capital to build scale. Consolidation followed—Accenture acquiring Tokyo design studios, BlackRock buying Preqin for £2.5 billion and HPS for $12 billion to control private-market data and infrastructure, GE HealthCare paying $2.3 billion for Intelerad to embed AI into imaging workflows.

The evidence

  • Web design: AI builders reached $6.3 billion market in 2026 with 26% YoY growth, capturing 60% of new websites while mid-market agencies race to the bottom on price.
  • Claims adjusting: AI adoption by carriers jumped from 8% in 2024 to 91% committed to deployment by end of 2026, promising 50-70% cycle-time cuts that threaten third-party adjusters.
  • Diagnostic imaging: Radiologist shortage reached crisis (961 unfilled residency spots in 2025; 130-day hiring cycle), while hospital consolidation and AI adoption squeeze independent centers facing 2.83% Medicare reimbursement cuts.
  • Portfolio management: Passive funds hold 55% of US mutual fund assets as of 2025; only 38% of active managers beat their benchmarks after fees, driving $1+ trillion in outflows and industry consolidation.

Who rides it

Winners own infrastructure or data. BlackRock controls both—they bought Preqin's private-market data (£2.5 billion in 2025) and HPS's platform ($12 billion in 2024) to dominate alternatives. Large web agencies survive by selling strategy to brands that won't commoditize. Hospitals consolidate imaging and capture 41.5% of outpatient claims. Carriers deploy claims automation in-house and disintermediate the adjuster middle. The pattern holds: scale matters. Consolidators win. Specialists with a judgment moat win. Everyone else competes on price in a market where price keeps falling.

Who's squeezed

Mid-market and solo professionals. The claims adjuster who isn't backed by a carrier or major network faces a choice: retrain as a complex-case specialist or leave. Independent diagnostic imaging centers struggle with 2.83% Medicare cuts and lack the capital to buy AI software they now need to compete. Mid-market web agencies can't afford to match the premium tier's strategy offerings or the AI tier's speed. Active portfolio managers managing conventional stocks and bonds watch their AUM leak away—$1+ trillion in 2025 alone—to passive funds. Radiologists don't disappear; they shift to hospitals and get salaried. The freelancer and small partnership, for now, still exist. They just stopped being the default path.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest tension is labor replacement speed exceeding retraining speed. Claims adjusters face 25% retirement by 2027 at the exact moment carriers are automating their jobs. Radiology training takes 5-6 years; the shortage is now, and AI can screen images today. Web design junior roles have collapsed (AI builders + platforms did that), so the pipeline to senior designer dries up. Portfolio managers in their 40s can't easily become alternatives specialists overnight. The worry isn't slow displacement—it's whiplash displacement, where the retraining ladder collapses before new rungs are built. Policy, schools, and firms haven't kept pace with the speed of automation.

The AI rewiring in a nutshell

Artificial intelligence made routine cognitive work cheap and gave permanent advantage to whoever owns the algorithm, controls the data, or operates at scale.
