A · The categories that went online first

Electronics go online

Commodity electronics led the retail exodus — tariffs, pricing power, and the smartphone gutted specialty stores, leaving only online retailers and the smallest experiential niches.

Electronics disappeared from Main Street first. Consumer electronics stores in the US still ring up $261.62 billion in 2026, but it's not because anyone is going to a shop anymore. Amazon owns 60.5% of all e-commerce electronics and appliances. The physical stores that built the category — Best Buy, independent computer shops, camera retailers — are all in structural decline, closing hundreds of locations a year. What happened is simple: phones made cameras obsolete, e-commerce made prices transparent, and tariffs made shelves too expensive to stock.

What changed

Consumer electronics went from a destination category to a default online purchase faster than any other retail segment. In 2022, there were 42,930 consumer electronics retail establishments in the US. By 2025-2026, that number had collapsed by 4.5% annually, a death march that accelerated when tariff rates on Chinese electronics hit 35% effective (25% Section 301 tariffs plus a 10% Section 122 surcharge) in early 2026, with some components facing rates as high as 145%. The tariff shock of April 2025 hit like a price shock: phone demand fell 37%, gaming consoles dropped 58%, laptops fell 68%. Retailers couldn't absorb that cost. Consumers at lower and middle incomes simply stopped buying. Even as tariffs moderated to 13.7% by February 2026, the damage held. Best Buy still commands $41.7 billion in annual revenue and has just announced its first store expansion in a decade — but only as small-format, high-touch shops in tech-forward metros, betting survival is boutique, not breadth. Appliances have outperformed because they're still a consultation buy, still installed at home, still a ticket item. Everything else — computers, cameras, gaming gear — is purchased online or not at all.

Computer retail fractured even faster. The segment was already thin at $39.6 billion in 2026, growing just 0.4% a year over five years. But tariffs devastated the supply side: US computer imports from China collapsed 70% to $10.8 billion in 2025. Retailers were forced to source from Mexico and Taiwan, a friction that added weeks and uncertainty. IDC forecast that PC shipments would fall 11.3% in 2026, with Q4 potentially down 20% year-over-year, and memory shortages will linger until the end of 2027. The average price of a PC rose 18.3% in 2026. Budget systems — the volume segment that feeds retail foot traffic — were projected to drop 28%. These weren't aspirational buys anymore; they were postponed buys. Apple, which built the premium computer retail segment, closed three US stores in mid-2026 while opening in only the highest-growth metros (Detroit, Miami), explicitly abandoning the mall. Best Buy shrank its computer footprint by 24-40 stores per year. The computer retail category is now a slowly-dying middle: too small to finance locations, too exposed to tariff shock, too transparent online. Independent computer retailers shrank from 5,258 locations in 2025 to a category that loses 6.6% of its store base per year.

Camera retail was first to near-total extinction. Fewer than 1,000 independent camera retailers remain — down from 1,180 in 2021 and 5,676 employees by 2021. The market is worth $5.4 billion in 2026, and it's nearly all online or rented. E-commerce owns 55% of camera sales. Smartphones handle 94% of all photos. Mirrorless cameras are 90% of interchangeable-lens sales, DSLRs are effectively dead, and the only growth segment is used gear — which online marketplaces (eBay, MPB, B&H Used) have monopolized. Tariffs on camera imports started at 10% baseline in April 2025, country-specific (Japan 15%, Thailand 19-46%, Germany variable), and by February 2026 climbed to 15% flat, raising retail prices 10-15%. For a category already running 1-2% margins (historically 1.9% in 2021), that was extinction velocity. Specialty camera shops survive only in high-population artistic hubs — NYC, LA, Portland — and only by serving professionals and enthusiasts who will pay for hand-holding and rental services. The surprise growth engine was rental: LensRentals and Adorama Rentals became essential revenue streams for both online retailers and the last specialty shops, because photographers who used to buy gear now rent it, use it once, and give it back. Margin-free retail became the business model for everyone else.

The evidence

  • Consumer electronics: Amazon owns 60.5% of US e-commerce electronics/appliances (2025); Best Buy reported $41.7B in 2026 full-year revenue with first positive comp sales (+0.5%) since fiscal 2022
  • Computer retail: US tariff rates on Chinese electronics reached 35% effective by early 2026 (Section 301 + Section 122); PC shipments forecast down 11.3% in 2026 with Q4 potentially 20% year-over-year decline
  • Camera retail: e-commerce holds 55% of US camera market share; tariffs raised retail prices 10-15% (April 2025 at 10%, February 2026 at 15%), compressing already razor-thin 1-2% margins
  • Tariff shock across devices: phones down 37%, gaming consoles down 58%, laptops down 68% during peak tariff period (2025); demand did not fully recover even as rates moderated to 13.7% (Feb 2026)

Who rides it

Amazon and the largest omnichannel players like Best Buy (one-third of revenue now from e-commerce) survive by owning digital distribution and pivoting to experiential retail in high-income markets. Online marketplaces (B&H, Adorama, eBay, MPB) that consolidated used-gear sales and rental services ride the shift: used camera gear sales projected to climb 13% annually, with eBay at 9.6% market share. Consumers who can navigate online pricing and tariff volatility gain access to wider selection and often lower prices (when tariffs don't spike). Professionals and enthusiasts find survival paths through rental services and specialized online communities.

Who's squeezed

Independent computer retailers (6.6% annual store closures), camera shops (down 7% per year annualized), and small-format consumer electronics chains lost to both Amazon's scale and tariff-driven cost floors. Consumers at lower and middle incomes were squeezed hardest: when tariffs spiked prices, budget systems were projected to fall 28%, and purchasing power simply evaporated. GameStop became the symbol of obsolescence — gaming went digital, digital distribution killed the retailer, and a failed attempt to acquire eBay couldn't reverse it. Sales associates and store employees (consumer electronics employment down 2.3% annually since 2021) lost jobs; $82.3 billion in 2022 physical retail shriveled into a much smaller experiential niche.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Tariff volatility is the single biggest risk to what remains. When tariffs spiked to 27% in April 2025, phone demand fell 37% and didn't recover fully even as rates moderated. The Section 122 surcharge was set to expire around July 2026, creating near-term pricing uncertainty heading into holiday shopping (2026). If tariffs reset or climb again, retailers already at 1-2% margins have zero room to absorb cost. The supply chain is still fragile: US computer imports from China collapsed 70%, forcing sourcing shifts to Mexico and Taiwan that add friction. PC memory shortages won't clear until the end of 2027. Any new tariff shock could finish off the remaining independent retailers and force Best Buy into even more aggressive consolidation or full retreat to e-commerce.

In one sentence

Electronics go online in a nutshell

Electronics went online first because prices became transparent, margins became indefensible, tariffs made physical inventory a liability, and Amazon had no rent.

A · The categories that went online first

Media & Hobby Retail

The store stopped being where you buy — Amazon and marketplaces hollowed out these categories, and only omnichannel giants and experential stores survive.

The channel shift hits different in media and hobby retail. Three categories, three endings: bookstores staged a print-fueled comeback, art supply stores collapsed under omnichannel pressure and tariffs, and hardware stores clung to survival as a DIY-driven niche. Each tells a story about what made physical retail matter again—and what doesn't.

What changed

Bookstores discovered that the store itself became the product. For fifteen years, print books lost ground to e-readers and online ordering. Then something flipped. Print sales dipped only 0.9% in the first nine months of 2025, a reversal from the 10% cliff of 2020. Gen Z and millennial readers rejected digital convenience for the tactile, discovery-oriented experience of physical bookstores. BookTok—a TikTok community centered on book recommendations—drove approximately 59 million print book purchases in 2024 and contributed 800 million euros in sales across Europe in 2025. Barnes and Noble, under CEO James Daunt, proved omnichannel worked by giving local store managers autonomy over inventory and merchandising, mimicking indie bookstore curation. The result: 67 new Barnes and Noble locations opened in 2025 (the highest single year in 15 years), and 422 independent bookstores opened that same year, up 31% from 2024. Since 2021, the indie bookstore count rose 70%. This category made scarcity valuable—the rare, curated, in-person discovery experience—and made abundance (digital convenience) cheap and unwanted.

Art supply and craft retail experienced the opposite compression. The market sat at $1.2 billion in 2025-2026, down from $819 million in 2022, but that number masks a brutal winnowing. Joann Fabrics filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2025 and announced closure of all ~815 stores, marking the collapse of another chain competitor. Tariffs hit hard: raw materials (Chinese pigments, European linen, Canadian timber) saw costs jump 22% in 2025, squeezing margins industry-wide. Yet demand for creative supplies was real—Michaels reported 40% earnings growth in Q3 2025 and 12% comparable store sales gains by building an omnichannel fortress (online plus physical). Online retail now accounts for 56.8% of art supplies market share as of 2026, with e-commerce growing at 7.4% annually while physical stores shrink. The category made omnichannel scale valuable and made specialty retail scarcity unsustainable. Small independent art supply stores survived only if they built community and expertise that Amazon could not replicate.

Hardware stores persisted as a grudging niche. The market was $42.8 billion in 2026, growing at 1.3% that year, but the structure was broken: big-box chains controlled 56% while small independents closed at record rates. The industry was anchored in a sustained DIY movement—74% of homeowners do maintenance projects, and 24% either do work themselves or hire labor while buying materials directly. But tariffs on imports ran 10-12.5% as of mid-2026, pushing supply costs up 15-30% for multi-site operations and stretching lead times from 6-8 weeks to 16-24 weeks. True Value Company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 14, 2024. Harpeth True Value Home Center, after 54 years, closed permanently on April 1, 2026. Carnation Ace Hardware, 56 years old, closed on October 25, 2025. Do it Best acquired the bankrupt True Value in late 2024, becoming the world's largest hardware cooperative, but even members reported closures due to inflation, unaffordable rents, and declining foot traffic. The category made deep expertise and local presence valuable—but made undifferentiated square footage cheap and expendable.

What made certain stores scarce and valuable was not inventory or convenience. It was curation, discovery, and expertise that e-commerce could not replicate at scale. Bookstores won by being experience platforms. Art and hardware stores lost by trying to compete on price and selection with omnichannel giants, and they collided with tariff shocks that erased thin margins. The survivors were those that pivoted to omnichannel leverage (Michaels, Barnes and Noble) or built credible expertise and community (independent bookstores, niche art suppliers, DIY specialists). The losers were chains caught in the middle: too expensive to be pure e-commerce, too generic to be experiential.

The evidence

  • Bookstores (2024-2025): BookTok drove 59 million print book purchases in 2024; indie bookstore openings surged 70% from 2021-2025, with 422 new indie stores in 2025 alone
  • Art Supply Retail (2025-2026): Michaels posted 40% earnings growth in Q3 2025 and 12% comparable store sales gains; online retail reached 56.8% market share growing at 7.4% annually
  • Art Supply Tariffs (2025): Raw material costs (pigments, linen, timber) jumped 22%; Joann Fabrics filed Chapter 11 in January 2025 and closed all ~815 stores
  • Hardware Retail (2024-2026): True Value filed for Chapter 11 on October 14, 2024; tariffs pushed supply costs up 15-30% with lead times stretching from 6-8 weeks to 16-24 weeks by mid-2026
  • Hardware Stores (2025): Harpeth True Value Home Center closed after 54 years on April 1, 2026; Carnation Ace Hardware (56 years) closed October 25, 2025 due to inflation and declining foot traffic

Who rides it

Barnes and Noble and Michaels—omnichannel consolidators with the scale to absorb tariffs and the sophistication to blend online and physical. Independent bookstores survived by becoming discovery platforms and community centers that TikTok and nostalgia fed. Specialty expertise retailers (niche art suppliers, local hardware shops with deep product knowledge) won by serving customers who valued advice over convenience. Home Depot and Lowe's gained ground as the default, because they had the scale to swallow tariff shocks that crushed smaller competitors.

Who's squeezed

Small independent hardware stores and specialty retailers caught between e-commerce undercutting and tariff inflation. Art supply chains like Joann Fabrics that tried to compete on breadth rather than expertise. Cooperative members who depended on stability but found True Value bankrupt and their own rents and labor costs unaffordable. Regional chains without omnichannel capability (Carnation Ace, Harpeth True Value) closed, betrayed by a model where the store was just an inventory warehouse, not a customer experience.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Tariffs are making the squeeze unsustainable even for winning retailers. Michaels and Barnes and Noble can absorb 15-30% supply cost increases; independent bookstores and art suppliers cannot. If tariffs stay at 10-12.5% for hardware and compound for craft materials, even omnichannel winners will pass costs to consumers, and price discipline will flip the DIY and bookstore booms into busts. The other risk: nostalgia is a volatile fuel. BookTok can reverse as suddenly as it appeared. If Gen Z stops treating physical bookstores as social experience and reverts to pure convenience, indie bookstores close en masse again.

In one sentence

Media & hobby retail in a nutshell

Bookstores found their way back by pivoting to curation and discovery; art supply stores and hardware stores got crushed between omnichannel consolidation and tariffs.

A · The categories that went online first

Apparel & the try-before-you-buy problem

Clothing shifted online despite fit friction; stores became showrooms, then closed.

For decades, apparel was the one category you had to try on. You went to a store, found a changing room, and made sure the fit was right before paying. That friction kept retail alive. But somewhere between 2021 and 2026, fit stopped mattering more than price and convenience. E-commerce captured half of women's clothing sales and a quarter of family apparel. Physical stores didn't disappear—they emptied out, closed down, and transformed into showrooms for online sales nobody would make in person anymore.

What changed

The apparel market was already shifting online before 2025, but three things hit simultaneously and shattered what remained of physical retail. First: tariffs made everything cost more at the exact moment when people stopped spending. When the de-minimis tariff exemption ended on August 29, 2025, all imports under $800 suddenly had duties applied. By December 2025, apparel tariff rates hit 35.1%, nearly 2.4 times higher than the January 2025 rate of 14.7%. That forced cost increase hit consumers immediately—apparel CPI jumped 5.1% year-over-year by March 2026, and monthly spending on apparel collapsed 21.7% from late 2024 to early 2025. Consumers, especially lower-income households, simply stopped buying clothes. Retailers had to choose between absorbing the tariff hit or passing it to a customer base that was already retreating.

Second: e-commerce dominance became complete and unstoppable. Women's clothing online reached $61.8 billion in 2025 while brick-and-mortar was still $66.4 billion in 2026—nearly parity. Family clothing saw e-commerce capture 24% of fashion retail in 2026, up from roughly 21% in 2024, growing 4.9% annually while traditional brick-and-mortar sales lagged by 62%. In footwear, the shift was sharper: e-commerce penetration hit 30-35% of total sales by mid-2025, growing at 7-9% annually. The stores that survived did so by becoming distribution centers for online orders, not by selling to people walking in the door. Online women's clothing employment grew 5.5% annually from 2019 to 2024, while brick-and-mortar employment in the same sector kept declining. The channel had flipped; the question was no longer whether online would win, but how fast physical retail would shrink.

Third: the industry consolidating and collapsing told the story nobody wanted to hear. Macy's announced closure of 66 stores in January 2025, part of a 150-store exit plan. Forever 21, once a ubiquitous fast-fashion fixture, filed Chapter 11 on March 16, 2025, and liquidated all 364 stores by May. Liberated Brands (which owned Volcom, Billabong, Quiksilver, and Roxy) filed Chapter 11 in February 2025 and liquidated 122 stores. Francesca's announced closure of 400 locations. Torrid planned 180 closures. Even luxury players weren't safe: Allbirds, which had a $4 billion IPO valuation in 2021, closed all remaining full-price US stores in February 2026 after being sold for $39 million. In footwear, the endgame became visible when Dick's Sporting Goods completed its $2.5 billion acquisition of Foot Locker in September 2025—the largest pure-play shoe retailer, no longer viable as a standalone business. Mall foot traffic declined sharply for the first time since the pandemic in late 2025, with super-regional malls down 1.2% overall during the holiday season. The stores had stopped being destinations. They were inventory graveyards waiting to be liquidated.

The evidence

  • Women's clothing: e-commerce at $61.8B (2025) vs brick-and-mortar $66.4B (2026) show near channel parity and structural shift
  • Family clothing: e-commerce grew 4.9% annually through 2026, capturing 24% share while brick-and-mortar lagged by 62% growth differential
  • Footwear: e-commerce penetration hit 30-35% by mid-2025, growing 7-9% annually, while Foot Locker—the largest pure-play retailer—acquired by Dick's in September 2025
  • Tariffs: apparel rates surged to 35.1% in December 2025 from 14.7% in January, triggering 5.1% CPI inflation and 21.7% spending collapse
  • Store closures: Forever 21 (364 stores, May 2025), Liberated Brands (122 stores, Feb 2025), Francesca's (400 announced), Allbirds (all full-price US stores, Feb 2026)

Who rides it

The winners are ultra-low-cost online platforms and value retailers positioned to absorb tariff shocks. Shein and Temu, despite controversies, continued gaining share as consumers cut spending and hunted for the cheapest option. TJX Companies (which owns T.J.Maxx and Marshalls) reported 5% comp sales growth in Q3 FY2026 and raised guidance, benefiting from price-conscious consumers rotating to off-price retail. Ross Stores projected 6-7% comp growth for FY2026 for the same reason. Retailers who went omnichannel and built localized warehousing—matching online order fulfillment to neighborhood hubs—survived by becoming infrastructure, not destinations. Nike and Adidas, by consolidating wholesale and pushing direct-to-consumer, bypassed the channel problem entirely (though Nike reversed some wholesale cuts after revenue impact). Employment growth in online clothing jobs showed clear winners: 5.5% annual growth 2019-2024 in women's clothing e-commerce versus ongoing declines in brick-and-mortar.

Who's squeezed

Mass-market and discount brick-and-mortar retailers got crushed. The store closures tell the story: 7,323 in 2024 and roughly 6,000 in the first half of 2025 alone. Forever 21, Francesca's, Liberated Brands, Torrid, and dozens of smaller chains liquidated or announced major exit plans. Women's clothing had 88,112 businesses in 2026 but was shedding locations constantly; brick-and-mortar employment in the sector continued declining. In footwear, the independent shoe store became obsolete—foot traffic at malls declined for the first time since the pandemic in late 2025, particularly hurting super-regional malls where larger shoe retailers clustered. Foot Locker's forced acquisition and closure of overlap stores proved the category couldn't sustain a pure-play model anymore. Family clothing retailers faced the worst squeeze: tariffs hit 35.1%, consumer spending collapsed 21.7%, and e-commerce took an additional 3 percentage points of share in just two years. Smaller, undercapitalized chains with high debt and inflexible leases simply couldn't survive long enough to rebuild online operations.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that tariff uncertainty and escalation cause a cascading insolvency wave through 2026 and beyond. The Trump administration imposed sector-specific tariffs up to 50% on some goods in 2025-2026, and footwear remained uncertain whether it would carry additional levies beyond the base 10% universal tariff. Retailers locked into Q1-Q2 2026 inventory sourced before tariff clarity will absorb the full cost hit, potentially pushing another wave of bankruptcies. Second: if e-commerce concentration continues unchecked and mall foot traffic keeps declining, landlords of regional malls will face a death spiral of empty stores, lower rents, and tenant defaults. Apparel CPI jumped 5.1% year-over-year by March 2026; if tariffs stay elevated, price resistance could cause permanent demand destruction—consumers may simply buy less clothing, not just shift channels. The category that defined retail is no longer retail.

B · The marketplace machine

The Marketplace Eats the Middle

The platform takes a cut of everything and sets the terms of survival for sellers.

When you buy online, you're increasingly buying from a marketplace platform, not a retailer. Amazon, Walmart, eBay, TikTok Shop — they all profit from the sale and from the seller's access to customers. The smaller the seller, the more punishing these economics become. Only the sellers who can afford the platform's take-rates, logistics standards, and demand for automation survive the squeeze.

What changed

E-commerce in the US hit $1,380 billion in 2026 and is growing 6.9% to 10.5% annually through the early 2030s, but that growth is not spreading evenly. Amazon's logistics supremacy forces all competitors to match delivery standards that only Amazon can afford — same-day, free, instant refunds. Walmart is fighting back with its omnichannel playbook: store-fulfilled delivery surged 50% in Q2 2026, and the company is targeting digital to be 25% of revenue by fiscal 2030. But Walmart's dominance is still regional; Amazon's remains national and unmatched. Mobile commerce now represents 60% of all online sales, and social commerce is growing 30% annually, with TikTok Shop claiming $20 billion in 2026 sales alone. This fragmentation actually favors the platforms more — sellers now have to show up on Amazon, Walmart, eBay, TikTok, and their own direct-to-consumer site, all simultaneously, all at different cost structures. The cost of being everywhere has never been higher.\n\nTariffs made the squeeze worse. The mid-2025 tariff shock — a 120% duty on Chinese goods and suspension of de minimis thresholds — forced import-dependent sellers to choose between raising prices (losing price-sensitive customers) and shrinking margins (losing money). E-commerce margins sit at 5.5% to 5.9%, already compressed by fulfillment costs, AI requirements, and platform take-rates that run 15-45% depending on the site. A small seller importing from China in May 2025 faced an instant 120% cost increase with no ability to pass it through to customers without losing them to a competitor three clicks away.\n\nReturn fraud has become its own crisis. Retailers lost $76 billion annually to fraudulent returns; 9% of all retail returns are now fake. Customers exploit 94.5% repeat-purchase standards by ordering multiples, returning the expensive ones, and keeping the cheap ones — or shipping back empty boxes. Retailers now deploy AI to detect patterns, but they face an impossible trade-off: stop the fraud and lose the customers who expect frictionless returns, or let it run and bleed margins. The platforms don't solve this; they profit from transaction volume regardless of whether goods go out and come back.\n\nIn grocery, the speeds are getting faster. Online grocery sales grew 20% year-over-year for six straight quarters through Q1 2026, and December 2025 saw a 32% surge as customers embraced pickup to avoid delivery fees. Walmart and Kroger are racing to profitability — Kroger expects digital profitability in 2026 — but profitability here means zero margin; it means they're breaking even on a volume play. For smaller grocery sellers, online channels don't exist. Only Walmart and Kroger have the store footprint and supply-chain density to make pickup pencil out. Everyone else is locked out or locked into the marketplace at whatever terms the platform sets.

The evidence

  • E-commerce: $1,380B market in 2026 with 5.5–5.9% margins, growing 6.9–10.5% annually but consolidating around platforms (Amazon, Walmart, eBay) and omnichannel incumbents
  • Tariffs: Mid-2025 duty shock (120% on China goods, de minimis suspension) forced import-dependent sellers to absorb costs or exit; e-commerce relies on imports
  • Grocery: Online grocery 20% YoY growth for six straight quarters; Walmart/Kroger targeting profitability in 2026 via store-pickup; small sellers locked out
  • Social commerce: TikTok Shop $20B+ annual sales in 2026, growing 30% annually, fragmenting seller channels and forcing multi-platform presence
  • Return fraud: $76B lost annually; 9% of returns fraudulent; retailers deploy AI while balancing fraud-prevention against repeat-purchase loyalty (94.5% of customers expect frictionless returns)

Who rides it

Walmart is the winner. Its omnichannel strategy — store-fulfilled delivery up 50% in Q2 2026, targeting 25% digital revenue by 2030 — is the only playbook that works at scale for a non-Amazon retailer. Walmart has thousands of stores; Walmart has supply chains that predate e-commerce; Walmart can absorb the fixed costs of dual fulfillment. Amazon remains the default, but Walmart is the only competitor making inroads. Amazon itself wins because competitors must match Amazon's standards to survive, and most never will. TikTok Shop wins in social commerce — $20B in 2026 sales with 30% annual growth — because it owns the attention and the checkout all at once. Small sellers lose. Big platforms win.

Who's squeezed

Smaller independent sellers are squeezed between Amazon's take-rates (15-45% depending on category), Walmart's controls, TikTok's uncertainty, and their own need to be visible on multiple channels simultaneously. Tariffs hit hardest — the mid-2025 duty shock on Chinese goods was an instant margin collapse for import-dependent sellers. They can't raise prices without losing customers to Amazon; they can't cut margins without going insolvent. Mid-market retailers without omnichannel infrastructure (stores + logistics + mobile app + returns automation) are locked in decline. Grocery is particularly brutal: only Walmart and Kroger can afford the store-pickup economics that consumers now demand. Regional and independent grocers have no online channel and no way to build one at competitive cost. The $76B in annual return fraud represents lost margin that gets passed to honest sellers who absorb higher fraud-detection costs.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that return fraud becomes systemic and unsolvable. At $76B lost annually and 9% of returns now fraudulent, retailers are deploying AI to detect patterns — but every fraud-prevention control that asks for ID, restricts refunds, or flags suspicious orders risks losing the 94.5% of customers who reward repeat purchase. If fraud accelerates (5x since 2024), retailers will either have to raise prices (killing volume) or tighten returns (breaking the loyalty loop). Smaller sellers have no AI, no fraud team, no data. They'll exit first. The platform dynamics make this worse: marketplaces profit from transaction volume regardless of fraud, so they have no incentive to solve it. The result is a system where honest sellers subsidize fraud detection, dishonest customers subsidize everyone else, and the platforms keep growing richer.

In one sentence

The marketplace eats the middle in a nutshell

Marketplace platforms profit from every sale and set the terms of seller survival — margins compress, tariffs hurt, fraud spirals, and only omnichannel incumbents or giant platforms survive the squeeze.

B · The marketplace machine

Direct-to-Consumer Brands

Small brands selling direct online are crushed by platforms and tariffs; only scaled omnichannel survives.

Direct-to-consumer was supposed to liberate brands from the middleman. Instead, the middleman became TikTok, Amazon, and Walmart. DTC upstarts that bypassed physical retail found themselves trapped in an even tighter squeeze: social commerce cannibalized discovery, logistics costs ate profits, and tariffs turned 2025 into a bloodbath. The brands that killed the store didn't survive the shift they started.

What changed

When brands went DTC in the 2010s, they promised direct relationships with customers and fat margins. That worked briefly for beauty and apparel. But by 2025, the structure inverted. TikTok Shop alone did $2.49 billion in US beauty sales in 2025, up 123 percent year-over-year, and that growth came directly from the wallets of brands still building email lists. Discovery moved to platforms; logistics became a commodity; tariffs arrived. In beauty specifically, the $69.3 billion US market in 2026 looks stable on the surface—up from $29.3 billion in 2022 under the old definition—but that's entirely Ulta and Sephora's doing. Ulta grew net sales to $12.4 billion in fiscal 2025 (ended February 2026), up 9.7 percent, because it aggregates and curates thousands of brands at scale. Smaller pure-play DTC brands didn't benefit. Glossier closed 75 percent of its stores. Pat McGrath Labs filed Chapter 11 in early 2026 after years of burning through DTC venture capital. Cover FX and Mally Beauty shut down in January 2026. Flower Beauty (Drew Barrymore's brand) closed in September 2025. All of them had followed the playbook: raise venture money, burn cash on customer acquisition, build a DTC site, hire Instagram influencers. None of it worked at unit economics that penciled.\n\nThe outdoor gear industry shows the same pattern differently. The US hiking and outdoor equipment market is now $6.3 billion in 2026, down from $7.1 billion in 2022—a real contraction after pandemic peaks. Here, Amazon and Walmart didn't just pressure margins; they moved upmarket with private-label tents and sleeping bags, and downmarket respectively, compressing the middle where independent shops and small brands live. REI, the largest outdoor co-op retailer, laid off 180 full-time and 248 part-time employees in January 2025 and shut down its Experiences division (tours and classes). In October 2024, it had cut another 257 retail jobs. Even with 23 million co-op members, REI cannot sustain the unit economics of the old model. Dick's Sporting Goods is launching elevated outdoor concepts to compete directly with REI, further fracturing shelf space. Smaller independent outdoor shops—the kind that used to cluster in mountain towns and college towns—are closing faster than they can pivot.\n\nWhat made DTC brands vulnerable was the same thing that looked like their strength: they operated in a world where the customer seemed close and loyalty felt real. But loyalty, it turned out, was just subscription frequency and Instagram algorithm reach. As soon as social commerce platforms figured out how to sell beauty and gear directly, the brands' entire moat evaporated. Tariffs in 2025 compressed margins further—health and beauty inflation cooled to 2.1 percent by mid-2025, a signal that consumers were trading down or buying less—and the venture-funded cash burn model that had sustained DTC growth hit a wall. Ulta-Target partnership ending in August 2026 eliminated a key distribution channel that was helping smaller brands get shelf space at scale. Amazon's forecast share of beauty is projected to climb from 10 percent in 2024 to 15 percent by 2030, while Sephora and Ulta's combined share dips from 20 percent to 19 percent. That's not a massive shift in the numbers, but it reflects the real fragmentation happening in customer discovery: the brands themselves lost control of the narrative the moment TikTok started selling it.\n\nThe playbook that was supposed to disintermediate retail—cut out Macy's, cut out department stores, sell your own site—actually transferred control to platforms with deeper pockets, better logistics, and network effects. Physical retail was the old tyranny. DTC was supposed to be freedom. What arrived instead was a new tyranny: algorithm dependency, customer acquisition cost inflation, and the brutal fact that margins below 40 percent cannot survive in a world where your payment processor and your logistics provider both take 20-30 percent. The brands that tried to go DTC without the scale to compete on fulfillment speed and price ended up playing a losing game against platforms that had no brand to build, only transactions to capture."

The evidence

  • Beauty & cosmetics: Pat McGrath Labs filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in early 2026 after years of DTC-only burn; Flower Beauty (Drew Barrymore brand) closed September 2025 due to tariffs and weak DTC sales; Cover FX and Mally Beauty shut January 2026.
  • Outdoor retail: REI (largest co-op chain) laid off 180 FT and 248 PT employees January 2025 and cut Experiences division serving only 40,000 of 23 million members; Dick's Sporting Goods Public Lands collapsed from 8 to 3 stores.
  • E-commerce capture: TikTok Shop drove $2.49 billion US beauty GMV in 2025 with 123% YoY growth; Gen Z/millennials now discover 70% of beauty digitally (TikTok, Instagram, social commerce).
  • Market contraction: US hiking/outdoor equipment declined -2.6% in 2025, market is $6.3B (2026) vs. $7.1B (2022); margin compression to 3.5-4.3% (2025-2026).
  • Beauty market bifurcation: $69.3 billion US beauty retail (2026), stable but structurally hollowed; Ulta's $12.4B (fiscal 2025, +9.7% YoY) masks failure of hundreds of smaller DTC brands; Amazon beauty share forecast 10% (2024) → 15% (2030).

Who rides it

Platforms (Amazon, TikTok Shop, Instagram) and scaled omnichannel aggregators (Ulta, Sephora, Dick's Sporting Goods with elevated concepts) are the winners. They control discovery, logistics, and customer trust. Ulta in particular is leveraging its margin and scale to absorb smaller brands into its ecosystem, while platforms handle the social commerce layer directly. Amazon is moving upmarket into premium outdoor gear with private labels. These players have the infrastructure to survive tariffs and absorb customer acquisition cost inflation.

Who's squeezed

Pure-play DTC beauty brands, outdoor startups, and small independent retailers. Glossier, Pat McGrath, Flower Beauty, Cover FX, Mally Beauty all folded. REI, despite its massive co-op base, had to cut 400+ employees and shut down its experiential division. Smaller outdoor shops continue to close as Amazon and Walmart upmarket/downmarket pressure compresses the middle. Any brand without scale to compete on fulfillment speed, tariff absorption, and logistics cost gets squeezed between platform commission, rising CAC, and margin compression.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that venture-backed DTC, which promised a new model of retail, simply transferred control to platforms with worse incentive alignment—algorithm-driven discovery that changes overnight, commission rates that rise with success, and customer data that the platform owns. A beauty brand that spent five years building a TikTok audience can wake up to algorithm changes or platform policy shifts that crater its business. Meanwhile, tariffs are a live risk: they squeezed margins throughout 2025 and consumer confidence in discretionary spending (beauty, outdoor gear) is fragile. If consumer spending retracts further, the omnichannel players (Ulta, Amazon) can absorb it by cutting smaller brands loose. The infrastructure advantage of the platforms means they can outbid DTC brands on fulfillment and pricing indefinitely.

In one sentence

Direct-to-consumer brands in a nutshell

DTC brands killed physical retail but lost to platforms that could sell faster, cheaper, and with network effects they could never match.

C · Who's holding on

Omnichannel or die

Big-box retailers survive the channel shift only by fusing online and store — ship-from-store, buy-online-pickup-in-store — or they fold.

Physical retail isn't disappearing. But the store's job has changed. It's no longer just a place to buy. It's a warehouse, a fulfillment hub, a place to see and touch before you commit. Retailers who treat their stores as part of a seamless online-offline system are holding margins and traffic. Those who don't are closing stores and losing ground to Amazon, marketplaces, and DTC brands.

What changed

The channel shift made scarcity out of *velocity*. A product sitting on a shelf in a store that only sells in-person is now a missed transaction — someone bought it online instead, or used it for research and purchased elsewhere. Omnichannel became a survival mechanism, not a luxury. Home Depot laid off 800 corporate staff and closed distribution facilities in Mexico, Missouri, and Tennessee in 2025-2026 to rebuild supply chains around ship-from-store logistics. Lowe's saw this coming and doubled down: professional services revenue surged 15% in 2024, a segment that depends on stores as hubs for consultation, staging, and same-day delivery. This wasn't about growing bigger — it was about making stores *do more*.

The cost structure shifted too. E-commerce didn't just take sales; it raised the floor on what customers expect. Amazon claimed 12% of online DIY sales ($6.1 billion in 2024, up 25% year-over-year), which forced Home Depot and Lowe's to match both price and speed. Smaller chains couldn't absorb this. Wren Kitchens, a $1+ billion kitchen specialty retailer, filed for bankruptcy liquidation and shuttered all 15 US locations in 2025. The home improvement store industry is flat — just 2.3% growth in 2025, barely 2% expected for 2026 — which means every competitor is fighting for the same dollar with higher friction costs. Meanwhile, sporting goods retail faced the same squeeze: Dick's Sporting Goods bought Foot Locker for $2.4 billion (announced May 2025, closed September 2025), merging 3,200+ stores globally to consolidate back-office, close redundant locations, and build a unified omnichannel engine. Online sporting goods sales reached $39.2 billion in 2025, but brick-and-mortar still accounts for the majority — which made consolidation a rational move to share fulfillment and service costs across more locations.

Auto parts retail shows the darkest version of this. The $77.1 billion market (2026) grew only 1.6% last year, and tariff volatility (25% on Chinese parts from April 2025, then a 90-day truce down to 30% in May, then ongoing uncertainty) made planning impossible. O'Reilly Automotive, the market leader, posted an 8.1% comparable-store-sales increase in Q1 2026 and diluted earnings per share up 16% year-over-year — but that required *scale*, tight inventory discipline, and integrated online fulfillment. Smaller competitors didn't have it. First Brands, a major supplier, filed Chapter 11 in 2025; Marelli (a Japanese parts group) also filed. Online auto parts sales (excluding marketplaces) reached $23 billion in 2025 and are forecast to grow 4.6% annually, while Amazon and eBay/Walmart push that to 6.7% when included. The store became valuable only if it could fulfill fast and keep costs low — which meant omnichannel or liquidation.

Tariffs and labor costs amplified the pain. Kitchen cabinet tariffs hit 15-20% in home improvement; material costs overall rose 4-6%, labor costs 6-8% annually. This margin compression made scale essential — and made omnichannel the only viable way to push higher-margin services (like Lowe's professional segment) while absorbing commodity-price and wage inflation in stores. Retailers who couldn't build unified demand signals, inventory, and fulfillment across channels became cost-uncompetitive.

The evidence

  • Home improvement retail: Amazon reached $6.1 billion in sales in 2024, up 25% year-over-year, while Lowe's professional services revenue jumped 15% in 2024 only by building omnichannel service delivery
  • Sporting goods retail: Dick's acquired Foot Locker for $2.4 billion (2025) to consolidate 3,200+ stores into one omnichannel system, as online sales hit $39.2 billion but brick-and-mortar remained critical
  • Auto parts retail: O'Reilly Automotive's comparable-store sales rose 8.1% in Q1 2026 through integrated fulfillment, while smaller competitors (First Brands, Marelli) filed for bankruptcy as tariffs and e-commerce squeezed margins
  • Home improvement stores: Market growth was flat at 2.3% in 2025; Home Depot laid off 800 staff and closed distribution facilities in 2025-2026, restructuring for omnichannel logistics
  • Sporting goods retail: Transactions declined 9% in Q4 2025-Q1 2026 due to tariff pass-through, forcing consolidation and profitability-through-scale strategies among survivors

Who rides it

Dick's Sporting Goods, O'Reilly Automotive, and Lowe's are the survivors. They had scale, technology spend, and the balance sheet to absorb tariff costs, build unified omnichannel fulfillment, and close redundant stores without destroying value. Dick's integration of Foot Locker, though costly, gave it a bigger store network to spread fulfillment and professional-service costs; O'Reilly's 8.1% comp growth in Q1 2026 shows that omnichannel done well can still squeeze margin expansion even in a flat-growth market. Lowe's professional services surge is proof that stores become profit centers when they're hubs for higher-margin services tied to online visibility and quick fulfillment. Amazon and online-pure-play brands also win — they never had the store-cargo problem and are systematizing the data advantage (buy online, ship from warehouse, show customer reviews). But the real winner is the integrated operator with 500+ locations, because they can amortize omnichannel infrastructure and absorb one-time restructuring costs.

Who's squeezed

Smaller chains and single-format operators get crushed. Wren Kitchens closed all 15 US locations in 2025. At Home, Miller's Hardware, and countless independent auto parts shops either liquidated or sold to consolidators. Foot Locker was the classic case: strong brand, but 4,000+ US locations optimized for mall traffic and wholesale-driven apparel, not omnichannel. It became acquisition prey for Dick's, which needed the real estate but had to write off redundancy and integration costs. Middle-income consumers also lose — tariffs on kitchen cabinets (15-20%), athletic apparel (10%+), and auto parts (fluctuating 25%-30%) get passed through, and the store's inability to compete on price or speed means less shopping overall. Workers in small retail shops face job cuts as stores close and consolidation automates back-office.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that omnichannel only delays the inevitable for legacy retailers. Tariffs, labor costs, and consumer retrenchment are structural headwinds. Home Depot foot traffic was flat to negative (−0.08% in Q1 2026) even as it invested in omnichannel. Sporting goods transactions fell 9% in early 2026. If consumer discretionary spending doesn't recover and tariffs stay elevated or get worse, even omnichannel scale may not be enough to support current store counts. The auto parts industry is the warning signal: electric vehicles structurally shrink the repair basket per vehicle (no oil changes, simpler drivetrains, regenerative braking), so adding scale and omnichannel logistics just slows the decline, it doesn't reverse it. A $77.1 billion market shrinking at 1.6% growth is still shrinking.

In one sentence

Omnichannel or die in a nutshell

Omnichannel is not a growth strategy — it is the price of survival, and only retailers with scale and margin discipline can afford to pay it.

C · Who's holding on

The experiential survivor

Expertise, immediacy, and in-person experience are the moats physical retail has left.

Physical stores are losing the commodity battle. You can get the thing cheaper online. But you can't get expertise, try-on, customization, or instant gratification through a screen. The stores that survive are the ones doing something e-commerce can't—and charging for it.

What changed

The channel shift has created a hard fork in retail. Brick-and-mortar jewelry stores contracted 12.1% in 2025 and 2.2% in 2026, with 167 US jewelry stores closing in just Q1 2025—a 21% increase from Q1 2024. The culprits are structural: gold prices surged 60% annually in 2025, peaking near $4,400 per ounce in October, pushing entry-level jewelry from $99 to $200-$500 and pricing out the mass market entirely. Tariffs on Chinese jewelry imports hit 145% by late 2025, forcing wholesale costs up 18-22% for retailers. But the real story is that online jewelry channels now capture an estimated 25% of global purchases, with mobile commerce accounting for over 60% of those transactions. Lab-grown diamonds have become the default—capturing 56.8% of the US engagement ring market as of late 2025—which means the floor for store visits isn't authenticity anymore, it's customization and styling. Stores like Claire's and Lugano Diamonds have filed for bankruptcy (Claire's in August 2025, its second bankruptcy in seven years) because they tried to compete on price in a channel shift world. The survivors aren't fighting that war.

Health stores face an identical squeeze. The brick-and-mortar health store sector grew only 3.8% year-over-year in 2025, while online supplements grew 11.4% annually. The Vitamin Shoppe and GNC—the two largest regional chains—both went through bankruptcy proceedings, with Kingswood Capital Management acquiring The Vitamin Shoppe in April 2025 for $193.5 million after Franchise Group's collapse. Tariffs on imported ingredients hit 10-34% depending on origin (China at 34%, Taiwan 32%), affecting 75-80% of imported raw materials used in vitamin and supplement manufacturing. Consumers buy vitamins from Amazon now, often not differentiating between generic and specialty brands. But personalized nutrition—subscription boxes, custom gummies, targeted formulations—is growing at 15% annually and specialty retailers are the only format equipped to stock and consult on it. The market is bifurcating: commodity supplements are being obliterated by Amazon and Target's private-label lines, but curated, personalized, and advice-driven health retail survives because the value isn't the product—it's the recommendation.

Convenience stores are the sharpest case study in what keeps stores alive. The US convenience store sector is massive ($43.7 billion in 2026) but nearly flat—just 0.2% CAGR from 2021-2026—because fuel margins are collapsing and organized retail crime is eating away at profit. Fuel sales fell to $476.3 billion in 2025 from $501.9 billion in 2024 as gas prices fell 5.9%. But prepared foodservice is now 39% of in-store profit and remains the only high-margin growth lever. 80% of operators expect foodservice to improve through 2026, betting on differentiation—think of this as betting on experience, convenience, and customization (hot sandwiches made to order, local pastries, regional specialties) rather than shelf inventory. The successful c-store chains are those adding experiential layers: Pilot Flying J is expanding EV charging to 50 new sites in H1 2026, turning the fuel stop into a destination with a 20-30 minute dwell time. Operators using AI-driven fuel pricing report 3.4% profit gains, which means the margin game itself is becoming an experience edge (knowing you're getting the deal). The failed mega-consolidation—Couche-Tard's $47.2 billion bid for 7-Eleven withdrew in June 2025—signals that scale doesn't solve the channel shift. Smaller, locally-optimized operators with strong foodservice and community presence are outperforming.

What the channel shift has made scarce is the commodity store itself. What it's made valuable is expertise, curation, and immediacy—especially for products where you want to try, touch, or talk to someone. Jewelry stores that survive now position themselves as design studios and custom workshops, not inventory warehouses. Health stores that survive are consultancies bundled with products. Convenience stores that survive are food destinations with fuel attached. The experiential moat is real, but it only works if you stop fighting e-commerce on its terms and start competing on presence, knowledge, and the thing you get right now instead of in two days.

The evidence

  • Jewelry: US market contracted 12.1% in 2025 and 2.2% in 2026; gold prices surged 60% annually in 2025 to $4,400/oz; 145% tariffs on Chinese imports; Claire's filed bankruptcy August 2025 (second in seven years)
  • Health Stores: Market grew only 3.8% in 2025 vs. 11.4% online; The Vitamin Shoppe acquired by Kingswood for $193.5M in April 2025 after Franchise Group bankruptcy; tariffs hit 10-34% on imported supplements (China 34%)
  • Convenience Stores: $43.7B market in 2026, flat growth (0.2% CAGR); fuel sales fell from $501.9B (2024) to $476.3B (2025); foodservice now 39% of in-store profit; organized retail crime cost $47.8B in 2025
  • Online Jewelry: Now captures estimated 25% of global jewelry purchases with mobile commerce at 60%+ of online transactions; fundamentally reshaping physical store value proposition
  • Personalized Nutrition: Growing 15% annually; subscription and custom formats thriving while commodity vitamin retail collapses on Amazon and Target private label pressure

Who rides it

Jewelry stores positioning as design studios and custom workshops (lab-grown diamonds, bespoke settings, styling consultation) survive the tariff and gold-price storm because they sell expertise and try-on, not commodity rings. Health retailers offering personalized nutrition consultation, subscription boxes, and curated recommendations (the 15% growth segment) win against Amazon. Convenience store chains betting on prepared foodservice, local differentiation, and experiential add-ons (EV charging that creates dwell time, regional specialties) win when fuel margins compress. They're all playing the same game: you can't click on it online, so come here for the experience, the advice, or the immediacy.

Who's squeezed

Mass-market jewelry retailers (Claire's, Lugano Diamonds) that tried to compete on inventory and price; specialty health chains that stocked commodity vitamins (The Vitamin Shoppe, GNC pre-bankruptcy restructuring) are getting hollowed out by Amazon and private-label alternatives. Convenience stores treating fuel as the profit center and foodservice as an afterthought; operators without local scale or brand identity. Tariff and margin pressure are accelerating the contraction—the 2025-2026 closures are the channel shift finally crashing the holdouts.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The experiential moat looks strong until inflation or recession dries up the customer base. Jewelry stores are already seeing a bifurcated market: affluent households remain confident spenders, but lower and middle-income households are squeezed by job market weakness and inflation, cutting off the middle of the market entirely. Convenience stores are being ravaged by organized retail crime ($47.8 billion in 2025, expected to hit $55 billion by 2028), which erodes the very margin gains that make experiential add-ons profitable. Health stores betting on premium personalized nutrition will win only if consumers have money to spend. The experiential survivor model requires a healthy middle class willing to pay for service and curation—if that customer disappears, the moat collapses.

In one sentence

The experiential survivor in a nutshell

Physical retail survives only when it does something e-commerce cannot—expertise, customization, immediacy, or presence—and every store that doesn't offer one of these is being methodically hollowed out by tariffs, online channels, and the channel shift itself.

D · The tensions

Tariffs & the de-minimis end

When the tariff loophole closed in August 2025, the price war moved offline—mass-market stores couldn't compete with Shein and Temu on cost anymore.

For years, Shein and Temu exploited a quirk in US import law: packages under $800 entered duty-free, making their unit economics unbeatable. On August 29, 2025, that ended. The de-minimis exemption closed globally, and suddenly every sub-$800 shipment faced tariffs. That same year, furniture tariffs hit 25% on upholstered goods. For mass-market retail already running on 2-3% margins, there was nowhere left to hide.

What changed

For two decades, the de-minimis loophole was the oxygen mask for ultrafast fashion and bargain electronics. Shein could ship a $3 tank top from China for $1.50 landed cost. No tariffs. No middleman. Customers in Nebraska got it in two weeks for $4.99. A store buyer paying $2.50 wholesale from a domestic vendor and selling for $12.99 couldn't touch that price. When the exemption ended in August 2025, the arithmetic inverted. A $3 Shein top now faced duty. Suddenly it cost Shein $3.50, or they had to raise the customer price to $6.99. That margin squeeze rippled backward through the entire supply chain—but here's the thing: it didn't hurt Shein the way it hurt department stores. Shein absorbed the hit, cut deeper, and passed a smaller damage to customers. A traditional mass-market retailer like Forever 21 or Value City Furniture was already operating so thin (2-3% net margin in women's clothing, 3% in furniture) that they had no buffer. The tariff didn't make them less competitive; it made them insolvent.

Forever 21 filed Chapter 11 in March 2025 and liquidated all 354 US stores. Liberated Brands (Volcom, Billabong, Roxy, RVCA, Spyder, Quiksilver) filed the same month and liquidated 122 stores. Macy's announced 66 closures in January 2025 as part of a planned 150-store exit. American Signature Inc. filed Chapter 11 in November 2025, closing Value City Furniture locations. Walker Edison Furniture and affiliates filed in August 2025 and sold for just $20 million to Twin-Star International. These weren't isolated stumbles. They were structural collapses driven by tariff pressure hitting retailers with no margin to absorb it.

The tariff also triggered a bifurcation that's still accelerating. The US women's clothing market was already split: $61.8 billion in online sales in 2025 versus brick-and-mortar staying flat at $66.4 billion in 2026 (a -0.3% annual decline since 2021). But after the de-minimis closure, traditional stores couldn't compete on price, so the online shift accelerated. Shein and Temu gobbled the price-sensitive shoppers, leaving traditional department stores and mass-market chains fighting for air. Meanwhile, premium and specialty retailers—luxury brands, niche segments like plus-size and athletic wear—kept growing. They weren't competing on $4.99 prices; they were competing on brand and fit. Employment in online women's clothing grew 5.5% annually from 2019 to 2024, while brick-and-mortar employment continued its decline. The tariff didn't create this split—but it accelerated it from a slow divergence into a cliff.

In furniture, the damage was compounded by housing weakness and tariff specificity. New home sales dropped 17.6% month-over-month in January 2026 and 11.3% year-on-year, hitting the core customer base. But the tariff was the knife: 25% duties on upholstered furniture and cabinets (effective October 2024) squeezed retailers between raising prices to consumers who were already retrencing, or eating the cost and eroding the already-thin 3% margin to zero. Online furniture captured 28% of market share by 2025 and grew 5-10% annually, with Wayfair alone holding roughly 14% of the US market. Wayfair could absorb tariff hits because scale and direct-to-consumer logistics gave it breathing room. Independent and mid-market retailers got crushed. At the same time, a premium niche emerged: 76% of consumers said they'd pay 9.7% more for eco-friendly furniture, and ergonomic gaming seating spiked as remote work held. The tariff made survival a choice between scale, brand, or niche—no middle ground.

The evidence

  • Women's clothing: Forever 21 liquidated all 354 US stores (March 2025), Liberated Brands liquidated 122 stores (February 2025), Macy's cut 66 stores (January 2025) as de-minimis closure and tariffs squeezed 2-3% margins past survival threshold.
  • Women's clothing: Online sales reached $61.8B in 2025 vs brick-and-mortar $66.4B in 2026 (-0.3% annual decline since 2021); employment in online grew 5.5% annually 2019-2024 while stores contracted.
  • Furniture: American Signature (Value City) filed Chapter 11 (November 2025); Walker Edison filed (August 2025) and sold for $20M; 25% tariffs on upholstered goods (October 2024) hit 3% margin retailers with no absorptive capacity.
  • Furniture: Housing demand collapsed 17.6% month-over-month January 2026 and 11.3% year-on-year; online furniture channels reached 28% of market share (2025) growing 5-10% annually, with Wayfair holding ~14% of US market.
  • De-minimis: August 29, 2025 closure ended duty-free entry for packages under $800 globally, forcing Shein and Temu to either raise prices (6% customer price increase) or accept margin compression; mass-market retailers with existing 2-3% margins had no escape valve.

Who rides it

Premium and specialty retailers, online platforms like Wayfair and direct-to-consumer brands, and niche segments like sustainable furniture (76% of consumers willing to pay 9.7% more for eco-friendly goods) and gaming ergonomic seating ride the channel shift. These businesses either have margin (premium brands), scale (online marketplaces), or differentiation (niche segments) to absorb tariffs and leverage the bifurcation. Shein and Temu themselves survive because they operate at massive volume and can subsume tariff costs into lower absolute prices; they out-scale traditional retailers. Remote work and consumer retrenchment favor DTC logistics and omnichannel models that cut inventory and physical footprint.

Who's squeezed

Mass-market and discount brick-and-mortar chains—Forever 21, Macy's, Value City Furniture, independent mid-market retailers—get squeezed into insolvency. They operated on 2-3% margins with the de-minimis loophole and tariffs as their only headwinds; when tariffs hit and the loophole closed, there was no margin to absorb the cost increase. Store closures accelerated: 7,323 in 2024 alone, roughly 6,000 more in the first half of 2025. Employment in brick-and-mortar women's clothing continued declining while online grew 5.5% annually. Consumers trading down to ultra-low-cost online hurt traditional mass-market the most; affluent consumers gravitate to premium brands, while price-sensitive shoppers found a cheaper path on Shein and Temu. The middle retail market—the $12-$30 apparel, the mid-range furniture—vanished.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is a second-order supply-chain contraction. If tariffs remain (or rise further) and domestic production doesn't scale fast enough, prices will ratchet higher across the board—not just for budget retailers but for omnichannel players and DTC brands too. A $70 sofa becomes $85. A Wayfair customer might switch to thrift or overseas sites using VPNs and forwarding services. Labor shortages in domestic furniture and apparel manufacturing mean replacing offshore production is slow and costly. The bifurcation could compress into a hourglass: ultra-premium at top, ultra-cheap at bottom, and almost nothing in the middle where most retail jobs exist. That's not a market; it's a hollowing.

In one sentence

Tariffs & the de-minimis end in a nutshell

The de-minimis tariff exemption closure in August 2025 and furniture tariffs gutted mass-market retail margins (2-3%), forcing store closures and accelerating the channel shift to online-only and niche brands while Shein, Temu, and DTC platforms captured price-sensitive and premium shoppers in the wreckage.

D · The tensions

The closure wave

Thousands of stores close each year; the real-estate and jobs fallout compounds.

Department stores and mid-tier retailers are closing at scale. Macy's alone closed 130 locations between 2024 and 2026. Saks Global—the merged Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf—filed for bankruptcy in January 2026 with $3.4 billion in debt. Real estate that anchored shopping districts empties. Jobs vanish. The store itself becomes obsolete at the very moment it was supposed to survive.

What changed

The channel shift made physical stores risky for full-line retail. The math breaks. The US department store industry sits at $227.1 billion (2026) but grew only 0.3% from 2022 to 2026—economically flat. Margins compressed from 6.1% (2024) to 6.0% (2026), and that's before tariff shocks. When import duties exploded from 14.7% in January 2025 to 35.1% by December, retailers faced a choice: absorb the hit (margins drop to 3.6% if fully absorbed) or raise prices. Either path loses customers. Macy's, Nordstrom, JCPenney, and others got caught in the middle—expensive to operate compared to off-price, expensive to compete with e-commerce, too mainstream to be luxury, too legacy to pivot fast. JCPenney's revenue hit $6.6 billion by FY2024, revenue that had nowhere to go. Discount stores and off-price players pulled the same customers away. Ross Stores saw comparable store sales jump 17% in Q3 2025 while announcing 110 new openings for 2026. Nordstrom Rack and Saks Off Fifth took market share, the very off-price banners that cannibalized their parent's full-line business.\n\nReal estate became stranded. A closed Macy's or department store doesn't become a tech campus or a village green—it's a 100,000-square-foot anchor tenant hole in a mall. Mall traffic fell because there were fewer reasons to drive to a destination. By end-2026, Macy's had closed 150 stores (50 by end-2024, 66 by end-2025, 14 more in early 2026). Each closure meant empty real estate in secondary markets, devalued malls, and lost property tax revenue for municipalities. JCPenney's comeback campaign, 'Yes, JCPenney,' lifted traffic 3% in May 2025, but that one tactical win couldn't reverse the structural. Nordstrom's family-controlled founders bid $3.8 billion to take the company private in late 2025, a signal they saw the full-line business as terminal and the real future in off-price Rack expansion.\n\nEmployees bore the cost. The department store sector employed 666,500 workers (2025), declining 2.87% annually through 2028—meaning 19,000 jobs vanishing every year from payroll shrinkage alone, on top of store closures. These aren't high-wage jobs for the most part—they're hourly, retail, in suburban and secondary-market towns where alternatives are scarce. A closed store means real unemployment, not just a transition to a new mall location. Wage pressures from 21 state minimum wage hikes in 2025 and warehouse labor costs rising 7.4% year-over-year only squeezed margins further, accelerating the incentive to close rather than modernize.\n\nThe bifurcation created a hollowed middle. Affluent households kept shopping at full-price retail or luxury; lower and middle-income households traded down to discount stores at five times faster rates in 2026. That left mid-tier department stores in the worst spot: not trendy enough to be destination, not cheap enough to be treasure-hunt, not online enough to be convenient. Saks Global's bankruptcy in January 2026 was the canary. When the luxury merger of Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman—three storied names—couldn't make the math work despite combining scale, it meant no department store was safe. Store productivity collapsed. Vendor payment delays cascaded. The bankruptcy filing sent ripples through the entire supply chain. Smaller bankruptcies followed: Rite Aid in May 2025 (second filing), At Home in June 2025 (100 store closures in home goods). The industry didn't face one shock—it faced four at once: tariffs, margin collapse, channel migration, and consumer bifurcation.

The evidence

  • Department Stores: Macy's 150-store closure plan (2024–2026) and Saks Global's $3.4B bankruptcy (January 2026) signal structural decline in a $227.1B industry growing only 0.3% CAGR.
  • Discount Retail: Ross Stores reported 17% comparable sales growth and 110 new openings in Q3 2025, winning share as consumers trade down five times faster in 2026.
  • Tariffs: Apparel import duties spiked from 14.7% (Jan 2025) to 35.1% (Dec 2025), compressing retailer margins to estimated 3.6% if fully absorbed, forcing price hikes or closures.
  • Employment: Department store payroll declining 2.87% annually through 2028 (19,000 jobs per year) as wage pressures from 21 state minimum hikes and 7.4% warehouse labor cost inflation squeeze profitability.
  • Off-Price Momentum: Nordstrom family bid $3.8B to take the company private (2025–2026) to focus on Rack expansion, while Saks Off Fifth and Nordstrom Rack cannibalize full-line traffic.

Who rides it

Off-price and discount retailers are the survivors. Ross Stores, Nordstrom Rack, TJX Companies (T.J. Maxx, Marshalls), and outlet malls are winning customers from traditional department stores. The "treasure hunt" experience—weekly-changing curated inventory at deep discounts—remains defensible against e-commerce in ways full-price mall retail is not. These players expanded aggressively: Ross added 110 stores in 2026, Nordstrom's founders invested $3.8B to take the company private and expand Rack, and discount store margins held at 6.9% (2026) even as traditional department stores compressed to 6.0%. Affluent consumers also win in one sense—luxury remains intact because it was never really competing in the mall anyway. But the real winner is e-commerce and direct-to-consumer, which didn't need to close stores because they never had the anchor tenant problem to begin with.

Who's squeezed

Department store chains and their landlords lose. Macy's, JCPenney, Nordstrom's full-line division, regional mid-tier department stores—these faces shrink or disappear. More than 666,500 retail workers employed in department stores face layoffs, wage stagnation, or forced relocation to discount formats at lower pay. Shopping mall landlords lose most of all. A closed 100,000-square-foot Macy's anchor tenant leaves a void that no lifestyle retailer wants to fill. Property values fall, operating costs rise, and the economic model of the destination mall fractures. Secondary and suburban markets lose downtown retail activity, tax base, and foot traffic.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The secondary and tertiary market real estate collapse is irreversible in a five-year window. When a Macy's closes in Des Moines, Springfield, or Allentown, there is no natural successor tenant. That real estate becomes functionally dead. Shopping centers go dark. Property tax revenue dries up for school districts and municipalities already squeezed. The social fabric of suburban retail—the meetup spot, the job entry point—erodes. At scale across hundreds of closed stores, this becomes a regional economic problem, not just a retail problem. The tariff environment may ease, margins may stabilize, but those closed stores won't reopen. The real estate damage is one-way.

In one sentence

The closure wave in a nutshell

Thousands of department and mid-tier retail stores close each year as tariffs, margin compression, and channel shift to e-commerce and off-price retail hollow out the full-line department store, leaving stranded real estate and jobs in secondary markets.

E · The big picture

The Channel Shift

The point of sale moved online; platforms and omnichannel scale win, standalone mid-market stores lose.

The store as the default place to shop is dead. Over the last five years, e-commerce has flipped from supplementary to primary, and the winners are platforms with massive logistics or brick-and-mortar chains that can do both at once. The losers are everyone else: independent stores, mid-market specialty chains, and any retailer still betting the physical location alone will pay rent.

What changed

What changed is simple and brutal: the economics of fulfillment. Amazon proved that if you own the warehouse, the truck, and the algorithm, you can deliver faster and cheaper than any store network ever could. That forced every competitor to either match Amazon's logistics footprint (impossible for most) or stop trying. The result has been a decade-long squeezing of the middle—the solo store, the small chain, the independent merchant. E-commerce in the US hit $1.38 trillion in 2026, up from $934.2 billion in 2022, a 48% jump in four years. But that growth is almost entirely going to Amazon, Walmart, and a handful of platforms like TikTok Shop (claimed $20 billion in 2026 sales). The margin compressed everywhere: e-commerce profit margins fell to 5.5-5.9% by 2025-2026, down from double digits a decade ago, because competition is ruthless and customer expectations for free shipping and instant returns are locked in. Small sellers on Amazon or Walmart Marketplace face take-rates of 30-50% after fees, logistics, and chargebacks, leaving almost no room to operate.

The bifurcation is real and it is deep. Women's clothing stores are the clearest case: online sales now run at nearly $61.8 billion (2025) versus brick-and-mortar at $66.4 billion (2026), a near-parity that would have been unthinkable in 2015. But the split is not even. Premium and specialty retailers—think Lululemon, Outdoor Voices, plus-size brands—are thriving both online and in selective physical locations because they have margins to invest in experience and fulfillment. Mass-market chains are collapsing. Store closures hit 7,323 locations in 2024 and roughly 6,000 more in the first half of 2025 alone. Forever 21 liquidated all 354 U.S. stores in March 2025. Liberated Brands (Volcom, Billabong, Quiksilver) filed Chapter 11 in February 2025 and liquidated 122 stores. Macy's announced the closure of 66 stores as part of a three-year 150-store exit. These are not anomalies. The women's clothing sector grew zero percent annually from 2021 to 2026, and that stagnation masks a violent reshuffling: thriving online segments and vanishing physical footprint. The tariff shock of August 2025—when the de-minimis exemption ended and all imports under $800 became dutiable—added $136 in estimated costs per family and forced price increases across imported apparel, which is nearly everything. Ultra-low-cost platforms like Shein and Temu, which had warehoused goods domestically to sidestep tariffs, now compete on pure volume and velocity.

Home improvement tells a similar but slightly different story. The sector is frozen by a housing crisis: low mortgage rates locked in a generation of homeowners who have no incentive to sell or move, so they are not buying new homes or renovating aggressively. Revenue in home improvement hit $294.6 billion in 2025, up only 2.3% from 2024, and growth is expected to stay flat to 2% in 2026. The category is splitting into professionals and pretenders. Lowe's reported a 15% revenue surge in professional services in 2024, outpacing DIY growth. Home Depot reported flat to negative foot traffic (negative 0.08% in Q1 2026 alone), suggesting consumers are not walking the aisles. Meanwhile, Amazon is quietly stealing share: its home improvement tool and equipment sales reached $6.1 billion in 2024, up 25% year-over-year. Tariffs are a rising cost burden—material costs up 4-6% on average, with kitchen cabinets and bathroom vanities facing 15-20% increases. Smaller competitors cannot absorb that. Wren Kitchens, a major kitchen specialty retailer, filed for bankruptcy and closed all 15 U.S. locations in 2025. Home Depot itself laid off 800 corporate employees and closed distribution facilities in 2025-2026. The omnichannel leaders—Home Depot and Lowe's—are surviving through scale and diversification, but the specialty player is extinct.

The channel shift did not destroy retail. It destroyed *store-based retail as a standalone business*. What survived, and what thrives, is omnichannel at scale: Walmart grew e-commerce 26% in Q2 2026 and store-fulfilled delivery surged 50%, with the company targeting 25% of revenue from digital by 2030. Online grocery grew 20% year-over-year for six straight quarters through Q1 2026; Kroger is expecting digital profitability in 2026. Grocery e-commerce exploded 32% in December 2025 alone when consumers discovered pickup and avoided fees. Mobile commerce now accounts for 60% of online sales. But this is also a story of new problems: return fraud has doubled in 18 months and now accounts for $76 billion in annual losses; 9% of all retail returns are now fraudulent. Small sellers and independent retailers face an impossible choice: invest in omnichannel infrastructure they cannot afford, compete on Amazon's terms (which means 30-50% take-rates), or exit. Most are exiting.

The evidence

  • E-commerce: US online retail jumped to $1.38T (2026) from $934.2B (2022) at 6.9-10.5% CAGR, but margins fell to 5.5-5.9% by 2025-2026, forcing small sellers into Amazon's 30-50% take-rate trap
  • Women's clothing: Online sales at $61.8B (2025) now rival brick-and-mortar's $66.4B (2026); mass-market stores collapsed with 13,323 closures in 2024-H1 2025, while premium segments thrived online
  • Home improvement: Market stalled at $294.6B (2025), up only 2.3% from 2024, with Amazon capturing $6.1B in tools alone (up 25% YoY) while specialty chains like Wren Kitchens filed bankruptcy
  • Tariffs: De-minimis exemption end in August 2025 added $136 per family to import costs and forced price increases across apparel, giving ultra-low-cost platforms (Shein, Temu) a localization advantage
  • Omnichannel winners: Walmart grew e-commerce 26% (Q2 2026) with store-fulfilled delivery up 50%; online grocery hit 20% YoY growth for six straight quarters into Q1 2026

Who rides it

Amazon, Walmart, and omnichannel-scaled chains. Walmart's store network became an asset instead of a liability—it can fulfill online orders from local inventory and beat Amazon on speed in many markets. Online-native and pure-platform players win too: TikTok Shop grabbed $20 billion in claimed 2026 sales by going after Gen Z directly, and Shein and Temu win through sheer velocity and tariff arbitrage (localized warehouses sidestep import duties). Premium and specialty retailers also survive if they own their own brand and margin: Lululemon, Outdoor Voices, niche athletic and plus-size labels can afford to build omnichannel and charge what customers will pay. The customer wins on speed, choice, and convenience—if they can afford it or tolerate the return fraud and data harvesting.

Who's squeezed

Independent stores and mid-market specialty chains. A solo bookstore, clothing boutique, or home-goods shop cannot compete on delivery speed, selection, or price. Small sellers on Amazon or Walmart Marketplace face take-rates of 30-50%, which erases profit. Mass-market chains like Forever 21, Macy's, and Liberated Brands could not differentiate fast enough and are liquidating. The small-city supplier and local distributor lose too: when consumers buy from Amazon or Shein directly, regional warehousing and local trucking disappear. Employment in brick-and-mortar retail is declining, with only professional services and specialty segments hiring. The tariff shock of August 2025 squeezed every import-dependent retailer, but small players had no scale to absorb the cost.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Return fraud and customer acquisition cost are spiraling and will eventually force price increases that undo e-commerce's savings promise. Retailers lose $76 billion annually to return fraud now (9% of all returns fraudulent), and the only defense is more friction (AI verification, restocking fees) which will drive customers back to … where? Also, Amazon's logistics dominance is not a competitive advantage—it is regulatory risk. Antitrust scrutiny is increasing, tariffs are being weaponized, and China's de-minimis workarounds (Shein's domestic warehousing) may trigger protectionist backlash. If tariffs spike further or Amazon faces forced divestitures, the entire omnichannel arbitrage collapses and prices spike across the board. The bigger risk: margins cannot compress any lower. When 5.5% is the ceiling and return fraud and labor costs keep rising, the economics of fulfillment break. That means either consolidation accelerates (fewer, larger players) or prices go up, and if prices go up, the whole value proposition of e-commerce—cheap, fast, frictionless—dies.

In one sentence

The channel shift in a nutshell

E-commerce won the sale, but omnichannel at scale and platforms with logistics won the customer; everyone else is closing stores and cutting jobs.
