A · Finance under the rules

The bank compliance load

How capital rules, KYC, and consumer regs turned compliance into a moat for the big four.

Banks used to be simple: take deposits, make loans, collect spread. But since 2008—and especially after the 2023 SVB collapse—the compliance engine has become industrial. A thousand regulatory demands (Basel III capital tiers, CCAR stress tests, AML/KYC databases, consumer disclosure rules) cost small banks millions to staff and audit. Big banks absorbed the cost decades ago. Small banks are still paying.

What changed

The compliance tax made capital itself scarce. After SVB failed in March 2023 and Signature shut down two days later, regulators tightened every capital and liquidity rule. The banking sector had to hold more—and more expensive—equity. The big four (JP Morgan, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup) already had the infrastructure: lawyers, compliance teams, automated reporting. When the Fed cut rates 1.75 percentage points between September 2024 and Q4 2025, net interest margins compressed. But here's the squeeze: a regional bank with $50 billion in assets pays 30+ people in compliance full-time. A community bank with $2 billion in assets can't afford that, so it outsources to consultants at $200–$400 per hour. That's a fixed cost per dollar of assets that kills ROA for small institutions. By Q4 2025, uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in a single quarter, meaning depositors moved money to safer names—the known big four. Small bank deposit costs didn't fall with Fed rate cuts; they stayed sticky because confidence evaporated. The result: net interest margins for community banks stayed compressed while big banks recovered to 3.39% by year-end 2025, highest since 2019.

Alongside deposit flight, capital rules made expansion impossible for small banks. Basel III capital minimums, stress tests that predict losses in a recession, and liquidity coverage ratios all require quarterly recalculation and board reporting. For a $10 billion bank, one mistake in the model can trigger a regulatory request for capital raises that costs 2–3% in dilution. For JPMorgan, the same mistake is a rounding error in a $2 trillion portfolio. Community banks faced another hidden cost: due diligence on climate risk, cybersecurity, third-party vendor management, and AI bias all rolled out between 2024 and 2026. These aren't optional; regulators issue cease-and-desist orders to banks that can't show controls. A small bank had to buy software, hire auditors, and train staff on frameworks that didn't exist five years ago. Big banks had already spent $1 billion building these systems and wrote the standards themselves through industry groups.

Compliance also made scale the only way to compete. The credit card issuing market is dominated: the top five issuers (Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, Bank of America) controlled over 50% of the $178.9 billion market in 2026. When Capital One closed its $35 billion acquisition of Discover in May 2025, it didn't shrink the market; it just consolidated it. Small issuers can't afford KYC infrastructure that screens for synthetic identity fraud (now the fastest-growing financial crime, costing $3.1 billion annually as of 2026). The Visa-Mastercard settlement pending regulatory approval threatened to cap interchange at 1.25%, which doesn't hurt JPMorgan (whose network effect and fee base can absorb it) but devastates a smaller player whose entire model depends on higher interchange. Fintech rivals (Affirm, Klarna) stole $70 billion in 2025 transactions by targeting BNPL, but they also sidestepped most traditional banking compliance—at least until regulators catch up.

The real cost lies hidden: commercial real estate. Banks hold $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure. By 2027, $1.26 trillion in CRE loans will mature, many originated at 4.3% now needing refinancing at 6.2%. Delinquencies are near decade highs. A bank regulator will demand proof that you stress-tested this portfolio, that you have a workout plan, that you can cover losses. JPMorgan has a 50-person CRE workout team; a small bank has one person wearing three hats. The compliance cost to hold, model, and resolve that risk is the same whether you're $2 trillion or $10 billion. It's a fixed cost of being a bank. Small banks are pricing out.

The evidence

  • Commercial banking: $1.5 trillion market (2026), but margins compressed as Fed rate cuts (1.75pp, Sept 2024–Q4 2025) eased deposit costs and depositors fled small banks post-SVB.
  • Credit card issuing: Top 5 control 50%+ of $178.9B market (2026); Capital One–Discover merger (closed May 2025) consolidated power as smaller issuers face $3.1B+ synthetic-ID fraud and pending Visa–Mastercard interchange cap.
  • CRE crisis: $1.26T in loans mature by 2027 at 6.2% (from 4.3% originals); banks hold $2.7T exposure with delinquencies at decade highs; compliance modeling cost is fixed regardless of bank size.
  • Deposit flight: Uninsured deposits surged $214.7B in Q4 2025 alone; SVB/Signature failures (March 2023) triggered regulatory tightening that small banks can't afford to staff.
  • Fintech disruption: BNPL stole $70B in 2025 transactions; synthetic-ID fraud costs $3.1B+ yearly (2026); small issuers lack KYC infrastructure to compete.

Who rides it

The big four banks (JPMorgan, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citi) win because they already had the compliance machines running. They absorbed the cost of building capital models, AML databases, and stress-test frameworks over decades. When the 2023 failures triggered regulatory tightening, they didn't build anew; they tuned what existed. Their deposit bases also benefit from a confidence moat: uninsured depositors fled smaller banks and moved to the known names, giving big banks cheap funding even as Fed rates fell. SVB's collapse was a gift that removed mid-size competitors (First Republic was sold to JPMorgan in May 2023) and reinforced that size equals safety in the eyes of regulators and the market.

Who's squeezed

Regional and community banks get squeezed. A $10 billion bank pays 30+ people full-time in compliance; a $2 billion bank outsources to consultants at $200–$400 per hour, pushing ROA below 1%. Their deposit costs didn't fall with the Fed's rate cuts because depositors—especially business owners—moved uninsured money to JPMorgan or Bank of America. Compliance costs for capital modeling, CRE stress-testing, climate risk, and cybersecurity are fixed regardless of asset size; they penalize small institutions on a per-dollar basis. Credit card issuers outside the top five face a similar wall: $3.1 billion in annual synthetic-ID fraud means KYC must be bulletproof, but building that system costs tens of millions that only big issuers can amortize. Small card programs are being acquired or shut down.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that compliance costs will become so high that the bottom 50% of banks (by asset size) consolidate or fail in the next five years, leaving only the big four and a handful of regional oligopolies. The $1.26 trillion CRE maturity wall means banks must hold more capital and model credit losses in unprecedented detail. Regulators will demand proof of controls on every emerging risk (AI bias, climate, third-party vendor cybersecurity). A small bank can't staff these functions; it also can't hire the consulting firms that big banks use because consultants prioritize large, profitable accounts. This creates a vicious cycle: small banks fall further behind, their ROA shrinks, they can't raise capital, and they become acquisition targets or failures. The market won't be more competitive; it will be more concentrated. Consumers will have fewer choices and face higher costs because the remaining players face no price competition.

In one sentence

The bank compliance load in a nutshell

Compliance rules that cost $50 million to implement at scale kill small banks on a per-dollar basis, handing deposits and market share to the big four.

A · Finance under the rules

Insurance & the regulators

State rules and new tech risks turn insurance into a compliance burden—and a margin game rigged for scale.

Rules are making insurance more expensive and more complicated. Health insurers are hiking premiums faster than anytime in 15 years. Cyber insurers are tightening underwriting and dumping risky firms to specialty carriers. Workers' comp carriers in California are exiting the market entirely. What changed is that compliance—to state data laws, to cybersecurity standards, to medical-cost regulations—has become inseparable from risk pricing itself.

What changed

Health insurance entered 2025-2026 in a state of violent repricing. Employer-sponsored premiums jumped 9 percent—the highest in 15 years—while ACA marketplace premiums for 2026 climbed 18 percent, with some benchmark plans jumping 26 percent beyond what insurers had even proposed. The real shock arrives December 31, 2025: enhanced ACA premium tax credits expired. That means an unsubsidized individual paying $888 annually in 2025 will face a $1,904 bill in 2026—more than double. Medicaid is shrinking for the first time since COVID, down 7.6 percent in 2025, as new work and reporting requirements in the 2025 reconciliation bill kicked in. What made this repricing possible is that the regulatory ground shifted. Subsidies vanished. Work requirements returned. Medicaid gates tightened. The largest threat to traditional insurers isn't regulation—it's that Amazon, GoodRx, and TrumpRx.gov are now siphoning off the most profitable segments. Amazon launched a GLP-1 management program through One Medical that charges as low as $25 per month in 3,000 cities (expanding to 4,500 by year-end 2026), undercutting traditional insurance entirely.

Cyber insurance shows the compliance tax in its starkest form. The market hit $7.02 billion in direct written premiums in the US in 2024, growing at 19.3 percent annually through 2026—still rapid, but slowed from the 25 percent-plus surge of earlier years as the market matured and competition squeezed rates. But then ransomware exploded. In the first half of 2025 alone, ransomware accounted for more than 90 percent of all cyber insurance claim severity. Initial ransom demands surged 47 percent year-over-year. Technology companies posted the highest average ransomware severity at $875,000, followed by finance and insurance at $731,000 and healthcare at $675,000. Even as claims accelerated, the market's combined ratio sat at 65.4 percent in 2025—still profitable, since breakeven is 100—but underwriters are signaling alarm. Third-party liability claims jumped 70 percent, the largest single-year increase on record. California's CCPA cybersecurity audit mandate took effect January 2026, requiring regular audits. AIG launched an AI-enhanced underwriting platform evaluating 700-plus cybersecurity variables per policy. The message is clear: compliance infrastructure—audits, penetration testing, staff credentials, incident response plans—is now built into pricing. Firms with loose security get denied outright or shunted to specialty carriers charging 2-3 times standard rates.

Workers' compensation insurance is caught in a different bind: regulation at the state level has fractured the market. Premiums nationally fell 3 percent to $41.6 billion in 2024, and the industry maintained an 86 percent combined ratio—the 11th straight year of underwriting gain. But claim severity jumped 6 percent in 2024, and medical costs are accelerating in certain states. Florida saw a 41 percent rate spike in 2025 after fee-schedule changes. California, home to 10 percent of US employment, posted a 127 percent combined loss ratio in 2026, forcing carriers to reduce capacity or exit entirely. This isn't a soft-market problem—it's a bifurcated market. Carriers with strong capital and predictive analytics are profiting. Smaller players, and those lacking technology to model state-specific medical inflation and presumption laws, are being pressured out. The compliance tax here isn't a single rule; it's a patchwork. Each state's medical-fee schedules differ. Each state's definition of compensable injury expands differently. Cumulative trauma and presumption-law claims are expanding the definition of injury faster than carriers can reserve for it. A carrier without 50-state medical compliance and claims analytics cannot survive.

The evidence

  • Health insurance market: $1.6 trillion (2026) with 9 percent employer premium increases (highest in 15 years) and unsubsidized ACA premiums doubling from $888 to $1,904 annually after December 31, 2025 subsidy expiration.
  • Medicaid shrinking 7.6 percent in 2025 (first decline since COVID) as new work and reporting requirements in 2025 reconciliation bill took effect.
  • Amazon launching GLP-1 management at $25 per month (April 2026) through One Medical, expanding from 3,000 to 4,500 cities by year-end, undercutting traditional insurance for high-margin segments.
  • Cyber insurance at $7.02 billion (2024) with ransomware driving 90 percent of claim severity in H1 2025; third-party liability claims surging 70 percent year-over-year, the largest single-year increase on record.
  • California CCPA cybersecurity audit mandate (effective January 2026) driving demand for cyber insurance; AIG deploying AI platform evaluating 700-plus variables per policy to tighten underwriting.
  • Workers' compensation bifurcating by state: Florida up 41 percent (2025), California posting 127 percent loss ratio (2026) and forcing carrier exits; claims severity up 6 percent in 2024 amid cumulative-trauma and presumption-law expansion.

Who rides it

Large, well-capitalized insurers with 50-state compliance infrastructure and advanced data analytics win. Aetna, UnitedHealth, and Cigna control health insurance and can absorb premium volatility and Medicaid shrinkage through scale. In cyber, Chubb, Travelers, and AIG are investing heavily in AI underwriting and can retain profitable segments by pricing in compliance overhead. In workers' comp, carriers like Zurich and Liberty Mutual with state-by-state medical expertise and machine-learning claims modeling are gaining share. Consultants, auditors, and security vendors win too—as compliance becomes pricing, demand for CCPA audits, penetration testing, and cyber-incident response planning explodes.

Who's squeezed

Small employers, small insurers, and startups get squeezed. A mid-market employer (100-500 employees) faces the full weight of a 9 percent premium increase in 2025-2026 while losing access to cloud-based compliance platforms that larger rivals subsidize. Regional workers' comp carriers in high-cost states like California face exit or absorption. The self-insured small business—once a competitive escape valve—now must hire compliance staff, run CCPA audits, and maintain incident response procedures, or lose insurability. For individual health insurance buyers, the subsidy cliff on December 31, 2025 is catastrophic: a $1,004 annual cliff pushes millions off the individual market entirely, reducing insurers' customer base but increasing claims concentration among the remaining enrollees.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The largest risk is a cascade failure in state-regulated markets. If medical cost inflation in Florida, California, or New York outpaces state fee-schedule adjustments, carriers will exit those states entirely, leaving self-insurance or high-cost specialty carriers as the only options. Simultaneously, if ransomware and third-party liability claims continue surging (third-party up 70 percent in a single year), the cyber market's 65.4 percent combined ratio will evaporate, triggering a hard market and denial of coverage for mid-market firms. The compliance tax then becomes a lock-in: only large firms with in-house security, actuarial, and legal teams can obtain insurance at any price, while smaller firms face uninsurable risk or massive premium shocks that force self-insurance or exit.

B · Healthcare's paperwork

Healthcare's Paperwork Machine

Hospitals bleed money on reimbursement shortfalls while drowning in regulatory overhead, forcing consolidation and pricing out independents.

US hospitals face a structural crisis: Medicare reimburses at only 82-87 cents per dollar of care, while operating margins have collapsed from 7.6% in 2022 to just 1-2% in 2025. At the same time, a thickening web of regulatory requirements—Medicare rules, AI governance, supply chain traceability, quality management systems—has made administration itself a massive, growing cost center. The result is ruthless consolidation, labor conflict, and the extinction of independent hospital networks.

What changed

The reimbursement math broke in 2024-2025. Medicare's shortfall—paying 13-18 cents less than the actual cost of care—combined with labor costs that jumped 42% since 2020, left hospitals with nowhere to hide. A hospital system can't cut patient care to fix the math. What it can do is consolidate, automate, and outsource. But doing any of that requires money and compliance expertise. Small regional systems don't have it. In January 2025, Prospect Medical Holdings filed Chapter 11 and shed 10 of its 16 hospitals. Steward Health Care's bankruptcy became the largest in the hospital sector in 30 years. Twenty hospital bankruptcies in 2025 alone, up from 15 in 2024.

Simultaneously, the regulatory load exploded. The FDA's Quality Management System Regulation, which took effect February 2, 2026, harmonized US device rules with ISO 13485:2016 and required new levels of supplier traceability and control. For device manufacturers, this meant restructuring decades of offshoring. Tariffs added muscle to the rule: a 10% global tariff on medical devices (April 2025), plus 50-100% tariffs on syringes and needles, forced major OEMs like J&J (facing $400 million in added cost for 2025) to rethink supply chains almost overnight. Smaller manufacturers couldn't absorb the hit. AI adoption accelerated in hospitals—75% of health systems now use at least one AI tool (up from 59% in 2025)—but almost entirely for tasks that don't directly generate revenue (note-taking, image analysis). The systems buying the tech, however, are the large consolidated ones with IT infrastructure and compliance staff to implement and defend these tools.

Scale became survival. In Q1 2026, hospital M&A rebounded to 22 transactions worth 14.5 billion—the highest Q1 in more than 5 years. Ascension spent 3.9 billion to acquire AmSurg, betting that owning ambulatory surgery centers (which now do 9% more procedures than they did in 2023) would give it control over profitable procedures that used to happen inside hospitals. Larger systems negotiate tariff-resilient supply chains. They absorb FDA compliance overhead. They can afford the IT teams to deploy AI and track its outputs. Regional hospitals and independents can't. Labor power shifted too: the Kaiser strike in January 2026, involving over 30,000 workers, exposed how labor unions now have leverage in an industry where staffing is the largest cost center and consolidation has reduced employer options. But unions only protect workers at large systems. Independent practices and small hospitals get crushed.

The FTC's new Healthcare Task Force, active in 2026, is blocking cross-market mergers and scrutinizing private equity deals to slow this wave. But the structural forces are stronger than any regulator. Medicare payment rules, FDA device rules, supply chain tariffs, and the automation threshold (it costs less to buy AI tools than hire staff at union rates) all point in one direction: hospitals must be big or disappear. The 5,875 hospital establishments in the US employed 5.8 million people in December 2025. That number will shrink.

The evidence

  • Hospitals: US hospital margins collapsed to 1-2% in 2025 from 7.6% in 2022, while Medicare shortfall widened to 13-18 cents per dollar of care
  • Device makers: Medical device tariffs (10% global, 50-100% on syringes/needles, April 2025) added $400M+ in annual costs to J&J alone
  • Labor: Over 30,000 Kaiser Permanente workers struck in January 2026; hospital bankruptcies rose to 20 in 2025, highest in years
  • Consolidation: Hospital M&A rebounded to $14.5 billion across 22 deals in Q1 2026, highest Q1 in 5+ years; Ascension acquired AmSurg for $3.9 billion
  • Regulation: FDA Quality Management System Regulation enforcement began February 2, 2026, tightening supplier controls; 75% of health systems now use AI tools (up from 59% in 2025)

Who rides it

Large hospital systems and medical device OEMs (Medtronic, Abbott, Boston Scientific, J&J, Edwards Lifesciences) win by absorbing compliance overhead and negotiating tariff-resilient supply chains. Ascension, buying AmSurg and ambulatory centers, captured profitable outpatient procedures. Health systems with IT infrastructure can deploy AI for automation and reduce reliance on union labor. Private equity and larger regional networks consolidate at fire-sale prices. Consultants selling compliance, supply chain restructuring, and AI implementation solutions capture a growing slice of hospital budgets.

Who's squeezed

Independent hospitals and regional chains disappear. Prospect Medical, Steward Health Care, and dozens of mid-sized systems can't survive the reimbursement shortfall or absorb tariff shocks and FDA compliance costs. Smaller medical device suppliers and contract manufacturers face impossible margins when tariffs hit 50-100% and they lack the scale to nearshore. Hospital workers at smaller systems lose leverage; labor unions protect workers at big systems, but independents are gone. Communities lose local control of healthcare infrastructure. Patients at remaining hospitals face fewer options as consolidation proceeds.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that consolidation accelerates healthcare inflation. Large hospital systems, freed from regional competitors, can raise prices and capture insurance reimbursement more aggressively. Meanwhile, the FTC's Healthcare Task Force is blocking cross-market mergers but can't stop within-market consolidation (one big system swallowing two smaller ones in the same region). The result: higher prices, fewer choices, lower quality. Simultaneously, regulatory pressure keeps pushing automation and AI, which large systems can afford but small ones cannot, deepening the divide. If consolidation continues at the current pace, within five years most Americans may have access to only one or two dominant health systems in their region, each facing no competitive pressure to keep costs down.</worry> </invoke>

B · Healthcare's paperwork

Data, Privacy & Cyber

Privacy and cyber rules raised the cost of holding data — and built a new profit machine for scale players.

Starting around 2023, the cost of keeping data safe went vertical. Privacy laws—GDPR fines exceeding €7.1 billion, California's CPRA, LGPD in Brazil, HIPAA in healthcare—stopped being legal abstractions. They became operational reality: compliance requirements embedded in hosting contracts, mandatory security audits, breach notification overhead, and staff time burned on paperwork. The infrastructure cost to hold data went from a commodity to a competitive moat.

What changed

Privacy rules made data expensive to hold. Start with the numbers: data processing and hosting services hit $485.7 billion in 2026, growing at 5.7% that year but forecast to grow at 16.8% CAGR through 2032. But there's a catch. Profit margins on basic hosting compressed from 6.7% in 2021 to near zero today because compliance and capex don't scale linearly—a small operator needs auditors, redundancy, and legal review almost as much as a big one. At the same time, GDPR fines exceeded €7.1 billion, and the EU AI Act hit full effect August 2, 2026, layering new obligations on any company processing data from Europeans. These rules don't cost nothing—they're sunk costs that a solo-operator host can't spread across enough customers.

The big players absorbed this differently. Hyperscalers—Amazon, Google, Microsoft—built compliance into the fiber of their infrastructure. AWS revenue hit $37.59 billion in Q1 2026 (up 28% year-over-year), and the company can afford to hire compliance teams, maintain HIPAA-certified zones, and build carbon-aware data centers because they have 31% market share and billions in revenue. For healthcare providers, research institutions, and mid-market firms, the path narrowed: either move to a big cloud vendor (Azure, AWS, Google Cloud—now with compliance baked in), or hire your own compliance staff and security engineers. Internet hosting services—13,817 establishments as of 2022, mostly under 10 people—faced a guillotine. Consolidation sped up: Newfold Digital (Clearlake Capital) folded Web.com into Network Solutions in June 2025, sunsetting the brand entirely. Technician wages rose 7%+ annually, driven by demand for people who understand both security and regulatory requirements. By 2025-2026, 53% of hosting providers said AI-driven automation was critical to survival, and 65% prioritized AI-powered malware detection—automation became table stakes just to compete.

The data processing layer felt the squeeze even harder. Seventy thousand enterprises operate in data processing, but consolidation is hollowing out the middle. The five largest hyperscalers spent $630 billion on infrastructure in 2026—up 36% from 2025—with $450 billion explicitly targeting AI. That money went to power, chips, and redundancy, not labor-saving automation. US data center electricity demand jumped from 23 GW in 2023 to 42 GW in 2026, and wholesale power prices near major data centers rose 267%. Meanwhile, 90% of data center operators cited staffing constraints as a bottleneck: demand for AI infrastructure specialists, high-voltage engineers, and cooling technicians vastly outpaced supply. Smaller data processing shops—the ones that might handle a hospital's imaging archive or a research lab's genomic data—couldn't compete for talent or power. The industry workforce grew from 636,786 employees in 2021 to a projected 753,671 by 2026, but those jobs concentrated at hyperscalers and tier-one operators. Tier-two and tier-three operators either specialized (edge compute, niche verticals) or exited.

What changed: privacy and cyber rules made the baseline cost of operating data infrastructure rise sharply, but scale masking that cost. Big players built compliance into their margins and hired domain experts. Smaller operators couldn't. At the same time, AI demand created a parallel crisis—power and talent became scarce, both expensive. For a healthcare provider or research institution looking to store sensitive data, the economic choice inverted: cloud giants with compliance teams and surplus power won, and the mid-tier hosting operator—the one that used to serve regional health systems and universities—disappeared.

The evidence

  • Data Processing & Hosting Services: $485.7B market in 2026 (5.7% YoY growth), forecast 16.8% CAGR through 2032; profit margins collapsed from 6.7% (2021) to near-zero (2025-2026) due to compliance capex and commodity pricing—hyperscalers (AWS $37.59B Q1 2026 revenue, +28% YoY) absorbed costs via scale; smaller hosts forced to specialize or exit
  • Internet Hosting Services: 13,817 establishments (2022), highly fragmented with <10 person average; market slowed to 4.9% growth (2025) from 11.9% pandemic boom; consolidation accelerated (Newfold Digital folded Web.com into Network Solutions, June 2025); technician wages rose 7%+ annually
  • Cloud Giants Market Share: AWS holds 31% cloud market share, Azure 23-25%, Google Cloud 11-12% (Q1 2026); all three integrated compliance zones and published carbon-aware APIs; price competition intensified (Google Cloud cut 8% across all regions, Q1 2026)
  • Data Processing Consolidation: 70,000 enterprises in data processing; hyperscalers' $630B infrastructure spend in 2026 (up 36% YoY) concentrated at tier-one players; CoreWeave/Digital Realty $200 MW lease (March 2026) and $21B M&A quarter (Q1 2026) show consolidation velocity at top; smaller operators specializing (edge, liquid cooling) or exiting
  • Compliance Overheads: GDPR fines exceeded €7.1B by 2026; EU AI Act fully applicable August 2, 2026; CPRA, HIPAA, LGPD embedded in hosting contracts (2025-2026); 65% of hosting providers prioritized AI-powered security, 53% cited automation as competitive necessity—compliance became part of baseline cost, not margin

Who rides it

Big cloud and hosting players. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and hyperscalers like Equinix, Digital Realty, and CoreWeave saw compliance become a competitive weapon—they could afford to build HIPAA zones, maintain GDPR certifications, hire security experts, and publish compliance roadmaps. Their scale let them spread compliance costs across billions in revenue. Meanwhile, consolidation rewarded aggressive M&A: Verizon paid $20 billion for Frontier (March 2026), Charter announced a deal for Cox, CoreWeave and Digital Realty formed a $15 billion joint venture—big players got bigger, smaller competitors' options narrowed to acquisition or exit. Data privacy regulation, meant to protect users, ended up being a moat for incumbents.

Who's squeezed

Regional and mid-market hosting and data processing shops. The compliance tax is a fixed cost: auditing, breach notification, legal review, security staff time. A solo-operator host or regional data processor pays nearly the same compliance overhead as a cloud giant, but spread across 10x or 100x fewer customers. Technician wages shot up 7%+ annually because everyone needed security experts at once. Power became scarce and expensive as hyperscalers monopolized available capacity. Smaller operators couldn't outbid for talent or power, couldn't spread compliance costs, and couldn't maintain the margin to reinvest in automation. Consolidation accelerated—Newfold folded Web.com, regional ISPs disappeared into Charter and Verizon deals—and independent operators exited entirely. For healthcare providers and research institutions, this meant fewer options: move to a cloud giant's compliance-ready infrastructure, or pay a regional operator's higher prices while they liquidate.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Compliance becomes a compliance moat, not user protection. The thicket of GDPR, CPRA, HIPAA, AI Act, and cyber mandates was meant to protect privacy. Instead, it created a high barrier to entry—only scale players can afford compliance teams, audits, and redundancy. Smaller operators, regional providers, and specialty hosts disappeared. Now healthcare systems, research institutions, and SMBs have fewer real choices: use an AWS zone or move to a hyperscaler. Compliance concentration mirrors infrastructure concentration. The irony: stricter privacy rules aimed at protecting data may have narrowed the competitive landscape enough to make data protection less competitive and more expensive. When there are fewer independent operators, competition for compliance excellence weakens, and prices rise for everyone except the scale winners.

C · The compliance-industrial complex

Who Profits from the Rules

Lawyers, auditors, and accountants are the new tax on compliance—they capture the windfall, even as their own model cracks.

When the rules multiply, three industries profit: law firms, audit shops, and accounting services. In 2025 and 2026, they celebrated record revenues even as demand growth stalled and their talent pools collapsed. The pattern is clear: compliance rules have made expert advisors scarce and indispensable, at least for now.

What changed

The US law firms industry hit a historic moment in 2025. The market reached $426.7 billion, up from $367.9 billion in 2022, but the growth masks something ugly underneath. Demand—the actual legal work companies need done—grew only 1.9 percent in 2025. Expenses, though, jumped 9.1 percent. Law firms made record profits not by doing more work, but by raising rates. Fees worked per lawyer climbed 16.8 percent in 2025 alone. Clients noticed. Fifty-nine percent of corporate clients surveyed said they see no savings from outside counsel using generative AI, yet law firms burned through 9.7 to 11 percent more on tech infrastructure in 2025 just trying to stay ahead. The industry is consolidating fast: 59 law firm mergers happened in 2025, up 18 percent from 2024, with at least 16 more deals announced for completion in 2026. Hogan Lovells and Cadwalader combined to create a $3.6 billion revenue firm. The squeeze is real. In-house legal departments, squeezed on budget, are moving work away from premium Am Law 100 firms to cheaper alternatives. Milbank's June 2026 salary scale—$235,000 for starting associates, $455,000 for eighth-year associates—signals desperation for talent.\n\nThe audit industry faces a different but equally stark paradox. The market is worth $56.3 billion in 2025, but talent is fleeing. Over 300,000 accounting professionals have exited the field in recent years. CPA exam takers are down 30 percent since 2016. Open audit roles now take 73 days to fill, 41 percent longer than comparable positions. The Big Four (PwC, Deloitte, EY, KPMG) audit 97 percent of the S&P 500, which means they own the compliance monopoly. So they are pouring money into AI. PwC announced end-to-end AI automation of audits by the end of 2026. EY deployed AI to 80,000 tax staff and rolled out 150 AI agents for data collection, document review, and compliance tasks. Yet accounting firm M&A hit a record 194 transactions in 2025, up 26 percent year-over-year, with financial acquirers leading at 54.8 percent of deals. The regulatory environment shifted sharply in 2025: SEC audit enforcement hit an eight-year low with only 2 actions in 2025 versus 58 in 2024. PCAOB enforcement dropped 33 percent year-over-year to 39 combined actions. Lighter-touch regulation means less pressure to tighten scope, and scope keeps expanding. Sixty-four percent of companies now expect auditors to assess AI use in financial reporting. ESG and sustainability assurance are mandatory or expected across most public companies and many private ones. Cybersecurity ranks as auditors' number one global concern.\n\nAccounting services paint the starkest picture of all. The US market grew from $141.8 billion in 2022 to $145-155 billion in 2025, projected to reach $187.58 billion in 2026. But this growth is not coming from more junior accountants doing tax returns. AI adoption quadrupled in 2024-2025, with LLM-based audit tools reducing document analysis time by roughly 50 percent. That shrinks junior labor demand fast. Eighty-seven percent of finance leaders report talent shortages. CPA exam participation has dropped 30 percent since 2016. Mid-size accounting firms are trapped: too small to invest in the tech and talent infrastructure of private-equity-backed platforms, but losing solo and small-practice client bases to self-service software and automation. Private equity consolidators (Blackstone, Cherry Bekaert, Aprio, Baker Tilly, Citrin Cooperman) are buying smaller and mid-market firms at 4 to 7 times EBITDA multiples, creating mega-platforms that chase scale and efficiency. KPMG received approval to launch KPMG Law US in 2025, the first Big Four law firm in the US under Arizona regulatory reform. KPMG's tax revenue grew 7.5 percent in 2025, outpacing competitors. The Big Four expanded workforces in 2025 while smaller firms struggled to hire.

The evidence

  • Law firms: 59 mergers in 2025 (up 18% YoY), rate hikes of 16.8% per lawyer despite 1.9% demand growth, yet 59% of corporate clients see no savings from AI spending by outside counsel (2025).
  • Audit services: Big Four audit 97% of S&P 500; PwC expecting end-to-end AI automation by Q4 2026; EY deployed 150 AI agents to 80,000 tax staff; PCAOB enforcement down 33% YoY to 39 actions (2025-2026).
  • Accounting services: AI adoption quadrupled in 2024-2025, reducing document analysis time by 50%; yet 87% of finance leaders report talent shortages and 194 M&A deals in 2025 (up 26% YoY) consolidate mid-market (2025).
  • Talent crisis: CPA exam takers down 30% since 2016; open audit roles take 73 days to fill (41% longer than comparable); over 300,000 accounting professionals exited the field; positions once taking 30-45 days remain open months (2025-2026).
  • Regulatory expansion: 64% of companies expect auditors to assess AI in financial reporting; ESG/sustainability assurance now mandatory or expected; cybersecurity is auditors' #1 global concern; SEC audit enforcement at 8-year low of 2 actions in 2025 vs. 58 in 2024 (2025-2026).

Who rides it

The Big Four (PwC, Deloitte, EY, KPMG) and mega-platform accounting firms backed by private equity profit most. They have scale to invest in AI and talent, control 97 percent of S&P 500 audit work, and face lighter-touch regulation. Premium law firms capture rate premiums from corporate clients stuck paying for regulatory complexity. Consolidators acquire mid-market practices at cheap multiples and integrate them into efficiency machines. These players turn compliance scarcity into pricing power.

Who's squeezed

Solo practitioners, small accounting firms, and mid-market law firms are squeezed out. They cannot afford the tech stack or talent costs of scaled rivals. Their client bases shrink as self-service software and automation handle routine work, yet they still face the same compliance burden. In-house legal departments, starved for budget, are forced to move work to cheaper alternatives or junior staff, eroding the traditional pyramid of billable-hour labor. Small businesses that once hired a local accountant now get pushed toward DIY software or AI tools they half-understand.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The model for advisor firms—selling scarce expertise at premium margins—breaks the moment the expertise becomes automated or abundant. PwC, EY, and Deloitte are investing billions in AI expecting to cut costs and grow profits. But if AI actually succeeds at automating audit work, demand for human auditors collapses, pricing power vanishes, and the industry consolidates further into a handful of mega-platforms. Law firms are already seeing this: rate hikes are running ahead of demand, clients are walking away, and mergers are accelerating. The real risk is that advisors have gotten so expensive that clients finally decide the compliance itself is the luxury they can no longer afford—and then the entire industry faces a demand cliff.

C · The compliance-industrial complex

Environmental & climate rules

EPA standards and climate mandates are turning environmental compliance into a $27.4 billion consulting market—feeding the Big Four while squeezing smaller operators with tariff costs and engineer shortages.

The EPA's 2024 PFAS drinking-water standards, CERCLA hazardous-substance designations, and methane regulations are creating multi-year remediation pipelines that flow directly through corporate and government budgets. Environmental consulting has grown into a $27.4 billion market in 2025, but the work is mostly expensive: site assessments, remediation planning, and compliance audits. The real story is who pays the bill and who makes the margin.

What changed

Environmental rules have flipped from an occasional cost to a permanent tax on operations. The EPA's April 2024 drinking-water PFAS standard—covering six forever-chemicals—triggered multi-year testing and remediation pipelines that flow through 2026 budgets and beyond. Three months later, in July 2024, PFOA and PFOS were designated as CERCLA hazardous substances, meaning any facility that touched them now needs legal support and site cleanup planning. These aren't one-time expenses. They're cascading: the PFAS rule alone created demand for environmental assessments, GIS mapping, ground-testing, treatment design, and litigation support. An updated methane rule taking effect in August 2025 will push 705 additional landfills toward capture systems, adding another wave of site-specific engineering work.

The cost advantage has shifted decisively to scale. Environmental consulting is a $27.4 billion market in the US (2025), growing at 1.6%, but that headline masks violent consolidation. In February 2025, WSP paid $1.78 billion to acquire Power Engineers, instantly adding depth in renewable-energy infrastructure and environmental design. Jacobs spun off its Cyber and Intelligence units to focus fire on infrastructure and environmental work. Montrose absorbed multiple boutique firms in 2024 and early 2025. The Big Four—Jacobs, WSP, Tetra Tech, and Stantec—are scooping up smaller regional competitors at valuations that reward size, client relationships, and the ability to staff 50-person teams on a three-month notice. Mid-sized firms operate at 8-9% EBITDA margins (2025), but consolidators are paying for 12-15% margin upside within 18 months.

Labor is now the bottleneck and the cost driver. Licensed environmental engineers are "the tightest in a generation" to hire (ACEC 2025). GIS specialists command noticeable premiums. Project managers with water remediation experience can name their price. This labor scarcity is compressing smaller firms harder than large ones: a firm with five engineers needs each one; a firm with 500 can rotate, cross-train, and absorb a departure without a client emergency. Simultaneously, tariffs are tightening the procurement side. US tariffs on steel and aluminum doubled to 50% in 2025, pushing the effective tariff rate toward 13% by early 2026. For site remediation, this means equipment costs, pipe, drilling rigs, and analytical instruments all cost more. Smaller contractors can't absorb the hit and pass it to clients; larger ones have supplier relationships and can negotiate. The result is that costs are rising faster than margins can expand, and only scale survives.

Data center demand for renewable baseload power is creating new contract opportunities, but they're captured almost entirely by established players. In 2025, data center electricity consumption surged 17%, and AI-focused data centers are tripling their power demand. Tech companies signed 40% of all new corporate renewable energy PPAs in 2025, and they're contracts with utility-scale operators, not local environmental consultants. Waste-to-energy plants, a $1.4 billion industry operating 64 facilities across 21 states, are seeing 18-25% EBITDA margins on this new demand. But the industry has only nine major operators, and consolidation is accelerating: Covanta rebranded to Reworld (April 2024) under EQT Infrastructure and shifted to regionalized service lines; FCC Environmental, a global operator with 12 international facilities, entered the US market in June 2025 by acquiring the Wheelabrator South Broward facility. Small regional waste operators face a choice: sell to a consolidator now or watch margin compression as commodity power prices fall.

The evidence

  • Environmental Consulting (Business Services): $27.4B market in 2025, 65,000 establishments, 165,000 employees; consolidators like WSP ($1.78B Power Engineers deal, Feb 2025) and Jacobs (spun off Cyber/Intelligence units, Dec 2024) hunting scale; PFAS and methane rules creating multi-year pipelines.
  • Waste-to-Energy Plant Operation: $1.4B market in 2025, nine operators, 64 plants; 18-25% EBITDA margins; Covanta rebranded to Reworld (April 2024), FCC Environmental entered US market (June 2025); data center demand surged 17% in 2025.
  • Landfill Gas & Methane Regulation: 598 active systems producing 64% of renewable natural gas (2025); 705 additional landfills now mandatory capture candidates under August 2025 EPA rule; 20 new projects in 2025 added 39.9 Bcf capacity.
  • Labor Scarcity & Tariff Squeeze: Licensed environmental engineers 'tightest in a generation' (ACEC 2025); steel/aluminum tariffs doubled to 50% in 2025; GIS specialists command premiums; mid-sized firms at 8-9% EBITDA, compressed versus large-scale consolidators.
  • Corporate Renewable Energy: Tech sector signed 40% of all new corporate renewable energy PPAs in 2025; data center power demand tripling with AI workloads; contracts captured by utility-scale operators, not regional environmental service providers.

Who rides it

Big consulting firms, especially Jacobs, WSP, Tetra Tech, and Stantec, are consolidating the industry at $1+ billion acquisition prices. They have the labor depth to staff multi-year remediation projects, the supplier relationships to absorb tariff hits, and the client trust to win government and Fortune 500 contracts. Waste-to-energy operators with scale—Reworld, FCC Environmental, EQT-backed players—are capturing data center power contracts worth 18-25% EBITDA margins. Tech companies building data centers are locking in long-term renewable energy PPAs at favorable rates, trading compliance risk for contract certainty.

Who's squeezed

Mid-sized environmental consulting firms (8-9% EBITDA margins) can't compete on project scale or labor bench strength. Small regional waste operators face margin compression from commodity power prices and consolidator entry. Facilities that touched PFAS—manufacturers, treatment plants, defense contractors, airports—now carry permanent remediation costs with no clear exit. Local contractors and engineering practices lose work to out-of-state consolidators who can underbid on the back of scale and spread overhead. Labor-constrained firms (especially those hunting licensed engineers and GIS specialists) either pay up and compress margins or miss contracts entirely.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The permanent shift in regulatory overhead has no off switch. PFAS remediation pipelines flow through 2026 and beyond; methane rules will keep expanding; climate and ESG consulting is eating into base environmental-assessment margins. Small operators can't exit compliance costs by doing less—they're pinned between statutory obligations and scale-driven competitors who can absorb multi-million-dollar bids and wait three years for ROI. The real risk is consolidation-driven monoculture: as Big Four consulting firms dominate, they standardize methods, raise prices for captive clients (especially mid-market and government customers), and lobby for rules that favor complexity. And if tariffs stay elevated or rise, procurement costs on remediation projects will keep compressing margin for everyone except the largest operators.

D · The tensions

The Small-Operator Squeeze

Compliance is a fixed cost, and small firms pay it the hardest.

Compliance cost is a flat fee. Whether you're a solo credit repair agent or a two-person team running a local IT bootcamp, you still need a lawyer to read the rules, software licenses to track them, and staff time to implement them. Scale the cost down across 50,000 customers and it disappears. Spread it across a five-person firm and it kills you. The patchwork of AI, privacy, climate, and cyber rules does not scale linearly—and that is the squeeze.

What changed

Credit repair used to be about telemarketing and customer volume. After the 2023 CFPB settlement—2.7 billion USD in fines and redress against Lexington Law and CreditRepair.com—the playbook broke. Small operators who ran call centers and used aggressive tactics suddenly faced existential legal risk. The settlement forced PGX Holdings to shut down approximately 80 percent of operations by 2024. But at the same time, machine learning made those call centers unnecessary. Modern platforms now use AI to analyze credit reports, auto-detect errors, generate dispute letters in seconds, and predict which disputes will succeed—making the old human-heavy model obsolete. For a solo credit repair agent or small shop, the compliance cost of avoiding CFPB violations (legal review, dispute letter audit trails, complaint handling, record retention) is identical whether you handle 100 customers or 1,000. That fixed cost lives on your P&L as a percentage of revenue. For the 29.6 percent of US consumers still holding subprime credit (September 2025), the demand is real—5.29 to 6.6 billion USD in market revenue in 2025—but employment in the sector dropped 4.7 percent year-over-year as of 2026. The work that remains goes to AI-enabled shops that can spread compliance overhead across scale.\n\nIT training and certification face the same squeeze, but inverted. The US business certification and IT schools market is 6.4 billion USD in 2026, up from 3.0 billion in 2022. That looks like growth until you zoom in. Enterprise-facing, compliance-linked credentials—cloud architecture, cybersecurity, AI engineering—are growing at 12 to 16 percent annually. Cybersecurity training alone jumped from 5.67 billion USD in 2024 to 6.66 billion in 2025, a 16.6 percent leap. Why? Because employers now tie these certifications directly to hiring, insurance discounts, and regulatory compliance. Compliance-adjacent credentials have pricing power. But entry-level bootcamps and generic IT skills training are in freefall. Large franchisors like 2U exited the university-partnered bootcamp space entirely in December 2024, citing weak junior hiring and AI displacement fears. Epicodus and the Southern New Hampshire University coding programs shut down between 2023 and 2024. The global coding bootcamp market is valued at 3.28 billion USD in 2025, but it is fragmenting because free alternatives—AI tutorials, corporate LLMs, MOOCs—now compete on equal footing. A small bootcamp operator cannot compete on curriculum or brand. They cannot spread the cost of compliance (employment law, advertising, accreditation, data privacy) across 1,000 students per year. They have 50.\n\nThe Coursera-Udemy merger (announced April 2026, 2.5 billion USD equity value) is the endgame signal. The combined company projects 1.5 billion USD in revenue, targets 290 million learners and 18,000 enterprise customers, and expects 115 million USD in annual cost synergies. Translation: economies of scale in compliance, content delivery, and enterprise sales are now non-negotiable. A regional bootcamp with 200 students cannot absorb a surprise change in data privacy law or a new cybersecurity insurance requirement. A 290-million-learner platform with enterprise contracts and dedicated compliance teams bakes it into the cost per user—a penny on a billion transactions. The small operator pays a dollar per student.\n\nWhat makes this system durable is that compliance is not optional and not uniform. The credit repair CFPB rules apply equally to a one-person operation and a 500-person firm. The cybersecurity certifications now demanded by employers require the same training infrastructure for both. There is no sliding scale. A boutique credit repair shop must hire a compliance officer or contract with a consultant. An independent IT bootcamp must carry employment lawyers, content auditors, and data protection software. The big player amortizes these costs; the small player files for bankruptcy. The result is not a level playing field tilted slightly toward scale. It is a field where the rules are the same, the cost is the same, but only large firms can afford to stay in the game.

The evidence

  • Credit repair: 43,810 businesses as of 2023, most 1-2 person operations, yet face identical CFPB compliance costs as the 2.7 billion USD settlement required in August 2023.
  • IT training: Cybersecurity credentials growing at 16.6 percent CAGR (2024-2025) while commodity bootcamps collapse; 2U exited bootcamp franchises entirely in December 2024 citing compliance burden and AI displacement.
  • Employment erosion: Credit repair employment fell 4.7 percent YoY as of 2026 despite 5.29-6.6 billion USD market revenue, proof that growth accrues to scale, not spread.
  • Consolidation signal: Coursera-Udemy merger (April 2026, 2.5 billion equity) targets 18,000 enterprise customers and 115 million USD cost synergies through scale in compliance and content delivery.
  • Subprime demand persists: 29.6 percent of US consumers hold subprime credit (September 2025), but market revenue concentrates upward as compliance costs eliminate small players.

Who rides it

Large platforms that can amortize compliance overhead across millions of users or thousands of enterprise contracts. Coursera, with 290 million learners post-Udemy deal, absorbs new privacy, employment, and cybersecurity rules as pennies per transaction. Enterprise-facing certification programs (AWS, Azure AI, CompTIA Security+) benefit from employer demand that subsidizes compliance costs through premium pricing. AI-enabled credit repair platforms that automate dispute generation and prediction cut the need for human-heavy call centers, making compliance infrastructure a smaller fraction of their margin."

Who's squeezed

Solo operators and two-to-five-person shops in credit repair and IT training. A one-person credit repair shop must still hire a lawyer or consultant to stay CFPB-compliant; a small regional bootcamp must maintain employment law expertise and data protection infrastructure with no scale to justify it. Regional bootcamp operators face competition from free alternatives (AI tutorials, MOOCs) while carrying the same compliance and wage costs as national platforms. Entry-level IT bootcamps are being priced out entirely, as evidenced by 2U's full exit in December 2024, Epicodus and SNHU closures in 2023-2024, and the fragmentation of the 3.28 billion USD coding bootcamp market."

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The compliance tax becomes a permanent barrier to entry. If an entrepreneur cannot afford to hire a compliance officer, outside counsel, and data protection infrastructure, they cannot legally operate a credit repair service or run a bootcamp. The result is not competition; it is consolidation and exit. The 43,810 credit repair businesses in 2023 will continue to shrink, folding into larger, AI-enabled platforms that can absorb regulatory costs. Small bootcamps will shut down or merge. The market revenue will grow (5.29-6.6 billion in credit repair; 6.4 billion in IT training), but it will flow upward to fewer, larger firms. Entrepreneurship in these spaces becomes a privilege of capital-backed ventures, not scrappy operators."

D · The tensions

Governing the Algorithms

New AI-governance rules land first on data, credit, and software—and they cost more to comply with than most midmarket firms can absorb.

The SEC is overhauling how rating agencies govern AI decisions. Europe already requires explainability of automated lending. Regulators want to know what the algorithm decided and why. That audit trail used to be optional. Now it is becoming the cost of doing business—and small players are bleeding out from it.

What changed

The compliance infrastructure around AI governance has turned explanation into a new operational burden. When a credit algorithm denies a loan or flags a transaction, the borrower can now demand to know why. That means the firm has to preserve the model's logic, document its training data, version its weights, and prove it didn't discriminate. Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian have all raised their compliance spending, and the SEC's proposed overhaul of rating agency rules (2026) will spike that further by requiring governance oversight, analyst independence audits, and methodology disclosure. This is not a one-time fix. Every model update triggers a new compliance cycle. Every breach—and the industry has suffered major ones: TransUnion exposed 4.4 million Americans' names and Social Security numbers in August 2025, and 700Credit exposed 5.8 million between July and October 2025—pushes regulators to demand tighter data handling, forcing bureaus and lenders to invest in security infrastructure that was considered optional five years ago.

What makes this worse is that the compliance tax compounds with scale. A startup credit bureau can hire a single compliance officer. A regional lender can buy off-the-shelf audit software. But when the SEC, FTC, and state attorneys general all want different documentation formats, different retention periods, and different explainability standards, the cost of coordination grows exponentially. Moody's reported $7.7 billion in revenue for 2025 with 9% growth in both analytics and core investor services, and crucially, operating income jumped 17% year-over-year (2025)—the big player absorbs the burden and passes it to customers. TransUnion's compliance costs are baked into their margins (averaging around 29% industry-wide in 2026), but they can spread those costs across millions of credit reports. A regional credit union or a fintech lender trying to build an AI lending system? They hit the same SEC requirements, the same explainability standards, the same data retention rules. They just can't amortize the cost across as many transactions.

Meanwhile, the software and AI-services layer is consolidating at breakneck speed. Salesforce spent billions acquiring Informatica (November 2025) for data integration and AI pipeline capabilities, Qualified.com (April 2026) for AI-driven sales acceleration, and Fin (June 2026) for AI customer support automation. These aren't feature acquisitions—they're acquisitions of compliance infrastructure. Building an AI agent that handles customer support requires not just the model but the governance layer: logging every decision, proving it doesn't discriminate, explaining why a customer was routed to a human, auditing for data lineage. A small software vendor can't afford that stack. So they get acquired, or they disappear. Seventy-two percent of SaaS M&A targets pitched AI as their core value in 2025, but what they were really offering was the compliance machinery already baked in. The enterprise software market is growing to $317.5 billion in 2026 (13.8% year-over-year growth), but that growth is concentrated at the top: big platforms expanding their compliance infrastructure, not new entrants building novel solutions.

The compliance tax here is turning simplicity into a luxury. A firm with established governance practices, existing audit trails, and deep regulatory relationships can layer AI into their products. They can afford the explainability audits, the annual security updates, the data-retention protocol changes. Smaller competitors, regional banks, independent lenders, and software vendors without enterprise backing—they face the same regulatory demands but can't spread the cost. Some will consolidate. Others will retreat into niches too small or too specialized for regulators to scrutinize heavily. The middle is being crushed.

The evidence

  • Credit bureaus: TransUnion exposed 4.4 million Americans in August 2025; Moody's reported 9% revenue growth and 17% operating income increase in 2025.
  • Enterprise software: $317.5 billion market in 2026 growing 13.8% year-over-year; Salesforce acquired Informatica (Nov 2025), Qualified.com (April 2026), and Fin (June 2026) for AI-governance infrastructure.
  • SaaS consolidation: 72% of M&A targets in 2025 pitched AI as core value, revealing that compliance-ready infrastructure is the new acquisition driver.
  • Alternative scoring: Zest AI demonstrated its model could approve 25% more loans while holding risk constant, disrupting the traditional credit-bureau moat.
  • Regulatory pressure: SEC's proposed overhaul of rating agency rules (2026) mandates governance oversight, analyst independence audits, and methodology disclosure.

Who rides it

Big platforms with existing compliance infrastructure win. Moody's, Salesforce, and other scale players can absorb the regulatory burden and amortize it across customers. Acquisition targets win temporarily—they get bought before the compliance tax makes them unviable. Consultants win. Every new regulation spawns demand for compliance auditing, governance frameworks, and integration work.

Who's squeezed

Regional credit unions, independent fintech lenders, and mid-market software vendors lose. They face the same SEC requirements, the same explainability audits, the same breach-response protocols as Moody's or Salesforce. They just can't spread the cost. Some will fold. Others will get acquired, shedding independence. The margin for a regional competitor shrinks faster than the market grows.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The consolidation cascade. As compliance costs kill mid-market players, the industry becomes more concentrated. Three credit bureaus, a handful of rating firms, a few software giants controlling the core infrastructure. That concentration makes regulatory capture easier and consumer choice nearly nonexistent. When one firm dominates and faces minimal competition, regulators lose their most powerful lever: the threat of market disruption if they overreach.

E · The big picture

The Compliance Tax

A patchwork of AI, privacy, climate, and cyber rules turns compliance into a rising cost that favors scale and feeds consultants.

Compliance used to be a cost of doing business. Now it's becoming a business model unto itself—and it's rewarding scale while crushing the small operator. Every new rule, from AI governance to data privacy to climate disclosure, requires legal expertise, IT infrastructure, and specialized talent that only large organizations can afford to maintain. The result is a form of regulatory tax that transfers wealth from small businesses to consultants, law firms, and the biggest players who can absorb the cost.

What changed

Compliance costs have become the new barrier to entry in nearly every sector. In finance, the 2023 bank failures (SVB in March, Signature Bank in March, First Republic in May 2023) triggered a regulatory backlash that has hit smaller banks hardest—they lack the compliance infrastructure that the big four now rely on to stay ahead of regulators. Commercial banking profit margins compressed to 19.7% in 2025 (down from higher historical levels before the rate-cut cycle), but the pain fell unevenly: large banks absorbed technology spending while smaller players watched deposit flows shrink and regulatory scrutiny intensify. This is not a temporary disruption—it's baked in. The $1.26 trillion commercial real estate maturity wall coming by 2027, with loans refinancing from 4.3% to 6.2%, will demand sophisticated compliance and risk management tools that only the largest institutions can build or purchase.

Healthcare is a living laboratory of compliance tax at work. US hospitals face reimbursement that covers only 82-87 cents per dollar of care, but they must still comply with Medicare's quality reporting, privacy rules, and increasingly, AI governance for diagnostic tools. AI adoption accelerated to 75% of health systems in 2026 (up from 59% in 2025), not because it improved margins but because regulators and payers started demanding it—and the compliance overhead of implementing, auditing, and documenting AI systems is enormous. Yet only large hospital systems can justify the investment. Steward Health Care's bankruptcy in 2025 (the largest hospital-sector bankruptcy in 30 years) and Prospect Medical Holdings' Chapter 11 filing (shedding 10 of 16 hospitals in January 2025) both point to the same story: regional operators with 5-50 hospitals could not scale compliance and operations fast enough to keep up. Meanwhile, consolidation surged in Q1 2026 with 22 transactions worth $14.5 billion—the highest Q1 in five years—because size now confers survival.

Law firms are the compliance tax's beneficiaries. The $426.7 billion legal services market posted record 2025 profits, but the underlying growth was only 1.9 percent while expenses surged 9.1 percent. That gap is pure compliance tax: firms raised rates (per-lawyer billing capacity up 16.8%) to pay for regulatory work, AI infrastructure (tech budgets up 9.7-11 percent in 2025 alone), and the merged-firm overhead needed to handle multinational regulation. Sixty-three law firm mergers occurred in 2025 (59 tracked by Fairfax Associates, up 18 percent from 2024), and at least 16 deals already announced for 2026 completion, because regulatory chaos forces corporates to hire bigger firms with deeper benches. But here's the tax: 59 percent of corporate clients surveyed in 2025 report no clear savings from outside counsel using AI, yet they still paid for that AI buildout. The rate hike was not about efficiency—it was about compliance volume.

In data processing and hosting, compliance has become a scarce resource itself. The EU AI Act reached full effect on August 2, 2026, triggering a global compliance architecture. US data center electricity demand surged from 23 GW in 2023 to 42 GW in 2026 as AI hyperscalers compete for power and cooling—but every new data center needs environmental compliance, grid approval, and labor certifications that tie up years of project timeline. Smaller hosting operators simply cannot navigate this. Consolidation accelerated in Q1 2026 with $21+ billion in data center M&A (the most active quarter on record), and the five largest hyperscalers will spend $630 billion on infrastructure in 2026, up 36 percent from 2025. Ninety percent of data center operators cite staffing constraints as a bottleneck, and demand for AI infrastructure specialists, high-voltage engineers, and cooling technicians far outpaces supply—another compliance tax: you must hire certified talent or you cannot legally operate.

The evidence

  • Banking: Commercial banking margins compressed to 19.7% (2025) as regulatory costs from 2023 bank failures (SVB, Signature, First Republic) hit smaller banks disproportionately hard relative to the big four's infrastructure.
  • Healthcare: US hospitals reimburse at 82-87 cents per dollar (2025-2026) yet must comply with AI governance; Steward Health Care bankruptcy (2025, largest in 30 years) and Prospect Medical Holdings Chapter 11 (January 2025) exemplify regional operators unable to scale compliance fast enough.
  • Legal Services: Law firms posted record 2025 profits on rate hikes (per-lawyer billing +16.8%), not efficiency gains; legal demand grew only 1.9% while expenses surged 9.1%—the gap is compliance and AI infrastructure costs passed to clients; 59% of corporate clients report no savings from AI tools (2025).
  • Data Centers: Five hyperscalers spending $630 billion on infrastructure in 2026 (+36% from 2025), with $450 billion targeting AI; EU AI Act effective August 2, 2026, forces compliance architecture; 90% of operators cite staffing constraints as bottleneck.
  • Consolidation: Hospital M&A hit 22 deals ($14.5B in Q1 2026, highest Q1 in 5+ years); 63 law firm mergers in 2025 (+18% from 2024); data center M&A reached $21+ billion in Q1 2026 (most active quarter on record); size is the survival strategy under compliance tax.

Who rides it

The big platforms win. JPMorgan absorbed First Republic in May 2023 and emerged stronger relative to smaller competitors. Larger hospital systems (like Ascension, buying AmSurg for $3.9 billion) grab market share from regional operators who cannot afford compliance overhead. The largest law firms (Hogan Lovells acquired Cadwalader to create a $3.6 billion revenue firm) consolidate regulatory work and raise rates because corporates have no alternative—and they pass the compliance tax to their smaller clients. In data processing, the five hyperscalers capture 90 percent of AI infrastructure investment because they alone can navigate power allocation, environmental compliance, and talent acquisition across multiple geographies. Consultants, advisors, and service providers also win: law firms, compliance technologists, and audit firms all benefit from the rising cost of rule-keeping.

Who's squeezed

Small and mid-sized operators get squeezed. Community banks cannot afford the compliance infrastructure that the big four now rely on, so deposits flow to larger institutions (uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 alone, suggesting clients are shopping rates toward bigger names). Regional hospital systems cannot justify AI infrastructure and compliance audits, forcing bankruptcies (20 healthcare bankruptcies in 2025, up from 15 in 2024) or acquisition at fire-sale prices. Small law firms lose corporate clients to Am Law 100 firms because multinationals need consolidated regulatory expertise under one roof. Mid-tier data center operators cannot compete for power, land, or talent in the hyperscaler arms race, leading to specialization or exit. The compliance tax is a wealth transfer from small business to scale, from operator to advisor, and from Main Street to Wall Street.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that compliance tax becomes self-reinforcing. As rules accumulate (AI governance, climate disclosure, privacy, cybersecurity, labor), the cost of staying compliant grows exponentially, not linearly. Small operators reach a tipping point where they cannot afford entry anymore—not because the rule is individually too expensive, but because the total compliance surface is too broad. This creates a permanent moat for the already-large and locks out new entrants. In healthcare, this already happened: Steward and Prospect bankruptcies were not caused by bad clinical care but by the inability to afford consolidated compliance, IT infrastructure, and regulatory staffing across dozens of facilities. The risk is systemic concentration—in every sector, compliance becomes an invisible tax that transfers market share from the distributed to the consolidated. If this continues unabated, we end up with a smaller number of larger operators, each one a more complex regulatory animal but with no real efficiency gain. We trade agility and competition for compliance theater and consolidation.

Compliance costs are becoming invisible taxes that reward scale, feed consultants, and lock out small operators—concentrating markets without delivering efficiency.

Larger hospital systems (like Ascension, buying AmSurg for $3.9 billion) grab market share from regional operators who cannot afford compliance overhead. The largest law firms (Hogan Lovells acquired Cadwalader to create a $3.6 billion revenue firm) consolidate regulatory work and raise rates because corporates have no alternative—and they pass the compliance tax to their smaller clients. In data processing, the five hyperscalers capture 90 percent of AI infrastructure investment because they alone can navigate power allocation, environmental compliance, and talent acquisition across multiple geographies. Consultants, advisors, and service providers also win: law firms, compliance technologists, and audit firms all benefit from the rising cost of rule-keeping.

Who's squeezed across the board

Small and mid-sized operators get squeezed. Community banks cannot afford the compliance infrastructure that the big four now rely on, so deposits flow to larger institutions (uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 alone, suggesting clients are shopping rates toward bigger names). Regional hospital systems cannot justify AI infrastructure and compliance audits, forcing bankruptcies (20 healthcare bankruptcies in 2025, up from 15 in 2024) or acquisition at fire-sale prices. Small law firms lose corporate clients to Am Law 100 firms because multinationals need consolidated regulatory expertise under one roof. Mid-tier data center operators cannot compete for power, land, or talent in the hyperscaler arms race, leading to specialization or exit. The compliance tax is a wealth transfer from small business to scale, from operator to advisor, and from Main Street to Wall Street.

The biggest tension

The one to watch

The single biggest risk is that compliance tax becomes self-reinforcing. As rules accumulate (AI governance, climate disclosure, privacy, cybersecurity, labor), the cost of staying compliant grows exponentially, not linearly. Small operators reach a tipping point where they cannot afford entry anymore—not because the rule is individually too expensive, but because the total compliance surface is too broad. This creates a permanent moat for the already-large and locks out new entrants. In healthcare, this already happened: Steward and Prospect bankruptcies were not caused by bad clinical care but by the inability to afford consolidated compliance, IT infrastructure, and regulatory staffing across dozens of facilities. The risk is systemic concentration—in every sector, compliance becomes an invisible tax that transfers market share from the distributed to the consolidated. If this continues unabated, we end up with a smaller number of larger operators, each one a more complex regulatory animal but with no real efficiency gain. We trade agility and competition for compliance theater and consolidation.
