E · The big picture

The Compute Super-Cycle

AI's hunger for power is reshaping the grid and everything plugged into it—whoever has electricity, land, and cooling near the data centers wins a once-in-a-generation buildout.

For 15 years, electricity was cheap and transmission was abundant. That era ended in 2024. AI data centers—training rigs burning 30–100+ kilowatts per rack, inference farms running 10–20 kW steady—have turned the US power grid from a taken-for-granted utility into a scarce, rationed resource. The entire economy is suddenly competing for electrons, and the winners are those who own generation, land, and cooling near demand.

What changed

Until 2020, colocation facilities competed on real estate—who had the most square footage. Today they compete on power. The US colocation market reached $72.37 billion in 2026 (up from $46.84 billion in 2025, a 54.6% jump in one year) and occupancy is at 1% vacancy, meaning there is nowhere left to build. The colocation industry's 11.5% CAGR through 2030 masks the real story: pricing has jumped 17–19% in just two years after 15 years of decline. Electricity access, not real estate, is now the moat. The grid cannot keep up. Interconnection queues exceed 1,400 gigawatts of stuck requests, with lead times stretching to four to five years in saturated markets like Northern Virginia, Dallas, and Phoenix. Federal regulators (FERC, December 2025) issued data-center-specific transmission tariffs for PJM, and states are rushing their own—Oregon signed the POWER Act in August 2025 mandating 10-year power-purchase agreements for any facility over 20 megawatts.

This squeeze on electricity has catalyzed what utilities are calling "The Great Re-Gassing." Natural gas generation remains at 40% of US electricity in 2026, but in March 2026, NextEra Energy announced a historic 10-gigawatt natural gas expansion in Texas and Pennsylvania, backed by the Trump administration, explicitly to meet AI data center demand. Duke Energy committed $103 billion in capex for 2026–2030, including 10 gigawatts of new gas procurement in the Carolinas. Southern Company is expanding similarly. The coal industry, which had been in steady decline, saw a temporary rebound to 17% generation share in 2025 (from under 15% previously) as Henry Hub natural gas prices surged 60% in 2025 and are forecast to rise another 30% by 2027. Coal retirements hit a 15-year low of 2.6 gigawatts in 2025, delayed by DOE emergency orders to keep plants online. None of this solves the underlying problem: utilities are racing to build generation and transmission infrastructure that will take years to permit and construct, while data centers are arriving now.

The transmission system is the true bottleneck. The electric power transmission market reached $536.2 billion in 2025 (up from $476.1 billion in 2022, a 12.6% increase in three years), but $1.4 trillion in transmission investment is planned for 2025–2030—and that may not be enough. Data centers will consume 75.8 gigawatts by 2026, accounting for nearly 90 gigawatts of total peak load growth. Wholesale power costs in PJM spiked 49% in 2025, with capacity costs up 262%, driven by data center demand outrunning supply. Profit margins at utilities have climbed to 15% of revenue in 2025, double the historical 7–8% norm. Companies like NextEra and Dominion merged in May–June 2026 (a $66.8 billion deal) to secure generation and transmission assets before constraints tighten further. Battery storage deployment is exploding—24 gigawatts planned for 2026 versus 15 gigawatts added in 2025—as operators scramble to buffer intermittent renewables and smooth demand peaks. Tech giants (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta) are responding by investing directly in generation: buying renewable energy, negotiating long-term PPAs, and signing deals with utilities for dedicated capacity.

This buildout is creating a secondary labor shortage. Data center construction spending hit $50.7 billion annualized in April 2026, up 28% year-over-year, and electricians are the constrained input. Journeymen electricians now earn $76,000–$110,000+, with specialists in solar, EV charging, and data center work commanding premium rates. However, tariffs have hit the industry hard: copper wiring prices jumped 18%, electrical panels 22%, squeezing smaller contractors' margins while consolidation accelerates. The electricians industry as a whole is $370.9 billion (2026) and has added businesses at a 3.7% CAGR, but residential construction has collapsed due to high interest rates, forcing the industry to depend on data center work as its growth engine. The structural mismatch is clear: the grid, generation capacity, transmission, and skilled labor are all becoming scarce at the same moment. Whoever owns renewable generation near cooling water, has transmission capacity, controls real estate, or can command electrician labor wins. Everyone else is stuck in a queue.

The evidence

  • Colocation facilities: Market cap reached $72.37 billion US in 2026 (up from $46.84 billion in 2025) with occupancy at 1% vacancy and pricing up 17–19% after 15 years of decline.
  • Electric power transmission: Market size $536.2 billion in 2025 (up from $476.1 billion in 2022); $1.4 trillion investment planned 2025–2030; utility profit margins doubled to 15% of revenue in 2025 from historical 7–8% norm.
  • Coal and natural gas power: Natural gas remains 40% of US generation (down from 42% in 2024); NextEra Energy announced historic 10 GW gas expansion in March 2026 for AI data centers; coal retirements hit 15-year low of 2.6 GW in 2025 due to emergency delays.
  • Electricians industry: Data center construction spending $50.7 billion annualized (April 2026), up 28% YoY; journeymen earn $76,000–$110,000+; copper wiring up 18%, electrical panels up 22% due to tariffs.
  • Data center interconnection: Queues exceed 1,400 GW with 4–5-year lead times; wholesale power costs in PJM up 49% in 2025 with capacity costs up 262%; NextEra–Dominion merger ($66.8 billion, June 2026) driven by need to secure generation and transmission assets.

Who rides it

Tech giants (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta) and utilities with existing generation assets or access to renewable energy sources win decisively. They can negotiate long-term PPAs, build their own solar and wind farms near data centers, and secure transmission capacity before constraints tighten. Equinix and Digital Realty, the two largest colocation operators (combined ~20% US share), win by raising prices and controlling capacity-constrained facilities. Renewable energy companies win in the near term by securing long-term power contracts. Utilities with coal or gas plants and transmission assets also win—profit margins have doubled—though the long-term bet is on gas expansion (not coal). Large, well-capitalized electrical contractors with data center specialization win; smaller, undercapitalized firms squeeze out.

Who's squeezed

Smaller colocation operators who lack power PPAs or renewable generation contracts lose. Residential construction and small electrical contractors lose because talent and capital flow to higher-margin data center work. Consumers face rising electricity rates as utilities pass through interconnection and capital costs. States without natural gas infrastructure or renewable capacity lose—California and the Mid-Atlantic remain capacity-constrained and cannot attract new major facilities. Coal plant workers lose as retirements resume once gas capacity comes online. Independent power producers without long-term contracts (like Pine Gate Renewables, which filed Chapter 11 in November 2025) lose to scale and consolidation.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is a misalignment between the speed at which data centers are being built and the speed at which the grid can be upgraded. Data center construction is running 28% year-over-year growth, but FERC interconnection rule changes won't take effect until 2026 at the earliest, and transmission buildout takes 5–7 years. If data centers are installed faster than generation and transmission can support them, the grid will experience rolling blackouts, forced demand destruction (shutdowns of data centers or other large loads), and a demand shock that crashes semiconductor and AI chip prices. Alternatively, utilities overbuild natural gas capacity to rush online, locking in carbon-intensive infrastructure for decades and wasting capital on stranded assets once renewables scale. A third risk: permitting bottlenecks remain unsolved. FERC rules help, but state and local permitting in data center hubs (Virginia, Texas, Arizona) is still a multi-year slog. The queue will get worse before it gets better.

AI made electricity and land scarce again, and the power-and-buildout chain is the trade of the decade.

The single biggest risk is a misalignment between the speed at which data centers are being built and the speed at which the grid can be upgraded. Data center construction is running 28% year-over-year growth, but FERC interconnection rule changes won't take effect until 2026 at the earliest, and transmission buildout takes 5–7 years. If data centers are installed faster than generation and transmission can support them, the grid will experience rolling blackouts, forced demand destruction (shutdowns of data centers or other large loads), and a demand shock that crashes semiconductor and AI chip prices. Alternatively, utilities overbuild natural gas capacity to rush online, locking in carbon-intensive infrastructure for decades and wasting capital on stranded assets once renewables scale. A third risk: permitting bottlenecks remain unsolved. FERC rules help, but state and local permitting in data center hubs (Virginia, Texas, Arizona) is still a multi-year slog. The queue will get worse before it gets better.

A · Renting the expert

The expert, on demand

Companies now rent senior judgment by the call or the project instead of hiring it full-time.

You used to hire a partner-level strategist for three years. Now you call them once, pay $2,000–$5,000 per hour, get what you need, and hang up. The expert networks business—which connects companies to on-demand senior talent for specific projects or judgments—is scaling on this shift. And it is being rebuilt from the inside by AI right now.

What changed

For decades, expert networks made their money one call at a time. A hedge fund needed to understand a biotech CEO's strategy; they called an expert network, got matched with a retired pharma exec, paid $2,000–$5,000 for the call, and got an hour of judgment. By 2025, the market for this—expert networks alone—sat at $1.8 billion in the US, growing about 4.3% that year, with an estimated 5,000–6,000 people working across roughly 65 independent companies. Five major players controlled 60% of it. The margins held at about 14%, down slightly from 15.6% in 2016 because labor and compliance costs had climbed. It was a steady, high-margin, boutique business.

Then AI broke the model. In June 2024, AlphaSense—the largest expert networks company by volume—bought Tegus, merging the two biggest libraries of past expert call transcripts under one roof. Suddenly, instead of scheduling a new expert call at $2,000–$5,000, a client could ask: "Give me the insights from every pharmaceutical CEO call we've ever taken." Within hours, an AI system could synthesize thousands of hours of conversation into a research memo. The marginal cost dropped from $2,000 to near zero. Research projects that used to take 2–5 days now take 2 hours. AlphaSense's CEO said openly that the future is not scheduling calls but building AI systems that learn from past conversations at scale. By April 2026, just two years later, AlphaSense had raised $650 million in new funding at a $4 billion valuation—almost entirely on the strength of this AI-powered consolidation story. Investors were betting not on expert networks as a labor business but on expert networks as a data monopoly.

The ripple is reshaping both ends of the market. First: the expert side. Sixty-one percent of expert networks now use AI-driven expert matching, meaning an algorithm picks the right person faster than a human coordinator did in 2020. Fifty-six percent can schedule a consultation within 24 hours. And by 2026, agentic AI systems—software agents that work autonomously—began automating entire end-to-end research workflows, cutting sourcing time from 2–5 days down to 2 hours. You no longer hire an expert for deep judgment; you rent the platform's ability to synthesize what it already knows. Second: the consulting side felt the pressure acutely. The US management consulting market was $370 billion in 2026, growing 4–5% a year, but hollowing from within. By 2025, for the first time in history, AI roles outnumbered entry-level consultant roles at top firms—a complete inversion from 2015, when there were nearly four junior consultants for every AI role. Hiring across consulting was down 20% from 2023 peaks. Consultant-specific roles were down 40%. Meanwhile, federal agencies cut roughly $5 billion in consulting contracts in early 2025, forcing immediate layoffs at Deloitte, Accenture, and IBM. Clients, exhausted by hourly billing, began demanding measurable ROI and pushing toward outcome-based pricing, subscriptions, and contingency fees. Traditional junior work—the on-ramp to the profession—was evaporating.

The consolidation accelerated. AlphaSense bought Tegus in 2024. Slingshot Insights bought Noble Insights in June 2025. Bridger bought Deepbench in February 2024. Levine Leichtman Capital Partners bought The Expert Institute's legal library in September 2024. The strategy was the same each time: control the transcript library, automate the matching, and undercut the pay-per-call model with AI synthesis. Compensation in consulting inverted: AI specialists commanded 56% wage premiums over traditional software roles by 2025, while junior consultant salaries stalled. The industry stratified into winners and losers fast. Big Four firms controlled the federal access and the scale to absorb the AI transition. Boutique specialists won on depth and agility, offering outcomes instead of hours. Mid-market consulting firms got squeezed between the two.

The evidence

  • Expert networks: $1.8B US market in 2025, but AI-driven consolidation (AlphaSense/Tegus, June 2024) reshaping the model from pay-per-call to transcript-library monopoly.
  • Management consulting: $370B US market in 2026 (4–5% CAGR), but AI roles now outnumber entry-level consultants at top firms for the first time—a reversal from 2015.
  • Federal spending collapse: Pentagon and US agencies cut $5B in consulting contracts in early 2025, forcing layoffs at Deloitte, Accenture, IBM.
  • Expert matching: 61% of expert networks use AI-driven matching by 2025; agentic workflows automate sourcing in 2–5 days down to 2 hours by 2026.
  • Consulting stratification: Big Four control scale; boutique firms win on agility; mid-market squeezed. AI specialists earn 56% premiums; junior consultant salaries stalled (2025).

Who rides it

Elite consulting firms and expert network platforms that own large call-transcript libraries win big. AlphaSense's $4 billion valuation (April 2026) signals that data monopolies on expert knowledge are worth more than labor. Boutique specialists who offer bespoke outcomes (not hours) and AI experts who can synthesize existing knowledge into actionable patterns capture wage premiums and job security. Senior strategists with rare judgment also benefit—they get paid well per call and no longer have to work full-time. Platforms that consolidate transcript libraries and automate matching reduce overhead and pricing pressure simultaneously.

Who's squeezed

Junior consultants and mid-market consulting firms absorb the worst of it. Entry-level consulting roles have been flat or declining as AI takes over routine analysis work. Federal austerity cut $5 billion in contracts in 2025 alone, forcing sudden layoffs. Mid-market firms lack the federal access of Big Four and the specialized depth of boutiques, so they are squeezed on both margins. Traditional expert networks that rely on one-off calls at $2,000–$5,000 each are being undercut by platforms that offer past research synthesized by AI at fraction of the price. Individual experts who are not rare or senior also lose—they compete with transcript libraries and AI agents that can search decades of prior calls for answers.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that AI synthesis of past expert calls creates a false sense of knowledge while hiding how out of date the underlying data is. If a platform like AlphaSense synthesizes insights from 10,000 pharma CEO calls recorded over the past five years, the answer sounds authoritative but may miss recent strategy shifts, new competitors, or regulatory changes that happened in the past quarter. Companies paying for AI-synthesized expert research instead of live calls could miss market inflection points. A second risk is consolidation around a few platforms means a few companies now control who gets asked for expertise and how expertise is monetized, creating new rent-seeking choke points.

The expert networks industry, which rents out senior expertise by the hour, is consolidating fast as AI makes past call transcripts instantly searchable and actionable.

A · Renting the expert

Fractional Leadership

Renting the expert: fractional CFOs and coaches replace permanent executives at smaller firms.

For decades, having a Chief Financial Officer meant hiring a full-time employee—salary, benefits, office desk, the whole thing. Now a company with $10 million in revenue can rent a fractional CFO for 10 hours a week at $150 an hour, getting expert judgment without the permanent headcount. The business coaching market alone is $20 billion in 2026, up from $10.9 billion in 2021. Fractional roles are not a niche anymore. They are how companies below Fortune 500 size now staffs their leadership."

What changed

The executive suite used to be binary: you either had a CFO as an employee, or you didn't. That constraint—the lumpy, all-or-nothing cost of permanent headcount—made expertise expensive and inaccessible. Now platforms and individual practitioners rent it by the hour. The fractional CFO and interim-executive markets grew because the economics shifted: companies need strategic guidance on cash flow, tax strategy, and board prep, but they do not need it forty hours a week, and they do not want to carry six figures in base salary plus benefits to get it. The interim executive market hit 120,000 workers by 2024, up from 60,000 in 2022—a doubling in two years—proving the demand is real and structural, not cyclical.

Business coaching is the clearest signal of this unbundling. The market grew from $10.9 billion in 2021 to $20.0 billion in 2026, but the growth rate actually slowed from 1.9% CAGR to 2.9% in 2026 because the market saturated. What changed is how coaching gets delivered: AI-assisted coaching segments grew at 22 percent to 28 percent annually, versus 3 percent to 5 percent for traditional one-on-one coaching. The number of business coaches exploded from 71,000 in 2019 to 145,500 in 2024. Most are nonemployees or solo practitioners working fractionally. What was once a luxury perk for the top 0.1 percent of executives—hiring a $300-an-hour coach—is now commoditized into monthly subscriptions at $100 bundled into HR platforms or delivered as a hybrid: 91 percent of clients perceive AI-augmented coaching as effective as in-person sessions, even as they still prefer the human touch for trust and continuity.

Executive search recruiters faced the hardest hit. The market was $8.8 billion in 2022 and is now $10.2 billion in 2026—growth that masks a 3.3 percent annual decline over the five-year period, followed by tentative recovery. The bottleneck is brutal: clients demand a shortlist in under a week, but executive search requires time for board-level due diligence and vetting. This gap favors large firms with AI workflows and global networks but crushes smaller practices. At the same time, fractional and interim executives—the very talent these recruiters used to place permanently—are mushrooming. Companies now hire external CEOs for 33 percent of successions in 2026, up from 18 percent in 2024, yet those hires are increasingly temporary or part-time rather than permanent. CEO turnover on the S&P 500 hit a twelve-point-five percent replacement rate in 2025, the highest in eight years, creating apparent tailwind. But the tailwind is illusory: those new external hires are often executives-for-hire, not permanent placements. Traditional search firms responded by diversifying into coaching (35 percent of top performers now offer it) and advisory consulting (30 percent), essentially admitting that the permanent placement business is contracting and they must capture fractional work to survive.

Regulation has tilted toward the fractional side. The International Coaching Federation updated its Code of Ethics in Q1 2025 to explicitly cover AI-assisted coaching, signaling that the hybrid "cyborg coach" model is here to stay. In January 2026, the ICF raised Minimum Skills Requirements for ACC and MCC credentials, immediately widening the gap between credentialed and non-credentialed coaches. This does not stop anyone from calling themselves a coach—there is no US licensing requirement—but it does create a two-tier market: high-credential, high-trust coaches can command premium fractional rates, while untrained practitioners undercut them. The search firms, meanwhile, face no such floor. Acquisition waves in 2025-2026—Advent LLP buying Heidrick & Struggles for $1.3 billion, Southfield Capital taking Metric Search for $100 million—signal that private equity is consolidating the fragmented search market, betting that scale and tech leverage can restore margins. But those deals come against the backdrop of structural decline, not growth.

The evidence

  • Business Coaching: Market grew from $10.9 billion in 2021 to $20.0 billion in 2026, now mostly delivered fractionally via online platforms and AI-augmented hybrid models (22-28% annual growth for AI segments).
  • Executive Search: Weakened by fractional alternatives—market declined 3.3% CAGR from 2021-2026, but CEO succession externalization rose sharply (33% of S&P 500 roles in 2026, up from 18% in 2024).
  • Interim Executives: Fractional and interim leadership market hit 120,000 workers by 2024, doubled from 60,000 in 2022, capturing permanent placement demand that traditional search firms once owned.
  • Coaching Workforce: Explosive growth from 71,000 coaches in 2019 to 145,500 in 2024; 88% are nonemployers, making fractional work the industry norm, not the exception.
  • Regulation Shift: ICF updated Code of Ethics in Q1 2025 to cover AI-assisted coaching; January 2026 raised credential floors (ACC/MCC), creating a two-tier market of credentialed premium and uncredentialed discount fractional coaches.

Who rides it

Platforms matching fractional talent to companies win big. Coaches with ICF credentials, tech-savvy delivery, and a strong referral network can command premium hourly rates ($150-$300) while working fractionally—no office overhead, no commute, multiple clients in parallel. Larger executive search firms with AI capability and global networks win on the placement side because they can deliver shortlists fast; they survive by layering in coaching and advisory, capturing the fractional revenue stream. Smaller mid-market companies win too: they get access to CFOs, CMOs, and executive coaches they could never afford full-time, allowing them to punch above their weight on strategy and execution.

Who's squeezed

Full-time executive employees are squeezed. If your company is $50 million in revenue and considering hiring a VP of Finance, you now compete against fractional CFOs who cost a third of the salary and carry no headcount risk. Mid-size search firms without AI, global reach, or diversification into coaching are losing ground—they cannot promise speed, they cannot layer advisory, and they watch permanent placements shrink as interim becomes the default. Entry-level talent gets hit too: there are 145,500 coaches in 2024, but 88% work as nonemployees, meaning no benefits, no stable income, and constant pressure to book the next client or sharpen skills to differentiate from AI.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is credential inflation and the erosion of trust. Right now, 91 percent of clients find AI-augmented coaching as effective as human coaching, which sounds like vindication for the platforms. But this perception can flip if fractional coaches become so commoditized that quality collapses—clients hire based on price, not judgment, and outcomes worsen. The second risk is that this market bifurcates permanently into premium credentialed coaches (ICF ACC/MCC, high price, high trust, tight supply) and a cheap, undifferentiated commoditized tier (unlicensed, AI-heavy, low price, high churn). A talented executive considering becoming a fractional CFO might instead stay in a full-time role for security, shrinking the supply of proven, experienced fractional talent and leaving the market to junior or mediocre practitioners. The third risk is platform capture: as Advent, Southfield, and other PE firms consolidate search and coaching platforms, they will prioritize margin extraction over quality, squeezing the fractional workers and leaving smaller firms with no way to compete on anything but price.

A · Renting the expert

Advice as a rented service

Whole functions like HR, marketing, and compliance now rent from expert consultants instead of building permanent teams—and the cut keeps shrinking.

Companies stopped hiring permanent staff for specialist functions. Now they rent. HR departments rent compliance advice from consultants. Marketing teams rent campaign strategy from agencies. Environmental risk gets outsourced to specialized firms. The effect is predictable: consultants multiply, but each one makes less.

What changed

The unbundling of permanent work into rented services made three things scarce and changed how advice works. First, in-house expertise became a luxury only the largest firms could keep. By 2025, HR consulting was a $39.4 billion market (up from $27.3 billion in 2022)—growth that came almost entirely from companies externalizing functions they used to staff. Instead of hiring a director of compliance, a firm rents compliance help by the hour. Instead of building a marketing team, they rent strategic guidance from an agency. Marketing consulting alone is now an $88.4 billion market (up from $63.4 billion in 2022), with 323,000 agencies competing for work. Environmental consulting sits at $27.4 billion (up from $23.6 billion in 2022), driven by EPA rules and corporate climate targets that are too dense for most companies to navigate alone.

But renting advice made the consultants' margins cheaper. HR consulting margins used to run 25-40% for mid-market work; by 2026, they'd dropped to 15-40% because competition flattened prices and three simultaneous headwinds hit consultants. First, software bundles like TriNet, Rippling, and Paychex now combine payroll, compliance, and employee analytics in a single platform—eroding the old advisory moat. Second, AI spending jumped 50% year-over-year in 2025 while overall HR budgets shrank, forcing consultants to pivot from selling system selection (easier, higher margin) to change management and upskilling (harder, lower margin). Third, regulatory density exploded: 48 states changed wage or leave laws in 2025, and pay transparency rules are now law in 30+ jurisdictions. This kept demand high but turned compliance advice into commodity work. Marketing consultants faced similar pressure: only 28% raised prices from 2024 to 2025 (down from higher rates in 2021–2022), while digital agencies saw net margins fall to 13% from historical highs, as clients demanded outcome-based fees instead of time-based rates. Environmental consultants got pinched too: tariff escalation in 2025 pushed steel and aluminum duties to 50%, stretching timelines and squeezing margins to 8-9% EBITDA as labor costs spiked and licensed engineers stayed scarce.

What became newly valuable was implementation and speed. When 78% of global organizations used AI by 2025 and 71% adopted generative AI, clients stopped buying advice on whether to adopt—they bought advice on how to execute it fast. McKinsey cut 3,000–4,000 jobs in 2025, concentrated in junior research roles where generative AI compressed delivery time. But the same consultancies pivoted hard to implementation-heavy work: IT consulting on AI strategy grew 89% year-over-year in 2025. Compliance consulting stayed valuable, but for a different reason: regulations multiplied and diverged. 20 US state privacy laws, GDPR, CCPA, and 30+ pay-transparency jurisdictions meant that clients needed expert translation of rules—but that work was ripe for automation and offshoring. The risk shifted. Renting advice made the firm's talent flexible (no payroll overhead), but it meant that advice quality depended on someone else's bench strength, not your own hiring and training. And the consultant's risk flipped: instead of managing long-term client relationships with stable margins, they competed in a commoditizing market with outcome-based pricing, regulatory complexity that required constant upskilling, and AI tools that automated junior work faster than they could hire.

The evidence

  • HR consulting hit $39.4 billion in 2025, up 44% from $27.3 billion in 2022—but growth slowed to 1.4% in 2026 as software platforms like Rippling and TriNet bundled away the advisory moat.
  • Marketing consulting is now $88.4 billion in 2025, with only 28% of agencies raising prices from 2024 to 2025—brutal price compression even as demand remained high because clients shifted to outcome-based fees.
  • Environmental consulting grew to $27.4 billion in 2025 but margins squeezed to 8-9% EBITDA due to tariff escalation (steel/aluminum duties to 50% in 2025) and acute engineer shortages described as 'the tightest in a generation'.
  • 48 states changed wage or leave laws in 2025 and 30+ jurisdictions enacted pay transparency rules—keeping compliance consulting demand high but turning it into commodity work competitors could undercut.
  • IT consulting on AI strategy grew 89% year-over-year in 2025, while McKinsey cut 3,000–4,000 jobs focused on junior research where generative AI compressed delivery—showing shift from advice to implementation.

Who rides it

Implementation specialists and niche expertise consultancies. Firms that built depth in one domain—AI change management, regulatory translation, climate risk modeling—won because they could charge more and automate less. McKinsey's cuts targeted junior research roles; their remaining headcount shifted to client execution and strategic transformation. Environmental consultancies that merged (WSP acquired Power Engineers for $1.78 billion in February 2025) won because they could knit together geographic reach and specialist depth. Small consultancies that stayed focused on one thing—one industry, one regulatory area, one AI risk—remained defensible. And the platforms themselves won: software bundles that reduced advisory need (Rippling, TriNet, Paychex) won because they automated the low-end advisory work and captured recurring revenue.

Who's squeezed

Generalist consultants and junior talent. The 10,000 US marketing jobs eliminated in the first seven months of 2025 due to AI automation were mostly junior roles. Agencies that sold execution rather than strategy lost margin because clients started doing basic execution in-house with AI tools. Independent consultants who competed purely on availability or time got undercut by software bundles and platforms. And the traditional training pipeline broke: two-thirds of agency owners worried about the disappearance of entry-level roles in 2025, meaning fewer junior consultants meant fewer senior consultants to train, which meant less depth for mid-market firms that couldn't afford the expensive specialists.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that advice becomes both commoditized and ungovernable at once. Regulations multiplied (48 states changed wage laws, 30+ enacted pay-transparency rules, EPA expanded PFAS standards), but the cost of keeping up with them fell on the consultant and the client jointly—and the consultant's margins can't absorb it. When only 28% of agencies could raise prices in 2025, the incentive is to cut corners or hire cheaper labor overseas. But if compliance advice gets outsourced to the lowest-cost provider, the client's risk exposure rises. Similarly, when implementation became more valuable than advice (89% AI-strategy growth), consultants faced pressure to promise faster execution with smaller teams, which means higher execution risk and lower quality. The worry is a two-tier market: expensive, brand-name consultants who capture the implementation work and can train their own people, and cheap commodity consultants competing on cost with growing risk of missed deadlines, compliance gaps, and botched executions that expose clients to liability.

Renting expert advice from consultants instead of hiring permanent staff made expertise abundant and cheaper, but it also made margins thinner, execution riskier, and junior careers disappear.

B · The platforms in the middle

Who places the talent

Recruiters and brokers become the bottleneck as work fragments — they control the match and take 5 to 15 percent off the top.

When work unbundles from permanent jobs into fractional gigs, someone has to do the matching. Recruiters, freight brokers, and staffing platforms have become indispensable middlemen. They take a cut of every placement—and they're tightening their grip as demand for flexible work grows and regulation bears down on fraud.

What changed

The executive search market shows what happens when matching becomes scarce and scrutiny tightens. The sector was valued at $10.2 billion in 2026, down 3.3 percent annually from 2021–2026, yet the work itself is fragmenting. CEO succession hit an 8-year high in 2025 at 12.5 percent of S&P 500 seats, but the nature of placement is shifting: fractional and interim executives have exploded to 120,000 by 2024, double the 60,000 in 2022. Firms still capture 10 to 15 percent margins on profitable placements, but they're squeezed from both sides. Clients demand shortlists in under one week, forcing speed over rigor. Smaller recruiters can't compete with large firms deploying AI-augmented workflows and global networks. Recruitment Process Outsourcing providers are eating into director and selective C-suite roles at lower margins, and in-house HR plus LinkedIn have eroded the monopoly on executive intel that recruiters once owned. The firms adapting survive: 35 percent of top performers now offer coaching alongside placements, and 30 percent bundle in advisory consulting. Recent consolidation—Advent acquiring Heidrick & Struggles for $1.3 billion in Q4 2025, Spencer Stuart buying Meyler Campbell, ZRG acquiring Aspen Leadership—signals that scale and specialization are the only defensible moats.\n\nThe freight brokerage market reveals the same pattern but at industrial scale and with regulatory teeth. The broad market was worth $169.8 billion in 2026, but the narrow freight brokerage slice was $20.64 to $22.39 billion, growing 4.48 percent annually from 2025 to 2032. The real story is in the capacity crunch and the regulatory noose. Spot freight rates jumped 43 percent year-over-year in June 2026, with dry van rates up 66 cents per mile, and tender rejection rates exceeded 15 percent—the highest since early 2022. This spike reveals how tight the matching becomes when capacity is scarce: brokers can dictate terms because they control access to the load. Simultaneously, double brokering fraud spiraled to over 8,000 complaints in 2025, costing the industry $700 million to $1 billion annually. The FMCSA cracked down by doubling surety bond minimums from $75,000 to $150,000 and mandating real-time load tracking starting January 2026. Margins compressed from 5.6 percent in 2021 to expectations of 6.3 percent by 2026, yet digital transformation—platforms like Flexport, transportation management systems, AI-driven optimization—moved from competitive advantage to table stakes. The firms with scale and technology survive; the rest are squeezed. The industry expanded to approximately 124,000 establishments by 2026 from 107,631 in 2021, and headcount grew from 395,612 to 495,000 to 500,000, yet consolidation is accelerating: RXO acquired Coyote Logistics from UPS for $1.025 billion in September 2024, becoming the third-largest freight broker, and Echo Global Logistics acquired ITS Logistics in January 2026.\n\nWhat these two industries share is the same structural shift: fractional and gig work requires constant matching, and matching requires a platform or network. The middleman becomes essential—and therefore powerful. Margins are modest (5 to 15 percent, depending on the service), but the volume scales with fragmentation. As permanent roles unbundle, the matching layer grows fatter and more centralized. Larger platforms with AI, global reach, or compliance infrastructure have moats; smaller brokers and recruiters face commoditization or acquisition. Regulation—whether FMCSA surety bonds or SEC rules on executive placement practices—creates barriers to entry that protect incumbents while squeezing smaller players. The matching economy isn't about creating value; it's about controlling scarcity and taking the cut."

The evidence

  • Executive search firms: CEO succession at 8-year high (12.5% of S&P 500 in 2025), external hires nearly doubled to 33% of successions, yet fractional/interim executives exploded to 120,000 by 2024 (2x the 60,000 in 2022).
  • Freight brokers: Spot rates surged 43% year-over-year in June 2026, tender rejection rates hit 15% (highest since Q1 2022), revealing capacity constraints and the middleman's newfound pricing power.
  • Executive search consolidation: Advent acquired Heidrick & Struggles for $1.3 billion (Q4 2025); Spencer Stuart bought Meyler Campbell; Southfield Capital took majority stake in Metric Search ($100 million), signaling PE-driven scale play.
  • Freight broker M&A: RXO acquired Coyote Logistics for $1.025 billion (Sept 2024); Echo Global acquired ITS Logistics (Jan 2026), as digital platforms (Flexport, TMS) moved from advantage to table stakes.
  • Regulatory squeeze: FMCSA doubled surety bonds ($75K→$150K) and mandated real-time load tracking (Jan 2026) to fight double brokering fraud (8,000+ complaints in 2025, $700M–$1B annual cost).

Who rides it

Large platforms with scale, AI, and compliance infrastructure win. In executive search, firms diversifying into coaching (35% of top performers) and advisory (30%) survive consolidation waves. Venture-backed and PE-backed platforms like Flexport in freight capture growth as digital becomes table stakes and regulatory burden rises. Small independent recruiters and brokers are getting crushed: they can't match the speed or technology of large networks, they can't weather regulatory overhead, and they have no defensible moat. The consolidation is brutal and accelerating.

Who's squeezed

Small and mid-size recruiters and brokers are squeezed from all angles. In executive search, internal HR plus LinkedIn eroded the monopoly, Recruitment Process Outsourcing providers undercut on price, and clients now demand impossible speed and rigor simultaneously. In freight, compliance overhead (doubled surety bonds, real-time tracking) creates barriers that small brokers can't afford. The 5,293 executive search firms and 124,000 freight brokerage establishments are fragmenting: scale wins, boutiques lose, and the work is hollowing out into commodity matching with razor margins.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The regulatory regime creates a perverse incentive: as compliance cost rises, it concentrates power in the hands of firms that can bear it—which then control the matching and extract rents. Fraud in freight brokerage spiraled to 8,000+ complaints and $700 million to $1 billion in annual losses because the fragmented market had too many bad actors and no transparency. FMCSA's response (doubled surety bonds, mandatory tracking) is necessary but will push more work through fewer, larger platforms. Similarly, executive search is consolidating upmarket into a handful of mega-firms while fractional and interim work (120,000+ by 2024) is splintering into unregulated gig networks. The result: a two-tier system where the matching layer is either massive and opaque or tiny and compliant. Workers in both tiers lose visibility and leverage—they're matched by algorithm, priced by the platform, and have no individual bargaining power.

In one sentence

Who places the talent in a nutshell

As work fragments, the platforms that match talent to opportunity become gatekeepers—they take 5 to 15 percent, control the flow, and their power grows as regulation and technology raise the cost of entry.

B · The platforms in the middle

Selling the Credential

Bootcamps, cloud certs, and AI tutorials collapse the time-to-hireable into weeks—and the platforms that certify them take the cut.

The gig labor market rewards credentials you can earn fast. Employers hiring freelancers and contractors want proof you can do the work—not a four-year degree. So the credential market split: enterprise certifications (cloud, cybersecurity) boomed, while basic bootcamps collapsed into commodity. The platforms in the middle—Coursera, Udemy, LinkedIn Learning—consolidated to capture the whole supply chain: platform, course, certificate, job board.

What changed

What happened is this. The old world was: university degree, then job, then training on the job. The new world is: credential, then gig, then credential again. That's what the gig economy demands. And when the time-to-hire becomes the time-to-credential—measured in weeks, not years—entire categories of training become either essential or worthless overnight.

Enterprise certifications exploded first. Cybersecurity training grew from $5.67 billion in 2024 to $6.66 billion in 2025, a 16.6 percent jump, and stayed on that trajectory through 2030. Cloud architecture bootcamps grew at 12.7 percent annually (2025-2032). These matter because employers link them directly to hiring decisions and insurance requirements. A CompTIA Security+ or AWS Solutions Architect credential is not just resume padding—it unlocks access to roles. In the enterprise world, that credential is scarce (you need to prove you have it) and expensive (companies pay $2,000-$5,000 per employee to certify). Meanwhile, the rest of the bootcamp market collapsed. The business certification and IT schools industry as a whole pulled in $6.4 billion in 2026, growing just 3 percent year-over-year in 2025. Margins compressed to 4.4 percent (and likely lower now). Big players exited: 2U announced in December 2024 that it was abandoning university-partnered bootcamp programs entirely (600+ centers), citing weak junior hiring and AI displacement fears. The coding bootcamp market overall was valued at $3.28 billion in 2025, but that figure masks a massacre. Free alternatives—AI tutorials, corporate LLMs, MOOCs—made generalist coding bootcamps structurally uncompetitive. The platforms consolidated to survive. Coursera completed its acquisition of Udemy in April 2026 for $2.5 billion in equity. The combined company controls 290 million learners, 18,000 enterprise customers, and 95,000 instructors. Udemy alone had made $786.6 million in revenue in 2024, but neither company was growing fast enough on its own.

What this force made scarce: legitimacy. Not every certification matters. Enterprise employers want certifications they can verify, that link to hiring standards, that (crucially) their insurance or compliance officer recognizes. What it made cheap: access to basic training. AI and free platforms have demolished the price floor for entry-level skills. You can learn Python from an LLM for the cost of a coffee. What it made risky: being a bootcamp operator. Margins are gone. Scale is required to survive. A single boutique bootcamp cannot compete with a platform that can subsidize courses, cross-sell job placements, and finance student loans. What it made valuable: the brand that gets you hired. A credential from a platform that enterprise HR departments already use (Coursera, LinkedIn, AWS) is worth 10x more than the same credential from an unknown provider. The credential market is now the credential platform market.

The evidence

  • Business Certification & IT Schools: cybersecurity training jumped from $5.67B (2024) to $6.66B (2025), then 16.6% CAGR through 2030.
  • Technology sector: cloud architecture bootcamps projected 12.7% CAGR (2025-2032), the only bootcamp category with sustained growth.
  • Online learning platforms: Coursera acquired Udemy for $2.5B (April 2026), consolidating 290M learners and 18,000 enterprise customers.
  • Bootcamp market: 2U exited university-partnered programs (December 2024), citing AI displacement and weak junior hiring across all coding bootcamps.
  • Education services: $9.58B AI-in-education market (2026), with 86% of education orgs adopting generative AI by 2025 to cut course production from 80+ hours to under 5 hours.

Who rides it

The winners are enterprise-credentialing platforms and compliance-linked certification bodies. Coursera and Udemy (now one company) control the on-ramp: they aggregate instructors, certifications, job boards, and employer relationships. They can subsidize and cross-sell. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and CompTIA own the credentials employers actually demand—cloud, cybersecurity, compliance. They can raise prices because the credential unlocks access to high-paying gigs and because HR departments and insurance carriers demand it. Individual instructors and niche educators who partner with big platforms also win, as long as they feed the platform's content engine and accept the revenue split.

Who's squeezed

The losers are independent bootcamp operators, regional training centers, and anyone betting on a stable bootcamp business without scale or a specific compliance niche. Margins disappeared. 2U's exit from bootcamps in December 2024 was the canary in the coal mine. Mid-tier bootcamps and coding schools that can't afford to become part of a larger platform are trapped: they can't compete on price with free AI tutorials, they can't invest in enterprise sales like Coursera can, and they can't offer the job placement guarantees that only big platforms can fund. Workers who completed bootcamps before the consolidation also lost: their credentials matter less now because the market is flooded with cheaper, faster alternatives. And students who took out bootcamp loans when margins were high (2019-2022) are now competing against free learners and AI tutors.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that credential inflation destroys the value of all credentials. If every platform offers AWS training and 90 percent of applicants have it, the credential stops being a signal. Employers then have to look past the credential to something else—maybe actual work samples, AI-generated portfolio projects, or tests conducted during the interview. That means platforms lose their gatekeeping power and their cut. The second risk is regulatory: if the government decides that bootcamps need to disclose job placement rates or outcome guarantees (like colleges do), the entire model breaks. Platforms have high marketing costs and no guarantee anyone gets hired. Forcing transparency could force many of them to either prove their worth or shut down. The third risk is that AI tutoring reaches parity with human instructors much faster than expected, making the platform's course library worth almost nothing. If a student can get the same certification by paying $9 to an AI tutor instead of $199 to Coursera, the platform's only leverage is job placement—and that's already a crowded market.

In one sentence

Selling the credential in a nutshell

Credentials have become commodities, so the platforms that verify them, bundle them, and connect them to jobs have become the real gatekeepers—and they're consolidating fast.

C · The tensions

The benefits gap

Fractional workers don't get health insurance or disability coverage — and the carriers are repricing the risk for those left behind.

When someone works as a fractional employee, contractor, or gig worker, they stop being covered by their employer's health plan or disability insurance. The employer stops paying for those benefits. The carrier stops seeing them as part of a stable group risk pool. The worker has to buy everything themselves — on an individual market where the prices are climbing fast and the subsidies are running out.

What changed

For decades, health insurance and disability coverage were locked together with a full-time job. The employer bought group plans from an insurer, and everyone in the group got the same premium. The risk was pooled — the healthy people subsidized the sick ones, and the young subsidized the old. Fractional work unraveled this. When a worker bounces between gigs, consulting clients, or fractional roles, there is no single employer to buy a group plan. The worker has to find their own coverage, alone, on the individual market. This happened gradually, but 2025-2026 is the moment the numbers broke. The US health insurance market was already $1.6 trillion in 2026 — and insurers just regained pricing power by hiking premiums 9% in 2025, the highest in 15 years, while ACA marketplace premiums jumped 18% for 2026 and benchmark plans soared 26%. Even worse: enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025. That means an individual who was paying $888 a year in 2025 will pay $1,904 in 2026 — more than double, overnight. These people had been surviving on subsidies. Now they face a cliff. Meanwhile, disability insurance — the income protection that catches you when you can't work — has barely touched the gig economy. Only 5% of the 70+ million gig workers in America have short-term disability access. The disability market is $20.2 billion as of 2025, and carriers like Prudential just launched gig-focused products, but they don't cover the fractional workers yet. The real dynamic is that fractional work makes a certain kind of worker — the one bouncing between clients — invisible to group plans and too risky for carriers to price fairly. Insurers are responding by withdrawing from individual markets entirely or repricing aggressively. MetLife and Unum deployed AI claims-automation platforms in 2024-2025 that cut processing time 25-30% and reject more cases using algorithmic underwriting. California raised its disability insurance rate from 1.2% to 1.3% in 2026, while New York cut it 28%, signaling that state regulators are treating gig and fractional workers as an occupational risk that varies wildly by region. The Medicaid enrollment shrinkage in 2025 (down 7.6%) is also significant — those people were getting coverage through government programs, but new work requirements in the 2025 reconciliation bill are pushing them off the rolls. They're joining the individual market just as it becomes less affordable.

The evidence

  • Healthcare: ACA marketplace premiums jumped 18% for 2026, with benchmark plans rising 26%, while enhanced subsidies expired December 31, 2025, causing annual premiums to double from $888 to $1,904 for subsidized individuals
  • Healthcare: Employer-sponsored premiums rose 9% in 2025, the highest in 15 years, as insurers like Anthem, UnitedHealth, and Humana regain pricing power after 2023-2024 margin erosion
  • Disability Insurance: Only 5% of 70+ million US gig workers have short-term disability access as of 2025, with Prudential launching its first gig-focused product only recently
  • Medicaid: Enrollment dropped 7.6% in 2025, the first decline since COVID, driven by work and reporting requirements in the 2025 reconciliation bill
  • State Insurance: California raised disability insurance rates from 1.2% to 1.3% in January 2026; New York cut rates 28% (from $24.75 to $17.68 per person annually), showing divergent state-level pricing of occupational risk

Who rides it

The big health insurers — Anthem, UnitedHealth, Humana, Aetna — win. They control the group market, which is stable and profitable, and they're raising premiums 9% in 2025. They're also benefiting from the expiration of ACA subsidies, which pushes more people into the individual market where prices are higher and margins fatter. Tech platforms like Amazon are also winning by carving out specific profitable segments — Amazon launched its GLP-1 management program in April 2026 with prices as low as $25 a month, undercutting traditional insurers on the most profitable drug categories. Disability carriers like Metlife and Prudential win by deploying AI claims automation; they process claims 25-30% faster and reject more cases using algorithmic logic. They're also starting to price gig-worker disability products at premiums that reflect the actual risk.

Who's squeezed

Fractional workers and gig workers lose. They don't have an employer buying them into a group plan, so they face individual market premiums that just jumped 18-26% in a single year. They also lose subsidies — the enhanced ACA tax credits that were propping up affordability expired December 31, 2025, so someone who was paying $888 a year is now paying over $2,000. They have almost no disability insurance; only 5% of gig workers have coverage. If they were on Medicaid, they're getting pushed off by new work requirements. They also lose to the new entrants like Amazon, which sounds good until you realize Amazon is only targeting the most profitable segments — GLP-1 drugs and primary care — which leaves the complex, expensive patients to traditional insurers, which then raise premiums further on the fractional worker who remains.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that the individual insurance market collapses under its own unsustainability. Premiums have now more than doubled for subsidized ACA enrollees, and enrollment is shrinking. Medicaid is shrinking due to new work requirements. Employer-sponsored plans are still rising. The only people left in the individual market are the ones who can't afford group coverage — the fractional workers, the self-employed, the gig workers. As that pool gets worse and worse, insurers will either withdraw entirely or price so high that nobody can afford it. That's already starting to happen in some states, and when it does, the fractional worker has nowhere to go. They can't get on an employer plan because they don't have a full-time job. They can't afford the individual market. They're not eligible for Medicaid anymore. That's when the risk becomes systemic — emergency rooms fill up with uninsured people, preventive care collapses, and the healthcare system has to absorb the cost.

In one sentence

The benefits gap in a nutshell

Fractional work stripped away employer health insurance and disability coverage, and now the insurers are charging the worker for the risk — while platforms like Amazon skim the most profitable segments off the top.

C · The tensions

The Firm Gets Thinner

Professional firms replace permanent staff with contractors, part-time experts, and outsourced work to survive an expense-demand mismatch.

Law and accounting firms used to run on a core of permanent staff—associates, junior accountants, paralegals—who built institutional knowledge and advanced up the ladder. That's breaking. Expenses are climbing faster than client demand, so firms are shedding permanent headcount and replacing it with a thinner core of senior people plus an outer ring of fractional workers, contract specialists, and offshored labor. The risk isn't obvious from the profit line yet. But it's coming.

What changed

Law firms celebrated record profits in 2025, but the windfall was built on rate hikes, not efficiency. Fees worked per lawyer jumped 16.8% in 2025—the firms simply charged more. Meanwhile, demand growth came in at only 1.9%, and expenses exploded 9.1%. That mismatch is the whole story. Firms are burning cash on AI infrastructure (tech budgets up 9.7% to 11% in 2025 alone) to replace junior work, yet 59% of corporate clients report seeing no clear savings from outside counsel using these tools. In-house legal teams, squeezed on budget, are moving work away from premium Am Law 100 firms to lower-cost alternatives and alternative legal service providers. The response has been consolidation—59 mergers in 2025, up 18% from 2024, with at least 16 more deals announced for 2026. Hogan Lovells and Cadwalader combined to create a $3.6 billion revenue firm. Firms are getting bigger, but the permanent payroll is not.

Accounting services face the same squeeze from a different angle. The Big Four (Deloitte, EY, KPMG, PwC) are expanding their talent pools, but the rest of the industry is hollowing. AI is automating 80%+ of individual tax returns and cutting document analysis time in half—junior accountant work is disappearing. The CPA shortage keeps getting worse: 87% of finance leaders report talent shortages, CPA exam participation dropped 30% since 2016, and open positions now sit vacant for months instead of the old 30-45 days. Mid-market accounting firms are caught. Too small to invest in AI platforms like the Big Four, too slow to compete with automation, they are losing solo-practice clients to self-service software and small-business clients to mega-platforms. Private equity is aggressively buying up smaller and mid-market firms (Blackstone, Cherry Bekaert, Aprio, Baker Tilly, Citrin Cooperman) at 4-7x EBITDA multiples, consolidating them into platforms, and squeezing out inefficiency by replacing junior staff with fractional specialists and offshore teams. KPMG launched KPMG Law in 2025 (the first Big Four law firm under Arizona regulatory reform), expanding the suite of services but also the reliance on specialist contractors for specific legal work. KPMG's tax revenue grew 7.5% in 2025, far outpacing rivals (EY ~5.5%, Deloitte ~5.5%, PwC ~1%), but the workforce growth isn't at the junior level—it's expert networks and fractional consulting roles.

In both industries, the permanent firm is not being replaced by remote work or asynchronous collaboration. It's being replaced by a hub-and-spoke model: a small permanent core of senior partners, directors, and relationship managers at the center, ringed by fractional tax specialists, contract litigators, part-time audit leads, and offshore junior labor. The US legal services industry spans 450,000+ establishments and 1.4 to 1.5 million employees as of 2025, but employment growth has slowed to 1-1.5% annually, even as the industry hits record revenue—a sign that revenue is being captured by fewer people, often through higher leverage, not broader hiring. Accounting meanwhile spans 95,421 firms and 609,491 employees, with headcount growth stalled at 0.77% annually through 2027, despite market expansion. The fracturing is invisible in aggregate numbers but clear in the firm structure: permanent payroll is the fixed cost firms are shedding first.

The evidence

  • Law firms: Fees worked per lawyer up 16.8% in 2025, but demand growth only 1.9%—a sign firms are thinning staff while raising rates (Thomson Reuters 2026 State of the US Legal Market)
  • Accounting: 87% of finance leaders report talent shortages; CPA exam participation down 30% since 2016, forcing mid-market firms to hire fractional specialists and offshore labor (KPMG, Deloitte, EY 2025-2026 reports)
  • Law: 59 mergers in 2025, up 18% from 2024; Hogan Lovells-Cadwalader deal created $3.6B firm—consolidation in place of organic growth (Fairfax Associates, June 2026)
  • Accounting: AI is automating 80%+ of individual tax returns and cutting document analysis time 50%, eliminating junior-level permanent roles (KPMG 2025 technology adoption data)
  • Professional services: US legal industry at 1.4-1.5M employees with 1-1.5% annual growth despite record revenue; accounting at 609,491 employees with 0.77% growth through 2027—permanent staff is not keeping pace with fee growth

Who rides it

Large firms and consolidators (Big Four accounting, Am Law 200 players, PE-backed platforms) are thriving. They have the capital to invest in AI, automation, and global delivery networks. KPMG's 7.5% tax revenue growth, Deloitte's expansion, and the 59 law firm mergers in 2025 show that scale and efficiency drive the winners. Private equity platforms buying mid-market accounting firms at 4-7x EBITDA are capturing the upside of automation and junior-staff replacement. Alternative legal service providers and legal process outsourcing firms are capturing deflected work from in-house teams cutting Am Law 100 spend. Fractional experts and contract specialists (tax, IP, audit, litigation) are capturing more work, though at lower rates and with less stability than permanent roles.

Who's squeezed

Mid-market and regional firms, especially in accounting, are squeezed between automation, talent shortages, and mega-platform competition. Solo practitioners and small practices are losing clients to self-service software and cheap offshore labor. Junior accountants and paralegals face narrowing permanent roles—the entry-level ladder is fracturing. Permanent employees in these firms face thinner advancement paths, lower compensation gains, and uncertainty as their firms shed headcount or merge to survive. In-house legal teams are winning on rate leverage (forcing premiums down), but senior partners at mid-size firms face margin compression and forced consolidation.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The structural risk is that professional services firms are optimizing for short-term profit by thinning permanent staff, but this hollows out institutional knowledge, training pipelines, and culture. In law and accounting, the permanent staff used to train the next generation; now that function is decoupled. Firms are converting senior-level work to fractional and contractor models, which is efficient but leaves no one accountable for long-term client relationships, regulatory risk, or ethics. If a recession hits and demand drops below the expense baseline (as it did in 2009-2011), firms will have shed so much permanent capacity that they cannot quickly rehire or rebuild. The AM Law 100 margin spread (14-78% among top firms) also suggests that premium pricing is fragile—clients see through the AI mirage and are walking to cheaper alternatives. That pressure will force deeper cuts, not just in junior staff but in senior consultant headcount.

The firm gets thinner in a nutshell

Professional services firms are shedding permanent staff to offset an expense-demand mismatch, replacing the traditional career ladder with fractional experts and offshore labor, and consolidating into mega-platforms that can automate and scale.

E · The big picture

The Fractional Worker

Permanent jobs unbundle into gigs, fractional roles, and expert networks — the firm rents talent by the hour, and the platform in the middle takes the cut.

For a hundred years, the employment contract was simple: you showed up, stayed put, got paid. Now it's splintering. The firm no longer wants to buy your time; it wants to rent your task. This shift is unfolding across three distinct markets—expert networks, management consulting, and business coaching—each showing the same pattern: permanent roles are being replaced by on-demand fractional work, platforms are racing to consolidate the data and the rolodex, and the burden of stability has shifted from the employer to the worker.

What changed

The fractional-work economy is being built on three layers, each with its own physics. At the top, expert networks—a $1.8 billion US market in 2025 growing 4.3%—are shifting from scheduling one-off $2,000–$5,000 phone calls with human experts to AI-driven transcript synthesis and agentic research workflows that compress a 2–5 day project into 2 hours. This inflection hit in mid-2024 when AlphaSense acquired Tegus, merging the two largest libraries of expert call transcripts under one roof and triggering a consolidation wave: Slingshot acquired Noble Insights, Bridger acquired Deepbench, and Levine Leichtman acquired The Expert Institute's legal library. By 2026, 61% of expert networks now use AI-driven expert matching and agentic AI systems are automating end-to-end research workflows—cutting sourcing time from days to hours. Margins are compressing (down from 15.6% in 2016 to ~14% in 2025), and the industry is consolidating rapidly: five major players now control 60% of a market with only ~65 independent companies and 5,000–6,000 workers. What used to be a network of thousands of accessible experts has become a data-moat play where those who own the transcripts win.\n\nIn management consulting, a $370 billion US market (2026), the pressures are more visceral. AI has become the industry's existential event. By 2025, AI roles outnumber entry-level consultants at top firms for the first time—reversing a 2015 baseline where there were nearly four junior consultants per AI role. Hiring is down 20% from 2023 peaks; consultant-specific roles are down 40%. Simultaneously, the U.S. federal government cut roughly $5 billion in consulting contracts in early 2025, forcing layoffs at Deloitte, Accenture, and IBM. Accenture announced an $865 million restructuring in April 2025, cutting 11,000 roles while doubling AI specialist headcount to 80,000—a stark rebalancing of the labor mix. Clients have also stopped buying hours: CEOs now demand measurable ROI and are pushing firms toward outcome-based pricing and subscription models instead of hourly billing. Compensation is inverting—AI specialists command 56% wage premiums over traditional software roles, while junior consultant salaries have stalled. The Big Four control scale and access, boutique specialists win on depth and agility, and mid-market firms are squeezed in between.\n\nBusiness coaching—a $20 billion US market (2026) growing 2.9%—is following a parallel arc, but in reverse. Instead of shrinking, the market is exploding in supply. Coaches numbered 71,000 in 2019 and jumped to 145,500 by 2024, mostly solo practitioners and small firms (88%+ are nonemployers). AI coaching segments grew at 22–28% annually in 2024–2025, far outpacing human coaching's 3–5% baseline. Yet here, workers are proliferating, not consolidating—entry barriers have collapsed because there is no US licensing requirement; anyone can call themselves a coach. The catch: 91% of coachees perceived AI coaching as effective as in-person delivery, and platforms now offer \"cyborg coach\" hybrid models bundled into HR software at $100/month. ROI has also become table stakes—86% of companies now report positive ROI from coaching, and it has shifted from discretionary C-suite perk to a strategic leadership-development tool embedded in succession planning. What this means is that coaching is being commoditized and stratified at once: a vast pool of fractional coaches competing for platform minutes, while those embedded in enterprise relationships (Korn Ferry, Heidrick & Struggles) or credentialed under new ICF Minimum Skills Requirements (raised in January 2026) are widening the gap.\n\nAcross all three markets, the pattern is identical: the unit of work is shrinking from the job to the task, platforms are racing to own the data (transcripts, call libraries, assessment histories), and the burden of sourcing, vetting, and staying constantly available has migrated entirely onto the worker. Expert networks used to build relationships with experts; now they run algorithms over transcripts. Consulting firms used to grow junior consultants into senior partners; now they hire AI specialists and outsource the rest to fractional labor or boutique shops. Coaching was once a luxury for the C-suite; now it's a commoditized \"cyborg\" service bundled into HR software. The commonality is that permanence is gone. Workers are paid by the task, platforms take the cut, and the risk of income volatility, benefits, and obsolescence sits entirely on the individual.

The evidence

  • Expert Networks (Business Services): $1.8 billion US market in 2025, consolidating rapidly after AlphaSense acquired Tegus (June 2024) to merge the two largest transcript libraries; five major players now control 60% of the market with only 5,000–6,000 workers and ~65 independent firms.
  • Management Consulting (Business Services): $370 billion US market in 2026 but hollowing—consultant-specific hiring down 40% from 2023 peaks as Accenture doubled AI specialist headcount to 80,000 in April 2025 while cutting 11,000 traditional roles; federal consulting contracts cut ~$5 billion in early 2025.
  • Business Coaching (Business Services): $20 billion US market in 2026, but supply exploded from 71,000 coaches in 2019 to 145,500 by 2024; AI coaching segments grew 22–28% annually in 2024–2025, yet 91% of coachees perceived no difference from human coaching.
  • Expert Networks AI Adoption: 61% of expert networks now use AI-driven expert matching by 2026; agentic AI systems automate end-to-end research workflows, compressing sourcing from 2–5 days to 2 hours and threatening the historical pay-per-call revenue model.
  • Consulting Labor Inversion: By 2025, AI roles outnumbered entry-level consultants at top firms for the first time, reversing the 2015 baseline where there were nearly four junior consultants per AI role; AI specialists command 56% wage premiums over traditional software roles.

Who rides it

Platforms and data-rich consolidators are the clear winners. In expert networks, AlphaSense (valued at $4 billion in April 2026) and five major players controlling 60% of the market win by owning transcripts and running AI synthesis at near-zero marginal cost, undercutting pay-per-call models and independent experts. In consulting, the Big Four and AI-focused boutiques win by controlling client relationships and AI capabilities; mid-market and commodity labor lose. In coaching, platform-embedded \"cyborg coach\" models and credentialed coaches embedded in enterprise relationships (Korn Ferry, Heidrick & Struggles) win, while solo practitioners fractionalizing into platform minutes lose bargaining power. Specialists who own irreplaceable depth—senior partners with deep client relationships, credentialed coaches with ICF credentials (raised in January 2026), niche industry experts—remain valuable. But everyone else competes as interchangeable fractional labor.

Who's squeezed

Ordinary workers lose on every dimension. Entry-level consultants and junior roles are being eliminated (hiring down 40%); expert networks employment is locked into 5,000–6,000 workers across five firms instead of a distributed network; 145,500 business coaches are competing for fractional minutes on platforms at commoditized rates. Stability evaporates: there is no pathway from junior to senior anymore in consulting (because juniors are being replaced by AI); no benefits or long-term income security for coaches or fractional experts; no incentive for employers to invest in training or career development when workers can be rented by the task. Mid-market consulting firms are squeezed between the Big Four's scale and boutiques' agility. And workers in these roles now bear all the risk: income volatility, benefits gaps, the burden of staying current on tools and AI capabilities, and the constant pressure to rebrand themselves as \"specialists\" to compete with commoditization. The premise of the employment relationship—stability and investment in you—is gone.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is the creation of a two-tier labor market where a small cohort of high-credentialed, high-data-access specialists (AI-trained consultants, platform-embedded coaches, expert networks embedded in consolidators) command rents while the vast majority of fractional workers are locked into a low-wage, low-power, perpetually contingent status. Evidence: Accenture doubled AI headcount to 80,000 while cutting 11,000 traditional roles; coaches jumped 105% in five years but are competing on platforms for $100/month slots; expert networks are consolidating around five firms with data moats. The path from commodity fractional labor to high-credentialed specialist is narrow and requires continuous re-skilling, which the market has no incentive to fund. Meanwhile, platforms and consolidators hold all the data and the client relationships, so bargaining power flows entirely upward. The true risk is not job loss—it's the normalization of permanent precarity, where \"flexibility\" and \"fractional work\" become a one-way ratchet toward lower incomes and zero security.
