A · The body wears out

Joint Repair & Surgery

Demand for knee and hip replacements floods in, but robotics become standard while Medicare cuts 26% of reimbursement in a decade.

Joints wear out. A 65-year-old body is not a 35-year-old body. The flood of aging Americans—10,000 turning 65 every single day—means orthopedic surgeries, eye surgeries, and the devices that go inside people's knees and hips are no longer niche. The market for orthopedic products hit $60.6 billion in 2025. But here's what changed: reimbursement cratered, robotics became table stakes, and consolidation crushed independents.

What changed

The orthopedic products business ($60.6 billion in 2025, growing only 4.3% annually through 2035) is being torn between explosive demand and a reimbursement wall. Ten years ago, a hip replacement or knee surgery was a specialty procedure. Now 34% of all inpatient procedures are people over 65, and Medicare's payment for hip arthroplasty has collapsed 39% since 2017. Not 2% cuts year after year—a 39% cliff. Meanwhile, the robot-assisted surgery piece exploded to $2.6 billion in 2026 and is growing at 16-17% annually, far outpacing the sluggish 4.3% of the traditional implant business. Stryker, which makes MAKO, now runs 67% of US knee replacements and 33% of hips on robotic platforms by end-2025. That's not a nice-to-have. That's the standard of care. Hospitals and surgery centers adopted the robot because it improves outcomes and reduces complications—but Stryker locked the market, and smaller implant makers have nowhere to hide. J&J spun off its DePuy Synthes orthopedic unit (valued north of $20 billion) because the core business of making knee implants can no longer justify the manufacturing footprint or R&D expense at acceptable margins.

Ambulatory surgery centers, which now handle many of these procedures outside hospitals, grew to $46.5 billion in 2026 and are consolidating violently. Ascension bought AmSurg for $3.9 billion in 2024 and went from 58 to 300+ centers overnight. Meanwhile, reimbursement grew only 2.4-2.9% annually—nowhere near wage inflation—so smaller independents got crushed. Large platforms like USPI hold 38.6% EBITDA margins by leveraging scale; smaller doctors' practices are down to the low 30s. CMS also threw a 2.5% efficiency adjustment at the industry in 2026 and added 560 new procedures to the ASC Covered Procedures List—cardiac ablations, lumbar fusion—but here's the catch: those complex procedures pay less at ASCs than at hospital outpatient departments. The reimbursement tables are deliberately tilted to keep complex, high-acuity work in hospitals. So centers have the permission to do the work but not the payment to make it attractive.

Eye surgery clinics ($2.0 billion in 2025, only 1.7% growth that year) are being squeezed from both ends. LASIK was the growth story for decades—elective surgery, cash pay, no insurance. Prices fell from $2,350 per eye in 2015 to $2,000-$5,000 today, which means younger, price-sensitive customers got priced in after waiting for deals, but the pool isn't growing. Cataract surgeries are covered by Medicare, so reimbursement is the limit. Meanwhile, there is a catastrophic shortage of ophthalmologists: 46% of eye practices report understaffing in 2025, and supply will fall 12% by 2035 even as demand grows 24%. That's a 36-point supply-demand gap. Hospital systems and private equity are acquiring regional clinics (Alcon bought STAAR Surgical for $1.5 billion in 2024; Zeiss acquired DORC) and bundling AI diagnostics to automate patient screening and reduce per-procedure costs. Independents can't match that. Roughly 40% of developers are now integrating AI—not as novelty but as a table-stakes move to compete. The result is a bifurcated market: large integrated platforms absorb the robot cost, the staff shortage, the reimbursement decline, and win through scale. Everyone else loses margin and volume.

The evidence

  • Orthopedic products: $60.6 billion market in 2025 with 26% Medicare reimbursement decline from 2016 to 2024, while robot-assisted surgery jumped to $2.6 billion in 2026 (16-17% CAGR).
  • Ambulatory surgery centers: $46.5 billion in 2026 growing only 2.4-2.9% annually, but large platforms like USPI maintaining 38.6% EBITDA margins while independents compress to low-30s.
  • Eye surgery: $2.0 billion market in 2025 with 46% of practices understaffed; ophthalmologist supply projected to fall 12% by 2035 despite 24% demand growth.
  • Robotic surgery dominance: Stryker's MAKO performs 67% of US knee replacements and 33% of hips by end-2025, making robotic assistance table stakes for competitive orthopedic practices.
  • Consolidation wave: J&J spun DePuy Synthes ($20 billion+) in October 2025; Ascension acquired AmSurg ($3.9 billion, 2024); Alcon bought STAAR Surgical ($1.5 billion, 2024).

Who rides it

Large hospital systems and PE-backed platforms win through scale and integration. They absorb the robot cost by spreading it across hundreds of cases, negotiate better Medicare rates by owning multiple sites, and deploy AI diagnostics to cut per-procedure costs. Stryker wins because MAKO is non-negotiable—surgeons switched because the robot genuinely works, then Stryker locked the market. Consolidated ambulatory surgery center networks like USPI and Ascension's expanded footprint can weather 2.4% reimbursement growth because they're not dependent on a single procedure or geography. They also have the capital to buy up stragglers at fire-sale prices. In eye surgery, hospital systems bundling cataract care with geriatric eye disease management and AI screening can underprice independents and defend market share through payer relationships.

Who's squeezed

Independent orthopedic surgeons and smaller implant makers get squeezed out. If you built your practice around a single implant line and can't afford Stryker's MAKO system or don't have capital to acquire one, you're losing surgeons to hospitals and surgery centers that have the robot. Small orthopedic device companies selling specialized knee or hip implants face a market where consolidation (J&J spinning DePuy Synthes, Globus buying Nevro for $250M in April 2025) is the only exit; organic growth at 4.3% doesn't justify standalone operations anymore. In ambulatory surgery centers, the 67% of independents are bleeding margin because reimbursement grows at 2.4-2.9% while their wage and supply costs rise faster. They're being acquired at multiples that reflect their distress. Independent eye surgery clinics can't match bundled platforms on cost, can't afford AI integration, and face a 12% ophthalmologist shortage—they lose volume and talent to hospital systems that own multiple practices, have recruitment power, and can cross-refer complex cases.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that Medicare reimbursement for orthopedic services collapses further and accelerates the erasure of independents before any new business model fills the gap. We've seen 39% cuts to hip arthroplasty reimbursement in a decade. CMS just applied a 2.5% efficiency adjustment in 2026 and is advancing site-neutral payment rules that could obliterate the ASC economics that depend on procedure price differentials. If Medicare goes after orthopedic services the way it went after cardiology a decade ago—capitated bundles, site-neutral pay, low utilization caps—the volume upside from an aging population evaporates into pricing pressure. Large platforms can survive on margin compression because they have scale and can cross-subsidize; independents cannot. The second worry is the robot lock: Stryker's 67% market share in knee replacement means surgeons who defect to MAKO have a hard time going back. If Stryker raises prices or restricts supply (as large players do when they dominate), the entire orthopedic supply chain is hostage. And the ophthalmologist shortage is existential—12% decline by 2035 against 24% demand growth means tens of millions of aging Americans cannot get routine cataract surgery, let alone advanced retinal work. No amount of AI screening or ASC efficiency gains that labor shortage away.

When the senses fade

Hearing and vision loss create steady aging-market demand, but reimbursement limits and tariff shocks are reshaping who captures the billions.

Thirty-seven and a half million Americans report hearing difficulty—one in three people aged 65 to 74 struggle to follow conversation. Vision losses are just as widespread: over half of adults over 75 need vision correction. These are not lifestyle upgrades. They are daily necessities. And the billions flowing into hearing aids, contact lenses, and eyeglasses reveal a market under stress: consolidation squeezing independents, tariffs doubling overnight, and big retailers capturing margin while manufacturers fight for scraps.

What changed

Hearing aid manufacturing—a $2.2 billion US industry in 2026—has fragmented into three distinct tiers as FDA deregulation since 2022 upended the entire market. Premium AI-driven devices from Sonova, Demant, and Starkey still command $2,400 to $3,000-plus and enjoy 3–5% annual growth among those who can afford them. The over-the-counter segment, now legal since October 2022, was supposed to democratize access with $800–$1,500 devices at retailers like Costco and Amazon. Instead, OTC has stalled at a niche 5–10% adoption rate—most people with mild hearing loss still delay treatment, and those who do buy often choose distribution over innovation. The real growth is happening at the margins: big-box retailers (Costco, Walmart, CVS) are now the fastest-growing channel by volume, but they demand ever-lower wholesale prices in return. Import penetration has settled at 48% of demand, but tariff threats and reshoring economics are making foreign suppliers less attractive; in July 2025, Nano Hearing Aids announced it was moving best-selling US models to domestic manufacturing to dodge tariffs. The industry's biggest structural shift arrived in 2026 when Amplifon (the world's largest hearing aid retailer) merged with GN ReSound (the third-largest global manufacturer) in a €2.3 billion deal—vertical integration that locks supply and retail together and raises the competitive bar for everyone else.

The eyewear market—$23.2 billion in retail, $7.7 billion in US manufacturing—is under a different kind of pressure. Contact lenses were growing at 7% annually through 2024, but decelerated to just 4% in 2025 as consumers pulled back on buying annual supplies, rebate programs contracted from 12-month to 6-month cycles, and e-commerce exploded from 35% to 40% of unit sales in a single quarter. Online retailers like Zenni and Warby Parker (which posted 15–18% growth through early 2025) undercut traditional brick-and-mortar prices by 20–70%, forcing optometry clinics to slash margins to match. Where is growth happening? Myopia management—soft multifocal lenses and orthokeratology (overnight corneal reshaping)—is now the bright spot, growing at 10.2% annually and reaching $2.8 billion by 2025, especially in affluent households and regions with insurance coverage. Specialty lenses (daily silicone hydrogel, toric) hold price power, but commodity frames and basic single-vision lenses are drowning in import pressure.

Then tariffs hit. In April 2025, duties on Chinese optical products jumped to 154.5%—contact lens tariffs alone—while plastic eyeglass frames from China faced combined tariffs of 64–155%. The Vision Council found that 50% of eye care providers expected to pass price increases directly to consumers. Tariff payments on Chinese optical imports alone are projected to nearly double from $160 million in 2024 to $333 million annually. Manufacturers scrambled: Bausch + Lomb, J&J, and others began near-shoring to Mexico and Southeast Asia, accepting 18% production cost increases to escape China penalties. Consolidation accelerated as cover—EssilorLuxottica acquired Optegra (70+ eye hospitals), Alcon scooped up Lensar and LumiThera, and J&J spent $1 billion-plus on manufacturing expansion in Jacksonville, Florida. By Q2 2025, the market had bifurcated: exam prices climbed 14% year-over-year, but volume of visits dropped 4.5%—people were spending more per visit but going to the doctor less often.

Blue-light-filtering glasses—a category that barely existed a decade ago—hit $2.9 billion in 2024 and is forecast to double to $5.8 billion by 2034 as screen time drives a new demand segment among younger users. But this growth sits atop a mature base where prescription inelasticity (you have to correct your vision to function) masks the real dynamics: aging baby boomers need hearing aids and stronger prescriptions, but they are price-sensitive and often delay treatment; affluent households can afford premium AI-driven devices and myopia control, while middle-income users are trapped between expensive retail prices and quality concerns about online OTC alternatives; and independent optometrists and small hearing aid dispensers are caught between margin compression from tariffs and online discounting on one side and vertically integrated mega-retailers and manufacturers on the other.

The evidence

  • Hearing aid manufacturing: US market $2.2B in 2026 with 3.6% YoY growth, but OTC adoption stalled at 5–10% since FDA deregulation (October 2022), while Amplifon-GN merger (€2.3B, end-2026) consolidates supply and retail.
  • Contact lenses: $4.42B US market in 2025, decelerating to 4% YoY growth from 7% in 2024; online retail now 40% of unit sales (up from 35% one quarter prior), exerting 20–70% price pressure on traditional optometry.
  • Eyewear manufacturing: $7.7B in 2025, growing only 2.4% YoY; plastic frames face 155% tariffs, Chinese optical materials 22–25% stacked duty, and manufacturers accepting 18% production cost increases to near-shore away from China.
  • Myopia control lenses: fastest-growth segment at 10.2% CAGR, reaching $2.8B in 2025; orthokeratology and soft multifocals gaining clinical adoption but cost-to-patient remains a barrier outside affluent regions with insurance reimbursement.
  • Tariff shock: April 2025 duties on Chinese optical products jumped to 154.5% (contact lenses), driving projected tariff payments from $160M (2024) to ~$333M annually; Vision Council survey found 50% of providers expected price pass-through to consumers.

Who rides it

Premium device makers (Sonova, Demant, Starkey, J&J Vision, Alcon) and consolidators (Amplifon-GN, EssilorLuxottica, Bausch + Lomb) who can absorb tariff costs and near-shoring expenses while offering specialty segments (AI-driven hearing aids, myopia control, therapeutic lenses) that hold pricing power. Big-box retailers (Costco, Walmart, CVS, Amazon) capture volume and margin by negotiating ruthlessly with manufacturers and offering convenience. E-commerce players like Warby Parker and Zenni win by exploiting the price gap between online and offline, though tariffs are beginning to compress their margins too.

Who's squeezed

Independent optometrists and small hearing aid dispensers are squeezed between margin compression from tariffs, online discounting, and pressure to match low prices while serving older, price-sensitive customers who delay treatment. Consumers in the middle—those with moderate hearing loss or vision correction needs who cannot afford premium AI-driven devices or myopia management and are wary of online OTC quality—face higher prices as tariffs ripple through and fewer low-cost options as consolidation continues.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The tariff shock of 2025 is structural, not temporary. Reshoring to Mexico and Southeast Asia adds 18% to production costs permanently; those costs cannot come out once tariffs are baked in. Manufacturers will pass them on or accept lower margins. Consumers will pay more and buy less—exam volume already dropped 4.5% in Q2 2025 even as prices climbed 14%. The real risk is that price-sensitive older adults delay hearing aid adoption or skip annual contact lens renewals, leaving potential demand unrealized and leaving the industry with overcapacity it built for demographics that never materialized at the prices it set.

As boomers age and demand for hearing aids and eyewear soars, tariffs, consolidation, and online discounting are fracturing the market into tiers the poor and middle-income cannot afford, while manufacturers and retailers fight over shrinking margin.

Annual growth rate for myopia control lenses (soft multifocal and orthokeratology), reaching $2.8 billion by 2025 and widening the premium-to-commodity bifurcation.

A · The body wears out

The chronic-disease machine

Kidney and heart disease scale with age into recurring, consolidated, reimbursement-dependent care.

America's 516,837 dialysis patients and millions with heart disease are locked into recurring clinical visits, medication refills, and device checks. This is the care machine: massive, unavoidable, profit-thin, and increasingly controlled by consolidators squeezing wages while Medicare slowly strangles reimbursement.

What changed

The boomers entering their 60s and 70s have made chronic disease the backbone of American healthcare. Kidney failure used to be rare. Heart disease was an acute event. Now both are chronic machines that run for decades—dialysis every other day, heart monitoring every week, medication adjustments every month. The dialysis industry alone hit $36 billion in revenue in 2025, growing at a steady 3.5% per year through 2035, treating more patients than ever before. But reimbursement is collapsing. CMS raised the ESRD base rate only 2.2% in 2026 to $281.71 per treatment, and for 2027 it's projecting a 1.1% increase to $299.55—both far below wage inflation and supply-chain costs. When Medicare pays slowly and grows slower, clinics stop buying new equipment. Dialysis equipment manufacturers face the same squeeze: they grew at 4.8% in 2025 but operate on razor-thin 5–6% margins, locked into a market where half the buyers are government programs with hard ceilings. Meanwhile, two giants—DaVita and Fresenius—control 65% of the dialysis market, using scale to absorb the margin pressure. Fresenius reported an 11.7% operating margin in Q2 2026, but independent and smaller regional operators can't match that. What was once a collection of local dialysis clinics is now a consolidated industry run by PE roll-ups and two public companies racing for cost control.

Cardiology tells the same story from another angle. The cardiologist shortage is real: for every 1,087 cardiac patients in 2025, there's one board-certified cardiologist. By 2035, that ratio craters to one per 1,700 patients. Heart disease still kills more Americans than anything else—one in four deaths—and obesity at 41.9% in 2025–2026 keeps pushing heart failure cases up from 6.7 to 7.7 million in under five years. But Medicare payments fell 29% from 2005 to 2021, while the paperwork load exploded. Ninety percent of cardiologists now work for hospitals or consolidators instead of private practice, because solo practice is dead. The 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule slashed payment for critical procedures: stress tests fell from $311.40 to $220.60 per visit, amyloid PET imaging was cut 57%, and left atrial appendage closures dropped 27% in work value. A cardiologist needs to see more patients or compress visits to earn the same income, both of which guarantee burnout. The field is projected to lose 547 cardiologists per year by 2031 from retirements and exits. Private equity made six cardiology practice acquisitions in the first half of 2025 alone—matching the entire 2024 volume—because consolidators can squeeze costs and automate admin in ways solo doctors can't.

What did the aging population make scarce? Cardiologists. Nephrologists. Qualified dialysis technicians. Rural capacity. Clinical time. What it made cheap? Labor for smaller operators, because the giants bid down wages by consolidating supply. What it made risky? Independence. Small regional dialysis operators and private-practice cardiologists face margin compression so tight they have to sell or fail. What it made newly valuable? Scale, automation, remote monitoring, and the ability to negotiate with Medicare. Baxter saw the writing on the wall in January 2025 and sold its kidney care business to Carlyle for $3.8 billion, spinning off Vantive with $1 billion committed to wearables and implantables by 2028—betting that home dialysis and portable devices are where real margins might exist. Fresenius doubled down, investing EUR 312 million in September 2025 to buy out non-physician stakes in Interwell Health, tightening control of home delivery networks. Both moves signal the same insight: the future profit is not in clinic visits or traditional dialysis but in portable, wearable, and eventually implantable therapies. Home dialysis grew from 8.5% of the US dialysis population in 2012 to 14.5% in 2025, and CMS is incentivizing the shift with expanded reimbursement codes and training add-ons. But that shift takes capital, R&D, and regulatory navigation—exactly what two big players and well-backed startups can do, not small clinics.

The evidence

  • Dialysis: DaVita and Fresenius commanded 65% of the $36B 2025 US market, with Fresenius reporting 11.7% operating margins in Q2 2026 on its 5008X CAREsystem deployed in 227 clinics.
  • Dialysis Equipment: US manufacturers faced tariff squeezes (25–54% US duties on Chinese devices in 2025, Mexico 35–50% on Chinese inputs from Jan 2026) while operating on 5–6% margins in a market frozen by Medicare rate caps.
  • Home Dialysis: Adoption climbed from 8.5% in 2012 to 14.5% in 2025, with Fresenius investing EUR 312M in Sept 2025 to acquire all non-physician stakes in Interwell Health, signaling capital-intensive consolidation around home delivery.
  • Cardiology Consolidation: Six PE-backed cardiology acquisitions occurred in H1 2025 (matching all of 2024), as Medicare cuts (stress tests −$91/procedure, amyloid PET −57%, LAA closure −27%) forced 90% of cardiologists into hospital or PE employment.
  • Cardiology Shortage: The field faces 1 cardiologist per 1,700 patients by 2035, losing 547 doctors annually by 2031, while heart failure cases grew from 6.7 to 7.7M adults in under five years and obesity hit 41.9% in 2025–2026.

Who rides it

Consolidators—DaVita, Fresenius, and PE firms backing regional roll-ups and cardiology groups—win by absorbing margin pressure through scale, cost control, and M&A. They can weather a 2.2% Medicare rate hike because they squeeze labor, negotiate supply, and deploy automation. Baxter and Fresenius win by pivoting toward home dialysis and wearable/implantable therapies, where margins might exist if they can beat the tariff squeeze and prove portable devices to regulators. Telehealth and remote patient monitoring vendors win by riding consolidator spend on automation and care-coordinate software—RPM revenue in cardiology hit $4.68 billion in 2025 as a cost-control tool, not clinical innovation.

Who's squeezed

Independents and small regional operators get squeezed out. The 142,000–156,000 dialysis workers face wage pressure as DaVita and Fresenius bid down labor in rural areas with leverage. Cardiologists lose: private practice is dead (down to 10% of the field), and those still employed watch reimbursement fall while caseload per doctor climbs from demographic demand. Solo or small-group practices can't negotiate with insurers and can't afford the backend admin and EHR costs that consolidators absorb. Rural areas and small-population regions lose access—clinics close or consolidate, forcing patients to travel farther. Equipment makers lose if they can't scale or consolidate: tariffs eat into the 5–6% margins, and frozen Medicare rates mean clinics defer purchases.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that consolidation and reimbursement pressure combine to worsen access exactly when demand is climbing. If dialysis clinics close in rural areas because Medicare rates don't cover costs, kidney patients have nowhere to go. If cardiologist shortages keep widening—projected to hit 1 per 1,700 patients by 2035—patients wait months for appointments, and acute heart events go unmanaged. Tariffs on medical devices could compress margins further and force more mergers or bankruptcies among equipment makers, collapsing competition and raising prices for clinics. The deeper risk: Medicare keeps cutting reimbursement to control costs, but the demographic wave—more kidney disease, more heart failure, longer patient lifespan—keeps increasing volume. Consolidators can handle it by ruthlessly controlling costs and wages. Everyone else exits or gets absorbed. The machine runs, but at lower quality and less competition.

In one sentence

The chronic-disease machine in a nutshell

Chronic disease is now the engine of American healthcare, but reimbursement caps and consolidation concentrate profit in two dialysis giants and PE-backed cardiology groups while squeezing out small operators, rural access, and clinical workforce.

B · Care leaves the hospital

Senior housing at scale

Boomer demand fills beds—but short staff and wage spirals are eating the margins.

The baby boom is moving into the frail years, flooding the assisted living and home care markets with demand. Occupancy rates hit their highest levels in a decade. But the very businesses capturing this wave are being squeezed by a caregiver shortage so acute that staffing costs are rising faster than revenue. The result: consolidators and deep-pocket operators thrive, while independent small homes get stuck choosing between losing money or rationing care.

What changed

In 2026, the senior residential care market is $415 billion in size and growing 6-9% annually—accelerating as the oldest boomers age into their 80s starting in 2027. The industry franchises alone (non-medical in-home care) hit $110 billion in 2026, up from $5.967 billion in 2021, a projection of $9 billion for that year showing explosive branching. Over 220,000 people now work in elderly services, compared to 163,813 in 2021; the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 711,700 new home care jobs between 2022 and 2032. Occupancy hit 88.7% nationally in Q3 2025, the 17th straight quarter of increases, meaning beds fill almost as fast as they open. The demographic engine is real and relentless.\n\nBut here is the bind: bed growth lags demand. Assisted living beds grow just 1-2% annually, while the over-80 population expands at 4%. That shortage pushes overflow demand into franchised home and community-based care, which sounds lucrative until you hit the staffing wall. Registered nurses, certified nursing assistants, and dietary staff report 40% annual turnover. Over half of home care agencies say they can't fill open positions. Wages for caregivers have climbed 31% since 2019 alone. Profit margins, which sat at 14.8% in 2021, are compressing as operators face a choice: pay the rising wage rates or lose staff and service quality. Even operators with the strongest market positions report that labor is now the binding constraint on growth.\n\nConsolidation is the response. In 2025, there were 871 M&A transactions in the senior care space—20.8% above the prior record of 721 in 2024. Assisted living made up 44% of those deals. On the current burn rate, 2026 is surpassing both prior years. Private equity sees the demographics as a tailwind and the fragmentation as an opportunity: the market includes 121,000 businesses in elderly and disabled services, most of them small operators with no economies of scale on purchasing, staffing, or financing. BrightSpring Health Services, backed by KKR, went public in January 2024, validating the thesis that institutional players can run home and community-based care at scale. The FTC and DOJ opened a formal investigation into PE acquisition surge in March 2024—still no enforcement, but the scrutiny signals a coming crack in the consolidation story.\n\nWhat the force made scarce is beds and caregivers both. Assisted living capacity is rationed by occupancy; home care workers are scarce and expensive. What became newly valuable is the ability to operate across multiple modalities (memory care, assisted living, home care, adult day programs) to smooth labor costs, negotiate with payers from scale, and absorb the M&A premiums consolidators pay. Private equity has the capital to roll up fragments and implement standardized staffing models—though those models often mean lower per-client touch, not higher quality. Independent operators and small chains, absent a buyer, face relentless margin compression and the risk of being undercut on price by a regional roll-up backed by institutional capital.

The evidence

  • Assisted living franchises grew from $5.967 billion revenue (2021) to a 2026 projection of $9 billion, with the workforce expanding from 163,813 (2021) to over 220,000 (2026).
  • Occupancy reached 88.7% in Q3 2025 after 17 straight quarterly gains, signaling severe bed scarcity and forced upselling into higher-cost home care modalities.
  • Home care agencies report over 50% ongoing worker shortages while caregiving wages climbed 31% since 2019, with operators squeezing margins or cutting service hours.
  • In 2025, 871 M&A deals (20.8% above prior peak) targeted senior care, with PE firms using institutional capital to roll up 121,000 fragmented operators into regional and national chains.
  • BrightSpring Health Services IPO (Jan 2024, KKR-backed) and FTC/DOJ scrutiny (Mar 2024) bracket the consolidation wave, validating scale economics while signaling regulatory risk.

Who rides it

Private equity and large regional operators win decisively. The wage spiral, occupancy crunch, and fragmentation reward capital, scale, and multi-modal operations. A PE-backed chain can absorb a 31% wage climb, negotiate payer rates from institutional leverage, and cross-subsidize margin-thin assisted living with higher-margin home care or memory care. Regional consolidators with 20-50 facilities can afford compliance staff, centralized purchasing, and trained front-line managers in ways a single 60-bed home cannot. The KKR thesis holds as long as reimbursement rates keep pace—and demographic tailwinds are strong enough that payers have limited leverage to push back.

Who's squeezed

Independent and small-chain senior housing operators get progressively squeezed. A 60-bed assisted living home with 70 staff members sees wage costs climb faster than occupancy revenue can absorb, especially if it competes with a PE-backed cluster that can move staff, negotiate insurance contracts, and subsidize losses with adjacent businesses. Operators without acquisition buyers face a choice: invest capital to modernize and staff competitively (a bet on their own operational improvement), merge quietly into a roll-up (often at a discount), or slowly lose both census and staff as residents transfer to better-funded homes. The 121,000 small operators are the residual—the unleveraged, the local-only, the under-resourced.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Reimbursement claws back faster than labor costs stabilize. Medicare and Medicaid (which fund 60%+ of assisted living and home care) are already cutting per diem rates and tightening home care hours in several states. If wage growth stays at 3-4% annually but payer rates flatten or decline, the margin story inverts—even consolidated operators hit a wall. PE valuations are being written assuming that revenue growth (occupancy and rate) outpaces cost growth (wages and benefit); if that flips, the 2025-2026 M&A wave looks like the peak before the squeeze. Small operators that relied on a buyer to bail them out will have sold at the wrong time.

In one sentence

Senior housing at scale in a nutshell

Boomer demand fills beds faster than operators can staff them, making scale and capital the only reliable path to profitability—and consolidation the only exit for everyone else.

B · Care leaves the hospital

Care comes home

Home care is booming as seniors flee hospitals, but razor-thin margins and a caregiver shortage have agencies turning away one in four patients.

The money now strongly favors keeping seniors out of hospitals and nursing homes. Medicare, Medicaid, and insurers all discovered that a home care aide costs less than a facility bed. Home care exploded from $109.6 billion in 2021 to $191.6 billion in 2026 — a 75% jump in five years. But the agencies running this boom are drowning in a simple problem: not enough workers, not enough pay, and payment cuts that get deeper every year.

What changed

The government made home care suddenly *necessary* by cutting what they pay for facilities and long-term institutional care. Medicare slashed reimbursement to hospitals and nursing homes so aggressively that shifting seniors to home-based services became the only way to make the math work. Home care is now growing at 6.7% annually (2021-2026), and in 2026 alone the market grew 3.9% while reaching $191.6 billion — that's real demand, not hype. The shift made home care *cheap* relative to the alternative, and suddenly valuable to every insurance company and government program trying to manage costs. It also made caregiver labor desperately *scarce*. Over 2.4 million home health aides work in the US in 2026, and that number is projected to grow 17% by 2034 — but the problem is turnover. Annual caregiver turnover sits at 75%, meaning half the workforce quit and needs replacing every 18 months. Wages climbed from $13.07 per hour in 2014 to $16.77 in 2024, but that's still low compared to other healthcare work, and it's not enough to fix the shortage. Ninety-five percent of agencies report moderate-to-severe staffing shortages as of 2026, and they're now turning away up to 25% of patient requests. That's capacity they can't fill and money they can't capture. Meanwhile, payment cuts keep coming: Medicare slashed home health reimbursement for four straight years, with 2026 seeing a 1.3% aggregate reduction worth $220 million — after CMS originally proposed a 6.4% cut in November 2025. These cuts are *risky* to smaller agencies, forcing closures in rural and underserved areas where margins were already near zero. Thirty-four percent of agencies reported profit concerns in 2025-2026, and those agencies are competing for the same scarce caregivers with bigger, better-capitalized platforms. The profit opportunity is still there — the best agencies target 15-20% SDE margins — but you have to scale to reach them, which means you probably need private equity backing or a tech platform that lets you manage caregivers and patients more efficiently. Private equity figured this out fast. Fifty-five home health and hospice deals closed in the first half of 2026 alone, with 41% backed by PE firms. General Atlantic paid ~$3 billion for TEAM Services Group in Q2 2026 — the largest home care deal on record. Kinderhook took Enhabit private for $1.1 billion in Q1 2026. Humana snapped up the remaining stake in Kindred Healthcare for $5.7 billion in 2024 to fully own the home care giant. The fragmented industry — 437,000+ independent agencies — is consolidating fast, with PE-backed platforms building scale, technology, and caregiver networks that smaller operators can't match. That consolidation is making the industry slightly *new* — value-based care models are shifting financial risk to lower-performing agencies through CMS rebalancing of quality scorecards, and cloud-based EMRs and remote patient monitoring are becoming mainstream. But integration is incomplete, and these technologies add administrative burden to agencies that are already stretched thin.

The evidence

  • Home care providers hit 2.4 million workers in 2026 but face 75% annual turnover despite caregiver wages rising from $13.07/hr (2014) to $16.77/hr (2024).
  • Medicare cut home health reimbursement 1.3% in 2026, the fourth year of cuts, forcing closure waves in rural areas where 34% of agencies reported profit concerns (2025-2026).
  • General Atlantic's $3 billion acquisition of TEAM Services Group (Q2 2026) was the largest home care deal on record as PE consolidates the fragmented 437,000-agency market.
  • 95% of home care agencies report moderate-to-severe staffing shortages in 2026, turning away up to 25% of patient requests as demand outpaces workforce growth.
  • The home care market jumped from $109.6 billion (2021) to $191.6 billion (2026) at 6.7% CAGR, but the best agencies only target 15-20% SDE margins while 34% struggle with profitability (2025-2026).

Who rides it

Private equity platforms and large integrated health systems that can scale. The best home care players now have technology platforms (cloud EMRs, remote monitoring), national caregiver networks, and enough volume to absorb margin cuts and ride out workforce volatility. General Atlantic, Kinderhook, and Humana are buying scale and consolidation power. Smaller PE-backed platforms that own home care assets directly benefit from rising demand and can squeeze out independent agencies. Technology vendors selling EMRs, patient monitoring, and caregiver scheduling software also win — agencies are forced to adopt these tools to manage stretched teams and improve reimbursement through value-based care scorecards.

Who's squeezed

Independent home care agencies, especially in rural and underserved areas where margins are already thin and caregivers are even harder to find. Closure waves are already underway. Smaller agencies can't compete for scarce caregiver talent — they can't match wages or offer career paths like bigger platforms do. Caregivers themselves lose too, despite wage growth: $16.77 per hour (2024) is still low for healthcare work, and 75% annual turnover means burnout and instability for the workforce. Patients in rural areas lose access as agencies shutter and agencies in other regions turn away 25% of requests.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The caregiver shortage is the single biggest risk to the whole model. If agencies can't hire fast enough, they can't take on more patients, which means demand stays unmet and the upside gets capped. Home care is growing 6.7% annually, but home health aide jobs are only projected to grow 17% by 2034 — that's real growth, but not enough to match demand if baby boomers age faster or migrate to underserved regions. Wages would have to spike much higher to attract workers from other fields, which would crush margins further and force more closures. Alternatively, agencies shift to lower-acuity, easier-to-staff services, which means higher-need seniors (the most expensive and complex patients) get pushed back into hospitals — defeating the whole purpose of the home care boom.

In one sentence

Care comes home in a nutshell

Home care is booming as payers shift seniors out of hospitals, but a caregiver shortage and four years of Medicare cuts mean agencies can only capture the upside if they scale fast or face closure.

The Specialists of Old Age

Age-skewed outpatient specialties boom as boomers age into their skin-cancer and chronic-pain years, but Medicare cuts and consolidation narrow the field.

The demographic wave hits hardest in specialties tied to aging bodies: dermatologists screen for skin cancer, allergists manage lifelong rhinitis, chiropractors treat the aching spine. The US dermatology market alone sits at $8-9 billion in 2026, growing 7-8% annually, while the allergy market jumped from $24.74 billion (2025) to $26.56 billion (2026). But reimbursement cuts and workforce scarcity are reshaping who survives.

What changed

Dermatology is a masterclass in the squeeze. The industry pulls in $8-9 billion (2026) with 7-8% annual growth, yet 85% of the ~12,000 practicing dermatologists still work in solo or small-group practices—exactly when Medicare threatens a 9% reimbursement cut in 2027. Cosmetic dermatology is the escape hatch: the medical aesthetics market exploded from $19.55 billion (2025) to $22.59 billion (2026), a 12.4% jump, with Botox alone valued at $9.84 billion in 2025 and on track to reach $18.76 billion by 2035. Dermatologists are buying Botox licenses and lasers to shift from insurance-dependent skin cancer screening (10-15% margins) into self-pay cosmetic work (30-50% margins). Meanwhile, private equity has backed 35+ multistate platforms—Schweiger, U.S. Dermatology Partners, Forefront, Pinnacle—and closed 16 deals through October 2025, including Schweiger's landmark acquisition of California Skin Institute. Solo practitioners fetch 3-5x EBITDA, small groups 4-9x, but the real prize is scaled platforms at 12-15x; solos are getting picked off.

Allergists face a different poison: the market is growing 8.8-9.1% annually through 2035, but practice consolidation is hollowing out the specialty. In 2023, there were 3,417 allergists (10% growth from 2015) but only 1,585 practices—down 11% from 1,782 in 2015. Allergists per practice doubled from 7 to 11, meaning the field is merging into multispecialty networks at breakneck speed. Young graduates post-2010 show 65% adoption of multispecialty groups versus 42% for earlier cohorts, a signal that solo practice is vanishing. Medicare reimbursement fell 3.4% in 2024 and another 2.83% in 2025 (the conversion factor dropped to $32.35), crushing margins that were already tight at 14.4-14.5% EBIT. At-home allergy testing kits ($60-200) now undercut office diagnostics, and telehealth is growing 17.4% annually—patients can consult remotely without visiting. Physician burnout affects 41.9% of allergists (2025), with staffing shortages and admin burden driving the exodus. The paradox: allergy incidence has risen 100% per decade for rhinitis and 21% for pediatric peanut allergies since 2010, so demand is surging, but the specialty can't capture it profitably at the solo level.

Chiropractors sit in the strangest spot: a $24 billion market (2026) with only 2.6% annual growth, 38,000 individual practitioners, and 70,000+ establishments, yet 70% are still independent. Franchise chains like The Joint (950+ locations, July 2026) and venture-backed digital startups (ChiroHD raised $26 million in 2025) are eating their lunch. Insurance reimbursement rates shrink annually; cash patients are priced out by high deductibles and cost-of-living stress. Digital competitors offer AI-driven diagnostics, employer contracts, and remote monitoring—things traditional chiropractors can't match. Private equity is hunting platform targets at 2.8x-3.8x EBITDA, betting consolidation unlocks profitability. But the industry's real hope—expansion of Medicare coverage to include evaluation, imaging, and non-manipulation services under the Chiropractic Medicare Coverage Modernization Act—has stalled at 167 House cosponsors as of August 2026, leaving practitioners in limbo. Without that legislative win, consolidation is the only path.

All three specialties are age-ready: dermatology rides skin-cancer screening in aging skin, allergies climb as boomers manage chronic rhinitis and food sensitivities, and chiropractic thrives on back pain in the 65+ set. But the economics reward scale, not specialization. Dermatologists who build cosmetic aesthetics operations escape into high-margin self-pay; allergists who join multispecialty networks share overhead and cross-sell to dermatology/ENT patients; chiropractors who franchise or go private-equity-backed survive. The lonely solo practitioner in any of these fields is facing an impossible choice: sell now, merge with a network, or build a cash-pay moat before reimbursement kills the model entirely.

The evidence

  • Dermatology: 12,000 practitioners, 85% solo/small-group; 35+ PE platforms consolidating at 16 deals through October 2025, with cosmetic aesthetics jumping from $19.55B (2025) to $22.59B (2026) at 12.4% CAGR (Healio, 2025).
  • Allergy: Market grew 7.3% to $26.56B (2026) while practice count fell 11% (1,782→1,585); allergists per practice doubled (7→11), signaling consolidation into multispecialty networks dominated by post-2010 graduates (IBISWorld, 2025-2026).
  • Chiropractic: $24B market with 2.6% growth; 70% still independent solos, but The Joint (950 locations, July 2026) and private equity (ChiroHD raised $26M in 2025) are capturing market share via franchises and digital diagnostics (Entrepreneur, IBISWorld, August 2026).
  • Medicare cuts: Dermatology faces 9% reimbursement cut in 2027; allergists saw 3.4% (2024) and 2.83% (2025) cuts; chiropractors waiting on legislative expansion (Medicare Coverage Modernization Act stalled at 167 House cosponsors, August 2026).
  • Margin squeeze: Dermatology's self-pay cosmetic segment (30-50% margins) vs. insurance skin cancer work (10-15%); allergy EBIT stable at 14.4-14.5% but at-home testing and telehealth (17.4% annual growth) compete directly; chiropractors at 2.6% growth with rising admin costs compressing the 19.5-19.7% margin (Healio, IBISWorld, 2025-2026).

Who rides it

Dermatologists who own cosmetic aesthetics operations escape Medicare reimbursement cuts into high-margin self-pay work; Botox is on track to reach $18.76 billion by 2035. Multispecialty networks win the allergy game—consolidated practices can negotiate better insurance rates, share overhead, and cross-sell dermatology and ENT services to the same aging patient. Franchised chiropractors and private-equity-backed platforms (ChiroHD, The Joint) win by standardizing workflow, adding AI diagnostics (ChiroTouch's Rheo, August 2025), and capturing employer contracts—advantages solo practitioners cannot match. Large platforms command 12-15x EBITDA multiples, a 2-3x premium over solos.

Who's squeezed

Solo practitioners in all three specialties are squeezed: dermatologists in low-margin insurance screening; allergists managing overhead with shrinking Medicare reimbursement (2025 conversion factor down to $32.35); chiropractors losing cash patients to cost-of-living stress and digital competitors. Physicians in group practices who joined early get diluted by at-home testing kits and telehealth. Young allergists face burnout (41.9%, 2025) and administrative burden with no path to ownership. Chiropractors are held hostage by Medicare expansion legislation that stalled at 167 House cosponsors, freezing them out of imaging and diagnostic coverage. The 38,000 independent chiropractors collectively lose market share to 950 Joint locations; the 1,585 allergy practices shrinking from 1,782 tell the story of consolidation grinding down autonomy.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that Medicare cuts accelerate and hollow out these specialties before consolidation can restore margins. Dermatology could see primary-care AI screening (DermaSensor FDA approval, January 2024) slash referrals faster than cosmetic demand can compensate. Allergists face a death spiral: Medicare cuts → burnout → exodus → fewer practices → higher costs → more cuts. And chiropractors have no Plan B if the Medicare Coverage Modernization Act stays dead—they are trapped between franchise consolidation and legislative hostage-taking, with no path to profitability at scale on their own. The aging population generates real demand, but the reimbursement model is breaking faster than the market can adapt.

In one sentence

The specialists of old age in a nutshell

Age-driven demand floods into dermatology, allergies, and chiropractic, but Medicare cuts and consolidation pressure force practitioners to sell, merge, or escape into self-pay and franchise models.

C · The money side of aging

Insuring a longer life

Living longer turns into an insurance and annuity market—but carriers face a pricing bind that's reshaping who wins and who pays.

The US life and long-term care insurance industry is worth $1.1 trillion as of 2026, but it's caught in a squeeze. Boomers are living longer, which should mean endless demand. Instead, carriers are wrestling with policies they priced wrong twenty years ago, new rate hikes that scare customers away, and a public Medicaid system that undercuts them on price. The money is there—but so are the headwinds.

What changed

The long-term care insurance market became a victim of its own optimism in the 1990s and 2000s. Carriers like Genworth and Prudential issued aggressive policies at rates that drastically underestimated both how long people would live and how expensive cognitive decline claims would be. The median time from an Alzheimer's diagnosis to a nursing home is 3.3 years—far costlier than underwriters predicted. Now the bill is coming due. Genworth alone is carrying $31.2 billion in cumulative rate increase approvals across all its policies. A 55-year-old woman buying coverage in 2025 pays roughly $3,750 per year; a man the same age pays $2,200. When policies renew, customers face sticker shock: increases of 10–25% are common, and some older policyholders see jumps of 40% or more. The market is shrinking because of it—growth was only 2.4% annually from 2020 to 2025, and the market size fell from $31.6 billion in 2021 to $25.6 billion in 2025. State regulators are tightening the screws. Connecticut passed legislation in May 2026 requiring public hearings for any rate hike above 10%, forcing carriers to justify their numbers in front of elected officials. The Federal Long-Term Care Insurance Program—which covered federal employees—remains suspended as of April 2026 because even the government decided pricing had become unsustainable. That's a signal.\n\nAnnuities and guaranteed income products, by contrast, are on fire. US retail annuity sales hit a record $464 billion in 2025, up 7% from 2024, marking the fourth consecutive record year. Every quarter now exceeds $100 billion in sales. The driver is simple: four million Americans hit retirement age each year, and they're terrified of running out of money. Fixed-indexed annuities (which offer upside participation in stock indexes while protecting against downside) nearly doubled to $126 billion in 2024. The newer Registered Index-Linked Annuities (RILAs) exploded, surging 270% from $24 billion in 2020 to $65 billion in 2024. These products appeal to affluent retirees who lived through 2008 and 2022 and want guaranteed income, not volatility. But this growth is happening in a shrinking population of traditional insurance buyers. The individual life insurance market is stalled. Sales are flat in 2025 and projected to grow only 1% in 2026, according to LIMRA. The problem is generational: Gen Z and younger millennials believe term life insurance costs ten to twelve times more than it actually does. They also lack the traditional triggers—marriage, children, mortgages—that pushed prior generations to buy coverage. The life insurance industry's regulatory capital hit an unprecedented $536 billion in Q3 2025, well above pre-pandemic levels, which freed carriers to chase yield in riskier assets. Insurance companies now hold 31.4% of their portfolios in private credit, up sharply as they hunt for returns in a low-rate world. That's a bet on defaults staying low.\n\nWhat became scarce is affordable protection for people in their late fifties and early sixties who want to lock in long-term care coverage before health issues price them out. What became cheap, paradoxically, is guaranteed income—record annuity sales mean fierce competition among carriers and aggressive distribution through fintech platforms and fee-only advisors. What became risky is holding the old playbook: the carriers who issued policies on 1990s mortality assumptions are now forced to choose between bleeding money or hiking rates so aggressively that customers flee to Medicaid (which is basically free for the poor) or skip coverage entirely. What became newly valuable is disciplined underwriting and curated care networks. Genworth's October 2025 launch of CareScout—available in 40+ states with 500+ pre-negotiated providers by end 2024—is a bet that the future of long-term care insurance looks less like "pay any provider" and more like a managed care network where carriers can negotiate rates and outcomes.

The evidence

  • Long-term care insurance (Genworth, Prudential): Market size $25.6B in 2025, down from $31.6B in 2021, with growth stalling at 2.4% CAGR (2020-2025) due to affordability crises and rate hikes of 10-25% annually
  • Annuities (MetLife, Lincoln National, Principal, Voya): Record $464 billion in US retail annuity sales in 2025, up 7% annually, with RILAs surging 270% from $24B (2020) to $65B (2024) as four million annual retirees seek guaranteed income
  • Life insurance (603 enterprises, largest players MetLife, Prudential): Market size $1.1 trillion in 2026 with 0.6% growth in 2025 but -1.4% contraction in 2026; individual life sales flat in 2025, projected 1% growth in 2026
  • Insurance regulatory capital (all carriers): Hit $536 billion in Q3 2025, driving 31.4% private credit allocations by end 2024 as carriers chase yield amid low rates and mortality normalization
  • Federal Long-Term Care Insurance Program (FLTCIP): Remains suspended as of April 2026 for new applications due to cost volatility and diminished market—a signal that even government pricing models failed

Who rides it

The big annuity and life insurance carriers—MetLife, Prudential, Lincoln National—win on guaranteed income. Retirees desperate for stability in a volatile world are buying annuities at record volumes, generating steady revenue and higher margins than volatile equity-linked products. RILAs in particular offer carriers a middle ground: upside participation that keeps customers happy, downside protection that keeps claims controlled. Fintech platforms and fee-only advisors also win, becoming the preferred distribution channel for annuities because they reach affluent retirees directly and handle the paperwork. Genworth wins by shifting away from the legacy long-term care playbook and launching CareScout—a managed network model that lets them control costs and outcomes instead of bleeding money on unpredictable claims. Connecticut regulators win because the new transparency rules (public hearings for rate hikes above 10%) force carriers to justify their numbers and protect consumers from the next round of shock increases.

Who's squeezed

Customers in their late fifties and early sixties lose because long-term care insurance is becoming unaffordable right when they need to lock in coverage. A 55-year-old woman pays $3,750 per year and will see that rise 10-25% annually. Many simply skip the insurance and bet on Medicaid, which is basically free for the indigent. Carriers holding legacy long-term care books lose because they're trapped: they issued policies at rates that don't cover claims, so they must either raise rates (driving customers away) or absorb losses. Genworth and Prudential are already struggling with this choice—Genworth alone carries $31.2 billion in approved rate increases it still has to implement. Individual life insurance agents lose as their market stagnates; Gen Z and millennials aren't buying because they either can't afford it or think it costs ten times more than it does. Insurance companies' private credit bets lose if the credit cycle turns and defaults spike—they're holding 31.4% of portfolios in private credit, a high allocation in a slowing economy.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that the long-term care insurance market collapses under the weight of rate increases that policyholders simply won't pay. If Genworth and Prudential try to implement their $31.2 billion in approved rate hikes all at once, customers will flee to Medicaid or drop coverage entirely, which will shrink the market further and push the remaining carriers toward insolvency. The Federal Long-Term Care Insurance Program's April 2026 suspension is a warning: even government can't make the math work. If carriers can't raise rates fast enough to cover claims, they'll either exit the market or demand state bailouts. A second worry is mortality risk in the annuity market: if recession drives unemployment and mortality spikes in vulnerable populations, or if long-term longevity assumptions prove wrong in the opposite direction (people live even longer than expected), carriers holding $464 billion in annuity liabilities could face margin compression or worse. The private credit bet—31.4% of insurance portfolios—is also dangerous: if the credit cycle turns, defaults spike, and liquidity freezes, insurers could face capital calls and forced asset sales.

In one sentence

Insuring a longer life in a nutshell

Boomers demand longer-life insurance, but carriers priced wrong twenty years ago and now face a choice: raise rates to unsustainable levels and lose customers to Medicaid, or absorb losses and exit the market.

C · The money side of aging

The drug that rewrote aging

GLP-1 medications obliterated the diet industry and forced pharmaceutical makers into a trillion-dollar reshoring sprint.

GLP-1 drugs did in five years what decades of fitness apps and diet programs could not: they made obesity treatable like a chronic illness. Adoption shot from 5.8% of American adults in February 2024 to 18% by 2026. That speed crushed an entire industry and remade pharmacology into a different business.

What changed

The weight loss services industry collapsed from $3.8 billion in 2022 to $2.6 billion in 2026—a 32% contraction in four years. This was not a slow decline. It was structural displacement. When obesity rates fell from 39.9% to 36.4% (2022–2026) almost overnight, the addressable market for traditional diet coaching shrank by millions of paying customers. Weight Watchers, which had survived 60 years of fad diets, filed for bankruptcy in May 2025 and emerged as a private company after shedding $1.15 billion in debt. The company's pivot—acquiring Sequence telehealth in March 2024 specifically to deliver GLP-1 prescriptions—showed the desperation. Legacy weight loss was not evolving; it was being replaced.

Meanwhile, brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturing leaped into overdrive. The U.S. market hit $293.9 billion in 2026 (up from $227.1 billion in 2022), though growth had flatlined at 0.0% CAGR from 2021–2025 before accelerating to 3.0% in 2026. The reason: GLP-1 obesity drugs alone created an $82.0 billion market segment growing at 12.4% annually. Oncology, another high-margin specialty, hit $286.6 billion and grew 11.8% per year. These two segments were eating the lunch of older blockbuster drugs—Humira biosimilars, Stelara, Eylea—whose patents expired in 2025–2026. Patent cliffs meant the industry could no longer coast on volume; it had to pivot violently toward specialty therapies and rare-disease treatments where margins stayed thick.

Then came the tariff shock. In April 2026, the Trump administration imposed 100% default tariffs on pharmaceutical imports, with 20% relief for companies pledging domestic manufacturing and 15% for allied-country suppliers. Big Pharma had no choice: within weeks, major manufacturers announced over $480 billion in reshoring commitments across 22 new manufacturing sites and 44,000 jobs. Eli Lilly pledged $27 billion, Merck $70 billion, J&J $55 billion. But reshoring takes years; no major U.S. plant would finish before 2029. The industry was caught between tariff penalties and supply-chain uncertainty for years. CDMOs—contract manufacturing organizations handling dose formulation—saw $24.86 billion in capacity investments globally in 2025, with $18.48 billion (74%) flowing to the United States, a sign of nearshoring desperation.

The IRA's drug price negotiation program, which kicked in January 2026, added another layer of margin pressure. The first 10 drugs faced 10–20% price cuts; the program expands to 20 drugs annually by 2028. Out-of-pocket caps for beneficiaries were capped at $2,000 per year. For manufacturers, this meant negotiated pricing eroding the premium-drug model that had justified decades of R&D spending. M&A spending spiked 81% to $240 billion across biopharma in 2025—companies desperate to consolidate pipelines, eliminate redundancy, and scale specialty-drug distribution before regulation bit deeper. H1 2026 alone saw $134 billion in deals (J&J acquired Intra-Cellular for $14.6 billion; BioMarin bought Amicus for $4.8 billion), a scramble to lock down supply chains and rare-disease portfolios that price-regulation could not touch as easily.

The evidence

  • Weight loss services: $3.8B market (2022) collapsed to $2.6B (2026), a 32% contraction as GLP-1 adoption reached 18% of U.S. adults.
  • Brand-name pharma: $227.1B market (2022) expanded to $293.9B (2026); GLP-1 obesity segment alone hit $82.0B growing 12.4% annually.
  • Tariffs: April 2026 Trump tariffs (100% default, 20% for onshoring, 15% for allies) triggered $480B+ reshoring pledges from Eli Lilly ($27B), Merck ($70B), J&J ($55B) across 22 sites.
  • M&A surge: Biopharma M&A spending jumped 81% to $240B in 2025; H1 2026 alone saw $134B in deals (J&J/Intra-Cellular $14.6B, BioMarin/Amicus $4.8B).
  • Price regulation: IRA Medicare negotiation program (January 2026) caps beneficiary out-of-pocket costs at $2,000 annually and mandates 10–20% manufacturer price cuts on first 10 drugs, expanding to 20 by 2028.

Who rides it

GLP-1 manufacturers and large telehealth platforms win decisively. Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and J&J dominate a market growing 12%+ annually and see room to expand globally. Hims, Ro, and noom—digital platforms that integrated GLP-1 prescribing—capture market share by offering direct-to-consumer convenience; Hims acquired Zava in June 2025 specifically for European GLP-1 distribution. Large CDMOs and nearshoring providers benefit from $24.86 billion in capacity investments (2025), especially the 74% flowing to U.S. domestic manufacturing. Specialty pharma as a category—oncology, rare disease, biologics—thrives as the industry pivots away from low-margin blockbusters toward high-margin, hard-to-replicate therapies.

Who's squeezed

Legacy diet and weight loss services are wiped out. Small and mid-market weight loss clinics that failed to integrate GLP-1 prescribing face margin collapse and closure; the industry shed 13,413 businesses by 2025. Regional practices without capital to invest in supply chains, digital infrastructure, or regulatory expertise get squeezed. Generic drug makers and CDMOs face tariff penalties and margin compression from both tariff shocks and IRA price negotiation. Patients on non-GLP-1 therapies see slower innovation pipelines as pharma diverts R&D spending to obesity and oncology specialties. Smaller biopharma firms without M&A war chests cannot compete in the $134 billion deal frenzy and risk being acquired at discount valuations or going dark.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is supply-chain fragmentation and tariff-driven shortages. No major U.S. pharmaceutical manufacturing plant finishes before 2029, meaning the industry remains dependent on foreign APIs and exposed to tariff escalation, geopolitical friction, or supply interruptions for 3–5 more years. A tariff escalation beyond the current 100% default could break the reshoring math and trigger shortage cascades. A second risk is price regulation eating into margins faster than expected: IRA negotiation expands from 10 drugs (2026) to 20 annually (2028), and if those drugs include major GLP-1 or oncology therapies, profitability could crater. Finally, GLP-1 adoption may plateau below 25% of adults due to side effects, manufacturing constraints, or insurance coverage limits, leaving the pharma industry with massive reshoring capex but slower-than-expected revenue growth to justify it.

In one sentence

The drug that rewrote aging in a nutshell

GLP-1 drugs turned obesity into a pharmaceutical market, obliterated the diet industry, and forced Big Pharma into a $480 billion domestic reshoring sprint—while tariffs and price regulation squeeze margins from both ends.

C · The money side of aging

Grey Leisure & the Active Old

Boomers retire with money to spend on leisure, but retail contraction, price resistance, and structural shifts are reshaping where the cash actually goes.

Active retirees have cash and time. You'd think leisure—hiking gear, amusement parks, campgrounds—would boom. But the money is crashing into a broken supply chain and a customer base getting pickier about what they spend on. The winners are those who control scarce supply; everyone else is fighting over a flattening pie.

What changed

The outdoor retail industry that peaked during the pandemic is now in freefall. Hiking and outdoor equipment stores shrank from $7.1 billion in 2022 to $6.3 billion in 2026, a contraction of roughly 11 percent even as 183 million Americans still reported outdoor participation in 2025. REI, the category leader, has become a cautionary tale: it shut down its entire Experiences division (tours and classes) in January 2025 after those offerings served only 40,000 of its 23 million co-op members. The company laid off 180 full-time and 248 part-time employees in the same quarter, trimmed another 257 retail positions in October 2024, and posted losses exceeding $300 million in 2022 and 2023. Dick's Sporting Goods, which tried to compete head-to-head with premium formats, abandoned its Public Lands brand after it collapsed from eight locations to three. The culprit is simple: boomers are browsing Amazon, comparing prices online, and buying less frequently. Margins are razor-thin (3.5 to 4.3 percent) because inventory still reflects pandemic-era ordering mistakes, and both Amazon and Walmart are moving upmarket on price, squeezing independents out of the middle. Smaller shops continue to close. Consolidation accelerates.

Amusement parks tell a different story—one of nominal growth masking real trouble underneath. The industry hit $33.4 billion in 2026, growing at a 9.7 percent CAGR since 2022, but the growth is heavily skewed by blockbuster new assets (Universal's Epic Universe opened in May 2025 with projections to serve 5.2 million visitors its first year and climb to 9.2 million by 2026). Disney's domestic parks attracted 76.5 million visitors in 2024—essentially flat year-over-year—and the company raised peak-day ticket prices to $224 at Disneyland and over $200 at Magic Kingdom in October 2025. That same move was accompanied by deeper discounts than the parks have offered in years, a signal that consumers are price-conscious and the market is stratifying: families with cash still spend; everyone else is staying home. Labor costs consume 35 percent of operating expenses and wage inflation remains sticky at 2.9 percent annually. The Cedar Fair-Six Flags merger, completed in July 2024, created a combined operator controlling 27 regional parks with a $5.5 billion debt load and declining attendance (down 1.4 million in Q2 2025 versus the prior year). Tariffs on imported ride systems and equipment are beginning to bite into capex budgets. Climate risk is now visible too: Hurricanes Helene and Milton imposed a $120 million operational cost on Disney in October 2024, a reminder that centralized destination parks carry infrastructure fragility.

The campgrounds and RV parks industry reveals the most interesting dynamic. Revenue grew 5.2 percent in 2025, but total reservations actually fell 1.0 percent for the first time in platform history—a textbook signal of a market shifting from volume growth to pricing power. Average nightly rates for medium parks jumped 16.6 percent to $83 per night. The sector is being remade by two forces: supply scarcity and generational mix. Building a new campground requires 24 to 48 months to permit and construct, at a cost of $60,000 per site, which creates a structural moat for existing operators and deters new entrants. That moat protects pricing. But who's using it? Glamping—upscale, experiential camping—is the only accommodation type growing; it surged 43.6 percent in 2025 while conventional RV parks stagnated. The money is going to premium, younger campers willing to pay for the experience, not to the core demographic of retirees in Class A motorhomes. Supply is so tight that cap rates (8.0 percent) sit above loan costs (8.7 to 9.3 percent), meaning new acquisitions start with negative leverage—returns depend entirely on operational improvements and rate optimization, not asset appreciation. The 2025 Guadalupe River flood and Hurricane Helene exposed uninsured waterfront risk and prompted Texas to tighten safety codes. Operators are retrenching: Sun Communities divested its entire Safe Harbor marina portfolio in October 2025 to exit marine leisure entirely. The RV industry itself is electrifying piecemeal (Ruby's Inn added Tesla Superchargers in July 2025), but infrastructure buildout is uneven and the passenger fleet remains overwhelmingly combustion-powered.

The evidence

  • Hiking & outdoor retail: market shrank from $7.1 billion (2022) to $6.3 billion (2026) with −2.6% annual decline and 3.5–4.3% margins; REI laid off 428 employees in January 2025 and closed Experiences division
  • Amusement parks: $33.4 billion in 2026, up 9.7% CAGR, but Disney's domestic parks flat at 76.5 million visitors (2024); peak-day tickets raised to $224 with offsetting discounts
  • Cedar Fair-Six Flags merger: completed July 2024; $5.5 billion debt load; Q2 2025 attendance down 1.4 million year-over-year
  • RV parks & campgrounds: $11.3 billion in 2026; reservations fell 1.0% in 2025 despite 5.2% revenue growth (pricing power not volume); glamping up 43.6%
  • Supply dynamics: 24-48 months to permit/build new campground at $60,000 per site; institutional cap rates (8.0%) exceed loan constants (8.7-9.3%), creating negative leverage

Who rides it

The winners are monopoly and near-monopoly operators in constrained categories. Universal's new Epic Universe was built to pull traffic away from competitors, not to grow the pie. Disney, despite raising prices and facing resistance, still controls the largest installed base. In campgrounds and RV parks, the 88 percent of the market still independently owned is being picked off: institutional operators like Sun Communities and KOA are consolidating supply, locking in pricing power, and betting that supply scarcity will keep rates rising faster than inflation. Glamping operators—younger, experiential, premium—are growing their segment at 43.6 percent annually because they're selling a different product to a different demographic. Equipment makers selling directly to consumers (brands like REI Co-op or private-label Amazon outdoor gear) sidestep retail erosion entirely. The losers in outdoor retail are losing so badly that REI, the co-op gold standard, had to destroy its own Experiences division to survive.

Who's squeezed

Retail chains and independent outdoor shops are being squeezed into irrelevance. Dick's Sporting Goods tried to compete on quality and failed: its Public Lands brand went from eight stores to three. REI, the stronger player, is now a shell of its pandemic peak, shedding staff and shuttering profitable-adjacent services. The entire outdoor retail category is contracting—1,382 establishments in 2025, losing establishments and employees (20,834 total) every quarter. Regional amusement park operators under the Cedar Fair-Six Flags umbrella are trapped: $5.5 billion in debt, flat or declining attendance, and labor costs consuming 35 percent of operating expenses with no way to cut further. Consumers buying RV park visits are being pushed into a choice between premium (glamping, which is up 43.6 percent) or commodified (cheap, no-frills parks). The middle—mid-range RV parks, mom-and-pop outdoor shops, regional theme parks—is hollowing out.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that this isn't cyclical—it's structural. Retail outdoor equipment probably won't rebound because consumers have permanently shifted to online browsing and price comparison. Amusement parks are dependent on blockbuster new assets (Epic Universe, new Magic Kingdom lands) to grow attendance; Disney is already at the limit of price resistance (peak tickets at $224) while operating margins erode from labor and tariff costs. Campgrounds face a convergence of climate risk (Hurricanes Helene and Milton exposed uninsured waterfront exposure) and infrastructure brittleness (RV charging, water systems, road access are aging). The real worry is that active, wealthy retirees—the supposed beneficiaries of the grey leisure boom—are being bifurcated: the very wealthy still spend freely on premium experiences and high-end gear (Epic Universe, glamping, $224 Disney tickets), but the mass affluent middle is becoming price-sensitive and trading down. If economic slowdown hits retirement accounts, grey leisure could contract sharply across the board. REI's collapse from category darling to layoff machine happened in five years; the system proved fragile.

In one sentence

Grey leisure & the active old in a nutshell

The boom in grey leisure is real, but it's concentrating in constrained supply (premium parks, glamping, branded experiences) while retail and mid-market recreation contract under price pressure and structural change.
