D · The tensions

Who pays for all this

Medicare Advantage is the card at the table, but the deck is rigged — premiums went vertical, but insurers are hemorrhaging money on the sicker population they said they'd manage.

Medicare Advantage owns the eldercare market now. These managed-care plans carved out $359.2 billion in 2026, pulling in 34 million seniors. But the deal that made sense five years ago — insurers take risk, trim fat, profit on efficiency — has inverted. The companies that bid to cover boomers are now pinned between rising demand they can't refuse and payment cuts they can't negotiate.

What changed

Medicare Advantage premiums surged because the math broke. Earned premiums rose 14.3% in 2025, yet insurers' actual claims climbed even faster at 15.5% — meaning they're losing ground on every policy, even after jacking up prices. Seventeen percent of MA contracts ran at a loss (above 100% medical loss ratio) in 2023, and another third live in the knife's edge between 90–95%, with no cushion for surprises. The surprise came: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic exploded as demand from obese and diabetic seniors flooded the system, and these drugs cost 2–3 times what insurers budgeted. Tariffs from the Trump administration tacked on another 2–3.6% to medical supplies and device costs in 2025–2026. The pricing power insurers grabbed — hiking premiums aggressively — has a shelf life. CMS is now running aggressive audits for "upcoding," where insurers get paid more by coding patients as sicker than they are. For 2026 alone, the agency launched enhanced audits targeting exactly this fraud, which means the margin squeeze can only tighten.

The insurer response has been swift and brutal. UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Aetna, and CVS all announced market exits and benefit cuts for 2026 MA plans in 2025. Cigna sold off its entire Medicare business (MA, Part D, supplemental) to Health Care Service Corp. in March 2025. Smaller regional carriers like Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare stopped offering Medicaid and ACA coverage entirely on January 1, 2026, keeping only MA. CMS predicted MA enrollment would fall from 35 million in 2024 to 34 million in 2025, but the real story is worse: 2.9 million seniors were forced to switch plans because insurers exited their markets. The insurers making money on Medicare Advantage today are not growing; they're retreating to the ZIP codes and risk profiles where they can still turn a profit.

Outside Medicare Advantage, the whole insurance ecosystem is in repricing shock. The broad health insurance market ($1.6 trillion in 2026, up from $1.13 trillion in 2022) is finally recovering margins after they crashed in 2023–2024 — but this recovery is built on squeezing both ends. Employer-sponsored premiums jumped 9% for 2026, the highest in 15 years. ACA marketplace premiums jumped 18% for 2026, and benchmark plans jumped 26%, far exceeding what insurers proposed. The December 31, 2025 expiration of enhanced ACA premium tax credits means that subsidized enrollees will watch their annual out-of-pocket premiums double from $888 to $1,904 in 2026 — a shock that will push millions into uninsured status or Medicaid. Medicaid itself is shrinking for the first time since COVID: enrollment fell 7.6% in 2025, driven by new work and reporting requirements in the 2025 reconciliation bill, and is forecast to grow only 0.2% in 2026.

Dental insurance tells the same story of payment collapse from a different angle. The market hit $99.9 billion in 2026, growing only 2.62% annually through 2035. Plan maximums — the annual cap on what the insurer will pay — are stuck at $1,000–1,500, which is 1/17th of their 1975 value in real dollars. Patients increasingly find procedures cheaper out-of-pocket than through insurance, rotting the fundamental value exchange. Dentist network participation cratered to 32% in major PPO networks by 2024, meaning most patients now pay out-of-pocket rates anyway. Dental service organizations (DSOs) have consolidated 16.1% of the market by 2024 (up from 7.2% in 2015), shifting bargaining power away from insurers to practice owners. Regulators intervened hard: 37 state dental insurance reform laws passed in 2025, the largest single reform wave in the industry, mandating minimum loss ratios, human review of AI claim denials, and transparency on retroactive denials.

The evidence

  • Health Insurance (broad US market): $1.6 trillion in 2026, growing 3.9% CAGR 2021–2026, margins recovering to 8.30% in 2025–2026 after collapse in 2023–2024 via premium rate increases
  • Medicare Advantage: $359.2B in 2026, but 17% of contracts above 100% MLR and 33% in 90–95% range; incurred claims grew 15.5% in 2025 vs. earned premiums 14.3%, creating per-policy losses
  • ACA Marketplace: Benchmark plan premiums jumped 26% for 2026; unsubsidized premiums double from $888 to $1,904 annually on Jan 1, 2026 after enhanced tax credit expiration
  • Dental Insurance: $99.9B in 2026, enrollment down 2.3% in 2025; plan maximums ($1,000–1,500) worth 1/17 of 1975 value in real dollars; 32% dentist network participation in major PPO by 2024
  • Medicaid: Enrollment fell 7.6% in 2025 due to work/reporting requirements; forecast growth only 0.2% in 2026

Who rides it

Big insurers are consolidating around Medicare Advantage and wringing pricing power out of employer and ACA markets — but only if they can exit the unprofitable MA ZIP codes and patient cohorts. UnitedHealthcare, Humana, and Cigna are retreating strategically: they're keeping the high-margin MA segments, hiking premiums 9–26% across employer and ACA, and buying time with policy exits. Employers with enough scale are winning too — they're self-insuring or moving to defined-contribution plans to escape premium inflation. Tech entrants like Amazon (GLP-1 at $25/month through One Medical as of April 2026) and TrumpRx.gov (direct-to-consumer pharma bypassing insurance) are siphoning off the most profitable and easiest-to-manage segments: primary care, drug fulfillment, and chronic condition management. Regional DSOs in dentistry are consolidating 16.1% of practices (up from 7.2% in 2015) and shifting bargaining power away from insurers.

Who's squeezed

Seniors on MA plans that stay open will see benefit cuts — narrower networks, higher out-of-pocket costs, more prior authorization. The 2.9 million seniors forced off plans in 2025–2026 are being pushed into traditional Medicare or replacement MA plans in worse zip codes. Unsubsidized ACA enrollees face a cliff: their premiums double from $888 to $1,904 on January 1, 2026, a shock that will drive millions into uninsured status or into Medicaid (which itself is shrinking by 7.6% in 2025). Dentists are squeezed on both ends: insurers keep reimbursement flat while DSO consolidation pressures independent practices to sell. Providers of all types (hospitals, medical device suppliers, dental practices) face margin compression: they face insurers holding the line on payments while tariffs and labor costs rise 2–3.6% annually.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is demand inelasticity meeting hard reimbursement ceilings. Boomers entering their care years have chronic diseases (diabetes, heart disease, obesity) that require continuous, expensive treatment — they can't skip care. But Medicare Advantage is losing money on every patient over 90–95% MLR, and CMS audits for upcoding are tightening the screws further. Insurers can't raise premiums fast enough to cover claim growth (15.5% in 2025 vs. 14.3% premium growth), and they can't negotiate down claims because seniors demand care and providers are consolidating into DSOs and hospital networks with more pricing power. The death spiral risk is real: as insurers exit unprofitable markets and raise out-of-pocket costs, only the sickest and most-vulnerable seniors remain, pushing MLRs even higher and triggering more exits. The 2026 MA contraction is just the start.

Medicare Advantage is the de facto payment system for elderly America, but it's trapped between seniors who need constant care and a government that keeps cutting what it pays for managing that care.

D · The tensions

The Caregiver Shortage

When 73 million boomers need care but nobody's home to give it, wages spike and profits crumble.

Demand for home care and residential senior services is exploding—the market hit $191.6 billion in 2026 and is growing 6.7% annually. But there's a hard wall: the people who actually do the work are vanishing. Ninety-five percent of home care agencies report moderate-to-severe staffing shortages, and caregiver turnover sits at 75% annually. The shortage is so acute that agencies are turning away up to 25% of patient requests. The math doesn't work.

What changed

The caregiver shortage isn't coming—it's already here, and it's reshaping the entire senior-care economy. Home care aides, certified nursing assistants, and registered nurses are the actual constraint. Home care wages have climbed from $13.07 per hour in 2014 to $16.77 in 2024, a 28% jump in a decade, yet turnover stays locked at 75% annually because the pay is still low compared to other healthcare roles and the work is physically grueling with no benefits. This wage spiral is being driven by sheer shortage: agencies can't fill positions fast enough, so they have to keep raising what they offer just to keep beds staffed. Meanwhile, the Census Bureau projects 711,700 new home care jobs will be created between 2022 and 2032. Where do they come from? They don't. Instead, agencies choose: lose money covering overtime, close beds and turn away patients, or merge with larger platforms that can absorb the costs.

The shortage is fragmenting the market but only for the small operators. Home care is the most fragmented healthcare sector in America, with 437,000+ establishments—mostly mom-and-pop agencies—and 75% annual turnover was already chewing up margins before wages started spiking. Now, 34% of home care agencies reported profit concerns in 2025-2026. Some are near zero or negative margins. The strong performers target 15-20% SDE margins, but they're the exception. Meanwhile, private equity owns 41% of M&A deal volume in 2026 and is aggressively rolling up the market: 55 home health and hospice deals in the first half of 2026 alone. Private equity can weather the labor cost squeeze better than independents because they can deploy technology (cloud-based EMRs, remote patient monitoring are now mainstream), hire corporate HR teams, and transfer workers across their portfolio. A single franchisee or small agency cannot. The consolidation is accelerating precisely because the shortage makes scale valuable.

The government is tightening the purse at the same time labor gets expensive. Medicare cut home health payments by 1.3% in 2026 (after proposing a 6.4% cut initially), and these cuts have run for four straight years. That's $220 million yanked out of the system in 2026 alone, even as caregiver wages demand upward pressure. This squeeze is already visible: rural and underserved areas are seeing agency closures because the reimbursement no longer covers the labor floor. Residential senior care franchises face the same pressure—occupancy is strong (88.7% in Q3 2025, a 17-quarter high), but it's also squeezed staffing: registered nurses, CNAs, and dining staff report 40% turnover, and over half of home care agencies still report ongoing shortages. Franchises have grown from $5.967 billion in 2021 to a projected $9.0 billion by 2026, but that top-line growth is noise if margins are collapsing. The industry is also shifting to value-based care models where CMS rebalances quality scorecards and pushes financial risk onto lower-performing agencies—another margin haircut for the fragmented base.

Assisted living beds are growing only 1-2% annually while the over-80 population grows at 4%. That mismatch is forcing demand into franchised home and community-based care, where operators should be enjoying wider margins. Instead, the staffing crisis is clamping them. Baby boomers enter the 80+ cohort starting in 2027, which will intensify all three pressures simultaneously: rising demand, falling supply of workers, and tighter reimbursement. The 2025 M&A wave—871 deals, 20.8% above 2024's record—shows private equity knows exactly what's coming. Assisted living deals made up 44% of those 871 transactions. But the FTC and DOJ opened a formal investigation into the PE acquisition surge in March 2024, signaling regulatory scrutiny of consolidation. That's the real risk: if regulators throttle roll-ups, the fragmented base won't have an escape route when labor costs go vertical.

The evidence

  • Home Care Providers: 95% report staffing shortages, 75% annual turnover, agencies turning away up to 25% of patient requests (2025-2026).
  • Residential Senior Care Franchises: Assisted living beds growing only 1-2% annually while over-80 population grows 4%, forcing demand into home care (2026).
  • Wages in home care have risen 28% since 2014 ($13.07 to $16.77/hr), yet turnover stays at 75% and 34% of agencies report profit concerns (2024-2026).
  • Private equity owns 41% of home health M&A deal volume in 2026; 55 deals in first half of 2026 alone, driven by consolidation pressure from labor squeeze.
  • Medicare home health payment cut 1.3% in 2026 after four straight years of reductions, forcing rural agency closures even as caregiver wages spike.

Who rides it

Private equity and large platform operators win. They can absorb wage inflation through scale, deploy technology (cloud EMRs, remote monitoring), transfer workers across their portfolio, and weather the margin squeeze that kills independents. The 41% of 2026 M&A volume that's PE-backed isn't accidental—consolidators see the shortage as a moat. Humana's $5.7 billion acquisition of Kindred Healthcare (2024), General Atlantic's $3 billion grab of TEAM Services Group (Q2 2026), and Kinderhook's $1.1 billion take-private of Enhabit (Q1 2026) show institutional capital betting that scale beats fragmentation in a labor shortage. Large franchises with multiple locations can also shift labor between branches and amortize HR costs across hundreds of facilities. For the franchisee segment (121,000 businesses), the demographic tailwind is real—73 million boomers entering retirement with guaranteed demand—but only the ones who can get bigger survive the labor cost floor.

Who's squeezed

Independent and small home care agencies get squeezed from both sides. Medicare is cutting reimbursement ($220 million cut in 2026 alone, after four years of cuts) while caregiver wages are rising 31% cumulatively since 2019. Rural and underserved area agencies are closing because the reimbursement floor no longer covers labor. Single-location franchisees and mom-and-pop operators face 40% CNA turnover and ongoing staffing shortages that force them to either lose money on overtime, turn away patients, or get acquired. The 34% of home care agencies reporting profit concerns in 2025-2026 are mostly small operators who lack the scale to absorb wage inflation or the cash to wait for consolidation deals. Patients in rural areas are the real losers—as agencies close and urban operators shed unprofitable branches, care deserts expand.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that labor shortages get worse before consolidation scales fast enough to fix them. Baby boomers enter the 80+ cohort starting in 2027, which will spike demand exactly when the workforce is still undersupplied. If the FTC and DOJ—which opened a formal investigation into PE acquisition surge in March 2024—begin enforcing restrictions on roll-ups, the fragmented base won't have an escape route. Private equity deals could slow, leaving thousands of small agencies caught between rising labor costs, frozen reimbursement, and the demographic wave. The result: more closures, more care deserts, and rationed care for seniors in underserved areas. The math simply doesn't close unless one of three things happens: wages stop rising (it won't, shortage is real), reimbursement goes up (Congress won't do it), or consolidation speeds up (regulators might block it).

E · The big picture

The Graying Market

Ten thousand Americans turn 65 every day, flooding industries built around aging—but the real winners fight over scraps as Medicare cuts reimbursement and care workers demand higher wages.

The US faces a demographic inevitability: 73 million baby boomers entering their care years guarantees explosive demand for orthopedic surgery, assisted living, home health, and long-term care insurance. But guaranteed demand does not mean guaranteed profit. Reimbursement cuts, labor shortages, and consolidation are reshaping who captures value—and many legacy players are being squeezed out of the market entirely.

What changed

The aging wave is making orthopedic surgery, senior housing, home care, and long-term care insurance scarce resources in the most literal sense: there aren't enough beds, enough workers, or enough willingness from payers to fund care at prices operators need. Medicare cuts have been surgical and relentless. From 2016 to 2024, Medicare reimbursement for orthopedic procedures fell 26%, with hip arthroplasty pay down 39% since 2017; in January 2026, CMS tightened further with a 2.5% efficiency adjustment. That is happening in an industry where orthopedic product manufacturing brought in $60.6 billion in 2025 and is supposed to grow at steady 4.3% annually through 2035, but real margin growth is strangled by pricing pressure of 1-2% per year. The only segment escaping this trap is robotic-assisted surgery: MAKO knee replacements exploded to $2.6 billion in 2026 and are growing at 16-17% annually—far outpacing the rest of the market—because hospitals can charge premium fees and Stryker now dominates with 67% of US knee procedures and 33% of hip procedures running on their platform by late 2025.\n\nThe senior care franchises face the opposite problem: demand is roaring, but they cannot find bodies to fill the beds. The residential senior care market hit $415 billion total in 2026, with non-medical home care franchises alone accounting for $110 billion, up from $5.967 billion in 2021. Growth is accelerating toward high-single-digit rates as boomers enter their 80s starting 2027, but wages are eating profits. Home care worker turnover runs at 40% and half of agencies report ongoing staff shortages. Since 2019, wages in the sector have climbed 31% cumulatively to pull bodies into the work, forcing operators into a brutal choice: lose margin or ration service. In 2025 alone, the industry saw 871 M&A transactions—20.8% above the prior record—with private equity firms betting that demographic tailwinds justify any acquisition price. Assisted living made up 44% of those deals. National occupancy hit 88.7% by Q3 2025, the 17th consecutive quarterly increase, showing demand is real and staying strong.\n\nLong-term care insurance carriers are caught in their own squeeze: they underpriced policies in the 1990s and 2000s, assuming claim frequency and longevity that proved wildly optimistic. Genworth now faces $31.2 billion in cumulative rate increases it has already secured from state regulators, and yet new customers still balk at premiums. A 55-year-old woman in 2025 pays roughly $3,750 per year for individual coverage—double what a man pays at $2,200—and faces rate hikes of 10-25% on renewal. Carriers are trying to escape the legacy trap by rewriting underwriting from scratch. Genworth launched CareScout in 2025 with a curated network of 500-plus providers by 2024, aiming for sustainable pricing on new business. Connecticut's 2026 legislation requiring public hearings for any rate hike above 10% signals that regulators are tightening oversight. The Federal Long-Term Care Insurance Program remains suspended as of April 2026 because even the government could not price it sustainably. This market brought in $25.6 billion in 2025 but is growing just 2.4% to 4.0% annually—far slower than the underlying aging population—because price-sensitive customers are either going without insurance or relying on Medicaid, which now has partnership programs in 40 states.\n\nWeight loss services tell the story in miniature. The industry pulled in $2.6 billion in 2026 but is shrinking at 2.4% annually from its 2022 peak of $3.8 billion because GLP-1 medications have displaced diet programs almost overnight. From 5.8% of adults using GLP-1s in February 2024, adoption soared to 18% by 2026, directly cannibalizing demand for traditional coaching. Weight Watchers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in May 2025 after 60 years in business. The future belongs to vertically integrated telehealth platforms like Hims and Ro that can secure steady GLP-1 supply and deliver it via apps and clinicians, not to coaching boutiques. The FDA crackdown on compounded GLP-1s in February 2026 accelerated this shift by favoring well-capitalized players with access to brand-name medications.

The evidence

  • Orthopedic Products Manufacturing: Medicare reimbursement cuts of 26% from 2016-2024; CMS applied 2.5% efficiency adjustment January 2026; $60.6B market (2025), 4.3% CAGR through 2035
  • Residential Senior Care Franchises: $415B total market (2026); 871 M&A deals in 2025 (20.8% above 2024 record); home care wages up 31% since 2019; 40% staff turnover and 50%+ agencies report shortages
  • Long-Term Care Insurance: $25.6B market (2025), 2.4% CAGR; Genworth secured $31.2B cumulative rate increases; women pay ~$3,750/year (2025) with 10-25% renewal hikes; Federal FLTCIP suspended April 2026
  • Senior Housing Occupancy: 88.7% occupancy by Q3 2025 (17th consecutive quarterly increase); assisted living dominated 44% of M&A deals in 2025
  • Weight Loss Services: GLP-1 adoption jumped from 5.8% (Feb 2024) to 18% (2026); industry revenue $2.6B (2026), down 2.4% annually from $3.8B (2022); Weight Watchers bankruptcy May 2025

Who rides it

The winners are consolidators with scale and deep pockets to absorb labor cost inflation and reimbursement cuts. In orthopedics, Stryker locked in dominance with its MAKO platform—67% of knees, 33% of hips—and can command premium pricing. In senior care, private equity firms like KKR (backing BrightSpring's 2024 IPO) are rolling up fragmented home and community-based care operators into unified staffing and procurement engines that can weather wage inflation. In telehealth weight loss, platforms like Hims and Ro with their own supply chains and digital infrastructure are buying up legacy assets and funneling everything through GLP-1 delivery. Vertically integrated, capital-heavy, late-consolidation businesses with pricing power over payers win. Regional and single-location operators lose.

Who's squeezed

The squeezed middle includes independent orthopedic device companies (J&J is spinning off DePuy Synthes as a $20B+ business because it is too small to survive alone), regional home care franchises unable to absorb 31% wage growth since 2019, and legacy long-term care insurers (Genworth and Prudential) burning through premium dollars on claims they underpriced decades ago. Independent weight loss clinics and diet programs that failed to integrate GLP-1 prescribing are being forced to shutter. The patients themselves get squeezed too: a 55-year-old woman buying long-term care insurance pays double what a man pays, faces double-digit renewals, and still may not be covered for cognitive decline. Regional Medicare Advantage plans face margin compression from CMS cuts. State Medicaid programs face spiraling costs as boomers enter, forcing them to slow eligibility or tighten benefit caps.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that reimbursement cuts and labor cost inflation spiral into a feedback loop that erodes care quality. Medicare is cutting orthopedic reimbursement by 2.5% efficiency adjustments on top of existing 39% hip arthroplasty cuts since 2017. At the same time, nursing assistants and home care aides face burnout and exit the profession because wages are not keeping pace with the cost of living despite 31% cumulative raises since 2019. When staffing is already 40% turnover and half of agencies report shortages, further margin compression could force operators to hire even less qualified staff or reduce hours per patient. The risk is not that the aging wave goes away—it doesn't—but that we end up rationing care to people who can afford it while pushing low-income seniors into understaffed, under-trained networks, creating a two-tier system. Long-term care insurance already prices out most middle-class workers. Medicaid is the fallback but is moving toward managed-care capitation that rewards plans for denying coverage. If that tightens much further, seniors and their adult children will face genuine gaps in coverage.

In one sentence

The graying market in a nutshell

The graying market is not a shortage of demand—it is a shortage of margin, labor, and political will to pay for what aging actually costs.

A · Rolling up healthcare

Private Equity in Medicine

Capital corners fragmented healthcare—dentistry, mental health, and dialysis.

Healthcare was built on independent practitioners and small regional operators. Dentists, therapists, psychiatrists, and clinic owners ran their own shops. Now PE and platforms are rolling them up fast. New graduate debt, thin margins, workforce shortages, and regulatory chaos have made independence—especially solo practice—too risky. The roll-up is happening at speed: DSO affiliation nearly doubled in two years; behavioral health M&A hit 104 deals in 2025; and dialysis giants are squeezing smaller players out of existence.

What changed

What this force made scarce is independence itself. The US dental market, worth $196.1 billion in 2026, is being reshaped by Dental Service Organizations (DSOs). In just two years, DSO affiliation nearly doubled—jumping from 16.1% of dentists in 2024 to 39% of practices by 2026. This didn't happen by choice. New dentists graduate with $297,800 in average student debt as of 2025, and Grad PLUS loans are being phased out for students starting in July 2026, forcing people to consider DSOs just to manage the debt. Meanwhile, reimbursement is stagnant: 60% of dentists report rates have flat-lined since 2021, and 25% say they've fallen. Operating costs are rising faster than revenue. In H1 2026 alone, 175+ dental practice locations sold to DSOs and other buyers. Staffing became the bottleneck—62% of dentists cite hiring as their top concern, dental hygienist shortages persist, and McKinsey projects 36,000 missing professionals by 2031. Solo practitioners can't compete on hiring or technology. Smile Doctors, a PE-backed platform, acquired myOrthos and its 70+ orthodontic practices across 13 states in 2025, signaling that specialty consolidation is the move.

The mental health sector is being crushed by a different squeeze: demand is exploding, but the system is broken. The residential mental health and substance abuse market grew to $33.2 billion in 2026, a 5.1% CAGR since 2021, but therapists and psychiatrists can't be hired fast enough. HRSA projects a shortfall of 327,000 behavioral health professionals by 2038. Mood and anxiety disorders alone drive 34.4% of the sector, and eating disorders among young adults are surging. Opioid overdose deaths have fallen from 110,000 in 2023 to 75,000 in 2025, but fentanyl still drives 75% of those deaths, keeping treatment demand relentless. The problem: Medicaid covers 45.6% of revenue but reimburses below cost in most cases. January 2026 gutted the enhanced Medicaid match (the 90% federal reimbursement that funded expansion), threatening state budgets. Then in May 2025, the administration stopped enforcing Biden-era mental health parity rules requiring equal coverage for mental versus physical health—leaving reimbursement in limbo. Small operators can't survive this: they lack scale to absorb low Medicaid rates, can't offer competitive wages, and have no safety net when policy shifts. PE saw opportunity: 104 behavioral health M&A deals closed in 2025, up from 73 in 2024. Mental health transactions alone exceeded 80, up from ~70 in 2024. Buyers are consolidating to create large platforms that can absorb regulatory chaos and negotiate with Medicaid.

Dialysis centers tell a starker story: two giants dominate and smaller players are nearly extinct. DaVita controls 38% of the market, Fresenius 27%, and the market is worth $36 billion in 2025, growing 3.5% CAGR. The two public giants are locked in a tightly controlled race: both guide for modest revenue growth (2–3% annually) but expand margins through relentless cost control and mix shifts. Fresenius deployed its premium 5008X CAREsystem (high-volume hemodiafiltration) across 227 US clinics by Q2 2026, performing 600,000+ treatments, signaling a shift toward higher-acuity, higher-margin dialysis. DaVita is countering with supply contracts for expanded high-efficiency dialyzers launching around 2028. Medicare rates are a cruel trap: the 2026 rate increase was only 2.2%; 2027 is projected at a mere 1.1% (with CMS setting the ESRD PPS base rate at $299.55 per treatment). These micro-increases lag wage inflation year after year, compressing operating margins to 11.7% on average—low for a capital-intensive business. Independent dialysis centers and small regional operators have been squeezed out. The industry treated 516,837 dialysis patients in 2025, but that volume is concentrated in two companies that can absorb low Medicare reimbursement through scale, supply chain leverage, and mix optimization. Home dialysis grew from 10% of the patient population in 2016 to 17.4% in 2022, and CMS is pushing this shift hard to cut costs. Small operators can't make the economics work on home dialysis without massive scale.

The evidence

  • Dentistry: DSO affiliation in US dental practices jumped to 39% by 2026 (from 16.1% in 2024), driven by new graduate debt averaging $297,800 (2025) and reimbursement stagnation that has frozen rates for 60% of practitioners since 2021
  • Mental Health: Behavioral health M&A accelerated to 104 deals in 2025 (vs. 73 in 2024) as fragmented regional operators faced a 327,000-person clinical workforce shortfall projected by 2038 and the January 2026 sunset of enhanced Medicaid FMAP (90% federal match)
  • Dialysis Centers: DaVita and Fresenius collectively hold 65% of the $36 billion market (2025); CMS rate increases (2.2% for 2026, 1.1% for 2027) lag wage inflation, compressing operating margins to 11.7% and squeezing independent operators
  • Dentistry: In H1 2026, 175+ dental practice locations sold to DSOs and other buyers; Smile Doctors acquired myOrthos' 70+ orthodontic practices across 13 states in 2025, signaling PE platform consolidation in specialties
  • Mental Health: Mood and anxiety disorders drive 34.4% of residential mental health revenue; eating disorders among young adults surging; opioid deaths fell from 110,000 (2023) to 75,000 (2025) but fentanyl still drives 75% of OD deaths, keeping treatment demand relentless

Who rides it

DSOs and PE-backed platforms in dentistry are winning. They absorb new graduates escaping debt, hire at scale, deploy technology (AI imaging, teledentistry is now 30% of consultations, up from near-zero in 2020), and negotiate with insurers as large networks. In mental health, consolidators can absorb Medicaid's below-cost reimbursement and hedge regulatory risk; small operators collapse under the volatility. In dialysis, DaVita and Fresenius win—they have the scale to manage CMS's micro-rate increases, the supply chain leverage to control costs, and the capital to invest in premium services like the Fresenius 5008X (deployed in 227 clinics by Q2 2026) that generate higher margins. Scale is the only winning strategy in all three. Technology adoption, workforce management, and payer negotiation all favor large platforms.

Who's squeezed

Solo dentists, small group practices, and independent therapists and psychiatrists are exiting. New dentists can't afford to go solo—$297,800 debt means DSO or bust. Solo practitioners can't compete on hiring (62% of dentists cite staffing as top concern; 36,000 dental professionals missing by 2031), can't afford technology, and get reimbursed at the same stagnant rates regardless of practice size. Independent behavioral health providers are being rolled up into large platforms or collapsing under Medicaid pressure, regulatory whiplash (SAMHSA grant termination then reversal in January 2026, parity rules non-enforcement in May 2025), and wage inflation they can't absorb. Small dialysis operators are already gone—the market is consolidated. Owner-operators who built private practices over decades are cashing out now before valuations fall further. The middle class of healthcare—independent practitioners and regional groups—is disappearing.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is system fragility. In dentistry, DSO consolidation is fast but unproven at scale—many DSOs are lightly capitalized platforms that manage practices but don't invest in clinical durability. If margins compress further (and they will as debt service costs rise and reimbursement stagnates), DSOs could collapse, leaving patients and hygienists worse off. In mental health, the risk is acute: regulatory chaos (SAMHSA swinging between grant termination and reversal in a single day) and the Medicaid FMAP sunset in January 2026 have shaken confidence. If state budgets tighten and enhanced Medicaid doesn't return, a huge population of poor and near-poor patients will lose access, and consolidators will abandon unprofitable markets. Dialysis is locked—DaVita and Fresenius control the industry—but that monopoly could trigger CMS price controls or tighter bundling, compressing margins further. All three sectors are dependent on Medicaid or stagnant commercial reimbursement, which means consolidation is a race to squeeze more value from fewer patients, not to improve care. That creates a hard floor on how consolidated the industry can become before regulators step in.

A · Rolling up healthcare

Scale in Devices & Generics

Medical device makers and generic pharma consolidate to absorb tariffs, regulation, and price cuts that independents cannot survive.

Healthcare manufacturing—medical devices, orthopedic products, generic drugs—faces a collision of tariffs, regulatory tightening, and relentless pricing pressure from hospital systems and pharmacy benefit managers. Small players have no room to maneuver. Scale wins because scale can absorb the shock, renegotiate supply chains, and invest in the automation and AI that regulators now demand.

What changed

Three shocks hit the healthcare manufacturing sector at once in 2025–2026, each making smaller operators uncompetitive. The tariff shock arrived in April 2025: a 10% global baseline tariff on all medical devices, plus 50–100% tariffs specifically on syringes and needles. J&J warned investors of $400 million in added costs for 2025 alone; Abbott issued similar cautions. For a small device maker running on 12% EBIT margins (the industry baseline as of 2026), a tariff hit of that magnitude is existential. Scale players like Medtronic, Boston Scientific, and Abbott can absorb it by reshoring high-complexity work to the US, nearshoring commodity parts to Mexico and Canada, and leveraging their size to negotiate supplier contracts that spread the cost. A 430-person generic drug maker cannot. The medtech M&A market responded: $36.5 billion in deals in the first half of 2026 alone, as large players rushed to scoop up smaller rivals before tariff shocks hit them even harder. The second shock was regulatory: the FDA's Quality Management System Regulation took effect February 2, 2026, harmonizing US device manufacturing rules with the global ISO 13485 standard. Compliance requires end-to-end supplier visibility, traceability systems, and continuous documentation—the exact kind of infrastructure that only large enterprises can afford. Fragmented outsourcing networks, once a cost advantage for nimble small players, became a liability overnight. The third shock was pharmaceutical pricing: the generic drug market shrank from $40.6 billion in 2022 to $28.5 billion by 2026, a 10% CAGR collapse. The cause is PBM (pharmacy benefit manager) consolidation and federal intervention. PBMs now control 80% of the market and have crushed prices on commodity generics to squeeze manufacturers toward higher-margin complex molecules and biosimilars. Congress finally acted in February 2026, delinking PBM compensation from drug prices—but that doesn't recover the margin that's already gone. Meanwhile, Indian and Chinese imports still account for 58% of US pharmaceutical imports by weight. India ships $10.5 billion in pharma to the US annually but depends on China for 70% of its APIs (active pharmaceutical ingredients). The Trump administration has signaled 100% tariffs on generic drugs by August 2028 and the PILLS Act is moving through Congress to incentivize US manufacturing. Generic drug makers must consolidate, shift to biosimilars (where Sandoz is leading the charge), or exit. A 50–100-person operation making commodity generics has no path forward. Orthopedic products face a different but equally brutal squeeze: Medicare reimbursement for hip arthroplasty has fallen 39% since 2017, and CMS applied another 2.5% efficiency adjustment in 2026. Robotic-assisted orthopedic surgery has become the competitive standard—the robot-assisted market grew to $2.6 billion in 2026 at 16–17% annually—but only Stryker, J&J, and a handful of scale players can afford to own the MAKO platform and the ecosystem around it. Stryker now dominates: 67% of US knee replacements and 33% of hip replacements are performed on MAKO as of year-end 2025. Smaller orthopedic device makers must either be acquired or retreat to niche segments that large players haven't automated yet.

The evidence

  • Medical device sector: $59.4B market (2026) with $36.5B in M&A deals in H1 2026, driven by April 2025 tariffs (10% baseline, 50–100% on syringes/needles) and February 2026 FDA Quality Management System Regulation
  • Generic pharmaceuticals: $28.5B market (2026), down from $40.6B in 2022 (10% CAGR decline), as PBMs (controlling 80% of market) crush prices and Indian/Chinese imports account for 58% of US pharma by weight
  • Orthopedic products: $60.6B market (2025) with robot-assisted surgery growing to $2.6B at 16–17% annually; Stryker controls 67% of knee and 33% of hip procedures via MAKO platform
  • Regulatory tightening: FDA Quality Management System Regulation (effective February 2, 2026) and GDUFA III efficiency gains (87 first-time generics approved in 2025) accelerate compliance costs and approvals
  • Pricing collapse: Medicare hip arthroplasty reimbursement down 39% since 2017, plus 2.5% CMS efficiency adjustment (2026); generic drug margins compressed to 5–15% on commodity, 20–40% on branded, with biosimilar expansion the only growth path

Who rides it

Large medical device OEMs (Medtronic, Abbott, Boston Scientific, J&J), robotic surgery platform owners (Stryker), and generic makers shifting to biosimilars (Sandoz, Teva pivoting away from commodity) win because they can absorb tariff shocks, afford compliance systems, negotiate tariff-resilient supply chains with nearshoring partners (Mexico, Canada), and invest in AI-driven manufacturing and quality systems. Stryker alone controls the orthopedic robot ecosystem. PE-backed consolidators win too—they roll up fragmented device makers and generic producers, strip overhead, enforce compliance at scale, and either sell them to larger players or flip them at a multiple. Hospital systems also win: consolidation concentrates their purchasing power, driving prices down further on the supplier side. The FDA's push for AI-enabled device software (952+ AI-device clearances by 2024, with the Predetermined Change Control Plan finalizing in August 2025) benefits only the players with in-house AI talent and capital to build it.

Who's squeezed

Small and mid-sized medical device makers (outside the top 10), independent generic drug manufacturers (especially those making commodity generics), and niche orthopedic device shops without robotic platforms lose hard. The 1,067 medical device establishments are concentrated among 10 major players; the 429 generic drug makers are shrinking at 2.4% CAGR annually. For a 50–100-person device maker or generic producer, the math breaks: tariff costs eat the margin, FDA compliance requires infrastructure they can't build alone, and hospital purchasing power forces price cuts they can't absorb. Owner-operators in these spaces face a choice: sell now at depressed valuations to PE or larger strategics, or watch their business erode under tariffs and pricing pressure. Family businesses and small-cap players selling to regional hospital networks are getting rolled up or shuttered. Specialty generic makers who don't pivot to biosimilars (and biosimilar approval timelines are long, even with GDUFA III gains) will be trapped in a shrinking commodity segment.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is tariff escalation colliding with reshoring inertia. The Trump administration has signaled 100% tariffs on generic drugs by August 2028 and tariff rates on devices are already at 50–100% for specific categories. But reshoring medical device and generic manufacturing to the US is not fast: it requires FDA-approved facilities, supply chain rebuilding (2–3 years minimum), and capital investment at a scale most independent makers cannot afford. Large OEMs can front this cost and amortize it over billions in revenue; small players cannot. If tariffs spike before reshoring capacity exists, it could trigger a cascade of bankruptcies among smaller manufacturers, further consolidation, and potential supply chain fragmentation for specialized or low-volume devices. The Indian pharmaceutical industry also faces tariff risk—it ships $10.5 billion in pharma to the US annually but depends on China for 70% of APIs. A tariff shock on Chinese APIs would ripple through US generic pricing overnight. Finally, there's regulatory whipsaw risk: FDA compliance is tightening, but AI-enabled device software is outpacing regulators' ability to set safety standards. Players who move fast in AI may face retroactive regulatory cracks, adding risk to the "AI is the path to competitiveness" narrative that's driving M&A.

B · Franchising Main Street

The Franchise Roll-Up

PE and franchising turn fragmented local services into scaled, financialized platforms — squeezing independent operators out.

Franchising has always promised local ownership with system support. But now private equity is buying up franchise networks, tightening standards, squeezing margins, and converting owner-operators into salaried managers. The shift is visible in two industries bearing the load: senior care and casual dining. Consolidation accelerates because demographic demand is certain and financialization makes scale profitable—even when it's not.

What changed

In senior care, demographic tailwinds created a franchise gold rush. The US has 73 million baby boomers entering retirement, and demand for non-medical in-home care is growing 6–9% annually (2026), with projections accelerating through the early 2030s as the over-80 cohort swells. Franchise revenue in residential senior care jumped from $5.967 billion (2021) to a projected $9.0 billion by 2026—a 51% climb in five years. That growth made the sector a perfect target for institutional capital. Private equity flooded in: 2025 saw 871 M&A transactions in senior care, up 20.8% from 2024's prior record of 721 deals. Assisted living made up 44% of those transactions. The pace is accelerating further into 2026, signaled by BrightSpring Health Services' IPO in January 2024 via KKR backing, validating the thesis that home and community-based care at scale was a safe bet. But the catch is immediate: labor is the binding constraint. Registered nurses, CNAs, and dining staff report 40% turnover rates. Over half of home care agencies report ongoing staffing shortages, forcing wage growth of 31% cumulatively since 2019. The industry is now caught between demographic certainty (occupancy at 88.7% nationally in Q3 2025, the 17th consecutive quarterly increase) and margin pressure that forces operators to choose between losing money or rationing service.

In chain restaurants, franchising confronts a different squeeze: structural cost inflation with nowhere to pass it along. Labor costs jumped 39% since pre-pandemic levels, with minimum wages now $16–$20 per hour in major states (California's FAST Act mandates $20/hour for national chains with 60+ locations starting 2024; Washington hit $16.66; Florida is heading to $15 by September 2026). Food inflation sits 34% above pre-pandemic baselines. Tariffs have forced 62% of operators to raise menu prices, yet consumer spending at restaurants is growing only 1.3% in real terms. The market itself is stalling: chain restaurant revenue fell -1.0% in 2026 after +1.7% growth in 2025, with margins already razor-thin. Forty-two percent of operators reported being unprofitable in 2025, and 60% report deteriorated business conditions. This is where franchising's promise breaks down. A franchise fee and marketing tax extract cash from the unit operator. When labor and food costs spiral and consumer demand softens, the franchisor still gets paid first. The franchisee absorbs the loss. The sector is cannibalizing itself: TGI Fridays and Red Lobster filed Chapter 11 in 2024, closing 130+ locations combined. FAT Brands (parent of Smokey Bones) filed Chapter 11 in January 2026, followed by closure of all remaining Smokey Bones locations. On The Border and Bravo Brio followed into Chapter 11 in 2025 (Bravo Brio for the second time in five years). Full-service casual dining was hit hardest, but even fast-casual is gasping: the 142,206 chain restaurant establishments (2025) are fighting over 15.8 million total restaurant industry workers where wages are non-negotiable.

The consolidation angle is now clear. In senior care, PE firms see demographic demand as a moat: occupancy gains are real, the tailwind is decades long, and rolling up 121,000 fragmented elderly/disabled services businesses into branded platforms with centralized procurement, training, and billing lifts margins. In restaurants, consolidation works differently—it's defensive. Casual-dining chains that survive (Chili's, Texas Roadhouse) do so by accepting lower check averages (sit-down meals at $12 undercut limited-service at $15) while ramping unit volumes. Smaller operators and independent franchisees cannot. The capital required to carry thin margins, absorb wage floors in high-cost states, and survive on 1–2% unit economics gets you to just enough scale that PE can buy you whole, strip out independent franchisees, and run you as a wage-labor operation. Franchising promised the franchisee a path to independence. Consolidation turns that promise into a trap: the franchise fee is now a wealth transfer from the operator to the institution, locked in whether the unit is profitable or not.

The evidence

  • Senior care: $9.0 billion franchise revenue projected by 2026, up 51% from 2021 baseline of $5.967 billion (2026 industry data)
  • Senior care: 871 M&A transactions in 2025, 20.8% above 2024's record; assisted living made up 44% of deals (Jan 2026 reporting)
  • Senior care: National occupancy at 88.7% in Q3 2025—17th consecutive quarterly increase, signaling sustained demographic demand (Q3 2025 data)
  • Chain restaurants: 62% of operators forced to raise prices due to tariffs; labor costs up 39% since pre-pandemic; 42% of operators unprofitable (2025-2026 data)
  • Chain restaurants: Market revenue declined -1.0% in 2026 after +1.7% in 2025; casual dining chapter 11 filings accelerating (Red Lobster, TGI Fridays, FAT Brands, On The Border, Bravo Brio in 2024-2026)

Who rides it

Private equity and scale-focused franchisors win. Demographic certainty in senior care makes consolidation a safe bet—KKR-backed BrightSpring's January 2024 IPO validated the thesis. Consolidation in restaurants lets survivors run leaner, absorb wage pressure with volume, and extract economics from scale that independents and small franchisees cannot. Institutional capital can carry thin margins longer than owner-operators can. Wage floors in states like California and Washington ($16–$20/hour) are fixed costs. Only franchisors with hundreds of units can absorb them and still turn a profit.

Who's squeezed

Independent franchisees and owner-operators are squeezed out. In senior care, 40% turnover of nursing and support staff forces wage growth of 31% since 2019—that margin pressure hits the franchisee first, before the franchisor. In restaurants, the franchisee absorbs labor inflation, food inflation, tariff costs, and consumer demand softness all at once. The franchise fee is a fixed extraction regardless of unit profitability. Sixty percent of operators report deteriorated conditions; 42% are outright unprofitable. Chapter 11 filings accelerated across casual dining (Red Lobster, TGI Fridays, FAT Brands, On The Border, Bravo Brio all between 2024–2026). The franchisee's only exit is liquidation or sale to a consolidator who will strip the brand and convert the unit to wage labor.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that consolidation in mature service franchises (restaurants, home care) will hollow out unit economics so aggressively that the survivor base becomes too thin to generate returns. Senior care has demographic tailwinds—occupancy is real and the boomer wave is decades long—so margin pressure is survivable at scale. Restaurants have no such moat. Chain revenue is already negative (-1.0% in 2026). Consumer defection to takeout, delivery, and at-home eating is structural, not cyclical. If PE rolls up casual dining and tries to run it on 1–2% margins while absorbing $16–$20 wage floors, the returns math breaks. The franchisee exits. But the franchisor still owns the real estate, the debt, and a network of units that no longer generate owner-operator entrepreneurship—just wage labor. That's when the moat inverts.

In one sentence

The franchise roll-up in a nutshell

PE rolls up franchised Main Street—absorbing owner-operators, tightening margins, and converting entrepreneurship into salaried labor—because scale and demographic certainty make financialization more profitable than independence.

B · Franchising Main Street

Consolidating Boring Services

Environmental, engineering, and architecture firms get rolled into regional platforms and PE-backed consolidators as independence becomes untenable.

Capital is hunting in the most unglamorous corner of the economy: engineers, architects, environmental consultants. These services are fragmented—thousands of small practices scattered across the country—and suddenly, they're not profitable enough to stay independent. Scale wins. Tariffs, labor shortages, and AI tooling all favor the big firms that can absorb these costs.

What changed

Environmental consulting was a $27.4 billion US market in 2025, growing just 1.6% that year but powering forward on EPA mandates. In April 2024, the EPA set drinking-water PFAS standards for six compounds; three months later in July 2024, PFOA and PFOS became CERCLA hazardous substances. Those two regulatory lines alone created a multi-year remediation pipeline flowing through 2026 budgets. At the same time, tariffs on steel and aluminum doubled to 50% in 2025, forcing project costs up and squeezing margins to the 8-9% EBITDA range typical for mid-sized firms. This is the kind of environment where only large, diversified consultancies survive: WSP paid $1.78 billion for Power Engineers in February 2025, hunting for specialist depth and geographic reach. The 65,000+ environmental consulting establishments in the US remain highly fragmented, but the consolidation wave is accelerating among the top tier.

Engineering services sits at $386.7 billion in 2026, growing at just 1.5% that year despite a decade of infrastructure money flowing from federal legislation. The infrastructure bill, data-center build-outs for AI, and renewable energy transition should be fueling explosive growth—and they are, in pockets—but over 382,000 engineering positions sat open in 2025 against an aging workforce (average age 46 by 2030) and accelerating automation. Tariffs hit hard: steel and aluminum duties up to 50% in 2025 directly compressed profit margins on projects already starved for labor. Firms cannot pass all these costs to clients without losing contracts. So they're consolidating instead. Over 55% of leading engineering firms deployed AI-assisted design, digital twins, and BIM systems by 2026, but you need scale to invest in those tools and absorb the labor shortage. In 2024 alone, 69 acquisitions happened among MEP giants; 2025 and 2026 are on track to exceed that. PRIME AE acquired Faller, Davis & Associates in December 2025; Salas O'Brien merged with Rock Brook in March 2026. The engineers with $5 million in annual billings cannot compete on technology or pricing.

Architecture is actually contracting. The market was $63.5 billion in 2026, growing at 0.1%—essentially flat—and down from $51.8 billion in 2022. The Architecture Billings Index hit 47.6 in October 2025 (anything below 50 means revenue is declining); 38 percent of firms reported falling revenue, and small practices under $250k annually expected a 7 percent revenue cut. Commercial office construction, which drives architecture demand, cratered because office vacancy rates hit 20.7% nationally in 2025, with San Francisco and Austin exceeding 26%. Nobody wants to build more offices. Smaller independent practices are getting squeezed hardest because they lack the geographic reach and service breadth to weather a single client segment's collapse. Meanwhile, AI software now automates site planning, code-violation detection, BIM workflows, and specification writing—shifting work toward firms that integrate these tools while threatening traditional junior-level drafting roles. The consolidation message is blunt: Stantec acquired UK firm Hydrock in May 2024, adding 950 professionals and increasing its UK presence by over 30%. The pattern repeats across all three sectors: independents cannot absorb tariff costs, cannot hire engineers at any wage, cannot invest in AI tools fast enough, and cannot weather cyclical collapses like the office-vacancy crisis.

The evidence

  • Environmental consulting: $27.4 billion US market (2025), 1.6% growth, tariffs doubled steel/aluminum to 50%, WSP acquired Power Engineers for $1.78B (February 2025)
  • Engineering services: $386.7 billion US market (2026), 1.5% growth, 382,000 open positions vs. aging workforce, 69 MEP acquisitions in 2024 alone with 2025-2026 exceeding that pace
  • Architecture: $63.5 billion US market (2026), 0.1% growth, office vacancy 20.7% nationally (San Francisco/Austin >26%), Billings Index at 47.6 in October 2025
  • Labor crisis across all three sectors: GIS specialists command premiums, licensed environmental engineers 'tightest in a generation' (ACEC 2025), 55% of leading engineering firms deployed AI tools to offset scarcity
  • Small practice collapse: Architecture firms under $250k annually expecting 7% revenue cut; 38% of architecture firms report falling revenue; independents cannot absorb tariff costs or invest in AI-driven workflows fast enough

Who rides it

Large, diversified engineering and environmental consultancies like WSP, AECOM, and Stantec are buying up regional specialists and niche practices at a fraction of what they'd cost to build organically. They absorb tariff costs across a diversified client base, they can invest in AI tools, and they can hire at scale. PE-backed consolidators (looking at architecture and engineering firms) can justify the upfront tech spend and weather cyclical downturns in single sectors because they own a portfolio. The winners are the firms with national footprints, data-center and renewable-energy client concentration, and the capital to integrate AI.

Who's squeezed

Independent practitioners and small regional firms are being squeezed from three directions at once: tariff inflation on materials and labor, inability to hire (average engineering workforce age 46 by 2030; licensed environmental engineers in acute shortage), and AI automation eating into traditional junior roles and drafting work. Architecture took a specific hit from the office-vacancy crisis (20.7% nationally, over 26% in major metros), making it a client-segment catastrophe. Small practices under $250k in billings expect 7% revenue cuts; they cannot compete on price with consolidators, cannot absorb tariff costs, and cannot afford the tech stack that's rapidly becoming table stakes. The exit ramp is narrowing: merge up or close.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that tariff escalation stalls infrastructure and commercial projects outright, which would crater the revenue pipeline that's supposed to be absorbing all these environmental remediation, engineering, and architectural services. If steel stays at 50% and aluminum follows, project economics break even for large firms. A recession would compound the damage: architecture is already down to 0.1% growth with collapsing office demand; engineering demand would evaporate in a credit crunch. The labor shortage is structural—you cannot automate yourself out of needing licensed engineers and environmental specialists—so firms cannot actually cut costs enough to offset tariffs and wage inflation. Consolidation becomes not a choice but the only path to survival, and the independents have no bargaining power.

In one sentence

Consolidating boring services in a nutshell

Capital is rolling up the fragmented world of engineers, architects, and environmental consultants—tariff costs, labor shortages, and AI tooling all favor scale, while small practices get squeezed into mergers or closure.

C · Scale in retail & food

Scale Wins in Retail

A few giant retailers absorb hundreds of competitors while smaller chains fade into bankruptcy.

Retail is getting smaller and bigger at the same time. The same category that used to support thousands of independent stores and small chains is now dominated by a handful of giants—Home Depot, Lowe's, Dick's, O'Reilly—while the middle disappears. Consolidation isn't coming; it's already here, and the cost of staying independent has become too high.

What changed

Home improvement retail has frozen in place. The housing market is stuck—locked-in mortgage rates from 2021 and 2022 have created what the industry calls the "lock-in effect," where homeowners refuse to sell because refinancing would cost them thousands more per year in interest payments. Housing turnover hit multi-decade lows. That means customers who used to flip houses or downsize are now just staying put, and their spending on renovations flatlines. In 2025, the market grew just 2.3% to $294.6 billion, barely keeping pace with inflation. The two leaders, Home Depot and Lowe's, can't grow; they can only split a frozen pie. But Lowe's found one angle that works: professional services. In 2024, its professional-services revenue surged 15%, because contractors still need work done even when consumers don't. Home Depot is now laying off ~800 corporate workers and closing distribution facilities to cut costs and rely more on AI for supply-chain routing. Smaller chains like Wren Kitchens, which had 15 locations, simply vanished—bankruptcy and liquidation in 2025. Meanwhile, Amazon is quietly climbing: it now captures 12% of online DIY sales and grew 25% year-over-year in home improvement tools, hitting $6.1 billion in 2024. The category is being hollowed out. Labor costs are rising 6–8% annually because workers are scarce. Material costs are up 4–6% on average because of tariffs—kitchen cabinets and bathroom vanities face 15–20% tariff increases, with some proposals pushing to 50%. Smaller retailers can't absorb these costs. They can't negotiate with suppliers. They can't shift to services or e-commerce. They fold.

Auto parts retail is shrinking because cars are changing. The US auto parts industry is $77.1 billion as of 2026, growing at just 1.6%—anemic for retail. The number of service occasions per vehicle is falling because electric vehicles need no oil changes, fewer spark plugs, simpler drivetrains, and less frequent brake service thanks to regenerative braking. The average car on the road is now 12.8 years old (a record), which should drive parts demand, but instead people are switching to service centers and dealerships because modern cars are too complex for DIY repair. E-commerce has captured the price-sensitive buyer: online auto parts sales (excluding Amazon and eBay) reached ~$23 billion in 2025 and are growing at 4.6% annually, but when you add Amazon's $13.7 billion (2026) and eBay Motors and Walmart, the e-commerce channel grows 6.7% annually—far faster than physical stores. Tariff shocks destabilized the entire supply chain. In April 2025, the US imposed a 25% tariff on imported auto parts. By May 2025, after a 90-day truce, that dropped to 30%, but the volatility alone broke smaller retailers' inventory planning and cash flow. Two major suppliers—First Brands and Marelli—filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2025, and analysts are warning of a wave of failures in 2026. The Big Four—O'Reilly Automotive, AutoZone, Advance Auto Parts, and NAPA—are surviving and thriving. O'Reilly posted record revenue in Q1 2026, with an 8.1% increase in comparable store sales and earnings per share up 16% year-over-year. They have scale, credit lines, and the ability to negotiate through tariff chaos. Smaller chains don't.

Sporting goods is consolidating in real time. Dick's Sporting Goods spent $2.4 billion to acquire Foot Locker in May 2025, finalizing the deal by September 2025 to create a combined entity with 3,200+ stores globally. Dick's controls roughly 10% of a highly fragmented $120.6 billion US sporting goods market (2026), but that 10% gives it enough leverage to close Foot Locker's unprofitable mall locations, consolidate back-office functions, and force suppliers to negotiate better terms. The market itself is barely growing—just 1.1% in 2026 and negative 0.5% CAGR from 2021 to 2026. Tariffs on imported footwear and athletic apparel are raising landed costs by over 10 percentage points in some categories, squeezing both wholesale margins and retail shelf prices. Consumers are retracting: middle-income discretionary spending is weakening, pandemic savings have dried up, and tariff pass-through has raised apparel costs. US sporting goods transactions fell 9% in Q4 2025 and Q1 2026. E-commerce is also pulling share—online sporting goods sales reached $39.2 billion in 2025, growing at 2.3% annually. Nike and other brands are rethinking direct-to-consumer strategies, which means they're cutting their own wholesale orders or raising prices to retailers, compressing Dick's margins just as it's integrating Foot Locker. Dick's reported FY 2025 consolidated net sales of $17.22 billion, up 28.1%, but that's because of the Foot Locker acquisition, not organic growth. The company's net margin is 4.7% as of Q2 2026—razor thin. Smaller specialists (Big 5, Academy, independent run shops) can't compete on price, can't negotiate supplier terms, can't build omnichannel systems, and can't survive a tariff shock. They're losing customers and cash simultaneously.

What's new is that scale has become a utility. In all three sectors—home improvement, auto parts, sporting goods—being small is no longer just a disadvantage; it's a terminal condition. A small retailer used to be able to compete on location, service, curation, or local brand loyalty. Now those advantages dissolve in months because e-commerce neutralizes location, tariffs destroy cash flow, supplier consolidation leaves no one to negotiate with, and consumers are switching to services (like Lowe's Professional) or direct brands (Nike, Amazon) rather than old-school retail. The independent hardware store, auto parts shop, or sporting goods specialist has become an endangered species because the margin structure can't support it anymore.

The evidence

  • Home improvement retail (Home Depot, Lowe's, Amazon): $294.6B market in 2025, 2.3% growth, professional services up 15% (Lowe's 2024), smaller chains bankrupt (Wren Kitchens 15 locations, 2025).
  • Auto parts retail (O'Reilly, AutoZone, NAPA, Advance Auto Parts): $77.1B market in 2026, 1.6% growth, O'Reilly comparable store sales +8.1% Q1 2026, smaller suppliers filing (First Brands, Marelli Chapter 11, 2025).
  • Sporting goods retail (Dick's, Foot Locker, Nike DTC): $120.6B market in 2026, 1.1% growth, Dick's acquired Foot Locker for $2.4B (May-Sept 2025), transactions down 9% Q4-Q1 2026.
  • Tariff impact across retail: auto parts 25% tariff April 2025 (dropped to 30% May 2025), home improvement materials up 4–6%, kitchen cabinets/vanities 15–20% increases, sporting goods footwear over 10 percentage points.
  • E-commerce penetration: Amazon $6.1B home improvement (2024, +25% YoY), online auto parts $23B excluding marketplaces (+4.6% CAGR), Amazon auto parts $13.7B (2026), sporting goods online $39.2B (2025, +2.3%).

Who rides it

Dick's Sporting Goods, O'Reilly Automotive, Home Depot, and Lowe's are the winners. They have scale, scale, and more scale. They can absorb tariff shocks by negotiating better supplier terms or shifting cost to consumers. They can close underperforming locations, consolidate back-office functions, and invest in e-commerce and services. Dick's swallowed Foot Locker to gain 3,200+ stores globally and eliminate redundancy. O'Reilly is posting record earnings while smaller competitors file for bankruptcy. Lowe's found a protected corner—professional services—where tariffs and e-commerce don't cannibalize as aggressively. They're not winning by growing; they're winning by absorbing competitors and cutting costs faster than rivals can.

Who's squeezed

Independent hardware stores, small auto parts chains, and specialist sporting goods shops. Wren Kitchens had 15 locations and it's gone. First Brands and Marelli filed for Chapter 11. Smaller retailers are losing to three forces simultaneously: tariffs that destroy cash flow, e-commerce that steals customers, and supplier consolidation that leaves no leverage for price negotiation. A small shop has to compete with Amazon's $6.1 billion home improvement operation, Dick's 3,200-store footprint, and O'Reilly's 8% store-sales growth. They can't. They're trapped between rising costs and falling margins, and the exit door is shrinking as acquisition offers dry up.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The structural risk is that consolidation breeds fragility. When three or four companies control an entire retail category, supply shocks ripple through with no buffer. The tariff swings of 2025—from 25% to 30% on auto parts in a single month—show how little control even the big retailers have over the cost structure. If tariffs stay high or ratchet up further, even O'Reilly and Dick's will struggle to pass costs to consumers without destroying volume. The second risk is that e-commerce and direct-to-consumer strategies will eventually cannibalize the winners too. Amazon is already taking 12% of online DIY and 25% growth in tools. Nike and other brands are recalibrating wholesale strategies, which means they could cut Dick's off or raise prices. If the big retailers get caught between rising supplier costs, tariff risk, shrinking transaction volumes, and brand price hikes, there's nowhere left to cut except payroll and store closures. That's when consolidation turns into a race to the bottom.

In one sentence

Scale wins in retail in a nutshell

Scale has become a utility in retail—too expensive to compete without it, and three or four giants now control categories that used to support thousands of independents.

C · Scale in retail & food

Scale in Food & Drink

Capital consolidates brewing, distributing, and slaughtering—independent operators face tariffs, automation, and a shrinking middle.

Consolidation is squeezing food and drink from both ends. Large producers with scale are automating, capturing retail space, and pivoting to premium categories—while thousands of independent craft brewers, small meat processors, and regional distributors face simultaneous margin collapse from tariffs, labor scarcity, and shifting consumer preferences away from their core products.

What changed

The US beer industry contracted 5.7% by volume in 2025, and craft brewery count fell 1.8% to 9,344 establishments by June 2026—but the real story is margin destruction. Aluminum tariffs hit 15% year-over-year in April 2025, canning costs doubled, and breweries paid labor rates exceeding $25 an hour. These cost shocks landed on a business model that was already fragile: only 54% of surveyed craft breweries reported growth in 2025, while 43% reported declines. Small regional players like Duck-Rabbit Craft Brewery (liquidated via Chapter 7 in April 2025) and Nebraska Brewing Company (Chapter 11 restructuring) couldn't absorb the hit. Meanwhile, large producers doubled down on automation and premium positioning. Molson Coors reported premium light beers adding 1.8 percentage points of market share by August 2024, with the Above Premium segment growing to 28% of net sales from 23% three years prior. Spirits-based ready-to-drink cocktails jumped 16.4% to $3.8 billion in 2025—a category entirely outside the traditional three-tier beer distribution system that small wholesalers depend on. This means craft breweries lost retail shelf space to RTDs, hard seltzers, and non-alcoholic beer (which exploded 111% from 2021 to 2025), all owned by larger players with consolidated supply chains.\n\nBeer wholesaling reveals the consolidation trap. The $95.4 billion beer distribution market grew just 1.0% from 2025 to 2026, stagnating despite overall beverage growth. The middle layer—1,393 beer distributors employing 115,900 workers—faced simultaneous compression: beer volumes fell 5.7% in 2025, tariffs fragmenting import segments (bottled and draft escaped 25% aluminum tariffs, but canned beer got hammered), and alternative categories bypassing the system entirely. Wages spiked 6.4% to $28.89 an hour even as employment ticked down 0.6% year-over-year—classic consolidation-era labor dynamics. Reyes, a mega-distributor, acquired 11 RNDC markets including a California exit in 2026, concentrating distribution power further. By April 2025, Trump administration tariffs on canned imported beer created a two-tier market: bottled and draft beer (61.5% of trade) remained tariff-free, but canned beer importers faced 25% duties. Mexico, which accounts for $6.3 billion of $7.5 billion in beer imports, bore the brunt. Smaller wholesalers who built their books around high-margin import cans suddenly faced inventory rot and margin collapse.\n\nMeat processing is the clearest consolidation win. The $387.7 billion beef and poultry sector is dominated by four firms—JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef—that hold near-monopoly power. But that power is being weaponized toward automation and scale escape. Beef cattle prices in 2026 averaged $240 per cwt, up 7% from 2025, while immigration enforcement tightened the labor supply beyond what wage increases alone could fix. Processors invested heavily in cobots and AI vision systems to replace de-hoofing, evisceration, and packaging roles—automating away the chronic labor shortages that have plagued the industry since 2020. Meanwhile, China locked out US beef in 2025, wiping out 96% of September exports (556 mt), and only restored partial access via a May 2026 trade deal. That export shock hit smaller regional processors and independent cattle ranchers hardest; the Big Four have global diversification and can absorb it. The DOJ opened antitrust investigations in 2025–2026, and price-fixing settlements ran into hundreds of millions—but enforcement hasn't disrupted the consolidation machine. Plant-based meat, hyped as an existential threat to the Big Four in 2023–2024, collapsed to 2–3% retail share as consumers rejected the taste and authenticity claims. The real threat to independents isn't innovation; it's scale. Tariff chaos created a 17% effective rate on food manufacturing in early 2025, but the Big Four leverage consolidated supply chains to absorb or pass through these shocks—while single-plant operators and regional cooperatives get caught flat-footed.

The evidence

  • Breweries: US beer production declined 5.7% by volume in 2025; 9,344 operating breweries as of June 2026 (down 1.8% YoY), with 481 closures in 2025.
  • Beer wholesaling: $95.4 billion market growing just 1.0% (2025–2026), while spirits-based RTD cocktails surged 16.4% to $3.8 billion (2025)—bypassing traditional distributors entirely.
  • Meat processing: $387.7 billion sector (2026) controlled by Big Four; beef cattle prices averaged $240/cwt (2026), up 7% YoY, driving automation investment while China lockout wiped out 96% of US beef exports in Sept 2025.
  • Tariffs: Aluminum tariffs hit 15% YoY (April 2025); canned beer importers faced 25% tariffs while bottled beer (61.5% of trade) escaped unscathed, fragmenting the import market.
  • Labor: Craft brewery labor costs exceeded $25/hour; beer wholesaling wages spiked 6.4% to $28.89/hour (2026), yet employment ticked down 0.6% YoY amid consolidation.

Who rides it

Large producers with automation and scale—Molson Coors, AB InBev, the Big Four meat processors (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef)—consolidate market share and shift to premium and alternative categories (non-alcoholic beer up 111% from 2021 to 2025, premium segments now 28% of sales). Mega-distributors like Reyes acquire smaller wholesalers outright (11 RNDC markets including California in 2026), concentrating gatekeeping power. Private equity and franchised production models can absorb tariff shocks and labor inflation through scale and capital access; automation investments ($4.5B global robotics market projected by 2033 at 9.2% CAGR) are only viable for the well-capitalized.

Who's squeezed

Independent craft breweries, regional breweries, and small meat processors face simultaneous margin collapse. Tariffs landed directly on their operating costs (15% aluminum, double-digit can inflation) at a moment when retail shelf space shifted to RTDs, spirits-based cocktails, and non-alcoholic alternatives. Duck-Rabbit Craft Brewery liquidated in April 2025; Nebraska Brewing restructured. Mid-sized regional breweries saw retail placement evaporate while competing on quality and story against automated premium beers from the Big Three. Independent meat processors and small ranches were blindsided by China's export lockout (96% volume wipeout in Sept 2025) and face automation-driven labor market tightening without the capital or efficiency to invest in cobots and AI vision systems.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Tariff fragmentation and category shift are destroying the business models that funded independents. The 25% tariff on canned beer created a two-tier market (bottled imports protected at 61.5% of trade), meaning small import-focused wholesalers saw inventory rot while large distributors pivoted to protected formats. More critically, the growth categories—spirits RTDs, hard seltzers, non-alcoholic beer—are all owned by large players with consolidated supply chains and retail muscle. Independents can't enter these categories without capital, and they can't compete in their core category without scale-driven automation. The middle layer (wholesalers, regional breweries) is being systematically squeezed out, not by innovation but by the combination of tariff shocks, labor inflation that only scale can absorb, and category migration controlled by giants.

In one sentence

Scale in food & drink in a nutshell

Tariff shocks, labor scarcity, and the shift to premium and alternative beverages owned by giants are consolidating US food and drink into the hands of a few automated, scaled producers while independents close or get bought out.
