D · The tensions

Fast Food's Reckoning

GLP-1, labor floors, and tariff-driven inflation squeeze margin so hard that chains abandon traffic for upsells, reformulate in desperation, or vanish.

Fast food chains face a three-front collapse. The appetite-suppressing effect of GLP-1 drugs is real enough that dinner spending at these chains dropped 6% among regular users—households with someone taking GLP-1 cut restaurant spending an average 5.3%. At the same time, labor costs have jumped structurally: California's $20/hour minimum for national chains (April 2024) forced operators to raise menu prices 8–12%, while tariffs and commodity inflation pushed food costs up another 34% above pre-pandemic levels. Customers aren't coming as often (traffic fell 0.3% in 2025, accelerating to -2% in Q4 2025), and when they do, they're less likely to spend big. The industry that built its empire on affordability and frequency is now locked in a death grip between shrinking visits and rising costs.

What changed

The $423.7 billion US fast food industry grew just 0.7% in 2026, dragging a structural decline backward from the 1.2% CAGR posted between 2021 and 2026. What changed is that the margin (already thin at 5.1% in 2021) collapsed under three simultaneous pressures. First came the wage floor: California's FAST Act mandated $20/hour for national chains with 60+ locations starting April 2024, an overnight 25% jump in labor costs for the largest franchisees. That forced menu prices up 8–12%, but price-sensitive customers can't absorb that without abandoning the category. Overtime was largely eliminated, hours were cut, and operators scrambled to offset lower ticket counts with higher average checks (which ticked up 3.3% year-over-year in 2025), but that's a trap—raise your burger to $10 in a category built on the $6 lunch special, and traffic falls faster.

Second came the tariff and commodity squeeze. Avian flu hammered poultry supplies, low beef inventories tightened across the board, and roughly 15% of all US food imports faced new tariff pressure. Food inflation ran 34% above pre-pandemic levels by 2025–2026. Operators absorbed much of that cost in their own margin because they couldn't pass it fully to traffic-conscious customers without losing volume they could no longer afford. Sixty-two percent of chain restaurants raised menu prices anyway, and 60% reported deteriorated business conditions in 2025. Half of all chain restaurant operators—42% of the segment—turned unprofitable.

Third came GLP-1. Dinner spending at fast food fell 6% among regular users; that's not a rounding error, that's structural demand destruction. Households with a GLP-1 user cut restaurant spending an average 5.3%. The industry can quantify it now: traffic declined 0.3% in 2025, but Q4 2025 vs. Q4 2024 the decline accelerated to -2%. That's not just maturity, that's deflation happening in real time.

The chains betting on automation—AI-driven order systems, robotic fryers, wage-replacement tech—are placing long-dated bets to survive what used to be their core margin: labor efficiency at scale. But while they automate, their customer base is shrinking, and every price hike to offset labor costs pushes more traffic away.

The evidence

  • Fast food traffic declined 2% in Q4 2025 vs. Q4 2024, driven by GLP-1 appetite suppression and consumer retrenchment (2025)
  • California's FAST Act ($20/hour minimum for national chains, April 2024) forced menu prices up 8–12%, absorbing a 25% labor cost jump
  • Dinner spending at fast food fell 6% among GLP-1 users; households with a GLP-1 taker cut restaurant spending 5.3% (2025–2026)
  • Food inflation ran 34% above pre-pandemic levels in 2025–2026; tariffs on 15% of US food imports added structural pressure
  • 42% of chain restaurant operators turned unprofitable in 2025; 60% reported deteriorated business conditions

Who rides it

Value-focused casual dining (Chili's, Texas Roadhouse) and grocery/convenience store takeout are winning. Casual dining's $12 sit-down deals undercut fast-casual's $15 limited-service entrees, pulling traffic from the middle. Grocery and convenience stores absorb the traffic that once went to QSR—at-home eating, convenience-store prepared food, and delivery apps are all cheaper and require no GLP-1 patients to leave the house. Premium fast-casual chains that reformulated their menus (higher protein, lower sugar, smaller portions that align with appetite suppression) are holding share better than legacy QSR. Automation vendors and wage-management tech are winning too: chains desperate to offset labor are placing long bets on robotic systems and AI-driven order platforms. But the real winner is the home kitchen and the convenience store—the category itself is leaking traffic.

Who's squeezed

Legacy fast food—especially the volume-dependent value player—is squeezed hardest. BurgerFi filed Chapter 11 in September 2024 after losses mounted from labor inflation and a failed 2021 acquisition; it couldn't absorb the wage shock. Casual dining took a hammer: TGI Fridays and Red Lobster both filed Chapter 11 in 2024 and closed 130+ locations combined. FAT Brands (Smokey Bones parent) filed Chapter 11 in January 2026; all remaining Smokey Bones locations closed. On The Border Mexican Grill filed Chapter 11 in March 2025; Bravo Brio filed a second time in August 2025. Even mid-market chains going private (Denny's sold for $620 million all-cash to a private-equity consortium in Q1 2026, leaving public markets after decades) signals that the operational model is broken. Franchisees in California and other high-wage states face an impossible math: they can't raise prices without losing traffic, and they can't absorb labor costs without cutting margin to zero.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is a debt spiral for overleveraged chains. Fast food is built on the franchisee model: individuals borrow against future cash flows to buy the right to operate a location. As traffic shrinks 2% per quarter and operators turn unprofitable (42% of chain restaurants in 2025), franchisees can't service debt or reinvest. Many locations will close quietly, creating a wave of underperforming assets. Large chains that double down on automation to replace labor are betting the company on technology adoption they can't fully control and customer willingness to pay for convenience—but if customers stop coming altogether, the robots run empty. The second-order risk is that as premium casual dining (Chili's, Roadhouse) captures traffic with sit-down deals, even those gains look fragile if the consumer recession deepens and households tighten further. GLP-1 adoption is also accelerating—if 5-10% of the population is on a GLP-1 analog by 2027, the demand destruction at fast food could move from a rounding error to a permanent 15–20% traffic erosion that no amount of automation or menu engineering can fix.

In one sentence

Fast food's reckoning in a nutshell

GLP-1 appetite suppression, $20/hour wage floors, and 34% food inflation have crushed the fast food model so thoroughly that chains are choosing automation over traffic, raising prices that drive away the customer base, or filing bankruptcy.

D · The tensions

Regulation & the Warning Label

Health warnings and sugar rules turn compliance into a repricing event.

Regulation doesn't kill the food and drink business. But it does make what you were selling yesterday suddenly cost more to sell today. A reformulation mandate, a tariff regime, or an FDA ban forces a reset: you either pay to change the formula, absorb the cost hit, or step aside. That reset is happening now, and it's remaking the energy drink and candy industries at the same time.

What changed

The US energy drink industry has doubled from $11.7 billion in 2022 to $23.9 billion by 2025—not because people drink more, but because the category is being remade. Sugar-free drinks now outsell full-sugar drinks for the first time, driven by consumers determined to cut sugar. Red Bull launched Red Bull Zero in November 2024 to keep pace. Celsius paid $1.8 billion for Alani Nu in April 2025 and then snapped up Rockstar through a distribution deal with PepsiCo in September 2025, racing to own the premium end before regulatory pressure and health consciousness make the sugar-heavy names untouchable. The FDA's ban on brominated vegetable oil (BVO) in August 2025 forced reformulation across dozens of brands—a small shock that signals bigger ones coming.

Tariffs have become a structural cost that reshapes economics overnight. When the Trump administration imposed tariffs in April 2025—10% baseline, 20% on EU goods, 31% on Swiss chocolate, and 145% on bulk shipments from China—candy production costs jumped 30% between December 2024 and September 2025. The US candy market, valued at $55 billion in 2025, is now projected to grow only 1.4% per year through 2030, a dramatic slowdown from earlier decades. That margin squeeze is forcing the industry to abandon cheap, commodity sugar drops in favor of premiumized, functional, and texture-driven innovations. Freeze-dried candy jumped to $1.31 billion globally in 2025 and is forecast to grow 12% annually through 2033, fueled by Gen Z craving crunch and seeing it on TikTok. Mars acquired Kellanov in December 2025—bringing Pringles, Cheez-It, and Pop-Tarts under the same roof—while Unilever paid $1.2 billion for the functional gummy brand Grüns in April 2026, betting that functional and premium are where the margin survives.

What makes this different from past regulatory cycles is speed and simultaneity. The BVO ban, the tariff regime, and the consumer shift all hit within months of each other, compressing the timeline for reformulation and repositioning. A company sitting in commodity sugar or standard production—the traditional playbook—faces tariff costs on imports, margin pressure on domestic production, and consumer indifference to what it's selling. A company owning a premium or functional asset, or one with the scale to absorb tariff shocks (Mars, Mondelēz), can raise prices or shift to higher-margin categories. Convenience stores, which took 65.5% of energy drink sales, are losing ground to warehouse clubs (19%) and supermarkets (10.9%) as bulk-buying and price-conscious consumers shift. The warning label—whether literal (FDA guidance on sugar and additives) or figurative (social media calling out synthetic ingredients)—has become a repricing event. Brands that can't reformulate or pivot up are stuck: too cheap to grow, too risky to hold.

The evidence

  • Energy drinks: Celsius acquired Alani Nu for $1.8B (April 2025) and Rockstar (September 2025) as sugar-free positioning becomes mandatory and regulatory risk makes legacy sugar brands untouchable.
  • Candy: Tariffs (10% baseline, 20% EU, 31% Switzerland, 145% China as of April 2025) drove production costs up 30% by September 2025, compressing margins on commodity sugar and forcing a pivot to premium and functional.
  • Regulation: FDA ban on brominated vegetable oil (BVO) in August 2025 forced reformulation across energy drinks and candies, signaling coming waves of additive and sugar scrutiny.
  • Freeze-dried candy: Jumped to $1.31B globally in 2025 and forecast to grow 12% annually through 2033, becoming a major escape route from commodity sugar positioning.
  • Consumer shift: 70% of consumers seek to limit sugar intake in 2025, and 47% of regular candy buyers actively seek healthier alternatives, making health-aligned positioning essential for survival.

Who rides it

Brands with scale and premium positioning—Mars (Kellanov acquisition December 2025, combined $36B global snacking portfolio), Mondelēz, and Celsius—can absorb tariff costs and shift to higher-margin categories. Functional and freeze-dried innovations, which grew at double digits, shelter from commodity economics. Companies that own the health-conscious narrative (Red Bull Zero, Alani Nu, Rockstar under premium distribution) and can reformulate without destroying margins survive the regulatory shock. Warehouse clubs (now 19% of energy drink sales) and supermarkets (10.9%) gain share as bulk-buying and price-sensitive consumers exit convenience stores (falling from 65.5%) seeking value in the new normal.

Who's squeezed

Mid-sized brands without reformulation budgets or premium assets get trapped: tariff shocks compress already-thin margins on commodity sugar products, and regulatory pressure makes old formulas legally or reputationally risky. Suppliers of additive-laden or high-sugar products lose shelf space as 70% of consumers demand lower sugar and brands move toward functional alternatives. Convenience stores, which relied on impulse purchases of high-margin, commodity energy drinks and candy, lose share to warehouse clubs and supermarkets. Smaller confectionery producers, already under pressure from the consolidated majors (Mars, Mondelēz, Ferrara), face tariff costs with no scale to negotiate or ability to pivot to premium positioning.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is a regulatory cascade. The BVO ban and tariff regime hit nearly simultaneously; if the FDA moves to restrict high-fructose corn syrup, further limit caffeine levels, or mandate sugar-reduction targets (as some countries have), the reformulation pipeline will choke. Brands already repricing to absorb tariffs cannot easily absorb a second round of compliance costs. Smaller producers will exit or consolidate, handing even more market power to Mars and Mondelēz. Consumer resentment at rising prices (86% notice and resent them in 2025) could trigger a retail or political backlash against tariffs, destabilizing the very cost environment companies are repricing into. Worse: if health-conscious consumers keep shrinking the addressable market for traditional candy and sugar-heavy energy drinks, the tariff-driven price increases will feel punitive rather than sustainable, leaving domestic producers with no escape route—they cannot lower costs enough to compete, and cannot raise prices enough to survive.

Regulation & the warning label in a nutshell

Regulation—FDA bans, tariff shocks, and the shift to cleaner labels—has made old-school sugar drinks and candies risky to hold, pushing billions into reformulation and reshuffling who survives.

E · The big picture

The Health Reckoning

GLP-1 drugs and the sober-curious wave are shrinking demand across food and drink; only premium and health-aligned businesses survive.

Three converging forces are rewriting consumer spending on food and drink. GLP-1 medications reached 18% of U.S. adults by 2026, pharmaceutical weight loss now outpaces behavioral coaching, and Gen Z is drinking 30% less than Millennials at the same age. Businesses that rode volume growth for decades are now in structural decline—and only those positioned for premium, health-conscious, or high-margin customers are staying upright.

What changed

The retreat from traditional consumption is reshaping entire industries. Weight loss services, once a $3.8 billion industry in 2022, contracted to $2.6 billion by 2026 as GLP-1 adoption accelerated from 5.8% of adults in February 2024 to 18% by 2026. This wasn't a gradual shift—it was seismic. Weight Watchers, the 60-year-old icon of diet culture, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on May 6, 2025, and emerged as a private company in June 2025 after cutting $1.15 billion in debt. Traditional coaching and accountability models became obsolete almost overnight. The industry consolidated around telehealth GLP-1 platforms like Hims, Ro, and Noom, which now function as prescription delivery networks rather than lifestyle programs. Obesity rates fell from 39.9% in 2022 to 36.4% by 2026, shrinking the addressable market for legacy diet services and forcing smaller regional clinics into margin pressure or shutdown.

Wine and beer faced a different structural wall: Americans simply stopped drinking. The U.S. adult drinking rate hit 54% participation in August 2025—the lowest in 90 years. Gen Z monthly wine occasions collapsed 34% since 2019, with 71% citing health and wellness concerns. GLP-1 drugs compounded this by reducing on-premise alcohol spending by 30% and home consumption by 22% among users. Wine bars, a $3.4 billion industry, barely grew (−0.7% in 2026) and bifurcated sharply: private equity-backed, experiential wine bars scaled 6.8% CAGR with premium positioning and staff expertise, while traditional independents faced margin compression. The 2025 Dietary Guidelines removed explicit daily drink limits (seemingly a win for the industry), but the U.S. Surgeon General simultaneously warned that alcohol linked to nearly 100,000 annual cancer cases. On-premise bar visits dropped 3.4% in 2025 versus 2024. The affluent, older drinker (55+) held loyalty, but that demographic is aging and numerically shrinking.

Fast food and energy drinks split into opposite trajectories, both driven by health and volume dynamics. Fast food entered freefall—traffic declined 0.3% in 2025, accelerating to −2% in Q4 2025 versus Q4 2024. Households with a GLP-1 taker cut restaurant spending by an average 5.3%; dinner spending at fast food dropped 6% among regular users. The $423.7 billion industry (2026) is growing below 1% annually, squeezed by labor costs (California's $20/hour minimum wage in April 2024 forced price hikes of 8–12%), tariff-driven food inflation, and disappearing customer frequency. BurgerFi, TGI Fridays, and Uncle Julio's filed bankruptcy or sold in foreclosure within three months of each other in late 2024, victims of structural demand collapse. Energy drinks, by contrast, exploded to $23.9 billion by 2025, up from $11.7 billion in 2022—a 104% increase. But the category underwent radical transformation: sugar-free surpassed full-sugar in dollar sales for the first time as 70% of consumers sought to limit sugar intake. Consolidation wars erupted as Celsius paid $1.8 billion for Alani Nu (April 2025) to capture younger, health-conscious women, and then acquired Rockstar through a PepsiCo distribution deal (September 2025). Red Bull launched Red Bull Zero in November 2024. The winners were companies that moved fast to offer zero-sugar, performance-oriented products; the losers were traditional, sugar-laden competitors left behind.

What these industries share is that volume is no longer the business model. Consumers are eating less, drinking less, and when they spend, they're trading down to premium or health-aligned alternatives. Fast food chains couldn't offset traffic loss with pricing—customers just stopped coming. Wine bars couldn't rely on Gen Z to replace aging Boomers. Traditional weight loss coaching died overnight because GLP-1s work better and cost less in the long run. Energy drinks that didn't reformulate to zero-sugar faced category extinction. The health reckoning isn't gradual disruption; it's demand collapse followed by margin compression for everyone except the premium and the purpose-built.

The evidence

  • Weight loss services: Market contracted 31% (2022–2026) as GLP-1 adoption hit 18% of adults and Weight Watchers bankruptcy marked the end of 60-year diet-program era (2025)
  • Wine bars: U.S. adult drinking hit 54% participation in August 2025—lowest in 90 years—while Gen Z wine occasions fell 34% since 2019, forcing industry bifurcation toward premium and away from volume (2025)
  • Energy drinks: Category doubled to $23.9B by 2025 (from $11.7B in 2022) as sugar-free surpassed full-sugar in dollar sales for the first time, with Celsius paying $1.8B for Alani Nu to capture health-conscious women (2025)
  • Fast food: Traffic declined 0.3% in 2025, accelerating to −2% in Q4 2025 vs. Q4 2024, as GLP-1 adoption reduced spending by 5.3% among user households and California's $20/hour minimum wage (April 2024) forced price hikes of 8–12% (2025–2026)
  • Telehealth GLP-1 platforms: Consolidation accelerated as Hims acquired Zava (June 2025) and Celsius expanded via PepsiCo partnership (September 2025), favoring large, well-capitalized providers over regional clinics and legacy services (2025–2026)

Who rides it

Premium and health-aligned businesses. Experiential wine bars scaled by private equity grew 6.8% CAGR with 22% higher retention than traditional formats. Zero-sugar energy drinks, led by Celsius and Red Bull, doubled market size while driving consolidation and acquisition wars. Telehealth GLP-1 platforms like Hims and Ro grew vertically integrated supply chains and became the default weight-loss solution. Restaurants and chains that embraced smaller portions, healthier options, and premium positioning—rather than relying on volume and value—maintained margins. The formula is clear: premium pricing, health messaging, and experiential elements beat volume plays.

Who's squeezed

Volume-dependent, mass-market businesses. Traditional weight loss coaching and diet programs are extinct—Weight Watchers' bankruptcy was just the symbolic capstone. Fast food chains dependent on frequent, high-volume traffic face structural traffic collapse as GLP-1 adoption reduces appetite and frequency. Wine and beer suppliers targeting Gen Z or mid-market drinkers lost 30% of on-premise spending per GLP-1 user and faced a generational defection (Gen Z drinks 30% less than Millennials). Full-sugar energy drink makers and suppliers got stranded as the category pivoted to zero-sugar overnight. Regional weight loss clinics, independent wine bars without experiential positioning, and fast-food franchises without brand power or premium tiers all face margin compression and closure.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is the floor beneath fast food and casual dining collapses faster than replacement demand materializes. Traffic is already down 2% year-over-year in Q4 2025. If GLP-1 adoption continues climbing (current trajectory suggests 25–30% of adults by 2027–2028), fast food may lose not just volume but consumer habit entirely—the customer stops visiting, finds alternatives, and never returns. Chains can't raise prices indefinitely without killing traffic further. Labor costs and tariff inflation are structural, not cyclical, so they can't cut their way to profitability. The bankruptcy wave (BurgerFi, TGI Fridays, Uncle Julio's in late 2024) may not be over; it may be the opening chapter. Regional fast-food and casual-dining operators—the 50,000+ independent franchises and small chains that lack scale to invest in automation or brand transformation—face wipeout.

A · The stores splitting apart

The department store falls

Mid-tier anchors of American malls hollow out as tariffs, luxury bankruptcy, and bargain hunting rip shoppers away.

The department store used to be the middle ground—not fancy, not discount, just normal. In 2025 and 2026, that middle ground vanished. Shoppers fled to luxury or bargain basements, tariffs compressed already-thin margins to breaking point, and Saks Global's bankruptcy in January 2026 proved even the merged mega-players couldn't hold the line.

What changed

The US department store industry sits at $227.1 billion in 2026, growing at only 0.3% annually and contracting 0.4% in 2026 alone. That flatness masks a violent hollowing: the market is cleaving into a luxury tier and a value tier, leaving everyone in the middle gasping. Start with tariffs. Apparel import duties exploded from 14.7% in January 2025 to 35.1% by December 2025—a 138% spike in one year. Even after the Supreme Court struck down country-specific rates in February 2026 and rates settled to a 10% flat China rate plus 15% EU ceiling by July 2026, the damage was permanent. Department store margins, already thin at 6.0% in 2026, had to absorb those tariff shocks. Retailers faced an impossible choice: eat the cost and watch profits evaporate, or pass it to shoppers and lose customers. Macy's chose the retreat. The company closed 50 stores by end-2024, then 66 more in 2025, with another 14 planned for 2026. Yet Q3 2025 showed modest comp sales growth of 2.5% to 3.2%, suggesting some stabilization—but only through aggressive pruning. The canary in the coal mine was Saks Global. In January 2026, the mega-merger of Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman filed Chapter 11 with $3.4 billion in debt. The theory was consolidation would save the luxury tier. Instead, store productivity cratered, vendor payments got backed up, and the merged entity couldn't survive. Even at the top of the market, the middle-market logic was broken. Meanwhile, shoppers were voting with their wallets. Discount department stores grabbed market share relentlessly. The off-price channel—Nordstrom Rack, TJX stores, Marshall's, Saks Off Fifth, outlets—became the place where real customers shopped. Ross Stores reported comparable sales up 17% in Q3 2025 and announced 110 new store openings for 2026. That's not marginal growth; that's velocity. Inflation, which pushed consumer price expectations up 4.1% year-over-year as of May 2026, was the accelerant. Affluent households absorbed higher prices and kept shopping full-price. Everyone else traded down five times faster, abandoning the mid-tier department store for bargain basements or going without. The industry lost 2.87% of its 666,500 employees annually through 2028, a steady bleed as stores closed and foot traffic never came back. The $227.1 billion market of 2026 looks almost unchanged from 2022's $139.6 billion growth projection, but the breakdown is everything: luxury collapsed, value exploded, the middle got wiped out.

The evidence

  • US department store industry: $227.1B market size in 2026 growing at 0.3% CAGR and contracting 0.4% in 2026; Macy's holds 7.8% share ($22.6B 2025 revenue) with 150 stores closing by end-2026 (2025-2026)
  • Apparel tariff rates spiked from 14.7% (January 2025) to 35.1% (December 2025), then settled to ~10% flat China rate plus 15% EU ceiling by July 2026 after Supreme Court ruling (2025-2026)
  • Saks Global filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy January 2026 with $3.4B debt after consolidating Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman; store productivity and vendor payments both collapsed (2026)
  • Off-price retail (Ross, TJX, Nordstrom Rack) captured market share: Ross comparable sales +17% Q3 2025 with 110 new openings planned; Nordstrom family launched $3.8B bid to take Nordstrom private while expanding Rack (2025-2026)
  • Inflation eroding purchasing power at 4.1% PCE year-over-year (May 2026) drove bifurcated consumer behavior: affluent absorbing prices, lower/middle-income trading down to discount stores at five times faster rates (2026)

Who rides it

Off-price retailers and true discounters win decisively. TJX, Ross, and outlet chains grab shoppers fleeing mid-tier department stores. The treasure hunt experience—curated inventory that changes weekly—proves defensible against e-commerce. Nordstrom's decision to go private and focus on expansion of Nordstrom Rack signals how the family is willing to abandon full-line department stores entirely to bet on off-price. Discount department stores as a sector stabilized at $107.2 billion in 2026, barely growing but holding ground, while traditional department stores hollow out around them.

Who's squeezed

Mainstream department store chains get squeezed from both ends. Macy's, JCPenney, and regional players are stuck in the middle: not premium enough to attract luxury shoppers, not cheap enough to compete with Ross or Walmart. JCPenney's 'Yes, JCPenney' comeback lifted traffic by 3% in May 2025 but revenue still fell to $6.6 billion in FY2024. Vendors lose too—payment backlogs cascade through the system (Saks Global proved that even merged players can't pay on time). Store employees hemorrhage: 2.87% annual job losses through 2028. The $227.1 billion market is essentially flat, but the floor is collapsing beneath the middle.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The structural problem is that tariffs made mid-tier retail unprofitable and consumers have already learned to shop elsewhere. Even if tariffs settle (they did, to ~10% flat by July 2026), that damage is permanent. Shoppers won't come back to Macy's because prices normalized. They've already switched to Ross or Amazon or stopped shopping department stores altogether. The second risk is cascading: if Saks Global—the desperate merger of the three biggest luxury/aspirational department stores—couldn't survive $3.4 billion in debt and vendor payment chaos, then regional and smaller chains have almost no runway. More bankruptcies will follow, accelerating the exodus.

The middle-market department store became undefendable in 2025-2026 when tariffs compressed margins beyond recovery and shoppers split into bargain-hunting and luxury, leaving undifferentiated mid-tier players like Macy's and JCPenney to close stores and hope for modest stabilization.

The Value Floor

Trading down powers dollar, convenience, and value formats.

When wallets tighten, shoppers don't just buy less—they move down. The value tier is where that traffic lands: dollar stores, convenience stores remaking themselves around cheap fresh food, ethnic supermarkets losing ground to mainstream copycats. The floor is crowded and it's profitable enough to hold, but it's no longer where growth happens.

What changed

Dollar stores and convenience stores moved from niche low-income destinations to mainstream trade-down venues. In 2024 and 2025, as inflation persisted and wage growth stalled, middle-income households began shopping dollar stores and convenience stores alongside existing low-income customers. Consumer sentiment tanked to a record low of 48.2 in May 2026, with Dollar General customers telling the company their own financial situation had worsened—a structural shift, not a cycle. The industry saw this coming: by 2025, 87% of Dollar Tree stores sat within five miles of a Walmart, proof that the format had matured and traffic was reshuffling, not growing. Dollar stores grew only 1.4% annually from 2021 to 2026, reaching $123.5 billion in revenue by 2026 (up from $101.3 billion in 2022), but the growth had gone flat. Convenience stores fared worse—only 0.2% growth over the same period, stuck at $43.7 billion in 2026. Neither format was dying, but both were gasping for air in a market where large discount chains (Walmart, Target) and Amazon offered better selection at comparable prices, squeezing the value middle from all sides.

Costs ravaged margins. Tariffs on imports hit hardest in early 2025: dollar and ethnic supermarkets saw collections on food and agricultural goods jump 647% compared to 2024, a shock that compressed already-thin margins (dollar stores at 4.7–5%, convenience stores at 1.5–2%). Organized retail crime cost the industry $47.8 billion in 2025 and was forecast to hit $55 billion by 2028—convenience stores, with their 24/7 cash-heavy operations, were prime targets, absorbing 6% of all robberies nationally. Labor kept shrinking profit: wages had grown 70% over a decade, making hiring difficult even as convenience stores desperately needed workers to keep shelves stocked and prepared-food stations running. Convenience store operators tried to fight back: those who deployed AI-powered fuel pricing reported 3.4% profit gains, but that was a Band-Aid. The real margin lifeline came from prepared food, which accounted for 39% of in-store profit, yet in-store foodservice sales sat flat in 2025 at $97.3 billion (out of $341.2 billion in total in-store sales).

Ethnic supermarkets faced a worse squeeze. The category had nearly stopped growing—just 0.1% in 2025, down from 1.9% in 2024—while the count of independent ethnic grocers fell 11.3% annually. Mainstream supermarkets (Kroger, Albertsons) had stolen their thunder by launching private-label ethnic foods, making the specialty itself a commodity. Tariff shock hit even harder for ethnic stores because their mix skewed heavily toward imported staples (Asian noodles, spices, fish sauce, Korean prepared foods) that bore the full tariff load. Large regional ethnic chains like Vallarta (49,000 sq ft flagship in Arizona, 2026; planning 15 stores over the next decade) and 99 Ranch (37,000 sq ft flagship in Flushing, 2026; expanding to Las Vegas) responded by going big: food halls, destination appeal, scale plays. But they were racing Amazon and Walmart on delivery networks they could never match.

The real reshuffling was customer behavior. Dollar stores responded to margin pressure and market saturation by investing heavily in fresh produce—DG Fresh, Dollar General's produce brand, had rolled into ~7,000 locations by 2025, a slow but deliberate pivot to compete on freshness and basket size. The company poured $150 million into labor and store remodels in Q1 2025 alone, driving a 5.2% same-store sales bump and a 61 basis point gross margin boost. Convenience stores, sensing that fuel was a race to the bottom (pump prices fell 5.9% in 2025 from $3.30 to $3.11 per gallon), bet their future on prepared food—80% of operators expected foodservice to improve in 2026, betting on personal pizzas and coffee to offset gas-margin collapse. The Couche-Tard attempt to acquire 7-Eleven (bid raised to $47.2 billion in early 2025, then withdrawn in June 2025) signaled that consolidation was the only survival path for smaller players. And it was starting: 88.9% of convenience-store M&A deals in 2025 went to strategic buyers, not financial players—a sign that the era of mom-and-pop c-stores was closing.

The evidence

  • Dollar stores: $123.5 billion market (2026), 1.4% annual growth 2021–2026; 9,400 companies, ~39,000 stores, 600,000+ workers; margins 4.7–5%
  • Convenience stores: $43.7 billion market (2026), 0.2% CAGR 2021–2026; 58,033 stores, ~175,000 employees; margins 1.5–2%, prepared food 39% of in-store profit
  • Ethnic supermarkets: $58.9 billion (2025), near-zero growth at 0.1% in 2025; 16,042 businesses (down 1.3% from 2024); annual closure rate 11.3% for independents
  • Tariffs: 647% spike in food/ag collections early 2025; organized retail crime $47.8 billion (2025), forecast $55 billion (2028)
  • Fuel margin compression: gas prices fell 5.9% in 2025 ($3.30 to $3.11/gallon); AI pricing automation yielded 3.4% profit gains for c-store operators

Who rides it

Walmart and Target win by weaponizing scale: they undercut dollar stores on price while offering fresher produce, prepared foods, and destination appeal that smaller value retailers cannot match. Large regional ethnic chains (Vallarta, 99 Ranch, H Mart) that can swing investment in flagships and food halls expand and consolidate territory, banking on brand loyalty and destination shopping. Convenience store consolidators—strategic buyers picking up small chains in 88.9% of 2025 M&A deals—win by eliminating redundant labor and standardizing operations to survive in a margin-compressed world.

Who's squeezed

Independent ethnic supermarkets and dollar stores without scale are getting crushed. Ethnic store closures are accelerating (11.3% annually), with mainline grocers stealing their ethnic-product differentiation through private labels (Kroger's Hispanic lines, Korean and Chinese meal kits, 2026) and Amazon/Walmart offering delivery at speed these stores can never match. Convenience store owners face a choice: consolidate or die. Mom-and-pop c-store operators are being pushed out as wage inflation and organized theft make labor and security unaffordable on thin 1.5–2% margins. Tariffs have weaponized import-heavy businesses—ethnic supermarkets bearing 647% tariff spikes cannot absorb the cost into already-thin 3% margins.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the value floor itself collapses if consumer sentiment doesn't stabilize. May 2026's record low of 48.2 signals that shoppers' financial strain is structural, not cyclical—if incomes continue to stagnate while inflation persists, even the value tier becomes unaffordable for millions, meaning traffic that should hold the format instead shifts to even cheaper formats (buy-in-bulk clubs, secondhand, food banks) or simply vanishes. A consumer recession would prove that even the floor has room to fall.

In one sentence

The value floor in a nutshell

The value floor stays crowded but stops growing—Walmart and large chains trade down from their upper tiers while small independents and undifferentiated mid-tier operators close or consolidate away.

A · The stores splitting apart

The premium ceiling

Affluent shoppers keep spending on premium jewelry and beauty, but the market splits—and middle-tier retailers fall apart.

Shoppers didn't stop buying jewelry or beauty products. But the people who buy them split into two groups, and the middle disappeared. Premium brands that cater to affluent consumers are thriving. Everything else is dying.

What changed

Gold prices nearly doubled in 2025, surging about 60% annually and peaking near $4,400 per ounce in October. That pushed entry-level jewelry prices from around $99 to $200-$500. Suddenly the mass market couldn't afford it. Store-after-store closed—167 jewelry stores shut down in Q1 2025 alone, a 21% jump from the same quarter the year before. By the end of 2024, the total was 747 discontinuances. The jewelry business contracted 12.1% in 2025 and another 2.2% in 2026, shrinking from a $61.7 billion market to something much smaller. Two major chains filed for bankruptcy: Claire's in August 2025 (its second bankruptcy in seven years) and Lugano Diamonds in November. Margins compressed to 3.0-3.4%, squeezed by tariffs, gold prices, and the shift to online shopping.

Beauty told a different story on the surface, but the mechanics were identical. Ulta Beauty, the premium player, posted $12.4 billion in sales for fiscal 2025 and grew 9.7% year-over-year, guided to 6-7% growth in 2026. But smaller specialty beauty brands evaporated. Pat McGrath Labs filed Chapter 11 in early 2026. Flower Beauty shut down in September 2025. Cover FX and Mally Beauty closed through their parent company's restructuring in January 2026. Glossier closed 75% of its stores. The market size—$69.3 billion in 2026—looked stable at first glance, but that hid a brutal consolidation where one player (Ulta) captured growth while dozens of smaller brands simply vanished.

Tariffs on Chinese imports hit 145% by late 2025, forcing wholesale costs up 18-22% through spring 2025. For jewelry, that meant $25-30 million in additional costs if applied to a full fiscal year. For beauty, tariffs became another squeeze on already-thin margins for anyone not large enough to absorb the hit. Online channels captured an estimated 25% of jewelry purchases globally by 2026, with mobile accounting for over 60% of online transactions. TikTok Shop alone posted $2.49 billion in US beauty GMV in 2025, a 123% jump year-over-year. Amazon's beauty share is forecast to climb from 10% in 2024 to 15% by 2030, while Sephora and Ulta's combined share dips from 20% to 19%.

Lab-grown diamonds reshaped the entire jewelry category. They captured 56.8% of the US engagement ring market by late 2025, fundamentally changing both product mix and what consumers would pay. The average lab-grown diamond went from 1.31 carats in 2019 to 2.45 carats in 2025—buyers got twice as much for the same or less money. That destroyed margins on traditional mined diamonds and forced traditional jewelers to retrain staff, restock, and reposition. Anyone stuck selling mid-tier jewelry got crushed between affluent buyers who wanted luxury and value buyers who wanted lab diamonds at deep discounts. The middle emptied out.

The evidence

  • Jewelry retail: $61.7B market (2025) down 12.1% YoY, with 167 store closures in Q1 2025 alone and gold prices up 60% annually to $4,400/oz in October 2025, pricing out the mass market.
  • Jewelry bankruptcy wave: Claire's filed Chapter 11 in August 2025 (second time in seven years) and Lugano Diamonds filed November 2025, as brick-and-mortar contraction accelerated.
  • Beauty premiumization: Ulta Beauty posted $12.4B in fiscal 2025 sales (up 9.7% YoY, guiding 6-7% growth in 2026), while Pat McGrath Labs filed Chapter 11, Flower Beauty closed (September 2025), and Glossier shuttered 75% of stores.
  • Tariff shock: Tariffs on Chinese imports hit 145% by late 2025, raising wholesale beauty and jewelry costs 18-22% as of spring 2025, with $25-30M annual impact per affected retailer.
  • Lab diamonds: Lab-grown diamonds captured 56.8% of the US engagement ring market by late 2025 (vs. negligible share in 2019), with average carat weight doubling from 1.31 to 2.45 carats, undercutting mined diamond margins.

Who rides it

Ulta Beauty and premium-focused brands thrive. Ulta's fiscal 2025 sales hit $12.4B with 9.7% growth, comp sales up 5.4%, and guidance for 6-7% growth in fiscal 2026. Amazon and TikTok Shop capture discovery and repeat purchases—TikTok Shop posted $2.49B US beauty GMV in 2025 with 123% YoY growth. Affluent consumers keep spending on status goods and premium beauty regardless of tariffs or gold prices. Lab-grown diamonds win, too—they capture 56.8% of engagement rings and let buyers get more carats for less money, reshaping the entire category.

Who's squeezed

Mid-tier jewelry and beauty retailers get crushed. Smaller specialty brands—Pat McGrath Labs, Flower Beauty, Cover FX, Mally Beauty, Glossier—collapse or nearly vanish. Traditional jewelry stores close by the hundreds. Margins compress to 3.0-3.4% for jewelers, a fraction of historical norms. Retailers stuck selling undifferentiated mid-tier goods can't compete upmarket against Ulta's scale and brand power, and they can't compete downmarket against online channels and lab diamonds. The Ulta-Target partnership ended in August 2026, further squeezing distribution for competitors.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The tariff shock is far from over. At 145%, tariffs on Chinese imports forced costs up 18-22% by spring 2025, and those pass through to consumers in 2026 and beyond. If tariffs stick or rise further, even affluent consumers may retrench on discretionary purchases. Jewelry and beauty both depend on discovery and impulse buying, and online channels (Amazon, TikTok) are redirecting that spending away from traditional retail. Lab-grown diamonds will keep undercutting mined-diamond margins. There's no price floor for mid-tier retailers—they have no cost advantage, no premium positioning, and no channel lock-in.

In one sentence

The premium ceiling in a nutshell

Premium jewelry and beauty retailers thrive while tariffs and gold prices destroy the middle market, leaving small brands and traditional stores to close or file bankruptcy.

B · Apparel & footwear bifurcate

Apparel splits

Fast-fashion and luxury grow; mid-price apparel chains close.

The American clothing industry is splitting in two. Shoppers at the top and bottom of the market are thriving—luxury brand DTC sites and ultra-cheap platforms like Shein and Temu pull customers and margin. Everyone else is crushed. The stores selling undifferentiated mid-market sweaters and jeans to average Americans are vanishing. Tariffs doubled import costs overnight. E-commerce captured a quarter of all fashion sales. And consumer spending on apparel just collapsed by a fifth in early 2025.

What changed

The apparel market has split into two incompatible worlds, and the middle is being evacuated. The family clothing retail market—the backbone of US mall shopping—reached $226.5 billion in 2026, but growth is nearly flat at 0.4%, masked by violent bifurcation below the surface. Women's clothing stores, which hit $66.4 billion in 2026, have exactly one story: premium and specialty retailers soaking up online growth (5.5% annual employment gains in online segments 2019-2024) while brick-and-mortar employment contracts year after year. Men's dedicated clothing stores are even worse off, declining at -1.7% in 2026 and shrinking to a $17.8 billion market from $8.3 billion in 2022—a deceptive compression that masks store closures and margin squeeze.

The tariff shock of late 2025 broke what remained of the middle. On August 29, 2025, the de-minimis tariff exemption expired globally, meaning every imported garment under $800 became subject to duty. Import tariff rates on apparel surged from 14.7% in January 2025 to 35.1% by December 2025—a 138% jump in nine months. McKinsey estimated that sourcing costs jumped 35% for apparel importers. A single family's cost of living went up $136 overnight. Apparel CPI reached 135.8 by March 2026, up 5.1% year-over-year, the fastest clip in years. Consumer response was immediate and brutal: apparel spending collapsed 21.7% month-over-month between Q4 2024 and Q1 2025. Price-sensitive households—the traditional customer for mid-market chains—pulled back furthest as inflation squeezed their budgets.

E-commerce has carved out a permanent quarter of the market. Online fashion sales reached $61.8 billion in 2025 and now account for nearly half of women's clothing sales overall. The growth isn't going to traditional department stores or branded websites, though. It's going to ultra-low-cost platforms like Shein and Temu that offer $5 blouses and $8 jeans. These platforms have invested aggressively in US warehousing to dodge tariffs and shipping delays. Meanwhile, department stores like Macy's—which still moved $22.5 billion in 2025 revenue—absorb menswear and women's brands at tighter margins, offering one-stop convenience that specialty retailers can't match. Amazon and brand-direct sites offer infinite selection and price transparency that small chains can't compete with.

The mid-market chains are gone or going. Forever 21 filed Chapter 11 on March 16, 2025, and liquidated all 364 stores by May 2025. Liberated Brands (the portfolio of Volcom, Billabong, Quiksilver, Roxy, RVCA, Spyder) filed in February 2025 and liquidated 122 stores. Macy's announced 66 store closures in January 2025, part of a 150-store exit over three years. Francesca's announced the closure of 400 locations. Torrid plans to shutter 180 stores. Store closures hit 7,323 in 2024 and approximately 6,000 in the first half of 2025 alone. The only retailer investing heavily is Tailored Brands, which filed for IPO in 2026 and plans to add 500+ stores over the next decade—but its strategy is to move upmarket into premium menswear and rental subscriptions, not defend the middle. Their fiscal 2025 revenue was $2.53 billion, up only 2.1% year-over-year, but gross margin expanded 145 basis points to 48.2%, meaning they are winning by shrinking the addressable market to affluent men willing to rent suits and use AI fit technology.

The evidence

  • Women's clothing retail in the US: $66.4B in 2026, growing -0.3% annually, as luxury and specialty online pull upmarket while Shein/Temu steal value customers from brick-and-mortar chains.
  • Men's clothing retail: contracted to $17.8B in 2026 (-1.7% in 2026), down from $8.3B in 2022, squeezed by department stores, e-commerce giants, and the normalization of casual athleisure (+10% annually).
  • Tariff shock: apparel import duties surged from 14.7% (January 2025) to 35.1% (December 2025), with McKinsey estimating 35% sourcing price increases, forcing retailers to raise prices 30-38% or absorb losses.
  • Consumer pullback: apparel spending collapsed 21.7% month-over-month (Q4 2024 to Q1 2025); apparel CPI hit 5.1% year-over-year by March 2026, fastest in years.
  • E-commerce penetration: 24% of fashion retail in 2026 (up from 21% in 2024), growing 4.9% annually; ultra-low-cost platforms (Shein, Temu) capturing share from traditional mid-market chains via aggressive US warehousing.

Who rides it

Discount and luxury retailers are the only winners. Value players like TJX Companies (TJ Maxx, HomeGoods) and Ross Stores are thriving: TJX reported 5% comp sales growth in Q3 FY2026 and raised full-year guidance, while Ross projects 6-7% comp growth for FY2026, both benefiting directly from the bifurcation—affluent customers want discounts more than they need brands, and price-conscious shoppers have nowhere else to turn. At the top, luxury and specialty DTC sites are growing online at 5.5% annually in employment terms, pulling wealthy customers into premium segments and niche categories like plus-size and athletic wear where margin is real.

Who's squeezed

The mid-market chain is being executed. Forever 21 (364 stores), Liberated Brands (122 stores), Francesca's (400 closures), and Torrid (180 closures) are the visible casualties, but the real victim is anyone dependent on selling undifferentiated apparel to average-income American families. Store closures totaled 13,323 in the 18 months from 2024 through mid-2025. Employment in women's brick-and-mortar clothing retail is contracting as specialty online grows. Men's dedicated clothing stores shed 1,126 jobs from 2022 to 2026 (38,126 → 37,000 estimated), a symptom of the category's irrelevance in a hybrid-work world where casual athleisure (growing 10%+ annually) has replaced suits and slacks. Retailers holding mid-market inventory face margin compression: net margins in family clothing sit at 2.3-5%, the thinnest in retail.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The tariff regime has created a structural price floor that may not reverse. A tariff rate of 35.1% on apparel imports is not temporary—it reflects the Trump administration's reciprocal tariff doctrine and shows no signs of easing. Retailers have until late Q1 or Q2 2026 for existing inventory to work through the supply chain, meaning the full tariff hit lands on Q1-Q2 2026 shipments. For retailers already operating on 2-5% net margins, there is no room to absorb a 35% cost increase. Either prices rise 30-38% (further crushing demand among price-sensitive customers) or they exit the category. The only escape valve is nearshoring to USMCA-qualifying countries like Mexico, Vietnam, and India, but production ramp-up is slow and won't relieve pressure until H2 2026 at the earliest. The tariff creates a lasting incentive for ultra-low-cost platforms like Shein and Temu to localize warehousing in the US, permanently locking in their competitive advantage against traditional retailers.

In one sentence

Apparel splits in a nutshell

The US apparel market bifurcates into thriving discount and luxury poles while mid-tier chains collapse under tariffs and e-commerce pressure.

B · Apparel & footwear bifurcate

Footwear & the niche

Specialty and athletic footwear thrive; generic mid-tier shoe retail shrinks.

The footwear market is splitting down the middle. Premium athletic stores and specialty labels are growing, while undifferentiated shoe retailers—the ones selling decent but unremarkable mid-priced sneakers—are disappearing. Tariffs, brand consolidation, and online channels have made it impossible to survive in the mushy middle.

What changed

For twenty years, shoe retail was simple. Nike and Adidas flooded wholesale, mall-anchor shoe stores sold volume, and margins stayed thin but predictable. That model broke in 2025-2026.

Start with tariffs. The Trump administration's 20-27% tariff regime on Chinese footwear (imposed April 2025, invalidated by the Supreme Court February 20, 2026, then reimposed under alternative authority) created three rounds of supply-chain chaos. A shoe that cost $50 to land now costs $62. Retailers with 3.8-3.9% EBIT margins cannot absorb that. They raised prices, watched traffic drop, and scrambled. Specialty running stores held steady because they offer fit expertise that online cannot match—57% of performance-oriented buyers still come to them. But generic shoe retailers collapsed.

Next, the brands took back control. Nike and Adidas spent three years cutting thousands of small retailers out of their wholesale networks to push customers toward their own websites and apps (higher margins, direct feedback, no middleman). Nike ended relationships with DSW, Urban Outfitters, and Olympia Sports in 2025. When Nike finally realized it was cannibalizing wholesale revenue, it reversed some cuts—but the damage was done. The largest pure-play shoe retailer, Foot Locker (which operated thousands of stores selling $17 billion worth of shoes in the 2021-2022 period), could not survive standalone. Dick's Sporting Goods acquired it for $2.4-2.5 billion in September 2025, absorbing 275 Foot Locker closures and 125 Champs Sports shutters (62.5% of that chain) by end of 2026. This is the end of the independent shoe retailer era.

Meanwhile, the market is hollowing out. E-commerce penetration in footwear reached 30-35% of total sales by mid-2025, growing 7-9% annually while physical stores flatlined. Mall foot traffic declined for the first time since the pandemic in the second half of 2025—particularly crushing the super-regional malls where mid-tier shoe chains clustered. The US shoe retail market, worth $41.8 billion in 2021, reached only $67.5 billion in 2025 but is now in structural decline (-1.0% projected for 2025 according to IBISWorld). Bankruptcies cascaded: Sneakersnstuff (Swedish parent SNS AB) filed for Chapter 11 in January 2025, closing stores in New York and Los Angeles. Soleply filed Chapter 11 in March 2025, closing 4 of 6 locations. Even Allbirds, the DTC-native shoe brand that went public for $4 billion in 2021, sold itself for $39 million in February 2026 after closing all full-price US stores.

What got scarce was the middle. You cannot compete as a mid-tier shoe store. Luxury and heritage brands (Cole Haan, Allen Edmonds, Allbirds-as-outlet) and online-first insurgents moved up or down. Specialty athletic stores and independent running boutiques survived because they sell expertise, community, and fit—not just shoes. Dick's now controls 3,200+ stores globally, bundling footwear with sporting goods so no single category has to carry margin pressure alone. The $32-42 billion athletic shoe retail segment grew 2.7-5.9% CAGR through 2030-2034, but only because consolidation and specialty focus are forcing out the undifferentiated players.

The evidence

  • Athletic Shoe Stores: $32-42 billion market (2025-2026) with 2.7-5.9% CAGR through 2030-2034; but only 3,678 locations (2025, +1.5% from 2024), meaning consolidation is squeezing unit count despite dollar growth
  • Foot Locker collapse: 275 of 1,200+ Foot Locker stores closing by end 2026 plus 125 Champs Sports closures (62.5% of chain), per Dick's September 2025 acquisition announcement
  • Nike wholesale pullback: Nike ended relationships with DSW, Urban Outfitters, Olympia Sports in 2025; Sneakersnstuff (SNS AB) filed Chapter 11 January 2025; Soleply filed Chapter 11 March 2025
  • Allbirds collapse: Sold for $39 million in February 2026 after IPO at $4 billion in 2021; closed all full-price US stores due to inability to compete mid-market
  • Tariff cascade: 20-27% Trump tariff on Chinese footwear (April 2025), Supreme Court invalidation (February 20, 2026), then reimposition under alternative authority—three rounds of supply chain disruption

Who rides it

Specialty athletic retailers and independent running stores are thriving. They sell expertise—gait analysis, fit guidance, community events—that Amazon cannot replicate. Fifty-seven percent of performance-oriented buyers still visit them because the right shoe prevents injury. Dick's Sporting Goods won by consolidating scale: it acquired Foot Locker's 3,200+ stores and leveraged bundled sporting goods to dilute margin pressure across categories. Heritage brands and luxury lines (Cole Haan, Allen Edmonds) survived by moving upmarket. DTC-native upscale brands like Skims and Savage X Fenty are capturing high-income customers willing to pay for design and brand. Even subscription and loyalty models are working for niche players like Adore Me (now part of Victoria's Secret) because they lock in repeat purchase. The winners all share one trait: they are not selling undifferentiated shoes to whoever walks in.

Who's squeezed

Mid-tier shoe retailers got crushed. Foot Locker, which once defined shoe retail and generated $17-19 billion in US volume (2021-2022), is now being dismantled. Smaller chains and independents selling Nike and Adidas at full price cannot compete when Nike itself sells direct online. Margin compression from tariffs (landed costs up 20-27% from April 2025) combined with e-commerce growth (30-35% penetration, growing 7-9% annually) left them no room to cut. Malls where these stores clustered lost foot traffic for the first time since the pandemic in late 2025. Brand-specific retailers—the ones betting their entire model on Nike or Adidas inventory—watched those brands pull wholesale relationships. Specialty chains without expertise advantage, without direct relationships with customers, and without the scale to bundle categories simply disappeared.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that specialty stores survive the tariff moment but then get crushed by Amazon penetration. Online footwear is already 30-35% and growing 7-9% annually. Specialty running stores hold 57% of performance customers now, but that assumes customers still value fit expertise enough to visit a store. If that assumption breaks—if younger shoppers accept misfit shoes because they are cheap online, or if VR fitting improves—then even the specialty segment disappears. Tariffs also risk spreading to tariffs on footwear from Vietnam and India, the secondary suppliers filling Nike and Adidas factories. If those tariffs land in 2026-2027, the landing cost squeeze deepens and even niche retailers with loyal customers may not survive. The hollowing out may be permanent.

In one sentence

Footwear & the niche in a nutshell

Tariffs and brand consolidation destroyed mid-tier shoe retail, leaving only specialty stores and DTC brands standing.

C · Eating & staying out

Dining bifurcates

The middle-market restaurant collapses as diners split to cheap QSR and premium sit-down experiences.

The restaurant middle is being crushed. For the first time since the pandemic, casual dining—Chili's, Texas Roadhouse, Olive Garden territory—is not just stagnant but actively collapsing. Fast food is hanging on. Premium sit-down is holding its own. But everything in between is hemorrhaging customers, closing units, and going dark. The math broke.

What changed

Labor costs have jumped 39% since pre-pandemic levels, with the California FAST Act setting a $20/hour minimum wage for national chain restaurants in April 2024 and other states following with $16-$20 floors now standard in major metros. This wasn't a gradual climb—it landed hard and structural. An operator who staffed a 150-seat casual-dining unit had to suddenly absorb ~$300,000 more in annual payroll, with no matching lift in customer traffic. Fast food could squeeze margins tighter (they sit at 5.1% as of 2021 and have only gotten leaner). Casual dining, already working single-digit margins, had nowhere to go. Food inflation sits 34% above pre-pandemic, compounded by tariffs now covering 15% of US food imports—beef, chicken, and dairy all trending up. Chains raised prices to cope (62% of operators raised menu prices in 2025), pushing a casual-dining entree from $14 to $18+ and a fast-food combo from $8 to $12. But consumers at the $18 casual-dining price point started asking: why not just go premium? Meanwhile, GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic are quietly reshaping behavior. Dinner spending at fast food dropped 6% among regular users, and households with a GLP-1 taker cut restaurant spending an average 5.3% overall. The appetites are smaller, the visit frequency is lower, and the middle is where traffic evaporates first. Chain restaurant market size is $230.6 billion (2026) with growth stuck at -1.0% that year, and 42% of operators reported being unprofitable in 2025. Meanwhile, fast food trudges ahead at $423.7 billion (2026) with 0.7% growth—not thriving, but stable enough to absorb defectors from the middle. Traffic in fast food declined only -0.3% in 2025, accelerating to -2% in Q4 2025 vs Q4 2024, but that's still a softer decline than the full meltdown hitting casual dining. What made scarcity: mid-tier seat traffic and the ability to charge enough to cover labor and food without customer rebellion. What became cheap: fast food, especially value bundles and dollar menus, which became the fallback for consumers priced out of casual dining. What became risky: operating a 150-seat restaurant with fixed labor costs, food inflation clawing at margins, and a price ceiling set by the neighbor's QSR down the street. What became valuable: either a locked-in fast food franchise model or a true premium experience (higher-income diners less price-sensitive and willing to visit less often but spend more per head).

The evidence

  • Fast-food minimum wage in California reached $20/hour in April 2024, forcing 25% cost increases and 8-12% menu price hikes across franchised QSR chains in the largest state market.
  • Chain restaurants (casual dining and above) contracted -1.0% in 2026 while fast food grew just 0.7%, with 42% of casual-dining operators unprofitable as of 2025.
  • Denny's—a casual-dining stalwart—went private via $620M all-cash acquisition in Q1 2026 after decades public; TGI Fridays and Red Lobster both filed Chapter 11 in 2024, closing 130+ locations.
  • Labor costs jumped 39% above pre-pandemic with tariffs now covering 15% of US food imports, creating a dual squeeze that casual-dining operators (already at 5.1% or lower margins) could not absorb.
  • GLP-1 adoption caused dinner spending at fast food to drop 6% among regular users and cut overall household restaurant spending by 5.3%, draining traffic from the mid-tier first and hardest.

Who rides it

Fast food and true premium. QSR chains can absorb margin pressure by cutting hours (overtime eliminated), raising prices modestly on price-insensitive customers, and relying on convenience and speed to drive traffic despite lower visit frequency. Premium restaurants (high-ticket steakhouses, destination fine dining) have customers less price-sensitive than casual dining and can pass through food inflation and labor costs—their customers expect to pay $70-$150 per head and visit less often. Both formats see growth or stability. Fast food has 224,000 establishments and 5.5 million employees by 2026; the chains large enough to absorb $20/hour minima and tariff costs are consolidating, not collapsing. Premium fine dining maintains pricing power and traffic among affluent, older diners less affected by GLP-1 and more willing to trade fewer meals for better experiences.

Who's squeezed

Casual dining chains and their employees. A 150-seat casual-dining restaurant with $18 entrees is now the worst position in dining: too expensive for price-conscious fast-food defectors, not special enough for the $60+ premium crowd, and stuffed with fixed labor and rent costs that labor inflation broke. Chili's and Texas Roadhouse are holding on by slashing prices to $12-$15 sit-down deals, but that only works if you're massive enough to absorb the margin hit (and Chili's parent is massive—Brinker International). Smaller casual-dining chains and regional players have no such cushion. TGI Fridays, Red Lobster, Bravo Brio, FAT Brands (Smokey Bones), and On The Border all filed Chapter 11 between 2024 and 2026. Meanwhile, the 15.8 million workers in the broader restaurant industry are squeezed: wage gains are real (your hourly rate went up), but so did the cost of food and rent. Visit frequency among households with GLP-1 users dropped 5.3%, meaning fewer shifts for casual-dining staff and more closure announcements.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The death spiral of casual dining accelerates and takes franchisees with it. As more casual-dining chains close units or go private (Denny's), franchisees stuck with leases, equipment debt, and payroll obligations have limited exit ramps. A franchisee owning a Chili's location now has to operate at 60-70% of historical traffic levels while paying $20/hour labor and absorbing 34% food inflation. Rent is fixed. Debt is fixed. The only lever left is pricing or closure. If casual-dining defectors swing fully to fast food, fast food will eventually saturate and pricing power will erode there too—meaning no one wins in the restaurant middle. And if GLP-1 adoption accelerates past the current 5.3% cut in household dining spend, overall restaurant industry traffic could tip negative across all formats. A recession or even mild job loss would finish the job by cutting discretionary dining entirely.

In one sentence

Dining bifurcates in a nutshell

Casual dining chains are caught between fast food's value dominance and premium restaurants' margin power, while labor costs, food inflation, and GLP-1 adoption hollow out the mid-tier entirely.

C · Eating & staying out

Hotels pick a lane

Budget and luxury boutique hotels boom while mid-scale motels face margin squeeze.

The US hotel industry split into two businesses in 2025. Luxury boutique hotels grabbed a six percent revenue jump with average daily rates hitting $452. Extended-stay properties grew four percent in supply—the biggest jump in four years—riding remote work and housing shortages. Meanwhile, the traditional mid-scale motel got caught in the middle, crushed by wages that rose 25.6 percent since 2019 and shrinking occupancy.

What changed

For decades, American hotels operated on a simple formula: rent rooms by the night, keep costs flat, watch margins grow. That model broke in 2024 and 2025. The fracture happened on two fronts.

First, labor destroyed the economics of mediocrity. Hotel wages climbed 25.6 percent against 2019 levels, and labor cost per occupied room jumped 21 percent from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025. Operating costs followed—insurance spiked one hundred percent, utilities up thirty percent. Those numbers sound abstract until you do the math: a mid-scale hotel operator paying $54.98 in labor cost per occupied room cannot absorb that squeeze while charging $110–130 per night. Luxury properties charging $452 per night could absorb wage increases and pass them to customers. Budget operators targeting $65–85 per night had already engineered skeleton crews with sixty to eighty percent annual turnover. The middle got destroyed.

Second, the demand split became irreversible. Luxury boutique hotels hit 70 to 75 percent occupancy in 2025 while economy segments flatlined. Extended-stay hotels filled a structural need: eighteen million Americans identify as digital nomads, four million homes vanished from the US housing supply, and over twenty-one million renters spend more than thirty percent of income on housing. Extended-stay properties expanded supply four percent in 2025—the most in four years—and bounced back to 76.7 percent occupancy by May 2026 after a rough 2025. Independent boutique owners watched their category become hot, but only if you had scale. Sonder—the poster child for boutique hotel tech—folded in November 2025 after Marriott killed its deal citing financial constraints. Revo Hospitality Group, operating 260 properties, filed Chapter 11 in January 2026 as refinancing walls peaked. What killed them was simple: small and mid-scale operators could not compete on brand distribution once metasearch and Google Hotel Ads commanded $8.2 billion in annual spend, and they could not absorb $21 percent labor jumps on $100–150 average daily rates.

The chains responded by converting the market, not building it. Economy properties shifted to extended-stay formats. Hilton launched Apartment Collection by Hilton in January 2026 with Placemakr, racing to offer furnished apartments at scale and compete head-to-head with Airbnb, which now offers one to two bedroom units in urban markets two times cheaper than hotel equivalents. Marriott opened StudioRes, a budget extended-stay brand, with eighty-five properties in the pipeline. IHG recorded a milestone: opening four hundred forty-three new hotels in Q1 2026 and passing seven thousand operating properties. The industry shifted from organic development to rapid conversion—lower capital expense, faster reopenings, and instant modern amenities. That path is not available to independent operators or mom-and-pop motels.

The evidence

  • Luxury boutique hotels achieved 6% revenue gain in 2025 with $452 average daily rates (IBISWorld), while mid-scale properties contracted.
  • Extended-stay hotels grew 4% in supply in 2025 and bounced to 76.7% occupancy by May 2026, the largest supply increase in four years (STR data).
  • Labor cost per occupied room jumped 21% from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025, hitting $54.98; wages up 25.6% versus 2019 (hotel operator surveys).
  • Sonder (Marriott-backed boutique operator) filed Chapter 7 liquidation in November 2025; Revo Hospitality Group (260 properties) filed Chapter 11 in January 2026.
  • Hilton launched Apartment Collection by Hilton in January 2026 and now operates 1,000 luxury and lifestyle hotels globally; IHG opened 443 new hotels in Q1 2026 and passed 7,000 operating properties.

Who rides it

Luxury boutique and extended-stay operators win. They have pricing power to absorb wage and operating-cost inflation. Boutique luxury hit 6 percent revenue growth in 2025 when the broader industry barely moved. Extended-stay hits 76.7 percent occupancy and 5.4 percent demand growth in Q1 2026 because they solve a real housing and work-pattern crisis. Large chains win by acquiring independents and converting portfolios: Hilton, IHG, and Marriott all rolled out collection brands and extended-stay formats to capture the split. Chains also win on distribution—metasearch and Google Hotel Ads now own the customer interface.

Who's squeezed

Mid-scale motels and independent boutique owners get squeezed from both sides. Wages rose 25.6 percent but they cannot raise room rates $300 more per night to compensate. Operating costs climbed across the board—insurance one hundred percent, utilities thirty percent—while occupancy stayed flat. Independent boutique operators who built a category watched Sonder and Revo implode on maturity walls and refinancing crises. Those still standing either sell to a chain (surrendering brand independence) or join a collection brand at scale. The mom-and-pop motel operator has no path forward except conversion to extended-stay or acquisition.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the bifurcation locks in and regional mid-market hotels disappear entirely. Once extended-stay and luxury capture the demand, volume-play economy properties become a commodity business with razor-thin margins. Chains can absorb losses on economy by cross-subsidizing from luxury. Independents cannot. If Airbnb continues undercutting hotel prices by two times in urban markets while digital nomads and housing refugees support extended-stay growth, the whole mid-tier category—not just weak players—could vanish within three to five years.

In one sentence

Hotels pick a lane in a nutshell

The US hotel industry bifurcated in 2025: luxury and extended-stay captured demand and pricing power, while mid-scale operators caught between wage inflation and flat occupancy face extinction or absorption into a chain.
