D · Experience & status

Paying for the Experience

Consumers splurge on blockbuster moments while casual experiences die—leaving mid-tier venues trapped.

Consumers are trading goods for moments. Amusement parks, concert venues, and movie theaters are pulling in record dollars—but the money is clumping at the extremes. A Disney guest pays $224 for a peak-day Disneyland ticket in 2025, while regional parks hemorrhage attendance. Concerts now average $144 per ticket, but small independent venues are disappearing. Movie theaters rake in billions, yet half the industry's independent chains filed for bankruptcy.

What changed

The shift from casual consumption to selective indulgence created a new scarcity: authentic, differentiated experiences. What happened is that pent-up leisure demand rewarded the spectacular and starved the ordinary. Disney's domestic parks pulled 76.5 million visitors in 2024—a nominal success—but the company is using a two-price strategy that screams bifurcation: peak-day tickets hit $224 at Disneyland and over $200 at Magic Kingdom (October 2025), while simultaneously offering the deepest discounts in years to maintain traffic. This is not margin expansion; this is elasticity breaking. Meanwhile, the Cedar Fair-Six Flags merger (completed July 2024, creating a 27-park combined operator) is drowning: a $5.5 billion debt load and Q2 2025 attendance down 1.4 million year-over-year. Pent-up demand is real, but it is not equally distributed. It flows to new spectacles—Universal's Epic Universe opened in May 2025 with five themed worlds (Harry Potter, Super Nintendo World, How to Train Your Dragon) and is projected to pull 5.2 million visitors in its opening year, climbing to 9.2 million by 2026, potentially boosting Universal Orlando's total attendance by 50%. That demand is stolen from everyone else. Concert and event promotion is experiencing a similar split. Live Nation reported record revenue of $25.2 billion in 2025 (9% year-over-year growth) and 159 million fans attending 55,000 concerts globally, with ticket prices averaging $144 (up 45% since 2019). The willingness to pay is there: 36% of consumers are willing to spend $100-$499 per ticket, and 17% will spend up to $1,000. But this premium consumption is a trap for the mid-tier venue. Rockwood Music Hall, an iconic NYC independent venue, closed in November 2024. The Music Hall of Williamsburg faces eviction at the end of 2026. Avant Gardner filed for bankruptcy owing $155 million. These were not marginal spaces—they were the scaffolding that built audience loyalty across genres and price points. Without them, the industry is a two-tier market: stadium-sized blockbusters with dynamic pricing algorithms and algorithmic yield management, and streaming alternatives at $15 per month. Movie theaters show the collapse most starkly. The industry recovered to $8.6–8.8 billion in 2025 but remains 23–27% below the 2019 pre-pandemic peak. Attendance dropped 34% (from 1.225 billion in 2019 to 780 million in 2025), but ticket prices rose 5.7% in 2025 to offset volume loss. AMC shuttered 200+ theaters; iPic, LOOK, and CMX filed Chapter 11. The survivors—Cinemark and Regal—were the low-leverage operators that could absorb years of margin compression. What remains is event-driven (Inside Out 2, Deadpool & Wolverine) versus everything else fails. This is not a recovery; it is a bifurcation with funeral pyres. The drivers are economic and structural. Labor costs consume 35% of operating expenses in amusement parks, with wage inflation stuck at 2.9% annually. Tariffs on imported ride systems and equipment push capital costs higher. Streaming made casual moviegoing obsolete—1.1 billion SVOD subscribers are now permanent (2x pre-pandemic), and studios have committed to 45-day theatrical windows or longer, forcing a détente that disciplines box office while protecting streaming. Yet all three industries are caught in the same squeeze: nominal growth masks a hollowing-out of the middle. Pent-up demand and willingness to pay fund the premium. Everyone else is forced to compete on price or disappear.

The evidence

  • Amusement Parks: Disney's peak-day Disneyland tickets reached $224 (October 2025) while offering deepest discounts in years; Universal's Epic Universe projected 9.2M annual visitors by 2026 (50% attendance boost to Orlando resort), while Cedar Fair-Six Flags faces $5.5B debt and Q2 2025 attendance down 1.4M.
  • Concert & Event Promotion: Live Nation $25.2B revenue in 2025 (9% YoY growth) with ticket prices averaging $144 (up 45% since 2019); April 2026 antitrust verdict found monopolistic ticketing practices (86% market share) while iconic venues like Rockwood Music Hall (Nov 2024) and Avant Gardner (bankruptcy) collapse.
  • Movie Theaters: Industry revenue $8.6–8.8B in 2025 but attendance down 34% (780M vs 1.225B in 2019); ticket prices up 5.7% in 2025 offsetting volume loss; AMC closed 200+ theaters, iPic/LOOK/CMX filed Chapter 11, survivors like Cinemark (18.6% EBITDA margin, 2025) thrive on consolidation.
  • US Streaming: 1.1 billion SVOD subscribers now permanent (2x pre-pandemic), forcing theatrical window détente; all major studios committed to 45-day exclusivity or longer (CinemaCon 2026) to protect downstream revenue.
  • Amusement Parks Labor: 35% of operating expenses consumed by labor; wage inflation sticky at 2.9% annually; tariff-driven equipment costs mounting pressure on regional operators with thin margins.

Who rides it

Premium operators and blockbuster experiences are printing money. Disney raised ticket prices to $224 while maintaining traffic through selective discounting. Live Nation's 2025 revenue hit $25.2 billion despite (or because of) $144 average ticket prices and willingness to pay soaring 45% since 2019. Universal's Epic Universe is cannibalizing regional park attendance but succeeding because it is genuinely new—five themed worlds that justify the premium. AMC strengthened cash to $778 million by Q2 2026; Cinemark reported 18.6% EBITDA margins in 2025 after paying down $700 million in COVID debt. The winners are the operators with scale, differentiation, or low leverage to absorb margin compression. They can afford tariffs, labor inflation, and intermittent closure (hurricanes Helene and Milton cost Disney $120 million in October 2024). They can invest in new spectacles. They own the consumer's discretionary moment.

Who's squeezed

Mid-tier and independent operators are being crushed. Cedar Fair-Six Flags, the second-largest regional park operator, carries $5.5 billion in debt and lost 1.4 million visitors in Q2 2025. Regional amusement parks lack the marketing capital or innovation velocity to compete with Disney and Universal. Independent concert venues are disappearing: Rockwood Music Hall closed in November 2024; The Music Hall of Williamsburg faces eviction in 2026; Avant Gardner filed bankruptcy owing $155 million. These venues once built audience loyalty across genres and price points. Now the industry is a two-tier market: stadium-sized blockbusters with dynamic pricing and streaming alternatives. Movie theater chains that were not Cinemark or Regal got eliminated. iPic, LOOK, CMX filed Chapter 11. AMC shuttered 200+ locations. The mid-market theater is now defined by event-driven movies (Inside Out 2, Deadpool & Wolverine) and nothing else. Casual moviegoing is dead. Labor costs (35% of operating expenses) and tariff-driven equipment expenses make it impossible for a mid-tier operator to compete on both experience and price.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that pent-up demand is not sustainable and that price elasticity is finally breaking. Disney's two-price strategy (peak $224 tickets plus deepest discounts in years) is a visible fracture. Concert ticket prices are up 45% since 2019, but 2025 data shows 36% of consumers willing to pay $100–$499 and 17% willing to spend $1,000—this is still early-adopter willingness, not mass-market endurance. If economic conditions soften (recession, job loss, credit card debt burden rising), the premium consumer will retrench, and there will be no mid-tier to catch them. The industry has eliminated the ladder. Labor costs will not deflate, tariffs may persist or climb, and capital-intensive attractions (new themed worlds, state-of-the-art theaters) will only remain economically viable at the largest scales. Climate risk is also invisible: hurricanes Helene and Milton cost Disney $120 million in October 2024. Centralized destination parks (Florida, Orlando) carry concentration risk.

In one sentence

Paying for the experience in a nutshell

Experiential spending splits into premium blockbusters and budget value, squeezing mid-market operators between pent-up demand and sticky costs.

D · Experience & status

Value's Revenge: The Dupe Economy

Cheap copies and private labels destroy the middle tier in beauty and supplements.

The mainstream middle in beauty and health retail is caving. Shoppers are abandoning the middle brands—the $40 serums, the mid-tier vitamins—for either cheap dupes and generics or for luxury. Meanwhile, the entire middle-market infrastructure that sold these goods is collapsing.

What changed

Beauty retail in the US hit $69.3 billion in 2026, but that headline number masks a brutal bifurcation. Ulta Beauty—the category's dominant player—posted $12.4 billion in net sales for fiscal 2025 (ended February 2026), up 9.7% year-over-year with same-store sales climbing 5.4%, because it's successfully climbing upmarket: higher average ticket, new premium store formats, and exclusive luxury brands. But the middle is hollowing out. Glossier closed 75% of its stores. Pat McGrath Labs filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in early 2026 and auctioned off its assets. Flower Beauty (the Drew Barrymore brand) shut down in September 2025. Cover FX and Mally Beauty closed via parent company restructuring in January 2026. These weren't fringe players—they were the $30–$80 premium-adjacent brands that defined the specialty beauty consumer for millennials and Gen Z. What killed them is not that premiumization ate their lunch (it did), but that value ate their breakfast. TikTok Shop—barely a player two years ago—posted $2.49 billion in US beauty GMV in 2025 alone with 123% year-over-year growth, almost entirely from cheap dupes, unknown Asian brands, and bulk discounts. Amazon is forecast to climb from 10% of beauty market share in 2024 to 15% by 2030. Sephora and Ulta's combined share is expected to dip from 20% to 19% in the same window. Gen Z discovers 70% of beauty digitally, and that discovery increasingly happens on TikTok and Instagram where a $3 lip tint that works "just like Charlotte Tilbury" spreads faster than any retailer could ever stock it. The Ulta-Target partnership ended in August 2026, eliminating in-store concessions that had been a key funnel for mainstream middle brands into Target's 1,900 stores.

Health and supplements tell the same story but with tariffs as the accelerant. The market hit $60.7 billion in 2025, growing 3.8% year-over-year—but online supplements grew 11.4% annually while brick-and-mortar stagnated. The Vitamin Shoppe, the category's biggest specialty chain, was acquired by private equity in April 2025 for just $193.5 million after its parent Franchise Group filed for bankruptcy in November 2024. GNC, the other regional titan, is still in bankruptcy proceedings as of 2026, seeking a rescue acquisition from a China-backed buyer. The physical footprint of brick-and-mortar specialty retail is shrinking 15–25% through 2026. Why? Consumers don't differentiate. A vitamin is a vitamin. They buy generic magnesium from Amazon at 40% less than what The Vitamin Shoppe charges, and the supplement works the same. Tariffs imposed in 2025 at 20–34% on imported raw materials (China 34%, Taiwan 32%, India 27%)—ingredients that account for 75–80% of US supplement imports—forced retailers to choose between raising prices to $12 for a basic B-complex or accepting margin compression that was already down to 5.5% in 2022. Meanwhile, upstream consolidation among supplement manufacturers created private-label entrants that bypass specialty retail entirely. Target launched an exclusive personalized vitamin line in 2021–2022. Online D2C brands grew in the fragmented middle while brick-and-mortar chains died. Personalized nutrition formats (gummies, subscription boxes) grew at 15% annually—exactly what specialty stores struggled to stock efficiently. The industry grew $72.9 billion overall in 2025 (+5.5% year-over-year), but that growth went to online channels, D2C brands, and private label. None of it went to the middle.

What made the middle scarce is exactly what made the dupes and generics newly valuable: brand credibility is now fully severed from retail distribution. Ten years ago, you had to walk into Sephora or Ulta to discover a new mid-tier brand. The brand's retail presence was its proof of legitimacy. Now a 19-year-old TikTok creator with 2 million followers can make a lip tint in Shenzhen, ship it directly to a US consumer, and that consumer never touches a specialty retail store. Luxury brands—Chanel, Dior, Tom Ford—can still command the retail floor and the price premium because they're aspirational. But the $50 serums and $25 eyeshadow palettes that used to justify a store visit? Replaced by a $5 Amazon dupe that does 85% of the job. For health, the commodification was even faster. Consumers learn that ascorbic acid is ascorbic acid. A 1,000 mg tablet of magnesium from Nature Made costs $6 at Costco. A specialty retailer's proprietary blend costs $14. The specialty retailer dies. The middle survives only if it differentiates—personalization, format innovation, subscription, expert curation. But that's expensive. Glossier tried curation and directness. It failed because it couldn't compete with price and convenience. The survivors will be Ulta (because it's premiumization + scale + logistics) and Amazon (because it's price + convenience + selection). The middle gets trapped between them.

The evidence

  • Beauty retail: Ulta Beauty's fiscal 2025 net sales reached $12.4 billion (+9.7% YoY), with same-store sales +5.4%, while specialty mid-tier brands (Glossier, Pat McGrath Labs, Flower Beauty) failed or filed bankruptcy (2025-2026).
  • Beauty retail: TikTok Shop captured $2.49 billion in US beauty GMV in 2025 with 123% YoY growth, nearly entirely from cheap dupes and value brands, threatening traditional specialty retail (2025).
  • Health retail: Online supplements grew 11.4% annually while brick-and-mortar stagnated; The Vitamin Shoppe acquired by private equity for $193.5 million in April 2025 after parent bankruptcy; GNC remains in bankruptcy (2025-2026).
  • Health retail: US tariffs imposed 20-34% on supplement raw materials in 2025 (China 34%, Taiwan 32%, India 27%), affecting 75-80% of imported ingredients and forcing margin compression or price hikes (2025).
  • Health retail: Supplement industry grew $72.9 billion in 2025 (+5.5% YoY), but growth concentrated entirely in online channels and D2C brands, not brick-and-mortar specialty stores (2025).

Who rides it

Ulta Beauty, Amazon, and D2C dupe brands win. Ulta wins because it's successfully premiumizing—higher average ticket, exclusive luxury brands, new store formats—while leveraging scale and logistics to compete with Amazon on convenience. Amazon wins because it has infinite selection and unbeatable price on generics and dupes. D2C dupe brands win because they can ship directly to consumers at $3–$5 and compete on social proof (TikTok reviews, creator endorsements) rather than retail shelf space. Private-label supplement makers win because they can bypass specialty retail entirely and sell direct to consumers or through mass market channels like Target and Costco.

Who's squeezed

The middle market gets squeezed from both sides. Glossier, Pat McGrath Labs, Flower Beauty, Cover FX, Mally Beauty, and smaller specialty beauty startups are shut or filed bankruptcy. The Vitamin Shoppe and GNC—the category leaders in health retail—collapsed into private equity and bankruptcy. Smaller multi-brand retailers and specialty store chains lose because they can't compete on price (Amazon) or prestige (luxury brands). Consumers in the middle income band lose too: they came to specialty retail for curation and discovery. Now they're trapped buying generics they don't understand or paying luxury prices they can't afford.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that tariffs and margin compression accelerate store closures faster than Amazon can build logistics to serve smaller cities and towns. If brick-and-mortar specialty retail dies entirely before Amazon builds out last-mile delivery and returns infrastructure to rural and secondary markets, there's a 2–3 year window where entire regions lose access to beauty and health products at any price. Second, regulatory scrutiny on supplement safety and efficacy—especially on imported Chinese ingredients—could create a bifurcated market where cheap dupes face recalls while consumers panic-buy at inflated prices.

E · The big picture

The Hollow Middle

Shoppers are splitting into two tribes—bargain hunters and the wealthy—and everyone selling the undifferentiated stuff in between is getting crushed.

The American retail landscape is splitting in two. On one side, bargain hunters are flooding dollar stores and Walmart looking for survival deals. On the other, the wealthy are still spending on luxury goods and premium experiences. Everyone stuck in the middle—department stores, chain restaurants, mid-tier jewelry shops—is getting squeezed from both directions at once. The math is brutal: if your margin is thin to begin with and your customers are choosing either cheaper or fancier, your business just stops working.

What changed

The middle market collapse happened because three forces hit simultaneously in 2025-2026. First, tariffs exploded. Apparel tariffs jumped from 14.7% in January 2025 to 35.1% by December 2025, forcing retailers to either eat the cost (crushing thin margins) or raise prices (driving price-sensitive shoppers away). Jewelry tariffs on Chinese imports hit 145% by late 2025, adding 18-22% to wholesale costs overnight. These weren't small headwinds—they were margin killers for anyone selling undifferentiated goods where customers compare prices obsessively. Second, gold prices surged approximately 60% annually in 2025, peaking near $4,400 per ounce in October. That simple fact pushed entry-level jewelry from around $99 to the $200-$500 range, cutting off the mass market entirely. Consumers didn't stop buying jewelry—the wealthy bought lab-grown diamonds (now 56.8% of engagement rings) and investment pieces, while everyone else just stopped. The middle customer evaporated.

Third, consumer finances bifurcated. Wage stagnation and persistent inflation created two shopping behaviors: survival shopping at dollar stores and Walmart, or quality shopping for things that last. In May 2026, consumer sentiment hit a record low of 48.2, signaling that middle-income shoppers were actually getting worse off, not better. Dollar stores saw trade-down behavior from middle-income households become structural—87% of Dollar Tree stores sit within five miles of a Walmart, intensifying the cannibalization. Meanwhile, department store margins compressed to 6.0% in 2026 as discounting escalated. Saks Global filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2026 with $3.4 billion in debt, collapsing the luxury tier that had once anchored department stores. Chain restaurants saw 42% of operators become unprofitable in 2025, with labor costs up 39% since pre-pandemic and food costs 34% above pre-pandemic levels. The casual dining segment—full-service restaurants at mid-price points—got hit hardest: TGI Friday's, Red Lobster, On The Border, and Bravo Brio all filed bankruptcy. Fast-casual's premium pricing ($15+ entrees) drove customers down to Chili's and Texas Roadhouse, who competed on sit-down deals at $12. But those deals killed margins too.

The bifurcation created two stable, opposite outcomes. At the low end, dollar stores and discount retailers locked in a resilient customer base making trade-down choices: 5.2% sales growth at Dollar General in Q1 2025, with gross margins actually expanding by 61 basis points from labor and store remodeling investments. Walmart and Costco weaponized their scale to undercut dollar stores while offering fresher food and better quality—they won the value game decisively. At the high end, the wealthy stayed confident spenders, keeping luxury jewelry and premium goods alive, though even luxury had to weather the tariff shock. What broke was the undifferentiated middle: retailers selling ordinary department store apparel at ordinary prices, or chain restaurants serving $15 burgers to price-conscious families. The US department store industry—$227.1 billion in 2026—grew only 0.3% annually through 2026 and actually contracted 0.4% in 2026 alone. Macy's executed a controlled retreat, closing 50 stores by end-2024, 66 in 2025, and 14 more planned for 2026. JCPenney launched a comeback campaign and saw 3% traffic lift in May 2025, but revenue still fell to $6.6 billion for FY2024. Jewelry stores saw the sharpest contraction: 12.1% decline in 2025 and 2.2% in 2026, with 167 US stores closing in Q1 2025 alone (21% increase from Q1 2024).

This isn't a cycle—it's a structural reshuffling. Tariffs punished importers of standard goods (apparel, jewelry) far more than they punished premium or domestic suppliers. Inflation hurt the price-conscious middle more than the wealthy. E-commerce and mobile commerce (over 60% of online jewelry sales) bypassed the middle-tier retail format entirely, moving volume straight to either Amazon and discount marketplaces or to direct-to-consumer luxury brands. The middle market wasn't squeezed by one competitor or one trend. It was squeezed by the fact that the customer it depended on—the middle-income American willing to spend a normal amount on a normal good—is either trading down to free up cash or trading up to buy something worth the price. The margin math no longer works for anyone selling the ordinary stuff in between.

The evidence

  • Department Stores: Saks Global filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2026 carrying $3.4 billion in debt; Macy's closed 150 stores (50 by end-2024, 66 in 2025, 14 more planned for 2026); tariff rates hit 35% on apparel by December 2025.
  • Dollar Stores: 87% of Dollar Tree stores are within five miles of a Walmart; consumer sentiment collapsed to 48.2 in May 2026; Dollar General Q1 2025 saw 5.2% sales growth and +61 basis point margin expansion (2025-2026).
  • Jewelry Retail: Gold prices surged 60% annually in 2025; tariffs on Chinese imports reached 145% by late 2025; Claire's filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in August 2025 (second bankruptcy in seven years) (2025-2026).
  • Chain Restaurants: 42% of operators unprofitable in 2025; minimum wages now $16-20 per hour in major states; TGI Friday's, Red Lobster, On The Border, and Bravo Brio filed bankruptcy in 2024-2025 as full-service casual dining segment collapsed (2024-2025).
  • Consumer Bifurcation: Wealthy remained confident spenders in luxury; middle-income households experiencing wage stagnation and persistent inflation shifted to survival shopping; lab-grown diamonds now 56.8% of engagement ring market as luxury consumers trade up while mass market exits (2025-2026).

Who rides it

Discount retailers and high-end luxury both won. Dollar stores and Walmart captured structural trade-down behavior from middle-income households—Consumer sentiment at record lows meant survival shopping became the norm. Off-price retailers (Nordstrom Rack, outlets) thrived as customers wanted deals. The Nordstrom family launched a $3.8 billion bid to take the company private in late 2025, betting on off-price expansion. At the top, wealthy consumers kept buying premium goods and lab-grown diamonds (56.8% of engagement rings), insulating luxury from the middle market collapse. E-commerce and direct-to-consumer brands bypassed traditional retail formats entirely, capturing 25% of jewelry purchases globally and growing 13% annually.

Who's squeezed

Mid-tier retailers selling undifferentiated goods got destroyed. Department stores with 6.0% margins in 2026 couldn't survive tariff shocks or discounting wars. Chain restaurants with 39% labor cost increases and 34% food inflation couldn't raise prices without losing customers—42% were unprofitable in 2025. Jewelry stores faced the sharpest contraction: 12.1% in 2025, 2.2% in 2026, 167 closures in Q1 2025 alone. Full-service casual dining (TGI Friday's, Red Lobster, Bravo Brio, On The Border) filed bankruptcy because their $15-20 entrees were too expensive for trade-down shoppers and not premium enough to command luxury margins. The middle customer—willing to spend normal money on normal goods—either doesn't exist anymore or is trading to one extreme.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that this bifurcation becomes permanent, not cyclical. If wage stagnation continues and consumer sentiment stays at record lows (48.2 in May 2026), the trade-down behavior locks in structurally. That means middle-income households stay locked into dollar stores and discount retail for survival, unable to graduate back to normal spending. Meanwhile, tariffs on imported goods remain high or ratchet higher, making it impossible for mid-tier retailers to ever rebuild margins through volume or pricing power. The retail labor force—666,500 in department stores alone, declining 2.87% annually—keeps shrinking. If the middle market never heals, we don't just lose retail jobs; we lose the economic engine that once connected small cities and suburbs to national consumer markets. The hollowed-out retail landscape becomes a symptom of a hollowed-out middle class.

A · The trades can't hire

The skilled-trades gap

The aging trades workforce and few new entrants push wages up faster than contractors can pass them on.

Electricians, plumbers, HVAC techs, and roofers can't find enough people to fill the work. The workforce is aging out, trade schools are half-full, and demand keeps climbing. So wages are spiraling—but the contractors taking those jobs can't raise their prices fast enough. The gap between labor costs and what customers will pay is crushing smaller firms.

What changed

The skilled trades faced a historic labor shortage starting in 2025. The US electrician shortage got so acute that Nvidia and Microsoft CEOs called it out as a concrete bottleneck for AI infrastructure expansion. Data center construction became the unexpected growth engine for electricians in 2026, spending reaching $50.7 billion annually (up 28% year-over-year from 2025), but there simply weren't enough hands to do the work. Journeyman electricians started commanding $76K to $110K and higher, with specialized work in solar, EV charging, and data centers pulling premium rates. Yet the 269,000 electrical contractors in the US struggled to pass those wage bumps to customers—most businesses operate on razor-thin 5-6% margins, and even top-quartile shops only hit 10-12%. Meanwhile, tariffs ravaged input costs: copper wiring jumped 18% and electrical panels shot up 22% in 2025-2026, squeezing the very contractors trying to hire.

HVAC contractors hit a different bottleneck. The industry's 590,000 workers faced an EPA mandate (effective January 2026) forcing technicians to retrain on new A2L refrigerants like R-454B and R-32, and installation costs jumped 10% overnight. Wages for qualified techs climbed 8% annually through 2025-2026. Residential HVAC work cratered because mortgage rates stuck near 6%, killing new home construction (single-family starts fell 5% to 909,000 units in 2025), but commercial HVAC exploded due to energy-efficiency mandates and AI-driven building automation. The industry bifurcated—commercial growing 8.27% annually while residential squeezed—but both needed more trained technicians than existed. Private equity saw opportunity and pounced: add-on acquisitions jumped 88% year-over-year through mid-2025, with Apex Service Partners alone rolling up 100+ brands by early 2026. Small independent shops got hollowed out; big platforms with scale could absorb wage inflation, small ones couldn't.

Roofing contractors faced perhaps the bleakest scenario. The $92.5 billion industry (2026) is 80% repair and maintenance work, not new construction. When June 2025 tariffs doubled steel and aluminum duties from 25% to 50%, metal roofing prices shot up 60%, asphalt shingles rose 6-10%, and single-ply membranes climbed 12-18%. General roofing material costs jumped 15-25% in 2026, pushing the national average roof replacement bill over $20,500. Meanwhile, 62% of roofing contractors reported difficulty finding skilled workers, and labor costs jumped 10-30% for most firms in 2025. The construction industry needed 439,000+ new workers in 2026 overall, and roofers were competing for every available hand. Smaller roofing contractors—the bulk of the 109,000-firm market—hit the wall: Ready Roofing filed Chapter 11 in June 2026, Ribbit Roofing in May, Snohomish Roofing in March, and Certified Roofing Solutions in July, all citing margin pressure and tariff impact. Supply chains consolidated hard too: Home Depot acquired SRS Distribution for $18.25 billion in June 2024, and QXO bought Beacon Roofing Supply for ~$11 billion in May 2025, leaving smaller contractors at the mercy of mega-distributors.

The core dynamic is the same across all three trades: wages became scarce (labor supply is fixed and aging; few young people enter the trades), which made experienced workers expensive and valuable (journeymen electricians $76K-$110K+; HVAC techs pulling 8% annual raises). Materials got expensive too (tariffs, supply chain chaos). But the ability to raise prices to customers didn't keep pace. Most contractors operate on 5-7% margins and can't pass through a 15-25% material cost bump or a 10-30% labor cost jump. The customer doesn't pay more; the contractor eats it.

The evidence

  • Electricians: US data center construction spending reached $50.7 billion annually in 2026, up 28% year-over-year, but electrician shortage is acute enough that Nvidia and Microsoft CEOs have publicly cited it as a concrete bottleneck for AI infrastructure expansion (2026).
  • HVAC: Heat pumps outsold central air conditioners and gas furnaces for the first time in 2025, with over 48% of US homes now using electrical heating, driving commercial HVAC growth of 8.27% annually (2025-2026).
  • Roofing: 62% of contractors reported difficulty finding skilled roofers, and the construction industry needs 439,000+ new workers in 2026, with labor costs jumping 10-30% for most roofing firms in 2025 (2025-2026).
  • Tariffs: June 2025 steel and aluminum tariffs doubled from 25% to 50%, causing metal roofing prices to jump 60%, asphalt shingles to rise 6-10%, and single-ply membranes to climb 12-18% (2025-2026).
  • PE Consolidation: Private equity add-on acquisitions in HVAC services jumped 88% year-over-year through mid-2025; Apex Service Partners (Apollo-backed) rolled up 100+ brands by early 2026, while QXO acquired Beacon Roofing Supply for ~$11 billion in May 2025 (2025-2026).

Who rides it

Big platforms with scale—private equity-backed consolidators like Apex Service Partners, QXO, and PE-funded HVAC and roofing roll-ups—win by absorbing wage inflation and supply disruption across hundreds of acquired shops. They can move workers between jobs, negotiate better terms with material suppliers, and spread financial risk. Tech infrastructure companies with deep pockets (Nvidia, Microsoft, AWS) win because they can outbid smaller construction firms for electrician capacity and pay the premium rates. Mega-distributors like Home Depot and the newly consolidated roofing suppliers capture pricing power when contractors have nowhere else to buy. Workers who have specialized skills—particularly in data center, solar, EV charging, and heat pump installation—command premium wages and can pick employers.

Who's squeezed

Small independent contractors get squeezed from both sides. The 269,000 electrical contractors, 120,000 HVAC shops, and 80,000+ roofing firms operating as nonemployers can't raise prices to keep up with wage and material costs. Most operate on 5-6% margins and hit the wall when labor jumps 10-30% and materials jump 15-25%. Residential builders and renovation firms lose because both labor and materials got expensive while customer demand softened (single-family starts down 5% to 909,000 units). Homeowners and small businesses lose because service prices climbed sharply—roof replacement now exceeds $20,500, HVAC retrofits cost 10% more, and electricians command premium rates—while quality dropped as contractors rushed workers and cut corners to survive. Some contractors just gave up: four midsize roofing firms filed Chapter 11 in 2026 alone.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that the labor shortage becomes permanent structural, not cyclical. If fewer young people enter the trades over the next five years, the shortage will only deepen. Wages will keep spiraling, driving more small shops out of business and accelerating PE consolidation. Critical infrastructure—data centers, electrical grids, HVAC systems keeping hospitals and offices running—becomes dependent on a shrinking pool of expensive workers employed by a few mega-platforms. At the same time, tariffs on materials keep rebounding (copper, steel, aluminum stay volatile), and supply chains stay fragmented, so input costs never normalize. Smaller contractors keep going bankrupt, urban and rural areas with thin margins get abandoned by contractors seeking only high-margin work, and the customer pool that can afford the new price floors shrinks. Regulatory mandates (A2L refrigerants, energy efficiency codes, EV charging infrastructure) keep adding retraining costs, but there's no corresponding rise in what customers are willing to pay.

In one sentence

The skilled-trades gap in a nutshell

Aging trades workers and few new entrants made labor scarce and expensive, but contractors can't pass the cost to customers, so smaller firms go bankrupt while big platforms buy up the survivors.

A · The trades can't hire

The People Who Build Things

Construction trades can't fill job openings fast enough, so tariffs and wage spirals are forcing consolidation and automation.

The trades that frame houses, pour concrete, and lay brick face a problem that money alone won't fix: there simply aren't enough workers. Residential construction is weak, but the shortage isn't cyclical—it's structural. Contractors need people faster than they can hire them, wage growth is outpacing pricing power, and tariffs are eroding margins that were already thin. The result is a race to automate or get swallowed.

What changed

The labor shortage in construction has turned into a margin squeeze that rewards scale and punishes small operators. Masonry, the most specialized of the trades, saw revenue shrink 1.6% in 2025 despite a $40 billion market, pinched between residential weakness (6%+ mortgage rates locked out buyers) and tariff shocks on materials—Mexican ceramic masonry jumped to 25% duty, Italian stone hit 10%, and steel tools climbed 50%. Yet masonry employment is creeping up only 2–3% per decade, leaving the trade 20,700 workers short annually just to replace retirees. Carpenters face the same squeeze at a bigger scale: the $63.5 billion carpentry industry shrank in establishment count (down 0.9% annually since 2021) while 65% of builders still can't fill positions. Carpenter wages hit $60,104 in 2026, up from $59,310 in May 2024, but material costs climbed harder—lumber tariffs (10% as of October 2025) stacked on 35% prior Canadian duties, and the 3–4% profit margins already compressed by labor costs are being erased by tariff cascades. Concrete is the clearest winner of the demand reshuffling, reaching $110 billion in 2026 (up from $73.3 billion in 2022) on the back of infrastructure law spending and data center buildout, but even there, margins have compressed 3–5 percentage points in 18 months as ready-mix prices climbed to $179–$195 per yard and 94% of firms report open positions they can't fill.

The tariff shock is accelerating a structural shift. In masonry, robotic bricklayers (capable of placing hundreds of bricks per hour with precision) and prefabricated panels are being tested by larger contractors, though adoption remains capital-intensive and early. In carpentry, modular prefabrication is moving components off-site; on-site work is shifting to finishing, custom details, and site-specific challenges—reducing the demand for general carpenters and raising the bar for those who remain. Concrete contractors are adopting telematics and automation to cope with 94% reporting open craft positions, and consolidation is running hot: Suncrete acquired ready-mix producers in Louisiana (April 2026, $31M+) and Texas (May 2026); Quikrete inherited ready-mix assets from Summit Materials and announced a deal with Martin Marietta for Texas ready-mix and cement assets. In 2025 alone, masonry subcontractor M&A activity jumped 38.6% year-over-year (366 transactions), driven explicitly by labor shortages—larger firms are buying smaller masonry shops to acquire skilled crews faster than recruiting can build them.

The consolidation and automation wave is reshaping who wins and who exits. Large regional and national operators can absorb tariff costs, finance robotic systems, and pass through wage inflation to customers with long-term contracts. Small masonry shops (22,035 establishments declining 0.6% annually) and independent carpentry crews (195,000 establishments down 0.9% annually) face a choice: invest in prefab and automation capital they may not have cash for, accept margin compression, or sell to a roll-up. Residential builders locked in below-4% mortgages (67% of existing homes) have no incentive to move or build new, so the market is bifurcating: new construction (nonresidential, infrastructure, data centers) is where wages and material costs are rising fastest and where consolidated firms can afford to operate; renovation and maintenance of existing stock is where smaller operators cluster and where pricing power is lowest. Geographic arbitrage is also beginning—contractors are relocating to regions where labor markets are looser or where nonresidential work is heavier, abandoning saturated residential markets.

The evidence

  • Masonry (US, 2026): $40 billion market, 0.5% CAGR 2020–2025, 146,100 workers (2024), declining at 0.6% annually in establishment count; 2025 revenue shrank 1.6% amid residential weakness and 25% Mexico-sourced tariff shocks.
  • Carpentry (US, 2026): $63.5 billion market, 0.3% decline in 2026, 923,000 carpenters employed; establishment count down 0.9% annually since 2021 despite 65% of builders unable to fill positions.
  • Concrete (US, 2026): $110.1 billion market, 4.2% CAGR 2021–2026, 285,000+ workers, 90,964 establishments; margins compressed 3–5 points in 18 months as ready-mix costs climbed $179–$195/yard.
  • Tariffs (2025–2026): Mexican ceramic masonry 25%, Italian stone 10%, steel/aluminum 50%, copper 22% YoY increase, Canadian lumber stacked to 45% effective; cement tariffs from Canada/Mexico took effect 2025.
  • M&A (2025–2026): Masonry subcontractor consolidation at 38.6% YoY (366 deals); Suncrete acquired Louisiana and Texas ready-mix; Quikrete inherited and announced major cement/ready-mix deals.

Who rides it

Large regional and national construction firms with the capital to invest in automation (robotic bricklayers, prefab systems, telematics) and the customer base to absorb tariff passthrough. Concrete contractors tied to infrastructure law spending and data center buildout are growing revenue (up to $110 billion) and consolidating market share. Firms that acquire skilled labor via subcontractor M&A are gaining scale faster than they could recruit it. Material suppliers with pricing power (cement, ready-mix, steel) and access to tariff-advantaged supply chains are capturing margin gains that contractors are losing.

Who's squeezed

Small masonry shops (22,035 establishments declining 0.6% annually) and independent carpentry crews (195,000 establishments down 0.9% annually) facing wage inflation and tariff pressures with no scale to pass costs through. Residential builders and contractors locked into low-margin work (renovations, maintenance, infill) in saturated labor markets. Self-employed tradespeople and small crews competing for labor with consolidators who offer steady work and benefits. New entrants to the trades face longer training timelines and lower perceived job security as automation and prefab reduce the demand for generalist carpenter and masonry positions.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The wage-tariff spiral could outpace productivity gains from automation, keeping trades chronically understaffed and expensive. Residential construction at 1.18 million units (May 2026, down 15.4% month-over-month) could collapse further if interest rates don't fall—leaving only nonresidential and infrastructure work, which concentrates demand in regions and sectors where large firms dominate. Automation adoption is still early and capital-intensive; if smaller operators can't finance robotic systems or prefab infrastructure, the fragmentation between large and small grows into permanent structural inequality, leaving thin-margin work for whoever's left and luxury work for whoever pays up.

In one sentence

The people who build things in a nutshell

Construction trades face a structural labor shortage that tariffs and wage inflation are turning into a capital-intensive automation race, winnowing out small operators and consolidating the industry into fewer, larger firms.

A · The trades can't hire

Hands for the Infrastructure Boom

The EPA mandates lead pipe replacement, states spend record billions on transit, and federal infrastructure funds flow—but there are not enough workers to swing the hammers.

The US has $70 billion in water and sewer line work to do. New York just got $68.4 billion for mass transit. Federal infrastructure money is real and ramping. But the workers to build it are not showing up. Labor shortages are now the ceiling on how fast any of this actually happens.

What changed

The EPA's Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (October 2024, effective December 2024) mandates complete replacement of all lead service lines within 10 years—by 2034. That means $423 billion in pipe replacement work nationally, with utilities already facing execution risk. The water and sewer construction sector alone is a $70 billion industry (2026) handling this work, but it is constrained by one thing: there are not enough people to do it. The construction industry is short 306,000 workers as of July 2025. Eighty-eight percent of firms report hiring gaps. Forty-five percent of contractors are already reporting project delays. Wages for skilled trades are rising 8-12% annually just to try to pull workers in, and it is not working.

Federal spending has opened the tap. IIJA disbursements ramped from $1 billion per year in 2022 to a $11 billion peak projection for 2027. New York committed a record $68.4 billion to mass transit in 2025. California announced $2.5 billion in transit and infrastructure spending in July 2026. The Federal BUILD program has awarded over $18 billion across 18 rounds. Heavy engineering construction jumped to $42.5 billion (2026), up from $26 billion in 2021. And yet the sector is shrinking in real terms. Home builders can barely move the needle—$166.2 billion in 2026, essentially flat from 2022, despite $10,900 in tariff-driven cost increases per home that they are absorbing just to stay alive. The money is there. The work is there. The workers are not.

Tariffs are making it worse. Steel tariffs of 50% and aluminum tariffs of 25-30% add direct cost to every project. Water and sewer contractors face tariffs on imported pipe equipment pushing material costs up 5-10% on top of base prices. Home builders report tariff costs of $10,900 per unit, with 60% of builders reporting tariff-driven cost increases (2026). Contractors respond by cutting margins—heavy engineering firms are down to 5-7.5% net margins, flat or falling from 2025, because they cannot pass costs to cash-strapped municipalities and states. Water and sewer construction margins sit at 3.6% (2022 data; 2025-2026 figures not publicly disclosed, suggesting worse outcomes). When you cannot hire and you cannot raise prices, you squeeze margin. And when margins evaporate, smaller players consolidate or exit. M&A among home builders doubled between August 2025 and June 2026—18% of builders now report acquisition approaches, up from 9%. Taylor Morrison, Tri Pointe, United Homes Group, and Holiday Builders all changed hands. Flatiron and Dragados merged to create a $18.5 billion backlog powerhouse. The sector is consolidating into fewer, bigger firms that have capital to swallow tariff shocks and wages, leaving smaller contractors margin-crushed.

Regulatory whiplash is piling on. The EPA finalized lead line replacement mandates in October 2024, but in May 2026 it rolled back Biden-era PFAS 'forever chemicals' regulations—rescinding limits on PFHxS, PFNA, and HFPO-DA—and pushed PFOA/PFOS compliance from 2029 to 2031. That creates short-term cost relief but long-term unpredictability. More immediately, IIJA authorization expires September 30, 2026. The water program faces elimination, and the FY 2026 budget proposal cuts EPA funding by 23% and Drinking Water/Clean Water State Revolving Funds by 31.5%. Award volumes in water infrastructure already fell 53% in the first half of 2025 due to executive orders and regulatory uncertainty. Contractors cannot recruit workers for a boom they are no longer sure is coming.

The evidence

  • Water and sewer construction: $70 billion market (2026) facing 306,000 unfilled jobs and 3.6% margins—federal mandates create demand but labor shortages cap execution.
  • Heavy engineering construction: $42.5 billion (2026), up from $26 billion (2021), but 92% of firms report hiring difficulties and margins squeezed to 5-7.5% by tariffs and wage growth.
  • Home builders: $166.2 billion (2026), flat since 2022, absorbing $10,900 tariff costs per unit while M&A doubles and small firms consolidate; 60% report tariff-driven cost increases.
  • Federal infrastructure spending: $68.4 billion New York MTA capital program (2025), $18+ billion BUILD awards through 2025, but water program authorization expires September 2026 with 23% EPA budget cuts proposed.
  • Tariff impact: Construction goods tariffs at 25-30% effective rate (2026), 50% on steel, with material costs up 5-10% on water/sewer projects and labor wages up 8-12% annually across trades.

Who rides it

Large, well-capitalized construction firms (Flatiron-Dragados with $18.5 billion backlog, MasTec acquiring McKee Utility Contractors for $276 million in March 2026) win because they can absorb tariff shocks, float higher wage bills, and hold shrinking margins until federal spending climaxes. Engineering consultants and automation vendors benefit as firms invest in BIM, AI, and electrified equipment to fill labor gaps—capex-hungry but necessary. Utilities and states that front-load projects before IIJA expires in September 2026 get first access to labor and federal funds.

Who's squeezed

Smaller contractors and regional water/sewer builders get margin-crushed and consolidated. Home builders outside the top tier face the worst: tariff costs of $10,900 per unit that they cannot pass on, 4% annual wage growth for skilled trades they cannot find, and margins collapsing from 6.1% (2022) to 6-8% (2026) while M&A activity doubles. Municipal utilities and states without federal backing face a 10-year mandate (lead line replacement by 2034) but shrinking federal support (31.5% cut to Revolving Funds proposed in FY 2026 budget) and rising contractor costs.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that federal infrastructure authorization expires September 30, 2026—the water program sunsets, and the FY 2026 budget proposal cuts EPA by 23% and Revolving Funds by 31.5%. Contractors and utilities built staffing and pricing assumptions on IIJA lasting longer. If spending collapses, a year or two of hiring will reverse into layoffs, and the mandated lead line replacement work (completing by 2034) will stall. Award volumes already fell 53% in H1 2025. A full cliff in Q4 2026 would strand workers, idle firms, and leave municipalities unable to meet their 10-year compliance window without raising taxes or borrowing at higher yields.

B · Care work runs short

The care-worker crunch

Nurses and home aides are the scarce input in a booming, demographically guaranteed sector—and margins collapse for anyone who can't pay up.

Care work—nursing, home health aides, residential support—is one of the few sectors with ironclad demand. Millions of aging Americans need care, and they'll keep needing it. But the workers who deliver that care have become the binding constraint. Wages have spiked, turnover is catastrophic, and providers face a brutal choice: raise wages and kill margins, or ration care and lose patients.

What changed

The demographic squeeze is forcing care to scale whether the industry is ready or not. US hospitals employ 5.8 million people and served a market worth 1.5 trillion dollars in 2025, but margins have collapsed from 7.6% in 2022 to just 1-2% today because Medicare reimburses at only 82-87 cents per dollar of care. Labor costs alone exploded 42% since 2020, hitting hospitals from both sides: wage bills spiral upward while reimbursement stays flat. The result is a consolidation frenzy—22 M&A deals worth 14.5 billion in Q1 2026 alone, the highest Q1 in five years, as larger systems cannibalize smaller ones for negotiating leverage. Larger chains can spread fixed costs and negotiate drug prices; regional hospitals and independent operators cannot. Bankruptcy filings reached 20 in 2025, up from 15 in 2024. The Steward Health Care bankruptcy in 2025 became the largest hospital-sector collapse in 30 years. Smaller, geographically isolated hospitals die. Large systems survive but with razor margins and constant labor pressure—Kaiser Permanente's 30,000+ worker strike in early 2026 over wages and staffing remains ongoing as of August.

Home care is even more vulnerable because the fragmentation is extreme. The market grew to 191.6 billion dollars in 2026 at a 3.9% growth rate, but 437,000 separate agencies compete in a race to the bottom on reimbursement. Medicare payment cuts have hit home care for four straight years, with a 1.3% aggregate cut in 2026 (220 million dollars) after a proposed 6.4% slash was partly averted. Agencies are closing in rural areas because they can't absorb the hits. But the real killer is staffing. Ninety-five percent of home care agencies report moderate-to-severe staffing shortages, turning away up to 25% of patient requests. Caregiver wages rose from 13.07 dollars per hour in 2014 to 16.77 dollars in 2024, a 28% bump, but turnover stays stuck at 75% annually because the work is brutal and low-pay relative to other healthcare roles. Home health aide positions are projected to grow 17% over the decade 2024-2034, but the supply of workers who'll take the jobs isn't keeping pace. Private equity sees a demographic safe bet and is sweeping up fragmentation: 55 home health and hospice deals in just the first half of 2026, with 41% PE-backed. General Atlantic bought TEAM Services Group for 3 billion dollars in Q2 2026—the largest home care deal on record. PE consolidation creates scale, but even scaled platforms can't escape the wage-turnover-margin squeeze because they're still filling the same shortage of bodies.

Senior residential care is riding the demographic wave but hitting the same labor wall. The market is 110 billion dollars in the non-medical in-home franchise segment alone, and occupancy reached 88.7% in Q3 2025, the 17th consecutive quarterly increase. Growth is accelerating as baby boomers enter their 80s (2027 onwards). But registered nurses, certified nursing assistants, and dining staff report 40% turnover, and over half of home care agencies report ongoing shortages. Wages have climbed 31% cumulatively since 2019, and operators face a binary choice: raise pay and shrink margins, or leave beds empty or understaffed. The industry is responding with historic consolidation: 2025 saw 871 M&A deals, 20.8% above 2024's prior record of 721. Assisted living accounted for 44% of those deals. On an annualized basis, 2026 is surpassing both years. The demand is locked in—73 million baby boomers, aging in place, needing assistance. But the supply of workers is tight, and whoever can consolidate fastest and achieve scale wins negotiating power over suppliers and access to capital for wage investments. The gap between occupancy demand and staffing capacity means winners take the market while losers shut down.

Across all three segments—hospitals, home care, residential senior care—technology is being pressed into service as a partial hedge. Seventy-five percent of health systems deployed at least one AI tool by 2025, mostly for note-taking and image analysis, to reduce administrative burden on nursing staff and squeeze more throughput from the same number of bodies. But IT infrastructure remains a bottleneck, and AI can't replace a human aide turning a patient in bed or monitoring someone's breathing at night. The labor shortage is real and structural. Whoever can pay up and retain staff wins. Whoever can't consolidates or fails.

The evidence

  • Hospitals: Medicare reimbursement at 82-87 cents per dollar, forcing consolidation—22 deals worth 14.5B in Q1 2026 (highest Q1 in 5 years).
  • Home care: 95% of 437,000 agencies report severe staffing shortages; caregiver wages rose to $16.77/hour in 2024, but 75% turnover persists.
  • Home care deals: General Atlantic acquired TEAM Services Group for $3B (Q2 2026), largest home care deal on record; 55 deals in H1 2026 alone, 41% PE-backed.
  • Senior care: 871 M&A deals in 2025 (20.8% above 2024), with assisted living at 44%; occupancy hit 88.7% in Q3 2025 (17th consecutive quarterly rise).
  • Kaiser strike: 30,000+ workers (nurses, service staff, clerical) struck in early 2026 over wages and staffing, ongoing as of August 2026—largest healthcare labor action in years.

Who rides it

Large health systems and private equity consolidators win by achieving scale. Kaiser, Ascension, Humana, and regional roll-ups can negotiate supplier contracts, spread fixed IT costs, and absorb wage pressures while still turning a profit on volume. PE-backed platforms acquire fragmented agencies, integrate technology, and sell scale and operational efficiency. BrightSpring Health Services, General Atlantic's latest deal (TEAM Services for 3 billion), and Kinderhook's 1.1 billion Enhabit acquisition show PE betting on demographic tailwinds as a structural safe play. Consolidated operators can afford to raise wages to retain staff, which smaller competitors cannot. They also get better access to capital for technology investments and real-estate collateral. Hospitals and senior care franchises that can absorb turnover costs and invest in retention programs survive and grow margins as smaller players exit.

Who's squeezed

Independent and regional hospitals, small home care agencies, and mid-market senior care operators get squeezed. A 2025 bankruptcy count of 20 hospitals, up from 15, and closures of rural home care agencies show the carnage. Providers that can't consolidate and can't command premium reimbursement face a brutal margin squeeze: Medicare cuts are mandatory (1.3% in home care, reductions in hospital reimbursement), wages are rising (16.77 per hour in home care in 2024, 31% cumulative growth in senior care since 2019), and they have no leverage to negotiate. Patients in rural areas lose access to care as agencies close. Workers at failing providers get laid off. Patients get rationed—95% of home care agencies are turning away 25% of requests because staffing is impossible. The middle market disappears; you're either big and consolidated or you're bankrupt.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that wage spirals and consolidation outpace demand growth, leaving the system unable to serve the booming number of aging Americans at any price point. Seventy-three million baby boomers are entering retirement, and 711,700 new home care jobs are projected 2022-2032, but the projected supply of workers in healthcare roles is not keeping pace with that demand. If consolidation doesn't produce enough efficiency or technology adoption doesn't reduce labor intensity enough, and if wages continue to spiral, the cost of care could exceed what Medicare, Medicaid, and middle-class families can afford. The government could then impose hard reimbursement caps, crushing providers entirely and causing wholesale care rationing. Alternatively, the shortage could force a cascade of wage theft, undocumented workers, and quality collapse in rural and poor neighborhoods. The demographic demand is guaranteed, but the delivery system's solvency is not.

In one sentence

The care-worker crunch in a nutshell

The care sector is growing fast because 73 million baby boomers need care, but the workers who provide it are scarce, costly, and leaving in droves, forcing providers to choose between losing money and losing staff.

B · Care work runs short

Clinical labor everywhere

Care work runs short

Three healthcare subsectors—mental health clinics, obstetrics, and ambulatory surgery—are all facing the same wall: acute clinician shortages that no wage hike alone can solve. The market is consolidating upward fast, with hospitals and private equity vacuuming up independent practices. But even the big players are getting sandwiched: reimbursement growth is crawling (2.4–3.9% annually) while labor costs are sprinting, margins are compressing, and the shortage just keeps getting worse.

What changed

Mental health clinics have become the clearest window into clinical scarcity. The industry hit $42.0 billion in 2026, growing at 4.8% CAGR from 2021, but the workforce numbers tell the real story: 301,246 employees in 2021 are projected to swell to 365,228+ by 2026—a 21% jump in five years. Yet 43 of 44 US states report active behavioral health workforce shortages right now, and demographers project a deficit of 43,660 to 93,940 adult psychiatrists by 2037. The shortage is so acute that M&A activity exploded: 104 behavioral health deals closed in 2025, up from 73 in 2024, with mental health subsector leading at over 80 transactions. Consolidation is the play for scale—Syra Health and Nora Mental Health announced a partnership in April 2026 explicitly to "expand access," which is code for pooling clinician rosters and leveraging shared infrastructure. Insurance reimbursement is adding pressure: telehealth claim denials jumped 84% from 2024 to 2025, and in May 2025 the Biden administration refused to enforce new parity rules that would have required demonstrated mental health benefit parity in practice. Margins in the sector were already thin at 5.8% in 2021, constrained by wage growth outpacing revenue growth, and they've stayed compressed.

Obstetrics and gynecology reveals a different but equally brutal scarcity: geography and law. The OB-GYN market is a $17.2 billion industry in 2026, growing at only 3.9% that year and a measly 0.4% CAGR over 2021–2026, yet the supply side is cratering. Idaho shed 35% of its OB-GYN workforce between mid-2022 and end-2024. Residency applications to abortion-ban states declined 6.7% in 2024 while applications to abortion-legal states rose 0.4%—a shift that signals long-term supply loss in entire regions. Meanwhile, demand paradoxes are playing out: fertility rates hit an all-time low of 1.6 total births per woman in April 2026, with only 3.6 million births in 2025 (down 1% from 2024). Maternity caseloads are shrinking. Yet OB-GYNs are irreplaceable for contraceptive access, preventive gynecology, and emergency obstetric care, so demand for the service doesn't evaporate—it just shifts. The consolidation response is swift: 47% of physicians are now in hospital employment (2024), and private equity has acquired 65% of physician practices from 2019 to 2023. The American Medical Association retired decades-old bundled billing codes (the maternity bundle) effective January 1, 2027, forcing a shift to individual E/M and procedure codes—a billing restructuring that works better for large, integrated operations than solo or small-group practices.

Ambulatory surgery centers are the third example, and here the labor squeeze is colliding with margin compression and coverage expansion. The ASC market hit $46.5 billion in 2026, with 6.3% CAGR growth, but large consolidated platforms (like USPI) are harvesting 38.6% EBITDA margins while smaller independents are compressed into low-to-mid 30s. Reimbursement growth is a paltry 2.4–2.9% annually, a pace that can't outrun wage inflation and clinical staffing costs. Anesthesia locums use jumped 17% since 2024 and is projected to climb another 5% in 2026—a sign that ASCs can't find permanent anesthesiologists and are renting them at premium rates. Nursing shortages are equally acute as hospitals poach staff. The consolation prize is CMS's 2026 expansion of the ASC Covered Procedures List, which added 560 new procedures including cardiac ablations and lumbar fusion—high-acuity work that sounds lucrative until you realize these procedures carry thinner margins at ASCs than at hospital outpatient departments due to site-of-service payment differentials. Consolidation is the antidote: Ascension's $3.9 billion acquisition of AmSurg in 2024 expanded the health system's footprint from 58 to 300+ ASCs across 34 states, the largest health-system ASC transaction on record. That kind of scale buys you staffing leverage and the ability to absorb margin compression.

The evidence

  • Mental health clinics: 43,660–93,940 psychiatrist shortage projected by 2037 (2025 estimate), with 43 of 44 states reporting active workforce gaps; M&A accelerated to 104 deals in 2025
  • Obstetrics: Idaho shed 35% of OB-GYN workforce in two years (mid-2022 to end-2024); fertility rate hit 1.6 births per woman (April 2026); residency applications to abortion-ban states down 6.7% in 2024
  • Ambulatory Surgery Centers: Anesthesia locums use up 17% since 2024; reimbursement growth only 2.4–2.9% annually (2025–2026) against wage inflation; Ascension's $3.9B AmSurg acquisition (2024) creates 300+ center platform
  • Mental health telehealth: Claim denials jumped 84% from 2024 to 2025, adding to reimbursement pressure despite demand (buprenorphine prescriptions at 15.4 million in 2024)
  • Health system consolidation: 47% of physicians in hospital employment (2024); private equity acquired 65% of physician practices from 2019–2023; large ASC platforms harvest 38.6% EBITDA margins vs. low-to-mid 30s for independents

Who rides it

Big health systems and scaled private equity platforms. Ascension swallowed 300+ surgery centers in a single acquisition. Large ASC platforms lock in 38.6% EBITDA margins by absorbing labor cost inflation across a wide roster of sites. Consolidators can cross-post clinicians between facilities, build shared call infrastructure, and leverage scale to negotiate supply contracts and staffing rates. Mental health M&A frontrunners like Syra and Nora can pool clinical talent and integrate digital tools (Spring Health, Lyra Health) to try to do more with fewer psychiatrists. If you're independent or regional, you either get acquired or watch your margins shrink every quarter as labor costs accelerate and you can't negotiate reimbursement power alone.

Who's squeezed

Independent practices, regional operators, and small health systems. Mental health clinics with 5.8% margins can't absorb simultaneous wage growth and 84% telehealth denial spikes. OB-GYNs in low-supply states (especially abortion-ban states) are watching younger doctors leave and can't compete for hires against hospital-backed consolidators. Smaller ASCs with margins compressed into the low-to-mid 30s can't afford the locums anesthesiologists or premium nursing wages that big platforms can. The CPT billing restructuring effective January 1, 2027 (retirement of the maternity bundle) favors integrated billing systems over solo billers. Solo or small-group practices are being squeezed into acquisition or closure.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

Consolidation doesn't solve the shortage; it just hoards the talent. When you have 43 of 44 states reporting workforce shortages and a 43,000–94,000-person psychiatrist deficit looming by 2037, buying up clinics doesn't create new clinicians. It just moves them into the bidders' portfolios. The second risk: if reimbursement growth (2.4–2.9% ASC, 3.9% OB-GYN, 4.8% mental health) continues to lag wage inflation (historically 3–4%, likely higher in healthcare), even consolidated platforms will face margin compression across the board. The third: insurance is actively fighting back (84% telehealth denial spike, parity rule refusal). If payers tighten reimbursement faster than consolidators can scale, you get a squeeze where labor stays expensive, reimbursement stays stingy, and consolidators can't arbitrage the gap anymore.

In one sentence

Clinical labor everywhere in a nutshell

Psychiatrists, OB-GYNs, and surgical nurses are vanishing faster than hiring can replace them, and whoever operates at scale wins while independent practices and regional clinics get squeezed.

C · Moving things & serving people

The driver shortage

Trucking's driver crisis meets freight cycles—automation doesn't move the needle yet, so wages spiral and carriers bleed out.

Trucking has a problem that no amount of technology has solved: there aren't enough drivers, and there never will be again. The average long-haul driver is 46 years old. The Department of State paused new employment visas for truck drivers in August 2025. Simultaneously, the industry is caught between tariffs that raised truck equipment costs by $10,000 to $35,000 per vehicle and freight demand that barely keeps pace. Carriers are going bankrupt. Rates are finally rising. But the margin squeeze is real.

What changed

The freight trucking market has entered a structural bottleneck, not because there isn't work, but because people won't do it at the wages the industry wants to pay. In 2022, the general freight truckload sector was a $212.2 billion market. By 2026, it had grown to $300.1 billion—a 41% expansion—but the number of carriers actually shrank. Ninety-three thousand trucking companies have exited the market since 2022. Bankruptcies hit a record high in 2025. Yellow Corporation, one of the largest LTL carriers, liquidated in 2024, and regional operators like Daniel Trucking and Davis Express filed Chapter 11 or ceased operations in 2025. Meanwhile, operating costs per mile hit an all-time high of $2.34 in 2025, with fuel alone eating up roughly 21% of total costs, driver wages climbing steadily, and tariffs adding new friction—25% duties on imported heavy trucks started in October 2025.

What got scarce was driver availability, not cargo. The problem isn't a recession in demand; it's an exodus of people willing to drive. Long-distance refrigerated trucking, which serves pharma and food cold chains, has roughly 22,000 to 24,000 drivers with an average age of 57—meaning retirements aren't coming in five years, they're coming now. The US trucking workforce is approximately 1.3 million people, but small carriers can't compete for talent when Walmart, Amazon, and other mega-employers are hiring at $20-plus per hour for warehouse and local delivery jobs with no six-week training requirement and no three weeks away from home. A March 2026 regulation barred asylum seekers and DACA recipients from obtaining commercial driver licenses, cutting off a pipeline that represented one in six truckers. The State Department paused hiring visas the month before, tightening the international supply. The industry's response was predictable: wages began climbing, but only fast enough to stop the bleeding, not fast enough to attract new entrants.

Spot rates climbed because spot rates *had* to climb. By late February 2026, van rates hit $2.41 per mile, up 20% year-over-year. In the reefer market—long-distance refrigerated—rates reached $3.35 per mile in May 2026, up a full dollar from $2.35 a year earlier. These look like victories for carriers, except they aren't. The reason rates rose is that small carriers were forced to exit. The industry didn't add capacity to meet demand; it shed unprofitable capacity and raised prices on the shipping customers who were left. Large carriers—Prime Inc., C.R. England, Schneider National—consolidated. The local trucking segment saw spot linehaul rates jump 23% year-over-year through February 2026, but contract rates only climbed 5%, meaning one-off loads got expensive while regular customers got protected. Tariffs accelerated this consolidation: a 25% duty on Class 8 trucks from Mexico and Canada (raised to 50% on Canadian goods in August 2026) added $10,000 to $35,000 per truck. Forty-seven percent of carriers delayed fleet replacement entirely. Small owner-operators, who make up 88.9% of the 660,000 to 795,000 truckload establishments in the US, couldn't afford new equipment and couldn't afford used equipment either.

What became newly valuable was scale, data, and automation—but slowly. Large brokers reported 30% productivity gains in quoting and load management through AI adoption by 2026, letting them move more shipments with the same headcount. E-commerce parcels hit 22.37 billion in 2024, and every parcel meant local last-mile trucking; that kept smaller carriers alive in their niches, but pricing power remained fragile. The regulatory squeeze on training providers—the FMCSA removed nearly 3,000 training schools from the registry in late 2025 and sent removal notices to 550+ additional CDL schools following 1,400+ onsite investigations in early 2026—meant that the supply of new drivers stopped just as demand for experienced drivers rose. Pharmaceutical cold-chain logistics hit $22.75 billion in 2025, growing at 9.12% annually, and only large carriers with compliance infrastructure and real-time monitoring could capture that margin. The industry needed workers and wasn't getting them. It needed investment and couldn't justify it. It needed automation and got quoting software instead.

The evidence

  • General Freight Trucking: $300.1 billion market in 2026 (up from $212.2 billion in 2021), but 93,000 carriers have exited since 2022, with operating costs at $2.34/mile and spot van rates at $2.41/mile in February 2026 (up 20% YoY).
  • Local Freight Trucking: $92.6 billion in 2026 (0.1% growth, compressed by tariffs and wages), with spot linehaul rates up 23% YoY to $2.01/mile in February 2026; 3,000 CDL training providers removed in late 2025.
  • Long-Distance Refrigerated Trucking: $13.6 billion (2025), growing 5.9% in 2026, but with 22,000–24,000 drivers averaging age 57; reefer rates hit $3.35/mile in May 2026, up $1.00 YoY, and bankruptcies continue (Daniel Trucking July 2025, Davis Express April 2025).
  • Tariff Impact: 25% duty on Class 8 trucks effective October 2025 (50% on Canadian goods August 2026) adds $10,000–$35,000 per vehicle, forcing 47% of carriers to postpone fleet replacement and deepening the margin squeeze.
  • Labor Scarcity: US State Department paused employment visas for truck drivers (August 2025); March 2026 CDL rule barred asylum seekers and DACA recipients, eliminating one in six truckers; average driver age is 46 (long-haul) to 57 (reefer), signaling retirement wave.

Who rides it

Large carriers with scale, compliance infrastructure, and digital logistics platforms win. Prime Inc., C.R. England, Schneider National—the carriers with 1,000-plus trucks—consolidated market share as smaller competitors exited. They can absorb tariff costs, navigate regulation, attract drivers with benefits packages and home-time policies that small fleets can't match, and run AI-powered load management systems that generate 30% productivity gains. Brokers with real-time monitoring and cold-chain expertise capture the high-margin pharma and vaccine lanes (the $22.75 billion segment growing at 9.12% annually). The mega-carriers also benefit from rate firming: spot van rates up 20%, reefer rates up 40% year-over-year. They have the balance sheet to survive a freight recession and the operational heft to thrive in the recovery.

Who's squeezed

Small carriers and owner-operators get crushed. Eighty-eight point nine percent of truckload establishments are nonemployers or micro-fleets, and they operate on less than 1% margins. When tariffs add $10,000 to $35,000 per truck, they can't replace aging equipment. When wages climb and the driver pool shrinks, they can't compete with large carriers for talent. Regional carriers—the mid-tier players who had some profitability—filed bankruptcy at record rates in 2025. Even as spot rates rise, contract rates (which feed the small carriers' bread and butter) only climbed 5% while spot rates jumped 23%, meaning the upside goes to the big players running spot markets, not to the local truckers. A driver shortage doesn't hurt the consolidated carrier; it hurts the small carrier who can't find a driver and can't raise rates enough to pay one.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The industry has no answer for the driver shortage yet. Automation looks good on a PowerPoint (AI in load matching, real-time monitoring, autonomous concepts years away), but it doesn't move the needle on the fundamental problem: there is no pipeline of new drivers entering the market at scale. Ninety-three thousand carriers exited since 2022, but new ones aren't being born to replace them. The FMCSA crackdown on CDL training providers (3,000 removed in late 2025, 550+ additional notices in early 2026) cut off the supply of newly licensed drivers. A March 2026 regulation eliminated asylum seekers and DACA recipients from CDL eligibility, slashing one in six truckers from the legal labor pool. The State Department paused hiring visas a month prior. Meanwhile, the average driver age is 46 (long-haul) to 57 (reefer), and retirement waves are coming this decade. If wages don't rise enough to attract new people, and regulation keeps cutting off labor sources, and automation takes five more years to mature, the industry faces a multi-year capacity crunch where rates keep rising but shipment velocity slows. Customers shift to alternatives (nearshoring, inventory buffers, local warehousing) to avoid the cost and unreliability. The rate spike becomes a demand destroyer.

In one sentence

The driver shortage in a nutshell

Trucking's driver shortage made workers scarce and wages expensive, consolidating market power to large carriers while small fleets bleed out and automation remains theoretical.
