C · Moving things & serving people

Aviation's people problem

Pilots got expensive, caterers got squeezed, and airports can't find the staff to handle record crowds.

Aviation is running full. Passenger load factors hit 84% in 2026—planes so packed there's almost no slack. But the people who move those planes and feed those passengers are scarce, expensive, and in control. Pilots negotiated 30-50% pay raises between 2023 and 2025. Catering workers have been in contract disputes for seven years. And the FAA is 3,000 controllers short of requirement, triggering thousands of flight delays every month. The labor squeeze has hit aviation hard, reshaping margins and consolidation patterns across the whole industry.

What changed

Labor became the single largest operating cost for US airlines. In 2026, labor represents 36.8% of airline operating expenses—a threshold reached after pilot pay surges of 30-50% negotiated between 2023 and 2025. That's not gradual inflation; that's a structural shift. The pilot shortage is real and measurable: a 24,000-pilot shortfall is projected to peak in 2026 from mandatory retirements. Airlines can't fill the gaps with inexperienced pilots—Federal rules require 1,500 flight hours minimum. So the shortage cascades into either canceled flights or higher wages, and higher wages then get passed to fares and absorbed by passengers. Jet fuel spiked 74% year-over-year in May 2026 (hitting $4.51 per gallon), but airlines have learned that they can raise fares when labor costs climb too, because the alternative—cutting flights—destroys revenue faster. The domestic airline market grew 9.7% CAGR from 2021 to 2026 (from $135.2 billion to $268.2 billion), yet net margins are expected to be only 3.9% in 2026. That's the squeeze in a single number: revenue doubled but profit is thin because wages ate the spread.

Ground crews and support staff face similar dynamics at airports. The US airport operations market is $17.9 billion in 2026, recovering to 104% of pre-pandemic passenger volumes by 2024. But airports employ only about 155,000 people to handle that traffic—a number that looks adequate until you ask why it takes five people to check a bag when one person could do it twelve years ago. The answer is the same: wages for skilled ground crews rose, so airports stretched remaining staff thinner or hired lower-wage workers and burned through turnover. The FAA air traffic controller crisis is the most visible scar: only 14,264 controllers on payroll in 2024 when the system needs 17,264. Government shutdowns in late 2025 made it worse—peak delays reached 8,000 flights on a single day. This isn't a temporary glitch; it's a structural bottleneck. Controllers are overworked, retiring fast, and training a new one takes three to four years. No airline can solve that. It's a tax on the whole industry.

Airline catering is the clearest picture of labor and margin collapse. The catering market is $3.9 billion in 2025 with razor-thin margins: 4-5% EBIT, about a quarter of what a healthy industrial company expects. Seven years of labor disputes at major catering firms—LSG Sky Chefs, Gate Gourmet, Flying Food Group—have run wages and tension higher without resolution. In July 2026, hundreds of Flying Food Group workers blocked airport entry at LAX over wage and safety claims. The industry's leverage is flipped upside down: airlines own the customer, so they dictate meal budgets. When fuel prices spike 30.9% in a single month (as happened in March 2026), airlines cut economy meals entirely rather than absorb the cost. Hawaiian Airlines eliminated free meals on all domestic flights except New York in July 2026, offering paid options at $10.99 to $16.99 instead. Caterers have to lay off workers or negotiate down—they can't push back. The only innovation breaking through is AI: Airbus deployed Smart Catering AI on Virgin Atlantic flights in 2025-2026 to track meal waste and optimize menus, which helps caterers defend margins against shrinking meal budgets.

Consolidation is speeding up because only big airlines can survive thin margins and wage pressure. Spirit Airlines, the last true low-cost carrier that could undercut the Big 4, ceased operations in May 2026, eliminating 17,000 jobs. Allegiant Air acquired Sun Country Airlines that same month. JetBlue has explored mergers with Southwest, United, or Alaska to get bigger and handle higher labor costs. The industry is absorbing thousands of employees into fewer, larger carriers. Small and mid-size airlines die. Workers lose individual negotiating power when they're absorbed. But the Big 4 get pricing power and scale to absorb wage inflation—at least for a while, until fuel prices spike again or recession hits and load factors drop below 80%.

The evidence

  • US domestic airlines: $268.2 billion market (2026), 3.9% net margin, labor at 36.8% of OPEX; pilot pay +30-50% (2023-2025) driven by 24,000-pilot shortage
  • US airports: $17.9 billion market (2026), 104% recovery to pre-pandemic passenger volumes, but FAA short 3,000 controllers, triggering 8,000 peak flight delays (late 2025)
  • Airline catering: $3.9 billion market (2025), 4-5% EBIT margin, 7-year labor disputes at major firms; July 2026 worker blockade at LAX over wages and safety
  • Jet fuel shock: 74% YoY cost increase (May 2026, $4.51/gal); airlines cut economy meals, shifting burden to catering workers; Hawaiian Airlines eliminated free meals except NY route (July 2026)
  • Consolidation wave: Spirit Airlines failed May 2026 (17,000 jobs lost); Allegiant acquired Sun Country same month; JetBlue exploring mergers with Southwest/United/Alaska to absorb wage pressure at scale

Who rides it

The big four airlines—United, American, Southwest, Delta—win by consolidating competitors and raising fares when labor costs climb. Load factors at 84% mean they can pass wage inflation to passengers without losing volume. They're exploring mergers to get even bigger, which gives them leverage to negotiate with unions while hedging fuel cost risk across a larger network. Airports in major hubs also win by charging airlines and passengers higher fees for scarce capacity and gates—traffic is booming and slot scarcity is real. Technology vendors like Airbus and gategroup win by selling AI waste-reduction tools to caterers struggling on 4% margins. And anyone already holding pilot licenses wins by having sellers compete for their time: new hires start at $60,000+ and scale to $200,000+ within ten years.

Who's squeezed

Regional and mid-size carriers lose because they can't absorb 30-50% wage increases at scale. Spirit went under; Allegiant swallowed Sun Country. Small airports lose because they can't compete for the hub traffic where margins are fatter. Catering workers lose in a strange way: wages have stalled in disputes for seven years, while the work is harder as meal budgets shrink and efficiency mandates rise (AI tracking waste means less slack). Ground crews and TSA screeners lose because they're often government or contractor workers locked into rigid pay bands while cost-of-living rises. Passengers lose initially because fares climb faster than wages for most workers; over time, fewer people fly and business shrinks. And the FAA loses because Controller pay hasn't kept up with private-sector alternatives—burnout, retirements, and three-to-four-year training cycles mean the shortage is self-reinforcing.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that labor shortages collide with recession before supply catches up. If a recession hits in 2027-2028, airlines cut capacity and lay off thousands of staff just when they finally trained enough pilots to fill the 24,000-pilot gap. Load factors drop, fares fall, and the margin squeeze reverses into a margin collapse—except wages don't fall as fast as revenue. Layoffs follow. The industry entered this squeeze with a 3.9% net margin and no cushion; a 15% recession-driven traffic drop would mean losses across the board. The consolidation into four carriers also means less redundancy in the network: if one of them hits distress (fuel shock, cyberattack on bookings, labor strike), it cascades. And the FAA controller shortage has no quick fix—training capacity is fixed, so even if Congress funded more jobs and raised pay, controllers won't show up in volume until 2029-2030. Delays, operational risk, and safety culture strain will simmer for years.

C · Moving things & serving people

The hospitality wage spiral

Servers and housekeepers got expensive; chains either automate, shrink their crew, or go bankrupt.

Fast food used to run on rock-bottom labor. California's $20 minimum wage for chain restaurants (April 2024) broke that math. Labor costs jumped 25-39% since 2019. Hotels watched housekeeping wages spiral while running skeleton crews with 70-80% annual turnover. The industry is bifurcating: luxury boutiques and extended-stay properties winning; economy chains and casual dining closing or filing Chapter 11.

What changed

For forty years, hospitality's margin came from paying the lowest wage the law allowed. That stopped in 2024. California's Fast Food Accountability and Standards Act mandated $20/hour for chain restaurants with 60+ locations—a number that sent shockwaves across franchised QSR. Other states followed: Washington hit $16.66; Florida is heading to $15 by September 2026. For a fast-food operator, this wasn't a small bump; chains absorbed 25% of operating-cost increases in the first six months, forcing menu prices up 8-12%. The math broke further because traffic didn't hold. Fast-food visits dropped 0.3% in 2025, then accelerated to a 2% decline in Q4 2025 versus Q4 2024. GLP-1 appetite suppressants added a hidden guillotine: households with one member on Ozempic or Wegovy cut restaurant spending by 5.3% on average, and dinner spending at fast food specifically fell 6% among regular users.

Chain restaurants got hit differently but just as hard. Labor costs rose 39% since pre-pandemic 2019. Food inflation (tariffs + avian flu pressuring poultry and beef) sat 34% above pre-pandemic by 2025. When 62% of operators raised menu prices to cover it, 60% reported deteriorated conditions in 2025, and 42% reported unprofitability. The casualty list grew: TGI Fridays and Red Lobster both filed Chapter 11 in 2024 and shut 130+ locations each. FAT Brands (Smokey Bones) filed in January 2026 and closed all remaining locations. On The Border filed in March 2025; Bravo Brio filed again in August 2025 (this was the second bankruptcy for that chain in five years). Full-service casual dining—the $12-$20 entree category—got hollowed out. Interestingly, value-driven casual brands like Chili's and Texas Roadhouse thrive by offering $12 sit-down plates that undercut limited-service chains' $15 entrees, revealing that consumer defection isn't just about price but about *perceived value per dollar spent*.

Hotels faced a labor squeeze with no good exit. Wages rose 25.6% versus 2019 while occupancy and RevPAR barely budged. The industry's answer: skeleton crews with 70-80% annual turnover—which means burned-out staff, empty floors, and guests walking. Luxury boutiques escaped the squeeze: they hit 6% revenue gains in 2025, with average daily rates of $452 and RevPAR of $307 (luxury segment average $263). Extended-stay properties grew 4% in supply in 2025—the biggest increase in four years—because they matched the hybrid-work decade and pulled project-employment demand. Economy properties, conversely, contracted. The industry shifted from building new hotels to conversion projects, which let operators reopen tired properties faster with lower capital spend and, critically, lower staff needs. The shock came from bankruptcies: Revo Hospitality (260 properties, 8,800 employees) filed Chapter 11 in January 2026. Sonder—the AI-powered, Marriott-backed startup that was supposed to be the future—filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in November 2025 after failing to integrate with Marriott's systems post-acquisition (August 2024).

The irony is that automation was supposed to be hospitality's wage escape hatch. Chains invested billions in kiosks, kitchen displays, and reservation systems. Sonder bet that AI housekeeping and checkout would eliminate labor costs entirely. Instead, Sonder's assets got liquidated, and fast-food traffic kept falling. The real winners aren't automating—they're pricing up and filtering down. Luxury hotels raised rates and let price-sensitive guests evaporate. Extended-stay captured hybrid workers who value long-stay discounts over turnover. Value casual dining (Chili's, Texas Roadhouse) won share by offering the perception of better value. The real losers are economy chain restaurants, midscale hotels, and anyone betting that higher prices would stick without losing traffic. In 2026, traffic didn't come back. Wage floors set by law—California's $20, Washington's $16.66, Florida's rising $15—no longer allow for the margin structure that built this industry. Whoever can't automate, can't raise prices, or can't migrate upscale is exiting the game.

The evidence

  • Fast Food (2026): California's $20/hour minimum wage (April 2024) forced menu prices up 8-12% and traffic declined 2% in Q4 2025 versus 2024; GLP-1 adoption cut dinner spending 6% among users.
  • Chain Restaurants (2025): Labor costs rose 39% since 2019; 62% of operators raised prices; 42% unprofitable; TGI Fridays, Red Lobster, On The Border, FAT Brands all filed Chapter 11 in 2024-2026.
  • Hotels (2025): Wages rose 25.6% versus 2019; economy segment contracted while luxury hit 6% revenue gains and extended-stay grew 4% in supply; Sonder filed for liquidation; Revo Hospitality filed Chapter 11 (January 2026).
  • Casual Dining (2025): Value-driven brands (Chili's, Texas Roadhouse) thrive with $12 sit-down entrees; full-service segment hollow; Bravo Brio filed bankruptcy again.
  • Extended-Stay Hotels (2025): Grew 4% in supply—largest increase in four years—by capturing hybrid-work demand at premium occupancy levels.

Who rides it

Luxury hospitality and value positioning won. Boutique luxury hotels achieved 6% revenue growth in 2025 with $452 ADR; extended-stay properties captured hybrid-work patterns and grew 4% in supply. Value casual-dining chains (Chili's, Texas Roadhouse) gained share by offering perceived value—$12 sit-down plates that undercut $15 limited-service entrees. The common thread: they raised prices *and* filtered downward, so only price-insensitive or efficiency-hungry customers stayed. Whoever could reposition upscale or downscale won. Whoever tried to hold the middle lost.

Who's squeezed

Economy chains and midscale properties got squeezed hardest. Full-service casual dining—the $12-$20 entree sweet spot—hollowed out: TGI Fridays, Red Lobster, FAT Brands, On The Border, and Bravo Brio all filed Chapter 11 between 2024 and 2026, closing 130+ locations each. Operators who refused to raise prices or cut service quality just went bankrupt instead. Franchisees in high-wage states—especially California after April 2024—either exited or were forced to cut hours and staff so hard that service collapsed. Economy hotels contracted as extended-stay and luxury grew. Workers in these collapsing formats lost jobs.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that wage floors no longer allow the margin structure that built this industry, and traffic won't return. Fast-food visits fell 2% in Q4 2025; even if wage floors stayed flat, traffic erosion from GLP-1 adoption (5.3% restaurant-spending cuts per household) is structural, not cyclical. Hotels are running skeleton crews with 70-80% turnover—a level that means burned-out staff, guest complaints, and future defection. If more states follow California's $20 model, or if inflation forces further nominal increases, the math breaks for economy and midscale operators all over again. Automation was supposed to save the industry; Sonder's liquidation suggests it doesn't yet. The risk is a long, slow exit of capacity and quality from the budget and middle tiers, leaving only luxury and discount extremes.

D · The responses

Automate or eat the margin

Labor shortages force a brutal choice: invest in robots or watch your profits vanish.

The labor shortage didn't hit all industries the same way. Some found their way out through automation. Others couldn't mechanize their core work and got crushed instead. This is where the labor squeeze reveals its harshest logic: if you can replace workers with machines, you do. If you can't, your margin dies.

What changed

Meat processing in the US tells the story most clearly. The industry is $387.7 billion (2026), with 539,000 workers doing jobs that are physically brutal—evisceration, de-hoofing, cutting—work that nobody wants at any wage. Immigration enforcement tightened the labor supply in 2025-2026 exactly when these plants needed more workers. Rather than fold, the Big Four processors (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef) raced to automate. They invested heavily in cobots and AI vision systems to replace the hardest-to-fill roles. The global automation robot market is projected at $4.5 billion by 2033 (9.2% CAGR), with meat processing as one of the largest adopters. At the same time, their input costs exploded—beef cattle prices averaged $240 per cwt in 2026, up 7% from 2025—so they had no choice but to mechanize or die. Tariffs made it worse. Trump's reciprocal tariffs hit food manufacturing at an effective rate of 17% in early 2025 (10% actual average paid). China locked out US beef in 2025, wiping out 96% of exports (down to 556 metric tons in September 2025 from prior years). Even after the May 2026 trade deal restored some access, US plants initially weren't approved to ship. These processors had to cut costs to survive, and automation was the only lever they had left.

Dairy is the darker version of the same story. The market is $153.0 billion (2026), but milk prices have collapsed. All-milk prices fell to $21.05 per hundredweight in 2025 and are forecast at just $19.25/cwt for 2026. That's deflation in a commodity market with rising production. Farm bankruptcies surged 46% year-over-year in 2025—315 Chapter 12 filings—with another 185 in the top 24 dairy states alone. Wisconsin, the nation's second-largest dairy state, has lost 76% of its herds over recent decades. Consolidation is now structural. But here's where automation hits different: dairy farms need milking labor that can't easily be replaced. Robotic milking covers only 5% of US farms versus 20-25% in Denmark and the Netherlands. Small and mid-size producers can't afford $300K-plus per unit. They've got no escape hatch. The US shed 155,000 ag workers between March and July 2025 alone. Many farms simply went out of business. Tariffs arrived in August 2026—50% duties on certain Canadian dairy imports (whey, powders, casein)—which protected the cheese producers (who still have 24.5% market share) but left commodity milk producers hanging. The big dairy firms like Leprino closed old facilities and consolidated into high-capacity plants in Texas (2025-2026), squeezing margins further. General Mills divested Yoplait for $2.1 billion to Lactalis USA (2025), reshaping competition in dairy segments. Small producers got nothing from these moves.

Vending machine operators are the surprising automators. The industry is only $7.9 billion (2026) and declining—down 1.6% CAGR through 2026, with 14,801 establishments shrinking at 3.8% annually from 2021-2026. But the operators who survived are the ones who invested in smart machines. Cashless payment now commands 58% market share (2025) versus 42% cash, and it raised average transaction value from $1.78 to $2.24. Nearly 6.5 million connected vending machines were deployed globally with AI and IoT monitoring by early 2026, with North America taking 34% of revenue share. Crane NXT launched AI-compatible cashless payment modules in January 2025 that work with 200+ vending models. These data-driven operators use AI for location scouting, dynamic pricing, and predictive inventory. They've cut out the need for human stockers and cash handlers. The top 20 global operators consolidated 40+ regional acquisitions from 2023-2025, with CapEx on connected hardware exceeding $1.4 billion in Europe alone (2024). The operators who went high-tech survived. The ones who didn't got absorbed or died. Micromarkets—unattended self-checkout kiosks—are now generating $20 per month per customer versus just $7 at traditional vending, further crushing traditional operators who couldn't automate fast enough.

The evidence

  • Meat processing: $387.7 billion market (2026) with 539,000 workers; Big Four racing to deploy cobots and AI vision systems to replace evisceration and cutting roles as beef cattle costs hit $240/cwt (up 7% in 2026)
  • Dairy: $153.0 billion market (2026) with milk prices at $21.05/cwt (2025), forecast $19.25/cwt (2026); farm bankruptcies surged 46% in 2025 (315 filings) while robotic milking covers only 5% of farms
  • US agriculture: 155,000 workers shed March-July 2025; immigration enforcement tightened labor supply exactly when meat and dairy needed to fill jobs
  • Vending: $7.9 billion market (2026, declining 1.6% CAGR); cashless AI-enabled machines now 58% market share (up from 42% cash), raising transaction value to $2.24; top 20 operators consolidated 40+ acquisitions 2023-2025
  • Trade: China locked out 96% of US beef exports (Sept 2025, down to 556 mt); Trump reciprocal tariffs hit food manufacturing at effective 17% rate (early 2025); May 2026 deal partially restored access but US plants initially unapproved

Who rides it

Companies that can automate are winning. Meat processors with capital to invest in cobots and AI vision systems replaced workers faster than wages could climb. They squeezed out more output per worker, cut costs when tariffs and input prices spiked, and survived. In vending, the top 20 global operators consolidated 40+ regional players (2023-2025) by investing in connected hardware—nearly 6.5 million AI-enabled machines by early 2026. These operators generate data-driven insights, optimize pricing, and eliminate human stockers. Big dairy firms consolidated too, closing old facilities and opening high-capacity plants, while divesting brands like Yoplait ($2.1 billion to Lactalis) to reshape competition in their favor. Winners are capital-rich, tech-first, and ruthlessly efficient.

Who's squeezed

Small producers and wage workers are getting crushed. In dairy, the 315 farm bankruptcies in 2025 were concentrated among small and mid-size producers who couldn't afford $300K-plus robotic milking units. Wisconsin lost 76% of its dairy herds over decades, and structural consolidation accelerated in 2025-2026. In meat processing, the Big Four's dominance has triggered DOJ investigations; consolidation squeezed the supply chain and left smaller players with nowhere to go. In vending, independent operators who didn't invest in AI-enabled machines got absorbed or died off. The US shed 155,000 ag workers March-July 2025 alone—workers had no say in whether their jobs would be automated or simply vanish.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The moment you can't automate, you're roadkill. Dairy is the canary. Robotic milking could cover 20-25% of farms in Denmark and the Netherlands, but it covers only 5% in the US because capital costs are prohibitive for small farms. Milk prices are in free-fall ($19.25/cwt forecast for 2026), and there's no automation escape hatch. Tariffs on certain Canadian dairy imports (50% duties, effective August 2026) protected some cheese producers but left commodity milk producers defenseless. The same logic applies to any industry where labor is hands-on, site-specific, and hard to mechanize—elder care, construction, hospitality. If you can't automate and labor is scarce, margins compress until you either consolidate or die. The labor squeeze isn't a temporary shock; it's forcing permanent structural change in industries that can adapt and destroying ones that can't.

In one sentence

Automate or eat the margin in a nutshell

Whoever can automate wins; whoever can't eats the margin hit and disappears into consolidation.

D · The responses

Passing the wages on

Service businesses try to pass wage inflation to customers — until price resistance bites and margins collapse.

When labor gets scarce and wages spike, the instinct is simple: charge customers more. Coffee shops, bars, breweries—the whole consumer-service stack tries it. But most don't have the pricing power. Customers walk. Margins vanish. And the places caught in the middle—independent operators, fast-growth concepts, regional players—fold.

What changed

In coffee, the wage squeeze meets commodity inflation head-on and the customer refuses to pay. Arabica prices surged 21% year-over-year in August 2025 and stayed 18.5% higher than a year prior as of April 2026. Tariffs whipped margins twice—10-50% rates hit in spring 2025, got pulled in November, then 10% snapped back on in February 2026. Starbucks, the industry giant, absorbed the hit: North America operating income dropped 41%, from $5.4 billion in fiscal 2024 to $3.2 billion in fiscal 2025. To cover labor costs, they spent $500 million on extra shifts in Q2 2025 just to handle mobile order volumes. The market itself is barely moving—$75.5 billion in 2026, flat at -0.2% growth that year. Three independents couldn't take it: Compass Coffee closed 10 of 30 stores after Chapter 11 in January 2026, then got bought for $2.9 million by Nerò. Red Bay Coffee and The Blend both folded. Meanwhile, the big players got bigger: Keurig Dr Pepper finished an $18 billion acquisition of JDE Peet's in April 2026, creating a $16 billion pure-play coffee company with 50+ brands. The customer shifted too—59% bought via drive-thru in fall 2025, 38% via app. Convenience and automation became the margin escape hatch.\n\nBars faced a different version of the same squeeze. Margins fell from 6.8% of revenue in 2022 to 5.4% in 2026—nearly 20% compression. The industry employed 392,915 workers in 2022 and was projected to grow to 424,379 by 2027, but that's across 70,000 venues with no chain holding more than 5% of the market. A typical nightclub's staff costs $70,416 per month, and bartender turnover runs 50-70% annually, which means constant hiring friction and wage pressure. Imported spirits hit with 15-20% price increases by mid-2026 after tariffs, and domestic spirits felt grain inflation and barrel constraints. Consumers, especially Gen Z, got selective. Gen Z's consumption rate actually rose to 73% in 2025 from 66% in March 2023, but 65% of Gen Zers said they intended to drink less. They drink fewer times per occasion—3.9 drinks instead of 4.4 in 2024—but spend more per drink when they do show up. Cheap volume is dead. The industry bifurcated: upscale experiential venues thrived, private equity started consolidating (Sun Holdings bought Bar Louie in 2025), and everyone else felt the margin squeeze. Themed venues surged 32.9% in 2025, and experiential dining was up 46% year-over-year with 34% more pop-ups and chef experiences. The customer was willing to pay, but only for something memorable.\n\nBreweries got hit worst of all. Production fell 5.1% in 2025 and another 4% in the first half of 2026. The industry had 9,344 breweries by June 2026, down 1.8% year-over-year, with 481 closures in 2025. The 191,000 craft brewery workers in 2025 had already declined 3% from the year prior. Labor costs topped $25 per hour for many, and aluminum cans jumped 15% due to tariff pass-through. Only 54% of surveyed breweries reported growth; 43% reported declines. Three went under: Alamo Beer Company filed Chapter 11 in February 2025, Duck-Rabbit Craft Brewery filed Chapter 7 in April 2025, and Nebraska Brewing Company filed Chapter 11. But the bifurcation was stark: consumers who call themselves craft beer drinkers are drinking more often (85% monthly consumption, up 10 points), and brewery visits rose to 5.5 per year. Market share by volume for craft held at 13.4%. Large producers with automation survived and gained share—Molson Coors' premium light beers added 1.8 percentage points of market share by August 2024, and the Above Premium segment was now 28% of net sales, up from 23% three years earlier. Non-alcoholic beer, the one segment exempt from volume collapse, jumped 111% in volume from 2021 to 2025. The small, independent brewer—caught between wage floors they couldn't automate away and customers who wouldn't pay for commodity beer—had nowhere to hide.

The evidence

  • Coffee & Snack Shops: Starbucks' North America operating income collapsed 41% (FY2025 vs FY2024) amid $500M labor investment to absorb wage costs; three independent chains folded (Compass, Red Bay, The Blend) while Keurig Dr Pepper closed $18B JDE Peet's acquisition in April 2026.
  • Bars & Nightclubs: Margins fell from 6.8% (2022) to 5.4% (2026); Gen Z drinkers moderated volume (-0.5 drinks per occasion) but premiumized spend; tariff-driven spirit prices rose 15-20% by mid-2026; experiential venues +32.9% (2025) while traditional venues struggled.
  • Breweries: Production down 5.1% (2025) and 4% H1-2026; 9,344 breweries operating by June 2026 (down 1.8% YoY); three filings (Alamo, Duck-Rabbit, Nebraska) in 2025; only 54% reported growth versus 43% reporting declines; labor costs exceed $25/hour with 15% tariff-driven packaging cost spikes.

Who rides it

The winners are the ones with scale and automation, or the ones who can charge premium prices to customers with real money. Starbucks survived its margin collapse by automating and investing in labor—mobile ordering captured 38% of sales by fall 2025, and drive-thru took 59%. Keurig Dr Pepper bought JDE Peet's for $18 billion and now controls 50+ brands with $16 billion in sales—consolidation lets them negotiate input costs and absorb labor inflation across a wider revenue base. In bars, upscale experiential venues thrived: themed bars up 32.9% in 2025, experiential dining up 46% year-over-year. Private equity started rolling up: Sun Holdings bought Bar Louie in 2025. In breweries, large producers with automation, like Molson Coors, gained market share—premium light beers added 1.8 percentage points and the Above Premium segment is now 28% of net sales. Non-alcoholic beer, the only segment with true volume growth, jumped 111% from 2021 to 2025 as consumers found an escape route. Whoever could automate away the labor or charge a premium escaped the squeeze.

Who's squeezed

The independents and regionals get squeezed the hardest. Compass Coffee, a fast-growth concept, filed bankruptcy and sold for $2.9 million. Red Bay Coffee and The Blend folded entirely. Alamo Beer Company, Duck-Rabbit Craft Brewery, and Nebraska Brewing Company all filed for bankruptcy in 2025. The craft beer sector lost 481 breweries in 2025 alone, with 191,000 workers, down 3% year-over-year. For smaller operators, the math is brutal: they have to pay $25+ per hour for labor, they can't pass tariff-driven aluminum costs (up 15%) to price-sensitive customers, and they can't afford automation. Margins vanish. Only 54% of surveyed breweries reported growth versus 43% reporting declines. In bars, the fragmentation is so extreme (70,000 venues, no chain over 5% market share) that independent owners face $70,416 per month in staff costs with turnover running 50-70% annually, and tariff-driven spirit prices up 15-20%, with no way to pass it through to younger customers moderating their intake. The customer in every category—coffee, bars, beer—is willing to pay, but only for something automated, scaled, or memorable. Commodity service at old prices is extinct.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is a wage floor that becomes unmovable while automation is still incomplete and consumers refuse to pay. Across all three industries, labor costs have no downward path—bartender turnover at 50-70% annually means turnover costs and wage pressure are persistent, and brewery labor exceeds $25 per hour with no alternative. If tariffs stay elevated (10% reimposed in February 2026 after removal in November 2025), commodity costs don't fall either. The customer will keep bifurcating: premium experiential and automated wins, while mid-market traditional loses. For a mid-sized regional brewery or an independent nightclub or a second-wave coffee shop, there's a long squeeze until either automation scales faster or the labor market loosens. The risk is sustained margin erosion and a wave of bankruptcies among anyone who can't afford to automate or doesn't have access to capital to acquire or rebrand.

E · The big picture

The labor squeeze

Workers got scarce — wages spiral, the trades can't fill the gap, and whoever can automate or pay up wins while everyone else eats the margin hit.

Labor just became the economy's binding constraint. Across electricians, home care, trucking, and fast food—industries that employ millions and touch every home—worker scarcity is forcing a painful choice: automate, consolidate, or die. The numbers are unambiguous: electricians now command $76K–$110K+ for specialized work; home care agencies report 75% annual turnover and can fill only 75% of job openings; trucking's average driver age is 46 with a retirement wave looming; and fast food traffic is collapsing even as chains raise wages to $20/hour in California and still can't find workers. For decades these were low-margin, fragmented industries. Now margin compression, wage pressure, and labor shortages are forcing a reshuffling that will concentrate wealth among scale players who can absorb the hit.

What changed

The electricians trade is being pulled in two directions and it is creating winners and losers fast. Residential construction has cratered because of high interest rates—the market that built the electrician industry—but data centers have become the unexpected growth engine. In April 2026, data center construction spending hit $50.7 billion annually, up 28% year-over-year. Nvidia and Microsoft CEOs have now publicly cited electrician shortages as a bottleneck for AI infrastructure. This demand for specialized labor—data centers, solar, EV charging—has driven wages and created a two-tier market. Journeymen earning $76K–$110K+ are commanding premium rates, especially for specialized work. But tariffs are crushing smaller contractors: copper wiring up 18%, electrical panels up 22%. Small independents cannot absorb that cost and cannot scale fast enough to chase the data center work. Consolidation is accelerating into 2026. The big platforms with capital and geographic reach can service the high-margin data center jobs while smaller shops fight over the shrinking residential market.

Home care is experiencing an even sharper squeeze: Medicare is cutting payments while demand explodes from an aging population. CMS finalized a 1.3% aggregate payment reduction for 2026, capping a four-year streak of cuts. At the same time, 95% of agencies report moderate-to-severe staffing shortages. Caregiver wages rose from $13.07 per hour in 2014 to $16.77 in 2024, but turnover stays at 75% annually because pay is still low relative to other healthcare roles and the work is relentless. The outcome is brutal: agencies are turning away up to 25% of patient requests because they cannot staff them. The market is now reshaping around private equity consolidation. General Atlantic acquired TEAM Services Group for approximately $3 billion in Q2 2026—the largest home care deal on record—and Kinderhook took Enhabit private for $1.1 billion in Q1 2026. These platforms have the capital to invest in technology (cloud EMRs, remote patient monitoring), absorb payment cuts across a broader cost base, and weather the wage pressure. Smaller independent agencies in rural areas are closing as they cannot compete on either dimension: they pay similar wages but cannot achieve the margins or efficiency gains that consolidation brings.

Trucking shows a parallel pattern of margin compression meeting driver scarcity. Operating costs per mile hit an all-time high of $2.34 in 2025. The US State Department paused new employment visas for truck drivers in August 2025, tightening labor supply on top of an aging driver workforce—average age 46, with a retirement wave expected over the coming decade. Small owner-operators and fleets under 1,000 trucks are being squeezed from both sides: rates are too soft to cover costs, and they cannot compete with large carriers on scale or financing. The only profitable segment is LTL (less-than-truckload) and mega-carriers with 1,000+ trucks. Spot van rates hit $2.41 per mile in late February 2026, up 20% year-over-year, signaling selective recovery, but this recovery is concentrated among large carriers that can optimize their network and wait out soft contract rates. A 25% tariff on imported heavy trucks starting October 2025 raised equipment costs, and cross-border freight dropped 5% in mid-2025 (Canada-bound traffic down 14.5%). The bankruptcies are reaching all-time high rates as small carriers exit.

Fast food shows what happens when a fragmented, low-margin industry meets labor scarcity with no room to automate. The market grew just 0.7% in 2026, and traffic is now declining faster. It fell 0.3% in 2025 and accelerated to negative 2% in Q4 2025 versus Q4 2024. The causes are structural: the GLP-1 appetite suppression effect is real (households with a GLP-1 user cut restaurant spending by an average 5.3%), and consumer spending is retracting under higher rates and reduced wage growth. California's $20 per hour minimum wage for fast food workers, effective April 2024, lifted operating costs roughly 25% and forced chains to raise menu prices 8–12%. But raising prices only works until customers stop coming. Tariffs have added another layer: avian flu has pressured poultry supplies, and 15% of US food imports are now tariffed, pushing commodity costs up steadily. Large chains with scale can absorb these hits through automation (kiosks, kitchen robots, delivery optimization) and by raising prices selectively at franchises with captive customer bases. Smaller chains and franchisees are not so lucky. BurgerFi filed Chapter 11 in September 2024, TGI Fridays in November 2024, and Uncle Julio's assets sold in foreclosure auction in December 2024. Each cited the same pressures: labor inflation, traffic loss, and an inability to pass full costs to price-sensitive customers. The survivors will be large platforms that can automate, consolidate, and tolerate lower margins while crushing independents.

The evidence

  • Electricians: Data center construction spending reached $50.7 billion annualized in April 2026, up 28% YoY, pulling specialized labor away from residential work and forcing wage pressure of $76K–$110K+ for journeymen.
  • Home care: CMS implemented a 1.3% aggregate payment cut in 2026 while 95% of agencies report moderate-to-severe staffing shortages; General Atlantic's $3 billion TEAM Services acquisition in Q2 2026 accelerates consolidation.
  • Trucking: Operating costs hit an all-time high of $2.34 per mile in 2025; the US State Department paused employment visas for truck drivers in August 2025, tightening labor supply as the average driver age is 46.
  • Fast food: Traffic declined 2% in Q4 2025 versus Q4 2024; California's $20/hour minimum wage (April 2024) raised operating costs 25%, forcing menu price increases of 8–12% while GLP-1 users cut spending 5.3%.
  • Cross-industry pattern: Tariff-driven material cost inflation (copper +18%, electrical panels +22%, tariffed food imports +15%) is crushing small, fragmented operators who cannot automate, consolidate, or absorb margin compression.

Who rides it

Scale players and consolidators dominate. Large electrical contractors and PE-backed platforms in home care can absorb tariff costs, invest in technology, serve high-margin customers (data centers, enterprise health systems), and tolerate lower margins on commodity work. Mega-carriers in trucking (1,000+ trucks) with optimized networks survive rate compression. Fast food chains with scale can automate (kiosks, kitchen robots) and raise prices selectively. Private equity is the big structural winner—TEAM Services, Enhabit, Kindred Healthcare all consolidating fragmented markets into platforms that can weather wage pressure, payment cuts, and tariff headwinds.

Who's squeezed

Fragmented, small operators get crushed. Independent electricians cannot scale to data center work or absorb tariff inflation. Small home care agencies in rural areas close as they cannot match platform efficiency or wage competitiveness. Owner-operators and fleets under 1,000 trucks are exiting trucking at record bankruptcy rates. Franchisees and smaller fast food chains cannot automate or absorb labor cost inflation—BurgerFi, TGI Fridays, Uncle Julio's all filed bankruptcy or foreclosure in 2024–2025 under these exact pressures.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest tension is whether wage growth and labor scarcity become a wage-price spiral that pushes inflation back up and forces the Fed to re-tighten, or whether automation and margin compression accelerate fast enough to prevent broad-based wage acceleration. Home care is the crux: if caregiver wages must rise further to fill the 25% of unfilled patient requests and retain staff below 75% turnover, that cascades into Medicare payment pressure and insurance costs. Fast food and trucking show the dark side: when wages and automation race, automation wins and workers lose. The risk is that labor scarcity becomes a structural feature—not a cycle—because demographic trends (retirements, low birth rates, immigration restrictions) mean the labor pool is actually shrinking in absolute terms. If that is true, then wage-price dynamics will stay inflated and consolidation will accelerate as the only lever to restore profitability.

The labor squeeze in a nutshell

Labor is now the binding constraint; winners consolidate and automate, losers absorb wage pressure and margin collapse.

A · Food gets squeezed

The Food-Producer Squeeze

Commodity, labor, and energy costs outrun what food makers can charge.

The U.S. food industry is caught in a margin vise. Bread makers, dairy producers, and meat processors face a collision of pressures: input costs are rising, labor is scarce, tariffs just landed, and consumers are shifting away from commodity products. Meanwhile, pricing power is flat. Only the biggest, the most automated, and the premium brands are escaping the squeeze.

What changed

Bread production tells the story most clearly. The U.S. bread market is $58.8 billion (2026) but growing at just 1.1% annually—a mature, flat market. Margins sit at 4.3%, leaving almost no room for cost shocks. Yet every input is moving up: wheat prices rose 11.1% year-over-year in June 2026. At the same time, consumers are leaving behind white bread and processed sandwich loaves, the volume drivers of decades past. Sourdough searches surged 178% in Q2 2025, and 67% of consumers now choose food based on health claims. Gluten-free bakery is forecast to grow 8.89% annually through 2031—reaching $12.99 billion by 2031 from $7.83 billion in 2025—but that's a niche. Automation is arriving fast: food manufacturing robot installations hit 21,000 in 2024, up 42% year-over-year. Bakeries are deploying AI-powered scheduling and robotic palletizing to escape the labor shortage. The winners are consolidators like Grupo Bimbo, which posted record full-year 2025 net sales of 427 billion Mexican pesos ($23.8 billion), up 4.6%, via five acquisitions and disciplined price increases. Flowers Foods holds the U.S. premium segment through Nature's Own and Dave's Killer Bread. The losers are regional commodity players who can't pass costs to customers and can't afford the automation build-out.\n\nDairy is worse. Milk prices have collapsed. All-milk prices fell to $21.05 per hundredweight in 2025 and are forecast at just $19.25 per cwt for 2026—a structural deflationary collapse despite production rising 1.3% in 2026. Farm bankruptcies surged 46% year-over-year in 2025, with 315 Chapter 12 filings and another 185 in the top 24 dairy states. Wisconsin, the nation's second-largest dairy state, has lost 76% of its herds over recent decades. The consolidation is structural now. Labor is the hidden crisis: the U.S. shed 155,000 agricultural workers between March and July 2025, and robotic milking covers only 5% of U.S. farms versus 20–25% in Denmark and the Netherlands. Tariffs landed in August 2026—the Trump administration imposed 50% duties on select Canadian dairy imports (whey, milk powders, casein), though cheese and fluid milk are exempt. Cheese demand is resilient at 24.5% market share, but plant-based alternatives are growing 13.8% annually and now capture 62.8% of the organic segment by 2026. In July 2025, General Mills divested Yoplait yogurt for $2.1 billion, and Lactalis USA acquired the U.S. operations—a sign that traditional players are stepping back from commodity dairy into higher-margin segments.\n\nMeat processing faces the sharpest collision. The industry is $387.7 billion (2026) with margins at 5.1%, healthy by food standards, but the inputs are soaring and labor is collapsing. Beef cattle prices in 2026 are forecast to average $240 per cwt, up 7% from 2025, driven by tight cattle supplies and strong demand. But plants can't fill de-boning, evisceration, and packaging roles at any wage—the work is physically brutal, and immigration enforcement has tightened labor supply. Processors are racing to automate: meat processors are investing heavily in cobots and AI vision systems to replace labor, and the global market for automation robots is projected at $4.5 billion by 2033 (9.2% CAGR). Export markets blew up: China locked out U.S. beef in 2025, wiping out 96% of sales (556 metric tons exported in September 2025, down 96% year-over-year), though a May 2026 trade deal restored some access. Plant-based competition, which was hyped as an existential threat in 2023–2024, has collapsed—it holds just 2–3% of retail share and falling as consumers cited \"lack of naturalness\" and taste issues. But antitrust is the real killer: the Big Four (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef) face DOJ investigations, and price-fixing settlements ran into hundreds of millions in 2025. Tariff chaos followed: Trump reciprocal tariffs in early 2025 created a 17% effective rate on food manufacturing (10% average paid), and China tariffs fell from 172% to 57% on pork after the May 2026 deal—but the damage to market confidence and planning is severe.

The evidence

  • Bread production (U.S.): $58.8B market in 2026, flat growth at 1.1% CAGR, 4.3% margins, disrupted by consumer shift to sourdough (+178% search surge Q2 2025) and automation (21,000 robot installations in 2024, up 42% YoY).
  • Dairy production (U.S.): $153.0B market in 2026, milk prices collapsed to $19.25/cwt forecast for 2026 (down from $21.05/cwt in 2025), farm bankruptcies surged 46% YoY in 2025 (315 Chapter 12 filings).
  • Meat & beef processing (U.S.): $387.7B market in 2026, 5.1% margins, beef cattle prices averaging $240/cwt in 2026 (up 7% from 2025), China lockout wiped out 96% of beef exports in Sept 2025 (556 mt).
  • Labor crisis across food manufacturing: U.S. shed 155,000 ag workers March–July 2025, robotic milking only 5% of U.S. farms vs. 20–25% in Denmark/Netherlands, meat processors investing in cobots and AI vision automation.
  • Tariff shocks landed Aug 2026: 50% duties on Canadian dairy imports (whey, powders, casein), 17% effective tariff rate on food manufacturing early 2025, China tariffs fell 172% to 57% on pork after May 2026 trade deal.

Who rides it

The biggest, most automated, and most premium escape the squeeze. Grupo Bimbo posted record full-year 2025 net sales of 427 billion Mexican pesos ($23.8 billion), up 4.6%, by consolidating via five acquisitions and enforcing price discipline. Flowers Foods holds U.S. premium bread through Nature's Own and Dave's Killer Bread, riding the consumer shift to gluten-free (forecast 8.89% CAGR through 2031) and protein-enriched products. Cheese makers thrive—cheese holds 24.5% of dairy market share and demand is resilient. Meat processors with capital for automation can replace labor and escape the plant-cutting bottleneck. Companies with export access (post-tariff) and antitrust clearance from the DOJ also gain pricing power from consolidation. And direct-to-consumer plays—flash-frozen bread subscriptions at $70–$100 per delivery—capture premium customers willing to pay for convenience and craft.

Who's squeezed

Regional commodity players are squeezed hardest. A small bread maker buying wheat at +11.1% can't raise prices fast enough in a 1.1% growth market. Dairy farms are collapsing: Wisconsin lost 76% of its herds over recent decades, and 2025 bankruptcies jumped 46%. Commodity dairy processors face falling milk prices ($19.25/cwt forecast for 2026) while labor shortages force them to invest in expensive automation they can't yet afford. Meat processors without antitrust exposure and automation capital are caught between soaring cattle prices (+7% in 2026) and chronically unfillable labor roles. Plant-based food companies, which were supposed to disrupt the industry, have collapsed to 2–3% retail share and are retreating. Tariffs also punish processors who depend on Canadian whey, milk powders, and casein inputs at the 50% rate imposed August 2026.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is that food prices don't keep pace with input inflation, leaving consumers with cheaper meals and producers with vanishing profits. Margins in bread (4.3%), dairy (2.8%), and meat (5.1%) are already razor-thin. If wheat, milk, and cattle prices stay elevated while consumer demand stalls in a recession, farm bankruptcies and plant closures will accelerate—consolidation will deepen, regional suppliers will disappear, and pricing power will shift entirely to the Big Four in meat and the handful of giants in dairy and bread. Automation can help long-term, but the upfront capital is brutal for smaller producers, and the payoff takes years. Tariffs add another layer of chaos: the 50% tariff on Canadian dairy imports and the shifting China tariffs create planning paralysis and supply-chain fragmentation. A supply shock—bad harvest, labor unrest, another trade war—could force rapid factory closures and worker layoffs. The food system will consolidate faster, become more brittle, and leave less room for regional producers and local supply chains.

In one sentence

The food-producer squeeze in a nutshell

Labor, wheat, milk, and cattle prices are all up; bread and dairy prices are down or flat—and only the largest, most automated, and most premium food makers can survive the squeeze.

A · Food gets squeezed

The Sweet-Goods Squeeze

Cocoa, sugar, and dairy tariffs crush indulgent-category margins, leaving only premium brands and automation escapes.

The candy, ice cream, and chocolate industries are not dying—they're restructuring around a brutal math. Tariffs jumped costs 30% since late 2024, but consumer willingness to pay rose only 10-20%, compressing margins that were already thin. The industry is splitting into winners (premium, automation, locked-in scale) and losers (middle-market brands with no pricing power).

What changed

Tariffs transformed sweet-goods economics overnight. In April 2025, the U.S. imposed 10% baseline tariffs on all imports, 20% on EU goods, 31% on Swiss chocolate, and 145% on bulk shipments from China. For chocolate makers, cocoa tariffs hit 21% on Ivory Coast imports and 10% on Ghana—the world's top two suppliers. Overnight, a chocolate producer's input costs jumped 30% between December 2024 and September 2025. Consumers did notice and resent it—86% of candy buyers now report seeing price hikes they notice and dislike. But they didn't double their spending; they simply paid 10-20% more for chocolate in 2025 versus 2024, with another 14% year-over-year increase in early 2026. That gap—30% cost inflation against 14-20% price pass-through—is the vise closing on the middle.

The squeeze is most visible in candy and ice cream. The U.S. candy market is $55 billion (2025), projected to grow just 1.4% annually through 2030. Margins in candy production, which sat at 4.5-4.7% in 2022, are now under structural pressure with no recovery in sight. The ice cream sector, worth $20 billion (2026), is growing only 2.66% annually. Both categories saw their tariff bills explode while consumer demand stayed flat. Chocolate fared slightly better—still a $28.9 billion market growing 4.58% through 2031—but only because chocolate is consolidating upmarket. Hershey, the dominant mass-market player with 33.5% share ($11.7 billion revenue 2025), is locked into retail channels where it has no pricing power against Walmart and Amazon. In contrast, single-origin and craft chocolate are accelerating at 10.15% and growing substantially via direct-to-consumer e-commerce (7.12% CAGR). The premium escape hatch is real: craft chocolate earned $842 million by 2032 and captures 40% higher purchase intent from younger consumers who will pay for story and quality.

What did this force make scarce and valuable? Premium positioning and automation. Unilever spun off its ice cream division as The Magnum Ice Cream Company (valued $9.1 billion, traded December 2025) precisely because ice cream is no longer a growth engine for conglomerates—but premium frozen desserts are growing. Plant-based ice cream jumped from $4.25 billion (2025) to $5.15 billion (2026), a 21% CAGR, as consumers trade regular bulk ice cream for higher-margin novelties. Single-serve impulse products now represent 42% of the ice cream market and are thriving. Meanwhile, technology adoption—3D printing, AI-driven coating sensors, IoT real-time monitoring—is accelerating in chocolate to reduce labor and yield variance, but adoption is uneven and expensive. Scale became newly valuable too: Mars spent $35.9 billion acquiring Kellanov (December 2025) to absorb Pringles, Pop-Tarts, and Cheez-It into its portfolio, a consolidation move driven by fear that only the very largest players can weather tariff shocks. Smaller players—like Kate Weiser Chocolate, a 12-year-old Dallas artisan brand—simply closed in April 2025, citing "the economy." What is now scarce: mid-market independence, low-tech profitability, and bulk commodity margins.

What did this force make cheap? Labor in manual confectionery and the ability to import finished goods at will. Tariffs inverted the economics of foreign manufacturing. When 31% tariffs on Swiss chocolate and 145% on Chinese bulk shipments kicked in, it became uneconomical for smaller U.S. brands to import finished products or semi-finished fills. Some producers shifted to lower-cost domestic sourcing or in-house automation to replace hand-packing. But labor itself (wages, benefits, turnover) did not cheapen—only the value of manual work diminished relative to automated alternatives. The industry employed roughly 24,500 in candy, 23,200 in ice cream, and 50,000 in chocolate (2022 baseline), with only 1% annual growth projected. Automation became the cheaper lever, not headcount cuts.

The evidence

  • Candy (2025): U.S. candy market at $55 billion growing only 1.4% annualized through 2030; tariffs and input-cost inflation compressing 4.5-4.7% baseline margins.
  • Ice cream (2026): $20 billion market growing 2.66% annually; plant-based segment exploding at 21% CAGR, while bulk ice cream declines; Americans' ice cream spending surged 26.5% month-over-month in May 2025 (inflation pass-through).
  • Chocolate (2026): $28.9 billion market growing 4.58% through 2031, but bifurcated—mass retail (Hershey 33.5% share) compressed, craft chocolate and single-origin accelerating at 10.15% CAGR, e-commerce at 7.12%.
  • Tariffs (2025-2026): 10% baseline, 20% EU, 31% Switzerland, 145% China; cocoa tariffs 21% Ivory Coast, 10% Ghana; chocolate input costs +30% Dec 2024–Sept 2025; early 2026 pricing +14% YoY against 30% cost inflation.
  • M&A (2025): Mars closed $35.9B Kellanov acquisition (December 2025); Unilever spun off $9.1B Magnum ice cream (December 2025); consolidation driven by tariff shock resilience and scale economics.

Who rides it

Premium, automation, and locked-in scale are escaping the squeeze. Unilever's spinoff of The Magnum Company signals that CPG giants can still profit in ice cream if they own the premium end; plant-based ice cream is the growth lever (21% CAGR), and single-serve impulse products (42% of market) thrive. Craft chocolate at $842 million (2032) captures 40% higher consumer intent and bypasses retail middlemen via direct-to-consumer e-commerce. Mars's $35.9 billion acquisition of Kellanov signals that only the very largest can absorb tariff shocks and restructure; smaller players who invest in automation (3D printing, AI coating sensors, IoT monitoring) are squeezing margin back via yield and labor reduction. Ferrara's launch of freeze-dried SweeTARTS and Lemonheads (August 2025) and M&Ms' POP'd Caramel (early 2026) both exploit a real trend: freeze-dried candy jumped from niche to $1.31 billion globally (2025) and is forecast to grow 12% annually through 2033. Unilever's $1.2 billion acquisition of Grüns functional gummy brand (April 2026) buys positioning in the 47% of regular candy buyers who now seek healthier alternatives—a escape from commodity pricing.

Who's squeezed

Mid-market, import-dependent, and labor-heavy producers are squeezed between tariff costs and consumer price resistance. A brand with no direct-to-consumer presence and retail-only distribution (like mid-size regional candy makers or smaller ice cream producers) faces a brutal choice: absorb the 30% cost shock and collapse margin, or raise prices 14-20% and lose volume as consumers trade down or switch brands. The 760 ice cream establishments in 2022 are consolidating via M&A; smaller players lack the capital to invest in automation or build premium positioning. Kate Weiser Chocolate, a 12-year-old Dallas artisan, simply closed in April 2025, citing "the economy"—but the real story is that without scale or direct-to-consumer reach, tariff shocks are unrecoverable. Hershey, despite its 33.5% market share, is locked into mass retail (Walmart, Target, grocery chains) where Walmart and Amazon dictate margins. Import-dependent producers who relied on finished goods or semi-finished fills from Switzerland (31% tariff) or China (145% tariff) face immediate uneconomical unit economics.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The structural bifurcation of the sweet-goods market into a premium top tier and a low-margin commodity bottom tier could tip into permanent capacity contraction and job losses. If tariffs persist through 2027-2028 and middle-market brands continue to fail, consolidation into 3-5 mega-players (Mars, Mondelēz, Hershey, Nestlé, Ferrero) will accelerate. The U.S. confectionery and ice cream industries employ roughly 100,000 workers combined (candy ~24,500, ice cream ~23,200, chocolate ~50,000 as of 2022), and most of those jobs are in manufacturing and packing. If automation becomes the only lever for profitability and tariffs force further margin compression, the incentive to automate aggressively will outpace new hiring. Second, the rise of health-conscious alternatives (47% of candy buyers now seek healthier options) and plant-based ice cream (21% CAGR) may be cannibalizing the traditional indulgent categories faster than margin compression alone explains. If consumption volume declines on top of margin pressure, even the big players will be restructuring for a permanently smaller market. Third, retaliatory tariffs on U.S. ice cream exports to China (125% tariff in 2026) are already capping export upside and stranding capacity.

In one sentence

The sweet-goods squeeze in a nutshell

Tariffs forced a 30% cost spike in sweet goods that consumers won't fully absorb, so only premium brands, automation, and mega-scale players escape the margin vise—mid-market producers are exiting or consolidating.

By the numbers
30%
Chocolate production costs jumped 30% between December 2024 and September 2025 due to tariff-driven input inflation (2025).
1.4%
U.S. candy market growth rate (annualized through 2030), down from historical ranges, as tariffs and pricing power mismatch constrain volume and margins (2025-2030).
86%
Share of candy consumers who report noticing and resenting price hikes on sweet goods (2025).
14%
Year-over-year price increase on chocolate in early 2026, following 10-20% hikes in 2025—a gap versus 30% cost inflation (2026).
21% CAGR
Growth rate of plant-based ice cream (2025-2026), versus 2.66% for the overall ice cream market; single-serve and premium driving category bifurcation (2026).
4.5-4.7%
Baseline margin in candy production (2022), now under structural pressure with tariff cost inflation exceeding pricing power (2022-2025).
$35.9B
Mars acquisition of Kellanov (Pringles, Pop-Tarts, Cheez-It) finalized December 2025—a consolidation-driven by scale economics and tariff shock resilience (2025).
40%

B · Serving food at a loss-leader price

The restaurant margin trap

Labor, food costs, and tariffs crush restaurant margins while customers stay home or eat cheaply.

Fast food and casual dining used to be a low-margin game: squeeze volume, train cheap, stay open late. That worked when labor was abundant, food prices stayed flat, and customers had spending room. Today, margins have compressed so hard that only the cheapest-to-operate, the most premium, or the locked-in chains escape without bleeding money. Between 42% of operators running unprofitable and bankruptcies hitting even established brands, the restaurant industry is learning the hard way that you can't serve food at a loss-leader price and stay alive when your inputs—labor, beef, coffee, cooking oil—are climbing 30-40% above pre-pandemic levels.

What changed

Fast food is hitting the structural wall. The $424 billion US fast-food market grew just 0.7% in 2026 with traffic declining 2% in Q4 2025, but here's the real problem: labor and commodities are rising far faster than restaurants can raise prices without losing customers. California's $20 fast-food minimum wage (April 2024) lifted operating costs roughly 25%, forcing menu prices up 8–12%. Across the sector, labor costs have jumped 39% since pre-pandemic, and food inflation sits 34% above pre-pandemic levels. Chains tried to offset this by raising average check (up 3.3% year-over-year in 2025) and cutting hours to eliminate overtime. But consumers responded by eating out less: GLP-1 adoption is slashing dinner spending—users cut restaurant spending by an average 5.3%—and traffic is deflating. Even worse, tariffs created a whipsaw on food prices: 15% of US food imports now carry tariffs, pushing beef inventories down (avian flu pressured poultry) and forcing repeated shocks in Q1 2025, then a removal in November 2025, then a 10% reimposition in February 2026 on coffee alone. Operators with 5.1% margins in 2021 have absorbed most of this in profit, unable to pass full costs to price-sensitive consumers without losing what little traffic remains.

Chain restaurants face a darker squeeze. The $231 billion market shrank 1% in 2026, and 42% of operators are unprofitable. Wage floors are $16–$20 per hour in major states (California's FAST Act, Washington at $16.66, Florida heading to $15), and 62% of operators have raised menu prices. Consumer spending is growing only 1.3% in real terms, and 60% of operators report deteriorated business conditions. The paradox is that weakness in fast-casual dining (where $15 entrees are standard) has saved casual dining: Chili's and Texas Roadhouse hold traffic by offering $12 sit-down deals that undercut limited-service prices. But this is a shrinking pie—consumers are defecting to grocery, convenience stores, takeout apps, and home cooking. The bankruptcies tell the story: Red Lobster and TGI Fridays closed 130+ locations in 2024; FAT Brands (Smokey Bones) filed Chapter 11 in January 2026 with all remaining locations closing; On The Border and Bravo Brio filed in 2025 and 2025 respectively. Even Denny's, a 60-year public company, went private in a $620 million all-cash deal (expected Q1 2026) because operational restructuring under public pressure became untenable.

Coffee shops and snack bars face an industry-wide margin squeeze from commodity and tariff shocks they cannot absorb. Arabica prices surged 21% year-over-year in August 2025 and sit 18.5% higher than a year ago (April 2026), far outpacing any menu increase operators dare impose. Tariff volatility—10–50% rates in spring 2025, removal in November, then 10% reimposed in February 2026—creates planning chaos: buyers can't hedge, inventory gets trapped, and prices swing wildly. The $75.5 billion US coffee market barely grew (−0.2% in 2026; 2.5% CAGR 2021–2026), and three prominent independents filed bankruptcy: Compass Coffee closed 10 of 30 stores after Chapter 11 and sold for $2.9 million; Red Bay Coffee and The Blend also collapsed. Starbucks, the sector leader, is the canary in the coal mine: North America operating income fell 41% to $3.2 billion in fiscal 2025 from $5.4 billion in fiscal 2024, forcing a $500 million "Green Apron Service" investment just to staff bottlenecks created by mobile-order volume. Meanwhile, technology is cannibalizing independent shops—59% of US consumers now buy coffee via drive-thru, 38% via app, and mega-consolidation is reshaping the landscape: Keurig Dr Pepper closed its $18 billion acquisition of JDE Peet's in April 2026, creating a global coffee giant with 50+ brands and $16 billion in sales. Independents cannot compete at scale or speed.

The evidence

  • Fast food: $424B market with 0.7% 2026 growth, traffic down 2% in Q4 2025; 224,000 establishments struggling to absorb 25% labor-cost spike from California $20/hr minimum.
  • Chain restaurants: 42% of operators unprofitable in 2025; $231B market shrinking 1%; 60% report deteriorated conditions as 39% wage inflation collides with 1.3% real consumer spending growth.
  • Coffee shops: Arabica prices up 21% YoY (August 2025) and 18.5% above April 2025; $75.5B market flat (−0.2% 2026); three bankruptcy filings (Compass, Red Bay, The Blend) signal margin death for independents.
  • Casual dining: Red Lobster, TGI Fridays closed 130+ locations (2024); FAT Brands (Smokey Bones) filed Chapter 11 (January 2026), all remaining stores closed; On The Border and Bravo Brio filed Chapter 11 in 2025.
  • Starbucks: Operating income fell 41% (fiscal 2025 vs fiscal 2024) to $3.2B; forced $500M labor investment just to handle operational bottlenecks; Keurig-JDE Peet's $18B mega-merger (April 2026) consolidates market power away from small players.

Who rides it

Premium casual and automated QSRs hold pricing power. Chili's and Texas Roadhouse keep traffic by offering $12 sit-down meals that beat limited-service entrees—casual dining's value positioning saved it from fast-casual's death spiral. Mega-chains with scale (Starbucks, McDonald's) can absorb labor costs through technology, app ordering, and purchasing power; smaller chains that went private (Denny's to a $620M buyout, expected Q1 2026) escape public market pressure and can restructure. Consolidators win hardest: Keurig Dr Pepper's $18B JDE Peet's acquisition gives it 50+ brands and $16B annual sales—scale that can hedge tariffs and negotiate labor contracts. Grocery and convenience stores cannibalizes restaurant traffic with cheaper meals and home-delivery apps, and they're winning the time-and-money trade.

Who's squeezed

Independent restaurants, especially full-service casual dining and coffee shops, are getting crushed. Independents can't negotiate tariff hedges or bulk labor contracts; they absorb 21% coffee-price swings, 25% labor-cost jumps, and tariff shocks one quarter at a time. Compass Coffee, Red Bay Coffee, The Blend, and dozens of smaller concepts filed bankruptcy or closed stores outright. Fast-casual, once growth, is hollowed out—caught between $20/hr wage floors and $15 limited-service pricing that leaves no room for rent, food, or profit. GLP-1 adoption, which cuts dinner spending by 5.3% per household, hits volume-dependent operators hardest; they can't raise prices to offset traffic loss without accelerating defection to cheaper channels.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

GLP-1 adoption is a silent erosion of traffic that restaurants can't price their way out of. A 5.3% cut in restaurant spending per GLP-1 household, scaling across millions of users in 2025–2026, is structural demand destruction—not cyclical. If adoption continues, restaurants face a 10–15% traffic cliff by 2027 while labor costs stay sticky (wages don't fall in recessions) and tariff uncertainty persists. Operators have already cut hours, closed locations, and gone private or bankrupt; the next shock—whether tariffs, recession, or faster GLP-1 adoption—will force consolidation or closure across the industry. The margin vise is now a choice between automation (which requires capital independents don't have), going premium (which locks out price-sensitive volume), or going dark.

In one sentence

The restaurant margin trap in a nutshell

Restaurants face a structural margin trap where labor, tariffs, and commodities rise 25–40% faster than pricing power, driving bankruptcies, consolidation, and customer defection to cheaper at-home and convenience channels.

By the numbers

39%
Jump in labor costs since pre-pandemic (2019) across US restaurants by 2025–2026.
$20/hr
California fast-food minimum wage effective April 2024, lifting operating costs ~25% and forcing menu prices up 8–12%.
34%
Food inflation above pre-pandemic levels by 2026, with tariffs affecting 15% of US food imports.
42%
Percentage of US chain restaurant operators unprofitable in 2025, up from stable margins in early 2020s.
5.3%

21%

41%

B · Serving food at a loss-leader price

The drinks squeeze

Tariffs, aluminum, labor, and collapsing demand make beverages impossible to price at the old margins.

A beer costs what it cost three years ago, but the aluminum can is 15 percent more expensive. Workers at breweries and distributors demand $28 to $30 an hour. Consumers drink 20 percent less juice than they did five years ago and are switching to hard seltzers and spirits RTDs instead. The middle cannot raise prices fast enough.

What changed

The drinks industry is experiencing a three-front squeeze that has no easy escape. First, tariffs arrived fast and hit hardest on packaging. In April 2025, a 25 percent tariff on aluminum cans went into effect. Aluminum itself was already up 15 percent year-over-year as of early 2025, so the combined hit pushed packaging costs up double digits overnight. A craft brewery making 20,000 barrels a year cannot absorb a 20 percent jump in can costs and stay profitable at a $6 or $7 retail price. The large breweries—Molson Coors, Anheuser-Busch—have pricing power and scale to negotiate tariff costs or shift to bottled beer (which faces lower tariffs). The 481 craft brewery closures in 2025 and the bankruptcy of names like Duck-Rabbit and Alamo Beer happened because margins went negative, not because their beer was bad.

Second, labor costs are climbing in a shrinking industry. Beer wholesalers saw wage pressure spike 6.4 percent to $28.89 per hour in March 2026, even as total employment ticked down 0.6 percent and volumes fell 5.7 percent in 2025. That is the worst dynamic: fewer workers demanded, but they cost more. Brewery jobs were down 3 percent year-over-year as of 2025, with 191,000 workers left in the craft segment, but wages still climbed because the skilled roles—head brewer, packaging line operator, QA—could not be filled. A 500-barrel-per-month brewery cannot cut a full brewer's shift and still make good beer. It pays the wage or closes.

Third, category collapse is cannibalizing beer's share. Spirits-based RTD cocktails surged 16.4 percent to $3.8 billion in 2025, and they completely bypass traditional beer wholesalers—they go through wine and spirits channels instead. That shift means beer volumes fall at the wholesaler level even if production is stable, so fixed costs (dispatch, warehouse, cold-chain) get spread over fewer cases per route. The wholesaler's margin, already thin at 4.8 to 5.0 percent of revenue in 2026, gets thinner still. Juice faces a different kind of demand cliff. Americans cut juice consumption by 20 percent from 2019 to 2024, viewing it as just another sugary drink despite being 100 percent fruit. The FDA's August 2025 proposal to lower the orange juice sugar standard from 10.5 percent to 10 percent Brix—the first standard cut since 1963—signaled regulatory surrender on traditional juice. Orange juice fell from 67 percent of juice beverage share in 2022 to 62 percent in 2024. The only juice segment growing is cold-pressed and premium, expanding at 8 percent annually as health-conscious consumers pay more for minimal processing. The mass market juice maker watching their 11 percent EBIT margin compress cannot compete there.

The evidence

  • Breweries: 481 closures in 2025; Duck-Rabbit Craft Brewery liquidated (Chapter 7) and Alamo Beer Company filed Chapter 11 (February–April 2025) as aluminum tariffs and margin compression accelerated.
  • Beer wholesaling: Wage pressure spiked 6.4% to $28.89/hour in March 2026 while beer volumes fell 5.7% in 2025 and RTDs surged 16.4% to $3.8 billion, fragmenting the three-tier distribution model.
  • Juice production: Americans cut juice consumption 20% from 2019 to 2024, and FDA proposed lowering orange juice sugar standard from 10.5% to 10% Brix in August 2025—first cut since 1963.
  • Aluminum: Up 15% year-over-year with an additional 25% tariff on cans (April 2025) and 25% on aluminum imports, pushing packaging costs up double digits for mid-sized makers.
  • Consolidation: 46 M&A deals across beverage alcohol in 2026 (YTD) vs. 26 in 2025; large players like Molson Coors gain premium segment share while mid-sized independents close or pivot to premium/experiential models.

Who rides it

Large breweries with scale and automation—Molson Coors, Anheuser-Busch—can negotiate tariff costs, shift to bottled imports (which face lower tariffs), and raise prices in the premium segment (Above Premium now 28 percent of Molson Coors net sales, up from 23 percent three years prior). Consolidators and private equity buying distressed regional breweries also win because they can integrate packaging, cut labor overhead, and repricing the brands. Coffee and premium beverage makers win by pivoting away from traditional juice and RTDs—Keurig Dr Pepper's $4 billion acquisition of JDE Peet's (closing expected Q2 2026) signals the exit from margin-squeezed juice into higher-margin coffee and specialty beverages.

Who's squeezed

Mid-sized regional breweries, craft independents, and traditional juice makers get squeezed from both ends. Craft breweries fell 4 percent in production in H1 2026, with 9,344 operating breweries down 1.8 percent year-over-year. The 481 closures in 2025 are happening at this tier because they lack scale to absorb tariffs, cannot negotiate on cans or aluminum, and face an increasingly automated supply chain they cannot match. Juice makers face structural demand collapse as consumers view juice as unhealthy (20 percent consumption drop since 2019) and regulatory pressure (FDA sugar standards) makes the mass-market business unprofitable. Beer wholesalers are trapped: volumes shrink, labor costs climb, and RTD growth bypasses them entirely.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that tariff policies become permanent before the supply chain diversifies. Mexican beer and juice are highly tariffed, but 61.5 percent of beer trade is bottled or draft, which faces lower tariffs—so large players will shift format and leave canned craft beer to absorb the 25 percent cost alone. If tariffs stay and aluminum stays high, the US craft beer industry could shrink from 9,344 to under 8,000 breweries within two years, consolidating production into 15 to 20 national brands. Smaller makers cannot compete at any scale, and the experiential model (taproom-first, food programs) only works in high-rent urban and resort markets, not in regional towns where 70 percent of small breweries operate.

In one sentence

The drinks squeeze in a nutshell

In 2025-2026, input costs on labor and tariffed packaging rose too fast for beer, juice, and soda makers to raise prices, so margins vanished and hundreds of mid-sized players closed.
