C · The payers hold the power

Who Holds the Purse

Insurers are regaining pricing power through premiums and audits, while Medicare Advantage collapses and squeezed providers have nowhere to go.

The insurers hold the purse in American healthcare. They decide how much to charge, what to cover, and how much to pay doctors and hospitals. In 2025-2026, they're pulling the purse tighter than it's been in 15 years—raising premiums aggressively, auditing providers, and exiting markets that don't make money. But the higher they raise premiums, the less room they have to negotiate, and the more providers fight back.

What changed

The big shift is this: for years, health insurers had thin margins and rising medical costs. Employers and patients paid more every year, but doctors and hospitals kept demanding higher fees. Starting in 2023-2024, that broke. Medical cost inflation squeezed insurer margins so hard that in 2025-2026, they stopped negotiating and started dictating. Employer-sponsored premiums rose 9% for 2026—the highest jump in 15 years. ACA marketplace premiums jumped 18%, with benchmark plans jumping 26%. Most dramatically, enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025, meaning unsubsidized individual premiums flipped from $888 to $1,904 annually—more than double overnight. That's not a gradual pinch; that's a market shock. But here's the rub: premiums rose while actual medical costs rose faster. Earned premiums grew 14.3% in 2025, but incurred claims grew 15.5%—insurers are losing money on individual policies even after those steep hikes.

Medicare Advantage is the canary in the coal mine. MA is supposed to be the profit engine—insurers get a capitated per-member fee and pocket the savings if they keep people healthy. Except they can't. In 2025, for the first time in two decades, MA enrollment fell. CMS expected it to drop from 35 million in 2024 to 34 million in 2025, and 2.9 million seniors were forced to switch plans because insurers simply exited unprofitable markets. Meanwhile, the costs were killing them. In 2023, 17% of MA contracts ran above 100% medical loss ratio (MLR), meaning insurers paid out more in claims than they collected in premiums. Another third sit in the 90-95% range with no cushion at all. GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic became surprise costs that no pricing model anticipated. So CMS, facing MA's collapse and its own budget pressure, launched aggressive audits starting May 2025, targeting "upcoding"—where providers report patients as sicker than they are to justify higher risk-adjusted payments. For the first time, CMS is auditing at scale and fast-tracking cases. The threat of clawbacks forces MA plans to tighten networks, cut benefits, and demand deeper discounts from providers.

This is what payer power looks like in practice. Dental insurance shows the same pattern at smaller scale. Plan maximums haven't budged since the 1980s—still $1,000 to $1,500 annually—meaning they're worth 1/17th their 1975 purchasing power. Dentists refuse to take those networks at those reimbursement rates. Network participation collapsed to just 32% by 2024 in major PPO networks. Insurers can't deliver the care their customers paid for. So they're raising premiums and shrinking benefits. Seventeen states passed dental insurance reform laws in 2025, and 30+ more followed in 2026, mandating minimum dental loss ratios, human review of AI claim denials, and bans on retroactive coverage denials. The insurers have less room to maneuver every month.

What makes scarcest right now is provider capacity at any price. Medicaid enrollment is shrinking for the first time since COVID—down 7.6% in 2025 due to new work and reporting requirements. Employers are defecting from group dental, down 2.3% in 2024-2025. And the unsubsidized individual market is about to crater when subsidies expire. Insurers need to raise premiums to cover rising medical costs, but raising premiums drives people out of insurance altogether, especially in the individual market. Volume is collapsing just as costs rise. Tariffs from the Trump administration added 2-3.6% to premium bills across device and supply costs, making it worse. Meanwhile, new entrants like Amazon—now offering GLP-1 drugs at $25/month through One Medical and same-day pharmacy delivery in 3,000 cities by mid-2026—are siphoning the most profitable segments. TrumpRx.gov, launched in February 2026 with GoodRx integration, lets patients buy drugs at manufacturer-discounted cash prices without insurance altogether. Insurers are losing pricing power over drugs even as they're trying to exercise it over providers.

The evidence

  • Health Insurance Market: US health insurance market hit $1.6 trillion in 2026 with 3.9% CAGR growth 2021-2026; margins recovered to 8.30% in 2022 baseline but came under severe pressure 2024-2025, rebounding via rate increases in 2025-2026.
  • Medicare Advantage: HMO provider market reached $359.2 billion in 2026 with 2.4% YoY growth, but profitability collapsed to 3-5% target margins, compressed from historical 4.4%, with 35 million members shrinking and 2.9 million forced exits in 2025.
  • Medicaid Enrollment: Medicaid enrollment shrank 7.6% in 2025 and is expected to grow only 0.2% in 2026 after new work and reporting requirements in the 2025 reconciliation bill, marking the first contraction since COVID.
  • Dental Insurance: Dental insurance market reached $99.9 billion in 2026 with 2.62% CAGR 2026-2035, but enrollment declined 2.3% in 2025 vs 2024 amid network collapse and 37+ state regulatory reforms passed in 2025 alone.
  • Amazon GLP-1 Platform: Amazon launched GLP-1 management program through One Medical in April 2026 offering drugs at $25/month with same-day delivery in 3,000 cities, expanding to 4,500 by year-end, bypassing traditional insurer intermediaries.

Who rides it

Large insurers like UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Cigna, and Aetna are taking back pricing power in 2025-2026 through premium hikes and aggressive cost management, especially in employer-sponsored plans where they can force employers to absorb increases. Dental service organizations (DSOs) are consolidating practices faster than ever (16.1% by 2024, up from 7.2% in 2015), concentrating supply-side bargaining power and reducing insurers' leverage—when one practice is worth negotiating with, insurers have to negotiate. Patients on employer plans with subsidies win by locking in coverage before unsubsidized premiums double. And new entrants like Amazon, bypassing insurance entirely with cash prices, are winning the marginal customer who can't afford premiums.

Who's squeezed

Providers lose hardest. Doctors and hospitals see MA network exits force them to renegotiate at lower rates or lose entire patient populations. Dentists watch network participation collapse as insurers refuse to pay, then get accused of leaving networks when they exit. Solo practices and small group practices can't absorb margin compression and are consolidating into DSOs or going cash-only. Patients in the individual ACA market lose access when subsidies expire—enrollment will crater when unsubsidized premiums double. Regional MA plans like Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare ceased all operations except MA by January 2026, abandoning hundreds of thousands of Medicaid and ACA enrollees. Medicaid beneficiaries lose most acutely: enrollment is shrinking for the first time since COVID, and states are cutting faster than CMS anticipated.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is that insurers can't actually keep raising premiums without destroying their own customer base. The individual market is one shock away from death spiral. When unsubsidized premiums double from $888 to $1,904 in 2026, enrollment will crater. Younger, healthier people will drop out, leaving only sick and older people in the pool. Claims per member will spike. Insurers will raise premiums again. More people drop out. Each cycle narrows the pool until the market doesn't exist. That's not speculation—it happened in the pre-ACA individual market in the 2000s. Meanwhile, the payer power itself is being undermined. CMS audits for upcoding and tariffs from the Trump administration are raising costs faster than premiums can follow. GLP-1 drugs cost more than anyone modeled. New entrants are siphoning profitable segments. And providers, especially consolidated DSOs and large hospital systems, are pushing back harder—consolidation means fewer players to negotiate with, and they can say no.

In one sentence

Who holds the purse in a nutshell

Insurers regained pricing power by raising premiums sharply in 2025-2026, but medical costs are rising faster, enrollment is collapsing, and new entrants are bypassing them entirely.

C · The payers hold the power

The independent-practice exodus

Solo dentists and mental health clinics sell to networks and PE to escape the pricing squeeze.

Reimbursement stagnation is forcing independent practitioners out. Dental practices that once thrived solo are now selling to DSO networks at record pace. Mental health clinics are consolidating just as fast, chasing economies of scale and digital scale that independents can't afford. The math is simple: margins compress, costs rise, and only large platforms can negotiate with payers and absorb the hit.

What changed

The pricing squeeze is real and measurable. In dentistry, nearly 60% of independent practitioners report that reimbursement rates have stagnated since 2021, and another 25% say rates have actually fallen. Yet patient demand is climbing—one in five Americans will be 65 or older by 2030, driving volume up. But volume doesn't matter if the price per visit keeps dropping. Dental practice margins fell from 15.3% in 2022 to 15–16% in 2026 as costs pressured profits despite higher throughput. The result is a stampede into DSO (Dental Service Organization) networks. In 2024, about 16% of dentists were DSO-affiliated. By 2026, that number nearly tripled to 39% of practices. In the first half of 2026 alone, 175-plus dental practice locations sold to DSOs and other buyers. New graduates are especially vulnerable: average dental school debt hit $297,800 in 2025, making the solo practice path financially treacherous when reimbursement is flat.

Mental health clinics face a parallel but slightly different squeeze. The market is growing at 4.8% year-over-year, and demand is real—buprenorphine prescriptions nearly tripled to 15.4 million in 2024, and overdose deaths fell from 110,000 in 2023 to about 75,000 in 2024. But reimbursement is tightening. Telehealth claim denials jumped 84% from 2024 to 2025, squeezing the revenue margin for clinics that depend on remote visits. Wages for psychiatrists and counselors are rising faster than revenue can keep up. A 2021 baseline margin of 5.8% is being compressed by wage inflation, and there's a projected shortage of 43,660 to 93,940 adult psychiatrists by 2037. The M&A boom accelerated to 104 behavioral health deals in 2025 (up from 73 in 2024), with mental health subsector accounting for over 80 of those transactions. Solo and small clinics are selling out because they can't compete on scale, technology, or digital reach.

What makes this collapse distinct from typical consolidation is that reimbursement doesn't improve much for the buyers either—they're not conquering the payers, they're just surviving better by cutting overhead, spreading fixed costs across more locations, and building the digital infrastructure payers now demand. A DSO can negotiate slightly more aggressively than a solo practice with 10 chairs, but not enough to reverse the trend. The exodus is driven by desperation, not ambition. The consolidators (PE-backed DSO platforms like Smile Doctors, which acquired myOrthos with 70-plus orthodontic practices across 13 states in 2025) and health systems don't win on price—they win on survival. They absorb the 5.8% margins in mental health and the 15–16% margins in dentistry, cross-subsidize with adjacent services, and outlast the independents.

Graduate debt policy is accelerating the shift. In July 2026, federal Grad PLUS student loans were eliminated for new dental students, and new income-driven repayment plans shifted to 1–10% income-based calculations. This reshapes the calculus: a dentist with $298,000 in debt can repay faster working inside a DSO with a guaranteed salary than betting everything on a solo practice in a reimbursement-flat market. The independence that defined the profession is now a liability, not an asset.

The evidence

  • Dentistry: DSO affiliation jumped from 16.1% in 2024 to 39% of practices by 2026, with 175+ practice locations sold in H1 2026 and average new graduate debt at $297,800 in 2025
  • Dental reimbursement: 60% of practitioners report rates stagnant since 2021, 25% report declines, only 7% received increases, compressing margins despite 1.9% market growth in 2026
  • Behavioral health: 104 M&A deals in 2025 (up from 73 in 2024), with mental health leading at 80+ transactions; market at $42 billion in 2026 growing 4.8% CAGR
  • Mental health reimbursement: Telehealth claim denials rose 84% from 2024 to 2025; margins constrained at 5.8% (2021) by wage inflation outpacing revenue growth
  • Behavioral health workforce: 43 of 44 US states report active psychiatrist and counselor shortages; projected deficit of 43,660 to 93,940 adult psychiatrists by 2037

Who rides it

DSO platforms and PE-backed consolidators. They don't win on negotiating better reimbursement rates—payers still have all the power. They win by spreading fixed costs across dozens of practices, reducing overhead per chair, and building the digital infrastructure (AI imaging, teledentistry, practice management software) that payers now expect. Smile Doctors acquired 70-plus orthodontic practices in 2025; health systems acquire mental health clinics in bulk. They also win on talent acquisition—a dentist fresh out of school with $298,000 in debt can take a guaranteed $200,000+ salary from a DSO, versus the 3-5 year grind of building a solo practice. The system survives by consolidating, not by fighting back against payers.

Who's squeezed

Independent practitioners and small practices. Solo dentists and solo mental health clinics are disappearing. Dental margins fell from 15.3% in 2022 to 15–16% in 2026. Mental health margins stay trapped at 5.8% or worse because wages rise faster than revenue. Staffing shortages—62% of dentists cite hiring as their top concern, and psychiatrist shortages project to 43,000–94,000 by 2037—make it harder for small practices to scale. New graduates are especially squeezed: they inherit $298,000 in debt and face stagnant reimbursement and workforce shortages. The independence that once defined these professions becomes a competitive disadvantage.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The consolidation doesn't solve the underlying problem—it just postpones it. DSOs and health systems are absorbing razor-thin margins and betting on volume and adjacency revenue to survive. Dental margins at 15–16% and mental health margins at 5.8% leave no room for error. If payer reimbursement tightens further (as it historically does during government budget constraints) or if wage inflation accelerates faster than productivity, even the big platforms will struggle. The other risk is that consolidation into 3–4 mega-platforms per region gives those platforms temporary negotiating power, which payers then crush with reference pricing or capitated contracts. The real danger: consolidation stops being an escape route and becomes just another trap.

The independent-practice exodus in a nutshell

When pricing power collapses, independent practitioners have no choice but to sell to DSOs and PE platforms—trading autonomy for survival in a volume-over-price market.

D · The tensions

Volume up, price down

Aging brings more patients, but Medicare's 82-87 cent payment per dollar of care means volume alone can't save anyone from margin collapse.

The aging population is real. US hospitals, home care agencies, and device makers are seeing patient and service volume rise year after year. Medicare expanded ambulatory surgery center procedures in 2026. Home care demand grew 6.7% annually from 2021 to 2026. But here's the trap: the more you grow volume, the more you bleed on price. Medicare reimburses hospitals at only 82-87 cents per dollar of actual care cost. Home care agencies face stacked payment cuts—2026 brought a 1.3% reduction after proposing 6.4%. You can't cost-cut your way out of that math.

What changed

Aging was supposed to be a tailwind for healthcare providers. The US population is getting older, and older people need more care—dialysis, joint replacements, wound care, home health aides. The industry grew to 1.5 trillion dollars in 2025 and is adding 2.4 million more home care workers by 2026. But volume without price power is a trap. Medicare sets the price, and it hasn't budged off its punishing rate: hospitals get 82-87 cents back for every dollar of care they deliver, leaving a 13-18 cent shortfall per case. Meanwhile, the hospitals that provide that care face labor costs that exploded 42% since 2020. Nurses struck at Kaiser in January 2026—30,000 workers—because wages haven't kept pace. Home care agencies confront a darker version of the same squeeze: caregiver wages rose from $13.07 per hour in 2014 to $16.77 in 2024, but the agencies can't raise prices to match because Medicare cuts keep falling. The industry absorbed a 1.3% payment cut in 2026 alone, on top of four straight years of cuts. No amount of volume compensates for that gap.

The math is forcing consolidation and collapse. Hospitals went from 7.6% margins in 2022 to just 1-2% by 2025—a structural profitability crisis. Hospital M&A fell to 46 deals in 2025, the lowest in 15 years, but rebounded sharply in Q1 2026 with 22 transactions worth 14.5 billion dollars as survivors went hunting for scale. Twenty healthcare bankruptcies hit in 2025, the highest count in years; Steward Health Care became the largest hospital-sector bankruptcy in 30 years, and Prospect Medical Holdings shed 10 of its 16 hospitals. Home care is worse: 34% of agencies reported profit concerns in 2025-2026, and many run at near-zero or negative margins. The industry is fracturing. Rural and underserved home care agencies are closing outright. Consolidation is aggressive: General Atlantic bought TEAM Services Group for 3 billion dollars in Q2 2026, the largest home care deal on record. Private equity now backs 41% of deal volume, betting that only platforms large enough to absorb the payment cuts and labor inflation will survive.

What's particularly brutal is that the volume growth is real but doesn't help individual providers. Ambulatory surgery centers—which don't carry hospital overhead—now do 9% more procedures than in 2023 and are stealing profitable work from hospitals. Hospitals know this, so they're buying ASCs themselves (Ascension's 3.9 billion dollar AmSurg deal), cannibalizing their own core business. Home care agencies report 95% of their workforce is under moderate-to-severe staffing stress and are turning away 25% of patient requests because they can't afford to staff up at current reimbursement rates. The turnover is grueling: 75% annual turnover among caregivers. Volume, in other words, is rising, but the people delivering it are leaving as fast as they're hired because the work is hard and the pay is low. Only large platforms with access to cheap capital, technology that drives automation (75% of health systems now use at least one AI tool, up from 59% in 2025), and enough scale to negotiate leverage can weather the margin collapse. Everyone else is being squeezed out of the market.

The evidence

  • Hospitals: US market at $1.5 trillion in 2025 with margins compressed from 7.6% (2022) to 1-2% (2025) as Medicare reimburses only 82-87 cents per dollar of care and labor costs rose 42% since 2020
  • Home Care: Market grew 6.7% annually (2021-2026) to $191.6B in 2026, but 34% of agencies reported profit concerns as Medicare cuts stacked for four straight years (1.3% cut finalized for 2026)
  • Consolidation: Hospital M&A dropped to 46 deals in 2025 (lowest in 15 years) before Q1 2026 surge of 22 transactions worth $14.5B; home care PE-backed deals hit 41% of volume
  • Labor: Hospital labor costs up 42% since 2020; home care caregiver wages rose to $16.77/hour in 2024 (from $13.07 in 2014) but 75% annual turnover persists as pay lags other healthcare roles
  • Technology: AI adoption in health systems jumped to 75% (up from 59% in 2025), and General Atlantic's $3B TEAM Services acquisition (Q2 2026) largest home care deal on record, driven by PE consolidation for scale

Who rides it

Large integrated platforms with AI capability and access to capital are winning. Hospital systems that can afford to consolidate, buy ambulatory surgery centers to recapture profitable work, and invest in technology are surviving the margin collapse. Private equity firms are betting on scale: 41% of 2026 home care deals are PE-backed, and the largest acquisitions (General Atlantic's 3 billion dollar TEAM Services buy, Kinderhook's Enhabit take-private) are all bets that only platforms with enough volume and automation can negotiate their way out of Medicare's pricing power. Humana's 5.7 billion dollar Kindred Healthcare acquisition ensures full ownership of a home care giant. These players can absorb the payment cuts, weather the labor shortage, and use technology to reduce headcount and improve margins on the back side.

Who's squeezed

Independent and mid-sized providers are getting squeezed out. Rural home care agencies are closing because they can't absorb Medicare's stacked cuts and can't compete on labor costs. Prospect Medical Holdings filed Chapter 11 in 2025 and shed 10 of 16 hospitals. Steward Health Care became the largest hospital-sector bankruptcy in 30 years. Mid-tier hospitals are consolidating up (M&A surged in Q1 2026 as larger systems acquired regional players for scale) or closing down. For home care, the pain is immediate: agencies turn away 25% of patient requests due to staffing shortages, and 75% caregiver turnover means the workforce itself is voting with its feet. Workers are squeezed too—caregiver wages rose, but not fast enough to offset the brutal conditions and low pay relative to other healthcare roles.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The system is fracturing, and access is degrading even as volume rises. Agencies are closing in rural and underserved areas. Hospitals in weak geographic markets have no scale to negotiate. Home care agencies are turning away a quarter of their patient requests. The underlying problem—Medicare's refusal to raise reimbursement rates while wages and supply costs inflate—is structural, not cyclical. Policymakers could change it, but doing so would require raising Medicare taxes or cutting benefits, neither of which is popular. So the squeeze will persist, leading to consolidation into a few large platforms, smaller providers exiting, and gaps in coverage for vulnerable populations in rural areas. The aging population will get the care it needs, but only if it can access the consolidated platforms that survive.

Volume up, price down in a nutshell

Volume is booming due to an aging population, but Medicare's flat reimbursement rates and soaring labor costs mean only consolidated platforms with scale and automation can survive the pricing collapse.

D · The tensions

The value-based bet

Providers and insurers are racing to move surgery and complex care out of hospitals and into cheaper sites — but reimbursement lags behind the costs of making it work.

Hospitals and insurers know they're losing money on every claim. The fix they're betting on: move surgeries and procedures out of expensive inpatient settings into cheaper ambulatory surgery centers, urgent care, and home-based models. Reimbursement is low. Labor is scarce. But if you can run at massive scale, the math might work.

What changed

The $46.5 billion US ambulatory surgery center market is the proving ground for this gamble. Hospitals and private equity are buying up independent ASCs at a frantic pace—Ascension Health paid $3.9 billion for AmSurg in 2024, expanding from 58 to over 300 ASCs across 34 states in a single swallow. Surgery Partners shed hospital assets (selling two Idaho hospitals for $1.15 billion to Intermountain in 2025), signaling a hard pivot: surgeries belong at ASCs, not hospital outpatient departments, because the site-of-service payment gap is real money.

The problem is reimbursement growth does not keep up with reality. CMS added 560 new procedures to the ASC Covered Procedures List in 2026—cardiac ablations, lumbar fusion, complex spine work that used to live in hospitals. But the payment rates for those procedures at ASCs are thinner than in hospital outpatient settings, by design. Meanwhile, wage inflation and operational costs have not slowed. Large platforms like United Surgical Partners (USPI) still hit 38.6% EBITDA margins in 2025, but smaller independents have been compressed into the low-to-mid 30s. Anesthesia shortages are acute—locum tenens use jumped 17% since 2024 and is projected to climb another 5% in 2026. Nursing shortages are equally severe, as hospitals and ASCs bid against each other for the same scarce staff.

The result is hard polarization. Scaled platforms—Ascension, Cleveland Clinic (via Regent Surgical), General Atlantic (via the National Platform acquisition of Legent Health in October 2025)—can absorb margin pressure because they negotiate at volume and spread overhead across hundreds of centers. They can also absorb the compliance burden. A solo or small-group ASC cannot. The value-based escape hatch works only if you run enough volume to drop the per-unit cost below what a hospital can achieve. That math is physics: if CMS pays the same rate for a cardiac ablation at an ASC as at a hospital outpatient department, but the ASC has half the overhead, the ASC wins on margin. But if the ASC has to pay locum anesthesia at $3,000 a day because staff is scarce, and the hospital outpatient department has staff on salary, the hospital wins. Scale determines which side of that crossover you land on.

The HMO side reinforces the pressure. Medical loss ratios (MLRs) are in crisis: 17% of Medicare Advantage contracts ran above 100% MLR in 2023, and another third sit in the 90–95% range with no cushion. Earned premiums rose 14.3% in 2025, but incurred claims grew 15.5%—meaning insurers are losing money on the policies themselves. GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic are surprise costs that no model predicted. CMS is auditing upcoding aggressively (May 2025 directive). And the aging population is not choosing cheaper sites—it is arriving sick and complex. So the only lever left is to steer volume away from expensive venues. Medicare Advantage enrollment itself contracted for the first time in two decades, falling from 35 million in 2024 to around 34 million in 2025, with as many as 2.9 million seniors forced to switch plans because insurers exited unprofitable markets. By January 2026, regional insurers like Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare had ceased all operations except Medicare Advantage itself—a kind of death spiral where the only line of business left is the one losing the most money.

The evidence

  • Ambulatory Surgery Centers: $46.5 billion market (2026) with 6.3% CAGR and 38.6% EBITDA margins for large platforms, but reimbursement growth of 2.4-2.9% annually fails to match wage inflation
  • Medicare Advantage HMOs: 17% of MA contracts above 100% MLR in 2023; earned premiums rose 14.3% in 2025 but incurred claims grew 15.5%, forcing insurers to exit unprofitable markets
  • Provider Consolidation: Ascension's $3.9 billion AmSurg acquisition (2024) and Surgery Partners' $1.15 billion hospital divestment (2025) signal hard shift from hospital inpatient to ASC-based care
  • CMS Procedure Expansion: 560 new procedures added to ASC Covered Procedures List in 2026, including cardiac ablations and lumbar fusion, but with site-of-service payment differentials favoring hospitals
  • Labor Market Squeeze: Anesthesia locum tenens use jumped 17% since 2024 and projected to climb 5% more in 2026; nursing shortages equally acute as hospitals and ASCs compete for staff

Who rides it

Scaled ASC platforms and integrated health systems win. They have the volume to negotiate rates, the capital to absorb margin compression, and the scale to absorb wage inflation across hundreds of centers. Ascension, Cleveland Clinic, and the new platforms launched by General Atlantic and Hospital for Special Surgery can move complex procedures to cheaper sites and still hit acceptable margins because they amortize overhead and staffing costs across massive patient volumes. For them, the pricing collapse is not a crisis—it is consolidation opportunity, a chance to buy independents at fire-sale prices and fold them into systems where the economics work at scale.

Who's squeezed

Independent and mid-size ASCs are squeezed. They cannot negotiate volume discounts with suppliers or labor. They pay locum anesthesia at market rates ($3,000+ per day) because they have no staffing bench. They lose higher-margin procedures to integrated platforms because health systems steer patients to their own ASCs. Small HMO providers and regional insurers are squeezed hardest—Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare have effectively surrendered, ceasing all operations except Medicare Advantage (the loss-making line) as of January 2026. Solo physicians who own ASCs are being bought out or pushed into ACOs where they lose autonomy and accept lower per-procedure fees in exchange for volume.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The value-based escape hatch depends on a bet that is not certain: that the cost of moving volume to cheaper sites will fall faster than reimbursement declines. But the data shows reimbursement growth (2.4-2.9% annually) is already lagging wage inflation and operational cost increases. Labor shortages are worsening, not improving—anesthesia and nursing are both under acute pressure, and there is no obvious way to automate those roles. If labor costs keep rising faster than reimbursement, the margin advantage of ASCs over hospitals evaporates, and the entire consolidation thesis breaks. Worse: if CMS audits upcoding more aggressively (as it promised in May 2025) and starts denying claims, or if it cuts ASC reimbursement to align with hospital outpatient departments, the economics reverse overnight. The scaled platforms can survive that shock because they have other lines of business. Independent ASCs and small HMO providers cannot.

The value-based bet in a nutshell

When price-per-unit falls, the only escape is to squeeze costs by moving procedures to cheaper venues like ambulatory surgery centers — a bet that only scaled operators can win.

E · The big picture

The Pricing-Power Collapse

Medicare cuts and payer power strip pricing from providers and device makers — volume rises with aging, but the price per unit keeps falling, and only scale survives.

Healthcare reimbursement is locked in a squeeze. Medicare cuts rates by 1–2% yearly while demand grows 3–4%, so you need to see more patients just to stay flat. Payers control the price, and only the biggest operators can absorb the margin compression.

What changed

The pricing-power collapse across healthcare has made volume abundant but price per unit scarce. Start with dialysis: the US industry treats 516,837 patients on dialysis in 2025, generating $36 billion in revenue at just 11.7% operating margin—and Medicare rate increases are running at 2.2% for 2026 and only 1.1% projected for 2027, far below wage inflation and labor costs. Fresenius and DaVita are both growing treatment volume 2–3% annually, but revenue-per-treatment is falling in their commercial mix, and CMS's final 2027 ESRD PPS base rate of $299.55 per treatment—a $17.84 increase—translates to only 1.1% total growth after phosphate binder bundling. The message is ruthless: you need more patients, not higher prices.

Orthopedic device makers face the same pressure inverted. Medicare reimbursement for hip replacements has fallen 39% since 2017, and all orthopedic procedures saw a 26% cut from 2016 to 2024, with CMS applying a fresh 2.5% efficiency adjustment in 2026. Yet the aging US population—10,000 Americans turning 65 daily, with 37% of diagnostic tests and 34% of inpatient procedures now driven by the over-65 crowd—still drives steady demand. Stryker captured 67% of US knee procedures on its MAKO robotic platform by year-end 2025, proving that robotic surgery (a $2.6 billion market growing 16–17% annually) is the only escape hatch from commodity pricing. The orthopedic industry margins compressed to 5.6% as of 2022, and consolidation is accelerating: J&J is spinning off DePuy Synthes (valued $20 billion+) precisely because the orthopedic business can't compete at scale against focused players.

Generic pharma is broken. The market contracted from $40.6 billion in 2022 to $28.5 billion in 2026—a -10% CAGR over five years—as PBMs took 80% control of the market and set prices to near-commodity levels. Teva reported 15% US generics growth in 2024 but issued subdued 2025 guidance under ongoing pricing pressure and patent cliffs. India and China now supply 58% of US pharmaceutical imports by weight, with India shipping $10.5 billion annually while depending on China for 70% of raw materials. Congress's February 2026 legislation delinking PBM compensation from drug prices is the most significant regulatory intervention in decades, but it won't raise manufacturer prices—it just shifts the PBM's profit model and leaves makers facing tariff threats (100% tariffs on generic drugs threatened by August 2028) and the race to biosimilars. Generic manufacturers with 5–15% margins are forced to exit the commodity business entirely and pivot to complex molecules and biosimilars (20–40% margins) to survive.

Finally, insurers are the one sector that just recaptured pricing power. After medical cost inflation crushed margins in 2023–2024, the Big Three (UnitedHealth, Humana, CVS/Aetna) are hiking premiums aggressively in 2025–2026: employer-sponsored premiums are rising 9%—the highest in 15 years—while ACA marketplace premiums jumped 18% for 2026, and benchmark plans jumped 26%. The expiration of enhanced ACA subsidies on December 31, 2025 means unsubsidized individual premiums will more than double from $888 to $1,904 annually. Medicaid shrinkage—down 7.6% in 2025 and growing only 0.2% in 2026 due to new work/reporting requirements—lets insurers shed the lowest-margin segment. But that power is temporary and defensive: tariff pressures are raising device and supply costs, Medicaid enrollment is evaporating, and new entrants like Amazon (which launched a GLP-1 management program in April 2026 at $25/month in ~3,000 cities) and TrumpRx.gov (a direct-to-consumer pharmacy that launched February 2026) are siphoning off the most profitable segments—employee health, primary care, and specialty drugs.

Made scarce: pricing power over units and premium growth. Made cheap: individual insurance coverage for the unsubsidized (due to subsidy cliffs), generic drugs (PBM leverage), and outpatient procedures (site-neutral payment rules). Made risky: being a small operator without scale or being locked into low-margin commodity products. Made valuable: being a consolidator with scale (dialysis giants DaVita and Fresenius), owning proprietary innovation (Stryker in robotic surgery), and being an insurer with enough enrollment to absorb margin compression through premium hikes.

The evidence

  • Dialysis: DaVita and Fresenius treat 516,837 US dialysis patients in 2025 at $36 billion annual revenue, 11.7% margin, yet face 2.2% Medicare rate increases for 2026 and only 1.1% projected for 2027—below wage inflation.
  • Orthopedic devices: Medicare reimbursement fell 26% from 2016 to 2024 (39% cut in hip arthroplasty since 2017), yet Stryker's MAKO robotic platform captured 67% of US knee procedures by end-2025, growing at 16–17% annually in a 4.3% overall market.
  • Generic pharma: Market contracted -10% CAGR from $40.6B in 2022 to $28.5B in 2026 as PBMs control 80% of pricing; India and China supply 58% of US pharma imports by weight, undercutting domestic margins.
  • Insurance: Employer premiums up 9% for 2025–2026 (highest in 15 years), ACA benchmark plans up 26% for 2026; expiration of enhanced subsidies December 31, 2025 doubles unsubsidized premiums from $888 to $1,904 annually.
  • New entrants: Amazon's GLP-1 program at $25/month launched April 2026 across ~3,000 cities; TrumpRx.gov (February 2026) offers direct-to-consumer drugs at manufacturer-discounted cash prices, bypassing insurer intermediation.

Who rides it

Consolidators with scale win. DaVita and Fresenius control 65% of US dialysis, absorbing Medicare cuts through operational efficiency and volume growth. Stryker owns the robotic surgery moat—67% of US knee procedures on MAKO by year-end 2025—and can charge premium prices because outcomes improve and hospitals depend on it. Insurers recapture pricing power in 2025–2026 through 9% employer premium hikes and 18–26% ACA increases, allowing them to pass cost growth to employers and individuals. New digital entrants (Amazon, TrumpRx) capture the most profitable segments: primary care, specialty drugs, and self-pay customers who bypass traditional insurance altogether.

Who's squeezed

Independent and regional operators get squeezed. Small dialysis operators can't negotiate with Medicare; small orthopedic device makers can't afford the R&D required for robotic platforms or biosimilars. Generic manufacturers are trapped: Teva's subdued 2025 guidance reflects pricing pressure that no cost-cutting can offset—commodity generics simply don't sustain 5–15% margins anymore. Unsubsidized individual insurance buyers face a cliff: when enhanced ACA subsidies expired December 31, 2025, annual premiums doubled from $888 to $1,904. Medicaid providers lose enrollment (down 7.6% in 2025) as work/reporting requirements shrink the pool, and the rates they receive don't compensate for complexity or volume loss.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is a political fracture over who bears the cost of volume growth. Aging is real—10,000 Americans turn 65 daily, and 37% of diagnostic tests and 34% of inpatient procedures are now driven by the over-65 crowd. Demand for dialysis, joint replacements, and heart procedures will keep growing 3–4% annually. But Medicare cuts reimbursement 1–2% yearly, insurers hike premiums 9–26%, and patients face subsidy cliffs that double their out-of-pocket cost overnight. At some point, the fraying middle (the newly unsubsidized) will demand price controls or break the insurer model entirely. Congress's February 2026 PBM legislation is the first domino; tariff threats on generic drugs and medical devices are the second. If tariffs land (100% on generics by August 2028 is being threatened), or if price controls spread from Medicare to commercial, the entire reimbursement architecture collapses, and no amount of scale will protect consolidators from a sudden repricing shock.

In one sentence

The pricing-power collapse in a nutshell

Medicare cuts reimbursement 1–2% yearly while demand grows 3–4%, making pricing scarce but volume abundant—only consolidators and proprietary innovators survive, and everyone else either exits, merges, or gets bought.

A · The office breaks

The office crisis

Hybrid work gutted office values while refinancing walls and conversion pipelines reshape American cities.

The office sector is in structural crisis. National office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025 and only fell to 17.7% by mid-2026 — a level that economists call unrecoverable. Hybrid work broke the occupancy math. Higher interest rates broke the refinance math. Both forces hit at once, and the collision reshaped the entire commercial real estate sector.

What changed

Hybrid work gutted office occupancy. When employees stopped coming in five days a week, vacancy exploded across secondary and tertiary markets. San Francisco and Austin — both tech hubs — saw vacancy rates exceed 26% by 2025. Class B and C office buildings became economically obsolete overnight. The only offices that stayed strong were Class A trophy assets in central business districts, the kind that multinational firms anchor with prestigious leases. Every other building — the mid-market office, the suburban corporate park, the regional tower — faced a choice: find new tenants who no longer existed, or die.

The refinance crisis turned distress into catastrophe. In commercial real estate, assets mature on predictable cycles: a loan taken out in 2013 comes due in 2023 or 2024. In 2025 alone, $957 billion in CRE loans matured. Through 2028, another $2.8 trillion comes due. Lenders who refinanced at 3% rates can now only get 6% or 7%. The math breaks. If occupancy is down 20 percent and rents are flat, the owner cannot service new debt at double the cost. CMBS delinquencies reached 7.29% in 2025 — the highest distress signal in the market. Chapter 11 bankruptcies hit a 10-year high, with 694 corporate filings in 2025, the most in 14 years.

Conversion became the survival strategy. Instead of fighting for tenants, real estate owners pivoted to adaptive reuse: tearing out office cubicles and building apartments. Office-to-apartment conversions reached 90,300 units in 2026, a 28% jump year-over-year. Now 47 percent of the entire 193,900-unit adaptive reuse pipeline is former office space. This signals defeat. It means owners acknowledged that the office market will not recover at historical occupancy rates. It means they see more value in apartments — a bet on the housing shortage (3.4 million homes short nationally) and the 105 percent premium to buy versus rent — than in rehabilitating their office towers.

Architecture felt the shockwave first and hardest. When office construction cratered, billings collapsed. The Architecture Billings Index hit 47.6 in October 2025, a reading below 50 that signals declining demand. Thirty-eight percent of firms reported falling revenue. Small independent practices, already thin on margins, took the biggest hit: firms with under $250,000 in annual billings expected a 7 percent revenue drop. Seventy percent of declining firms cited fewer new projects ahead. AI software accelerated the squeeze, automating site planning, specification writing, code-violation detection, and BIM workflows. Larger, consolidated firms integrated these tools fast; smaller practices could not compete and faced pressure to merge or shut down. Meanwhile, consolidators like Stantec acquired UK firm Hydrock in May 2024, adding 950 professionals and signaling that private equity saw opportunity in rolled-up, consolidated practices. The sector is consolidating under pressure, not from growth, but from survival.

The evidence

  • Real Estate: $957 billion in CRE loans matured in 2025 alone, with another $2.8 trillion maturing through 2028 as refinance rates doubled.
  • Real Estate: Office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025 and only fell to 17.7% by mid-2026, forcing Class B and C buildings into obsolescence.
  • Real Estate: Office-to-apartment conversions reached 90,300 units in 2026 (up 28% YoY), now representing 47% of the entire adaptive reuse pipeline.
  • Architecture: The Architecture Billings Index hit 47.6 in October 2025, with 38% of firms reporting falling revenue and small practices facing 7% cuts.
  • Real Estate: Multifamily net absorption hit 124,600 units in Q2 2026 with investor transaction volume up 39.5% YoY, the strongest sector as capital flees offices.

Who rides it

Real estate investment trusts and large, consolidated architecture and engineering firms are riding the conversion wave. Capital rotates into multifamily assets (124,600 units absorbed in Q2 2026) powered by the housing shortage and 105% buy-versus-rent premium. Industrial real estate thrives: 940 million sq ft leased in 2025, the second-best year on record, as e-commerce tenants account for 56% of retail goods sales growth. Large consolidated practices — especially those backed by PE capital — integrate AI tools, absorb smaller competitors, and win the shrinking pool of projects. Only Class A trophy offices in CBDs retain premium occupancy; owners there hold pricing power.

Who's squeezed

Mid-market and Class B/C office owners face decade-long losses and forced debt restructuring. Small independent architecture practices are squeezed hardest: facing revenue declines of 7 percent, unable to afford AI tools, and losing deals to consolidated competitors. Junior architects and traditional drafting roles face automation. Real estate development firms focused on office are obsolete or in bankruptcy. Regional and suburban office markets see permanent demand destruction as hybrid work reshapes occupancy norms. The $63.5 billion architecture sector grows at 0.1% in 2026, a practical standstill, as commercial construction remains dormant.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is a cascading debt spiral. CMBS delinquencies are already at 7.29%, but the real wave hits 2027-2028 when the bulk of the $2.8 trillion refinance wall matures. Owners who cannot reposition (convert, or sell at a loss) will default, flooding the market with distressed assets and depressing pricing further. A debt standstill among major commercial landlords could choke both capital availability and development momentum for years. If conversion pipelines saturate and apartment supply finally catches up to demand, the single remaining exit for office owners closes, and a permanent loss spiral begins.

Office vacancy broke the revenue model for real estate and architecture, forcing a decade-long reckoning on distressed towers and refinance cliffs.

A · The office breaks

Adaptive Reuse & Conversion

Dead offices get gutted and rebuilt—but the contractors doing it are starving on thin margins.

Hybrid work killed the demand for traditional office space. Rates stayed high. So millions of square feet of Class-B and Class-C office buildings now sit half-empty, especially in secondary markets. That creates a real opportunity: tear out the cubicles, rewire for apartments or mixed-use, and sell the landlord a comeback story. But the contractors doing that work are trapped between material inflation, tariff shock, and a grinding shortage of skilled workers—all crushing margins that were already razor-thin.

What changed

Hybrid work erased 41% of demand for office space since 2019. New office deliveries fell 26% in 2025 alone. National office vacancy sits at 17.6% (April 2026), but the real problem is concentrated: Miami's at 12.5%, but Seattle's bleeding at 25.2%. Class-A trophy towers still command premiums and find tenants; it's the older Class-B and Class-C buildings—the bread-and-butter stock in every American city—that are now dead weight. Those buildings can't compete on price because their rents don't cover debt service at 5.7–6.6% mortgage rates. The math just doesn't work. So owners are forced to either sell at a loss or convert.

That conversion is real work, and it's real opportunity. An office building can become apartments, hotels, co-working, light industrial, storage, mixed-use retail-and-housing. The Commercial Property Remodeling market is $39.8 billion (2026), up from $45.2 billion in 2022 in dollar terms—but that's nominal inflation, not growth. The CAGR from 2021 to 2026 is just 0.8%. In 2026 alone, the market grew only 1.5%. Meanwhile, material costs surged 40.3% from January 2021 to April 2026. Tariffs added another layer: 50% on steel and aluminum, 15% on industrial equipment, 10% on softwood lumber. Contractors are reporting total project escalation of 6–10% just from tariff stacks. That eats the margin. Contractors were already squeezing 3.6% margins (2022), and those are probably compressed further by 2026 due to tariffs and labor inflation.

Labor is the second guillotine. Commercial building construction has a 500,000-worker shortage that costs the industry $10.8 billion annually. The shortage is structural: retirements and chronic underinvestment in trades training mean there simply aren't enough HVAC techs, electricians, plumbers, and framers to go around. Wages are climbing faster than inflation itself—residential construction wages jumped 9.2% year-over-year in mid-2025. Contractors can't turn to offshore labor or automation for the craft work involved in adaptive reuse; every old building is different. They either hire at inflated wages or they turn away jobs. For mid-market remodeling, many are turning away jobs.

But there's an undertow of consolidation happening. Commercial HVAC and mechanical trades are being rolled up by private equity—Blackstone/Legence, Morgan Stanley/Sila, Leonard Green/Wrench—and subcontractor acquisition volume jumped 38.6% year-over-year to 366 deals in 2025. The theory is that larger platforms can absorb tariff inflation through volume, leverage supply chains better, and lock in labor by offering better benefits. Meanwhile, commercial chapter 11 filings hit a 10-year high in 2025 and surged another 76% year-over-year in January 2026 versus January 2025. With $875 billion in commercial mortgages maturing in 2026, refinancing is a bloodbath for anybody who overlevered into office.

The evidence

  • Commercial building construction: Data center construction starts reached $77.7 billion annually in December 2025, a 190% year-over-year surge, with monthly spending averaging $6.5 billion in December 2025 (2025)
  • Commercial property remodeling: Market size $39.8 billion in 2026, up nominally from $45.2 billion in 2022 but growing only 0.8% CAGR; margins at 3.6% in 2022 and compressed by 2026 (2026)
  • Construction labor: 500,000-worker shortage costs the industry $10.8 billion annually; residential construction wages up 9.2% year-over-year mid-2025 (2025)
  • Office market: Office vacancy improved 210 basis points year-over-year to 17.6% by April 2026 (first sustained positive absorption in 18 quarters), but regional spread is severe: Miami 12.5%, Seattle 25.2% (2026)
  • Tariff impact: Material costs surged 40.3% January 2021–April 2026; tariff stacks (50% steel/aluminum, 15% equipment, 10% lumber) pushing total project escalation 6–10% (2026)

Who rides it

PE firms and consolidators win. Blackstone/Legence, Morgan Stanley/Sila, and Leonard Green/Wrench are rolling up mechanical and HVAC trades to build platforms that can absorb tariff shocks and labor wage inflation through scale and better supply-chain leverage. Subcontractor M&A volume jumped 38.6% year-over-year to 366 deals in 2025. Larger contractors with balance sheets can also wait out the remodeling cycle, pick the best projects, and refuse margin-killing work. And the mega-firms doing data center construction (Amazon, Microsoft, Google) are the only segment genuinely thriving—$77.7 billion in starts in 2025 (up 190%) makes office look like a graveyard by comparison.

Who's squeezed

Mid-market and small remodeling contractors get squeezed into bankruptcy or consolidation. The industry has 29,469 highly fragmented establishments with no player over 5% share and 80,000–90,000 workers. Those contractors can't absorb tariff inflation or wage pressure without cutting margins below viability. They can't wait out the cycle; they need work now. They face a choice: merge up into a PE platform, specialize narrowly (only luxury conversions, only historic preservation), or exit. Office landlords holding Class-B and Class-C stock also suffer, especially those who financed at 3% and now can't refinance the maturity wall; $875 billion in commercial mortgages maturing in 2026 will force fire sales or extended holding patterns.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The conversion pipeline could stall entirely if labor wages and tariff costs don't stabilize. Adaptive reuse is inherently expensive and unpredictable—every old building is different. Contractors need predictable material costs and stable labor to bid those jobs. Right now, a 6–10% tariff-driven escalation can blow a project's underwriting and tank the deal. If tariffs stay at 50% on steel through 2026–2027, and construction wages keep climbing at 9%+ annually, the math breaks. Owners might simply hold empty buildings and wait for a recession or tariff relief rather than convert. That would freeze a sector that's supposed to absorb the 41% decline in office demand, leaving millions of square feet in limbo and small contractors permanently damaged.

In one sentence

Adaptive reuse & conversion in a nutshell

Hybrid work and higher rates created a $39.8 billion adaptive-reuse opportunity, but tariffs and labor shortages are crushing the margins of the fragmented contractors supposed to build it—pushing capital upmarket to PE rollups and away from the small firms that do most of the actual work.

B · Where capital rotates

The Housing Squeeze

High rates freeze buying and pressure multifamily even as housing stays scarce.

The housing market faces a squeeze from two sides at once. Buyers can't afford to buy because rates stay near 6%, while landlords in rent-controlled cities can't raise rents fast enough to cover soaring insurance and labor costs. The result: a frozen market where builders cut prices and offer mortgage buydowns, apartment companies merge into mega-REITs to survive, and smaller operators face bankruptcy.

What changed

Higher interest rates broke the math on both sides of the housing market. On the homebuilding side, a buyer who could afford a $400,000 house with a 3% rate now can't afford that same house at 6%. Builders saw housing starts crash 15.4% from January to May 2026, hitting 1.177 million units—the lowest since May 2020. Rather than wait for demand to return, they've started cutting prices by an average of 5% and offering to pay down mortgage rates for buyers just to move inventory. At the same time, construction tariffs hit 25-30% in 2025, raising the cost of each home by about $10,900, and labor shortages cost the industry $10.8 billion annually. Builders are getting caught between higher input costs and lower prices—a squeeze that squeezes margins from 6.1% in 2022 down to 6-8% by 2026. In response, the industry is consolidating fast. Between August 2025 and June 2026, the share of builders reporting acquisition approaches doubled from 9% to 18%, and major deals like Taylor Morrison going to Berkshire Hathaway, Tri Pointe to Sumitomo Forestry, and United Homes Group to Stanley Martin show that only scale survives. The US home builders industry is now flat at $166.2 billion in 2026 revenue with near-zero growth, a far cry from the building boom of 2021–2023.

On the rental side, the squeeze takes a different form. After years of climbing rents—double-digit growth in 2021–2023—the apartment market hit a wall. Vacancy rates climbed from 6.3% in 2021 to 7.0% in Q2 2025, and luxury segments sit at 11.4% vacant. Developers chased the rent-growth tailwind and built aggressively in the Sun Belt and Mountain West, but when occupancy tightened, owners stopped raising rents and started offering concessions instead. The apartment rental market is still huge at $305.7 billion in 2026 revenue, but growth has slowed to 1.7% annually. Worse, rent-controlled markets like New York and California face a cruel squeeze. Tenants pay record-high percentages of their income for housing, yet landlords cannot raise rents fast enough—NYC caps increases at 2.75%–5.25% per year, California at 5% plus inflation capped at 10%—to cover surging insurance, labor, and maintenance costs. Multifamily loan delinquencies hit 1.37% in Q3 2025, a 3.4× increase over two years and the highest since 2008. Smaller leveraged owners and rent-stabilized properties face the worst of it: Pinnacle filed for bankruptcy in May 2025 with $500M in mortgage debt; 5,100 of its rent-stabilized NYC apartments went to auction. Sonder, the short-term rental company, collapsed entirely when Marriott terminated its licensing deal and it filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in 2025. Consolidation is the only exit. AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential announced a $69 billion merger to create the nation's largest apartment REIT with 180,000+ units and $175M in cost cuts expected within 18 months—a vote of no confidence in independent operators' ability to survive.

What became scarce? Affordable housing, paradoxically, even though oversupply is pushing rents down in competitive markets. In rent-controlled cities, supply is locked in place by regulation, and demand for those cheap units far exceeds supply. What became cheap? Single-family homes, at least in hot markets like Florida and Texas where builders are cutting prices to clear inventory. What became risky? Leverage on apartment buildings, especially those with rent-stabilized portfolios that can't cover rising costs. What became newly valuable? Scale and capital strength. Big builders like D.R. Horton and Lennar can absorb tariff shocks and rate headwinds; small builders get acquired or disappear. Big REITs like the new AvalonBay-Equity Residential colossus can negotiate better insurance rates, automate labor, and hide losses in diversified portfolios; small mom-and-pop landlords go bankrupt.

The evidence

  • Homebuilding (Construction): US housing starts collapsed 15.4% from January to May 2026 to 1.177 million annualized units, lowest since May 2020, as tariffs at 25-30% effective rate added $10,900 per home and rates stayed near 6%.
  • Homebuilding (Construction): M&A activity among builders doubled between August 2025 and June 2026, with 18% reporting acquisition approaches; major deals include Taylor Morrison to Berkshire Hathaway and Tri Pointe to Sumitomo Forestry.
  • Apartment Rental (Real Estate): Apartment vacancy rates climbed to 7.0% in Q2 2025 from 6.3% in 2021, with luxury segments at 11.4% vacant, ending years of double-digit rent growth and forcing concessions.
  • Apartment Rental (Real Estate): Multifamily loan delinquencies hit 1.37% in Q3 2025, 3.4× higher over two years and highest since 2008, driven by rent-stabilized properties squeezed between frozen rents and soaring costs.
  • Apartment Rental (Real Estate): AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential announced a $69 billion merger closing in 2026 to create 180,000+ unit mega-REIT with $175M in cost cuts, reflecting consolidation as smaller operators face bankruptcy.

Who rides it

Big builders and mega-REITs win. D.R. Horton, Lennar, and PulteGroup have the scale and cash to absorb tariff shocks, hold price through a down cycle, and buy distressed competitors. On the rental side, the AvalonBay-Equity Residential merger creates a giant that can negotiate insurance discounts, invest in automation to replace expensive labor, and diversify risk across 180,000 units. Capital flows to winners who can play a multi-year game.

Who's squeezed

Small builders and independent landlords get squeezed out. A builder with a handful of projects can't absorb a $10,900 per-unit tariff cost while cutting prices 5% and offering rate buydowns—margins don't pencil. A mom-and-pop landlord with a rent-stabilized building in New York faces a $5,000-per-unit per-year gap between frozen rents (capped at 2.75%–5.25%) and soaring insurance and labor costs. Bankruptcy becomes the only exit. Pinnacle, Sonder, and countless unnamed operators are liquidated to pay debt, and their portfolios get picked up by REITs at distressed prices.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The debt wall. Multifamily delinquencies at 1.37% in Q3 2025 are already at financial-crisis levels, and most distressed debt is still working through the courts or negotiating workouts—the real wave of defaults could take years to clear. If commercial real estate debt—maturities are heavy in 2026–2027 for office and weaker multifamily—has to refinance at higher rates, the pain spreads to the banks that hold the mortgages and the insurance companies that insure the loans. A cascading default scenario could freeze credit and tip the broader economy into recession.

In one sentence

The housing squeeze in a nutshell

Higher rates and tariffs trapped homebuilders in a margin crunch while rent controls left apartment owners unable to cover surging costs, forcing both sides to consolidate around winners with scale and capital strength.

B · Where capital rotates

Logistics & Data Centers: Capital Finds Electricity

Warehouses and data centers pull capital from office towers because they move goods and compute, not people—and the race for power has reshaped what matters most.

Hybrid work killed the case for downtown office towers. But it also turned AI and e-commerce from trends into infrastructure problems. Developers and capital are no longer fighting over square footage. They're fighting over power, grid access, and the industrial real estate that can handle 30-100 kW per rack or move packages at scale. The U.S. colocation market has nearly doubled in five years—from $26 billion in 2021 to $72 billion in 2026—and that money is still moving.

What changed

For fifteen years, colocation facilities were cheap and plentiful. A data center operator could lease space, plug in servers, and compete on price. That game is over. AI training demands 30 to 100 kilowatts per single server rack. Inference at 10 to 20 kW per rack still looks simple until you multiply by thousands. The constraint flipped: electricity is now the scarcity, not space. North American colocation occupancy hit 1% vacancy in 2026. Operators are buying sites not for acreage but for power—proximity to hydroelectric dams, natural gas plants, or utilities willing to guarantee grid capacity. The Texas hyperscale campus that ECP and KKR announced in July 2025 (part of a $50 billion AI infrastructure partnership) exists because Texas utilities have capacity. The U.K. subsidiary acquisition by Digital Realty ($200 million, July 2024) happened because London has grid slots.

The electrical grid itself became the bottleneck. Grid interconnection requests now exceed 1,400 GW stuck in queue, with lead times of four to five years for high-capacity connections in saturated markets like Northern Virginia, Dallas, and Phoenix. In December 2025, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) broke the dam by issuing data-center-specific transmission tariffs for the PJM Interconnection—the largest regional grid operator. Starting January 2026, data centers had to follow new rules about how they buy power and pay for grid upgrades. Oregon's POWER Act (August 2025) flipped the model: facilities over 20 MW now must sign ten-year power-purchase agreements with renewable generators. California and Virginia followed with large-load tariffs starting at 25-40 MW thresholds. Power pricing jumped 17-19% in the last two years—the first sustained spike after fifteen years of decline.

Capital is flowing to the operators and utilities that control power, not space. Equinix and Digital Realty—the two largest U.S. colocation companies (10.28% and 9.98% market share in 2024)—are consolidating smaller operators and bidding aggressively on grid contracts. The market is growing at 11.5% compound annual growth in the U.S. through 2030, and globally at 14% CAGR, but that growth is narrowing to companies with utility partnerships, real estate in high-power zones, and access to capital to build custom cooling (liquid-cooled racks need specialized design).

Meanwhile, logistics real estate is less dramatic but just as locked in. Warehouses that move boxes—parcel hubs, last-mile centers, regional distribution nodes—have become essential to the e-commerce flywheel. That demand is steady and boring, which is exactly why capital moved there. Unlike offices (uncertain occupancy) or data centers (capital-intensive, technically risky), logistics is a proven yield play: ground leases at 6-8% on income-producing assets in tier-1 nodes (Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, Chicago). The rents on well-located warehouses have held firm even as office space craters, because the goods still have to move.

The evidence

  • Colocation (Technology & Digital): U.S. market grew from $26 billion in 2021 to $72.37 billion in 2026, with 11.5% annual growth through 2030 driven by AI infrastructure.
  • Data centers: Occupancy at 1% vacancy in 2026; 1,400+ GW of grid interconnection requests stuck with 4-5 year lead times in Northern Virginia, Dallas, and Phoenix.
  • Power costs: Colocation pricing jumped 17-19% in two years (2024-2026) after 15 years of decline, and FERC mandated data-center-specific transmission tariffs (December 2025).
  • Logistics (implied from real estate capital flow): Warehouse rents in tier-1 nodes (Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, Chicago) holding firm at 6-8% yields even as office vacancy spikes.
  • Regulatory shift: Oregon POWER Act (August 2025), California and Virginia large-load tariffs (2025-2026), and FY 2026 federal infrastructure authorization cliff (September 2026) reshaping regional competitiveness.

Who rides it

Operators with power contracts win—Equinix and Digital Realty (10.28% and 9.98% U.S. market share) consolidate smaller rivals and ink utility deals. Regions with stable renewable power or utility capacity (Texas, Oregon, parts of the Pacific Northwest) attract the bulk of new hyperscale investment. Logistics operators in tier-1 nodes see steady demand and pricing power because goods still need to move, and e-commerce growth is inelastic to recessions. States and utilities that act fast on power policy—Oregon's fast-track PPAs, FERC's new tariffs—become migration magnets for AI infrastructure capex that used to flow to office parks.

Who's squeezed

Developers who own empty office towers get squeezed as capital rotates to power-constrained data centers and logistics hubs. Mid-market colocation operators without utility partnerships face margin collapse as power costs rise 17-19% and occupancy is already maxed. Construction firms building data center campuses face labor shortages and tariffs on materials—heavy engineering construction margins are compressing from 7.5% to 5% even as labor wages jump 8-12% annually. States without power capacity or outdated grid infrastructure lose AI capex entirely; Northern Virginia is saturated, and grid queues now favor greenfield sites in deregulated regions.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The power grid itself is the single biggest fragility. Interconnection queues exceed 1,400 GW with four-to-five-year waits for new capacity in saturated markets. If AI demand keeps accelerating and utilities can't build capacity fast enough, data center operators will face forced load-shedding, outages, or have to build their own on-site generation (hugely expensive and regionally constrained by fuel supply and environmental permitting). A hard recession could stall the federal infrastructure funding that has propped up heavy construction, since authorization expires in September 2026 and state/local budgets are already tight. If grid tariffs or renewable PPAs become unaffordable, AI capex could freeze or migrate offshore to cheaper electricity zones, leaving U.S. colocation operators with expensive build-outs and no demand.

In one sentence

Logistics & data centers in a nutshell

Capital flowed from office real estate to logistics and data centers because they move goods and compute—but now the constraint is electricity, not space, and power access has become the only moat that matters.

B · Where capital rotates

Owning the Land

Land leasing and RV parks shift from growth to scarcity—a steady, consolidating landlord business serving renters priced out of home ownership.

Office real estate lost its tenant base to hybrid work and rising interest rates killed its financing math. But capital doesn't disappear—it rotates. Into land. Into RV parks. Into manufactured housing communities. These asset classes are small, sleepy-sounding, and boring by design. They're also consolidating fast, commanding near-total occupancy, and printing 47% margins while traditional property chokes.

What changed

Land leasing in the US is a $16.0 billion market (2026) moving at 0.6% CAGR since 2022, but growth is accelerating right now because housing is genuinely unaffordable. The industry serves two overlapping populations squeezed out of homeownership: price-conscious renters who can't afford stick-built homes, and retirees who are aging through their 60s and 70s and don't want property maintenance. RV adoption stayed high after the pandemic as remote work made mobility realistic. Occupancy rates sit near 95%—nearly full—and land leasing operators pushed through 7% rent growth in 2025 without backing down. That pricing power comes from scarcity. New community development is stuck. Zoning boards in most states treat manufactured housing as a nuisance, forcing developers to spend 24-48 months and $60,000 per site just to get a new campground or mobile home community open. Each year the supply stays constrained, existing operators become harder to dislodge.

Regulators are starting to notice the rental squeeze and pushing back: Washington state capped annual lot rent increases at 5% in May 2025, and Florida and Virginia are loosening zoning to allow more manufactured homes. But these policy moves won't matter if supply stays locked. In campgrounds and RV parks—a subset of land leasing that's $11.3 billion and flat to declining in volume—the structural play is even clearer. Total reservations fell 1.0% in 2025, the first annual decline in platform history, but revenue rose 5.2%. Operators raised prices instead of filling more sites. Average nightly rates at medium parks jumped 16.6% to $83. This is the opposite of growth-through-expansion; it's yield-through-power. Glamping—luxury camping with comfortable beds and hot showers—grew 43.6% while regular RV parks flatlined, revealing that younger, remote workers are willing to pay premium prices for a mobile lifestyle. Consolidation is accelerating. Sun Communities spent $457 million in October 2025 acquiring 14 manufactured housing and RV communities, then immediately divested its 129-property marina portfolio to exit a riskier business. KOA added new communities in North Carolina and Massachusetts in 2025, but these are rare; most capital is flowing into consolidation of existing sites, not greenfield development.

The economics are becoming clearer too. Cap rates for institutional investors sit at 8.0%, but the actual cost of borrowing runs 8.7-9.3% per year. That means day-one leverage is negative; returns depend on slowly paying down debt and repositioning the asset, not on cash-on-cash returns. This is not a get-rich-quick play. It's a bond-substitute play: you're taking operational leverage and accepting single-digit cash flow yields in exchange for inflation-protected rent growth and full occupancy. The 47.3% EBIT margins for land leasing (2026) are remarkably stable because the operator is just charging rent and maintaining infrastructure; there's no variable cost to scale. Labor is rising—parks struggle to hire groundskeeping staff—but that's a cost of maintaining the asset, not a margin killer. The 2025 Guadalupe River flood and Hurricane Helene exposed uninsured waterfront risk and prompted Texas to tighten safety codes, but this just favors larger REITs who can absorb insurance costs and regulatory adaptation. There are ~98,000 land leasing operators in the US (2026), ranging from one-person lot rentals to huge REITs like ELS (452 communities, 173,201 sites) and Sun Communities (5,000+ communities). Consolidation is accelerating because small operators can't navigate zoning friction, insurance risk, and regulatory patchwork anymore.

The evidence

  • Land leasing: US market at $16.0 billion (2026) with 47.3% EBIT margins, serving ~98,000 operators and 129,000 employees, anchored by REITs like ELS (452 communities, 173,201 sites) consolidating smaller landlords.
  • RV parks and campgrounds: $11.3 billion market (2026) with 15,000+ establishments, 88% independently owned; revenue rose 5.2% in 2025 while total reservations fell 1.0%—pricing power over volume growth.
  • Occupancy and pricing: Manufactured housing communities near 95% occupancy (2025-2026) with 7% YoY rent growth; campground nightly rates jumped 16.6% to $83 average (medium parks, 2025).
  • Premium shift: Glamping grew 43.6% in 2025 while conventional RV parks flatlined, attracting younger remote-work-enabled demographics willing to pay higher prices.
  • Supply barrier: New campground development requires 24-48 months permitting and costs $60,000 per site, creating durable scarcity that protects incumbents and drives consolidation—Sun Communities spent $457 million acquiring 14 communities (October 2025).

Who rides it

Real-estate investment trusts (REITs) like Sun Communities and ELS benefit from consolidation as regulatory complexity and insurance risk make small operators unviable. Large campground networks like KOA can adapt faster to premium demand (glamping growth +43.6%) and absorb financing costs. Operators of existing land leases and RV parks win through scarcity—95% occupancy and 7% rent growth with no volume pressure. Younger, remote-enabled travelers and retirees willing to accept mobile or manufactured housing get access to affordable shelter, though at rising costs.

Who's squeezed

Small, independent land-leasing operators (majority of the 98,000 total) are squeezed out by zoning friction, insurance risk, and consolidation pressure. Mid-market campground owners face negative day-one leverage (loan rates 8.7-9.3% exceed cap rates 8.0%) and rising labor costs, forcing them to sell to REITs or abandon expansion. Renters and retirees face 7% annual rent growth and shrinking affordable housing supply as policy pushback (Washington's 5% cap, zoning loosening) lags actual demand. Conventional homebuyers remain locked out as mortgage rates stay high and land-lease communities capture inventory.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is a recession that halts remote work and RV adoption, collapsing demand just as occupancy sits at 95% and operators have locked in high debt levels with negative day-one leverage. If a downturn hits, operators can't cut rates fast because they have fixed debt service; they'd face forced sales or defaults. Second, policy intervention accelerates: if Washington state's rent-cap model spreads to other states and federal regulators tighten land-lease oversight, margins compress and the investment case collapses. Third, climate risk is becoming real—Hurricane Helene and Guadalupe River flooding exposed uninsured waterfront campgrounds and forced safety code tightening in Texas, a leading RV park state; catastrophic loss could hit leverage and insurance costs across the sector.

In one sentence

Owning the land in a nutshell

As office towers empty and traditional housing becomes unaffordable, capital quietly rotates into land leasing, RV parks, and manufactured housing—where occupancy stays near 95% and pricing power grows because supply is stuck.
