C · Hospitality & retail property

Hotels as Real Estate

The lodging market bifurcates into high-margin luxury and extended-stay while economy motels collapse as chains financialize the category as an asset class.

The US hotel industry is stuck. Market size inched from $258.1 billion in 2022 to $286.5 billion in 2025, but that 0.5% growth masks a story of radical bifurcation: luxury boutiques pulled 6% revenue gains while economy properties contracted, extended-stay hotels captured supply growth, and Sonder's November 2025 bankruptcy shocked the market. Higher rates broke the capital math for conversion plays and independent operators, and labor scarcity made skeleton crews the new normal.

What changed

Higher interest rates killed the conversion-play economics that had kept the hotel pipeline full. For years, investors could acquire distressed motels, pour capex into a refresh, and refinance at a spread over treasuries. By 2025, that math inverted: debt service on empty properties became toxic, maturity walls hit Q4 2025 through Q1 2026, and Revo Hospitality Group's 260 properties landed in Chapter 11. Sonder, the Marriott-backed boutique tech startup, collapsed in November 2025 after the licensing deal severed, stranded guests mid-stay, and left its asset base in limbo. The refinancing crisis was real: hotels that could not roll over loans were forced to sell, compress capex, or file for restructuring.

Simultaneously, the labor cost wall inverted the margin ladder. Wages for hotel staff rose 25.6% versus 2019, and labor cost per occupied room jumped 21% from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025, hitting $54.98 by year-end. Operating costs exploded too: insurance premiums up 100%, utilities up 30% from 2024 to 2025, while demand flatlined after the pandemic recovery bounce. Large chains could absorb these hits by running skeleton crews with 70-80% annual turnover and automating guest-facing functions. Independent operators and smaller chains could not. By 2026, boutique hotels with tighter unit economics faced compression of average margins from 18.4% in 2016 down to 15.1% in 2026, making refinancing harder and forcing consolidation.

What made lodging newly valuable was scale and distribution, not the property itself. Luxury boutique hotels achieved average daily rates of $452 in 2025 with RevPAR of $307, well above the industry-wide luxury average of $263, because they could command premium pricing from high-frequency travelers and corporate accounts. Extended-stay hotels grew supply by 4% in 2025, the largest increase in four years, occupying 12.4% above industry-average occupancy because they served project-based employment and hybrid work relocations, not one-off travelers. Casino hotels bifurcated by destination: premium Las Vegas resorts remained resilient with higher-value customers per room, while mid-tier regional casinos faced slower traffic and price competition, reflecting geographic pricing power. What made rooms cheap was economy lodging: traditional midscale and budget properties faced contraction because their occupancy could not sustain their debt loads at 2025 borrowing costs.

The real money rotated to asset financialization. IHG opened a record 443 hotels in Q1 2026, passing 7,000 operating hotels with 1.03 million rooms, and signed 694 additional properties, converting franchising into a real-estate brokerage. Hyatt acquired Playa Hotels & Resorts for $2.6 billion in 2025, and Blackstone purchased Hamilton Island for $1.2 billion, treating resort properties as collateral-backed income streams rather than hospitality operations. Fertitta Entertainment offered $7 billion for Caesars Entertainment (a $31.5 billion deal including debt) expected to close late 2026 or early 2027, consolidating casino properties into a mega-operator with 60 casinos. VICI Properties acquired Golden Portfolio properties (7 casinos) in April 2026 for $1.15 billion and Gamehost assets in Canada for $141 million in June 2026, positioning itself as a landlord to casino operators rather than an operator itself. Hilton launched its Outset Collection with 60+ properties in pipeline, targeting independent owners seeking global distribution without losing brand autonomy. In essence, the property became the collateral, the franchise became the moat, and the occupancy rate became the bond yield.

The evidence

  • Luxury boutique hotels: 53.5% of boutique market revenue in 2025 with 70-75% occupancy and RevPAR climbing 5.3%, while economy segments declined (2025)
  • Extended-stay segment: Grew 4% in supply during 2025, driven by project-based employment and hybrid work patterns, occupying 12.4% above industry average (2025)
  • Labor crisis: Wages rose 25.6% versus 2019, turnover 70-80% annually, with cost per occupied room up 21% from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025 (2025)
  • Casino hotels: Labor cost per occupied room jumped 12.8% in 2025, compressing margins from 12.2% baseline; premium Las Vegas resorts resilient, mid-tier regional casinos face price competition (2025-2026)
  • Consolidation wave: Hyatt acquired Playa Hotels & Resorts for $2.6B (2025); Fertitta offered $7B for Caesars Entertainment ($31.5B including debt, expected close late 2026); IHG opened record 443 hotels Q1 2026, signed 694 additional properties (2025-2026)

Who rides it

Large chains and asset financiers win. IHG, Hilton, and Marriott capture franchise fees and brand licensing without owning physical properties, turning landlords and independent operators into renters of their systems. Blackstone, VICI Properties, and other pension-backed real-estate players acquire distressed assets at discounts, hold them as collateral-backed income streams, and lease them to branded operators, earning spread and optionality. Luxury boutique properties and extended-stay conversions win because their occupancy and RevPAR justify the debt load: boutiques achieved $452 average daily rates in 2025, extended-stay captured 12.4% above industry occupancy, and their guests pay premium rates or sign longer leases. Digital distribution platforms win too: metasearch and Google Hotel Ads commanded $8.2 billion in annual spend in 2025, bypassing traditional OTA channels and giving chains direct customer data.

Who's squeezed

Independent hotel owners and economy-segment operators lose hard. Sonder's November 2025 collapse and Revo's January 2026 Chapter 11 bankruptcy forced asset sales into an unfriendly debt market, and survivors faced margin compression from 18.4% in 2016 to 15.1% in 2026. Economy and traditional midscale properties contracted throughout 2025 because their occupancy could not justify their debt service at higher rates and their labor costs could not be absorbed by lower RevPAR. Mid-tier regional casinos lost pricing power and foot traffic, forced to compete on discounts rather than experience. Guests in stranded Sonder locations lost access mid-stay. Workers in hospitality faced the highest wage gains (25.6% since 2019) but also the highest turnover (70-80% annually), suggesting jobs became temporary and unstable despite raises.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is a debt spiral among the remaining independent and mid-tier operators. Maturity walls peaked Q4 2025 through Q1 2026, meaning a wave of loans reached renewal exactly when refinancing rates remained high and occupancy had plateaued. Hotels that cannot roll over debt at acceptable rates will be forced into emergency sales, flooding the market with distressed inventory and crushing pricing for those still solvent. Regional casinos face regulatory fragmentation: Illinois, Indiana, Hawaii, Maine, and others are legalizing online casinos and micro-betting, which will siphon players from land-based resorts and require operators to choose between maintaining price and defending volume. If online expansion accelerates, mid-tier regional casinos could face a 10-15% revenue loss within three years, triggering another wave of bankruptcies and asset fire-sales.

In one sentence

Hotels as real estate in a nutshell

Higher rates and labor scarcity bifurcated the hotel market into high-margin luxury and extended-stay winners and contracting economy properties, while large chains and asset financiers consolidated control by franchising brands and acquiring distressed real estate as collateral.

C · Hospitality & retail property

Retail's Property Fallout

Store closures are flooding retail real estate onto the market as tariffs and e-commerce crush the department store model.

Department stores, the backbone of American shopping malls for decades, are imploding. Tariff rates jumped from 14.7% in January 2025 to 35.1% by December 2025, crushing margins. Saks Global—which had just merged Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman—filed for bankruptcy in January 2026 carrying $3.4 billion in debt. Macy's is closing 150 stores by end-2026, dumping prime retail real estate onto the market faster than it can be repurposed.

What changed

For decades, a department store on Main Street or in a regional mall was money: stable anchor tenant, foot traffic, reliable credit quality. That math broke in 2025-2026. Tariffs on apparel imports exploded—14.7% in January 2025, climbing to 35.1% by December 2025—compressing margins industry-wide from 6.1% in 2024 to an estimated 3.6% if retailers absorbed the costs. Retailers had three bad choices: eat the tariff hit and wipe out profit, pass it to customers and watch traffic tank, or manufacture differently. None worked. Saks Global, carrying $3.4 billion in debt after its December 2024 merger of three iconic luxury banners, hit a wall in January 2026 when vendor payment delays cascaded and store productivity collapsed. That bankruptcy was the signal. It told landlords that even prestige retail was vulnerable.

Mainstream department stores followed. Macy's executed a controlled retreat, closing 50 stores by end-2024, then 66 in 2025, with 14 more planned for 2026—that's 150 doors gone, each one freeing a landlord to either hold vacant space, discount massively, or let the tenant walk. JCPenney's FY2024 revenue fell to $6.6 billion despite a 'Yes, JCPenney' comeback campaign that lifted May 2025 traffic by 3%. Nordstrom's family launched a $3.8 billion bid to take the company private in late 2025-2026, signaling they saw more value in the off-price Rack format than in traditional department stores. The shift was structural, not cyclical. Consumer spending bifurcated: affluent households kept spending; lower and middle-income households traded down to discount stores at five times faster rates in 2026, with inflation (PCE up 4.1% year-over-year as of May 2026) driving the wedge. Discount stores and off-price retailers (TJX, Ross) won that migration. Department stores were caught in the middle, losing traffic to cheaper channels above and below them.

The real estate consequence is cascading vacancy and repricing. Mall anchors are no longer anchors. Department store real estate—prime 50,000-100,000-square-foot boxes in regional malls and downtowns—is flooding the market with no clear next tenant. The 666,500 employees in US department stores are declining 2.87% annually through 2028; fewer jobs means weaker demand for nearby service space, parking, and logistics. Landlords face a choice: hold space at distressed rents, convert to fitness, dining, or entertainment, or accept lease terminations and redevelop. Each option destroys value vs. the pre-2020 model. Off-price and discount retail are expanding—Ross Stores reported comparable store sales up 17% in Q3 2025 and announced ~110 new store openings for 2026—but those boxes are smaller, lower-rent, and serve different locations. They won't fill the real estate vacuum left by department store collapse.

The evidence

  • Department stores market: $227.1B in 2026, declining at 0.4% in 2026 alone with 6.0% margins compressed by tariffs and discounting (IBISWorld 2026).
  • Apparel tariff shock: rates climbed from 14.7% (Jan 2025) to 35.1% (Dec 2025), cutting retail profit margins by estimated 2.5 percentage points if absorbed (US trade data, 2025-2026).
  • Saks Global bankruptcy: $3.4B debt January 2026 after luxury merge; Macy's 150-store closure by end-2026; Nordstrom family $3.8B take-private bid (2026 retail consolidation).
  • Consumer trade-down: lower/middle-income households shifting to discount stores at 5x faster rates in 2026 with 4.1% PCE inflation (May 2026 consumer behavior data).
  • Off-price winning: Ross Stores +17% comp sales Q3 2025 with ~110 new openings for 2026; TJX gaining share from collapsing mid-tier (Q3 2025 earnings).

Who rides it

Off-price and discount retailers are the clear winners. Ross Stores posted 17% comparable store sales growth in Q3 2025 and announced 110 new store openings for 2026. TJX and other value formats are capturing traffic from the collapsing mid-tier. The "treasure hunt" experience of curated, changing inventory remains defensible against e-commerce, so discount stores are outperforming traditional department stores across the board. Nordstrom's family, betting $3.8 billion on taking the company private, sees the future in Rack expansion, not in full-line department stores. Logistics and alternative uses for vacated real estate may also win—repurposed department store boxes can become storage, fitness, dining, or entertainment venues if landlords are creative.

Who's squeezed

Department store landlords and the vendors, workers, and service providers that depend on them are getting squeezed. Macy's is closing 150 stores by end-2026; JCPenney is fighting for survival despite a 3% traffic bump; even luxury collapsed (Saks Global bankruptcy). Department store employees are declining 2.87% annually through 2028. Mall owners are losing their anchor tenants. Landlords are either holding vacant space, offering fire-sale rents to attract new tenants (who may never come), or accepting lease terminations and redevelopment losses. Regional malls that built their entire model around department store anchors are facing existential questions about their future.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The biggest risk is the speed and cascade of store closures creating a real estate death spiral in regional malls and secondary downtowns. Macy's 150 stores, Saks Global bankruptcy, JCPenney's struggles, and smaller retailers' exits are all happening in 2025-2026 simultaneously. As landlords lose anchor tenants and traffic, they cut maintenance, raise rents on remaining tenants (squeezing smaller shops), and the mall spirals down. Secondary and tertiary locations are most vulnerable—a mall in a smaller metro loses its Macy's and has no clear alternative anchor. If landlords can't find new uses or tenants fast enough, you see vacancy cascades, property value crashes, and forced sales at steep discounts that ripple through REIT portfolios and commercial property financing.

In one sentence

Retail's property fallout in a nutshell

Tariffs and e-commerce broke department stores; now their real estate is flooding the market with no clear next tenant, forcing landlords to either discount massively, hold vacant space, or accept redevelopment losses.

D · The tensions

The commercial-debt wall

When $2.8 trillion in maturing loans hit refinancing at higher rates, the math breaks.

The commercial real estate sector is running into a wall. Not the office crisis, though that's real and getting worse—the problem is simpler and more mechanical. Billions of dollars in debt is maturing, and the math that made sense at 4.3% does not work at 6.2%. Banks are getting squeezed, borrowers are getting squeezed, and the reckoning is happening right now.

What changed

The Federal Reserve cut rates sharply from September 2024 through the end of 2025—a total of 1.75 percentage points—to ease pressure on banks and borrowers after the 2023 banking crisis took down SVB, Signature, and First Republic. But that relief was temporary and one-directional. The real problem sits in the debt that was issued years earlier, when rates were lower and office buildings still looked like safe bets. Between 2015 and 2022, commercial real estate borrowers locked in loans at rates around 4.3%. Now those loans are maturing. In 2025 alone, $957 billion in CRE loans came due for refinancing. Through 2028, $2.8 trillion more will mature. Today's rates for new CRE financing sit at 6.2%. The spread—190 basis points—is not a rounding error. For a $100 million office building loan, that's $1.9 million more per year in interest expense. Scale that to a portfolio or a whole asset class, and the math breaks.

The refinancing wave exposes a deeper structural problem. Office properties refinancing at 6.2% often cannot generate enough rental income to service the debt at the new rate. Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities (CMBS) delinquencies hit 7.29% in 2025—the highest distress signal in years. Chapter 11 bankruptcies in the real estate sector hit a 10-year high in 2025, and corporate bankruptcies broadly reached 694 cases, the highest count in 14 years. The market knew this was coming, but knowing and absorbing it are different things. Banks are holding $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure on their balance sheets, concentrated in regional and community banks that lack the diversification of the mega-banks. When office tenancy fails and cap rates reset, the collateral value drops. A building worth $60 million based on rents six years ago might be worth $35 million based on what rents and interest rates say today. That gap is where losses live.

The Fed's rate cuts from mid-2024 into 2025 actually compressed banks' net interest margins even as they recovered slightly to 3.39% by Q4 2025—the highest since 2019—because deposit costs were sticky and slow to fall. Meanwhile, competition for deposits intensified. Uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 alone, a sign that corporate clients and sophisticated investors were chasing yield and moving money to banks offering better rates. Banks needed higher yields on their loan books to offset deposit-cost pressure and compensate for credit losses on troubled CRE. But borrowers already stressed by rate resets cannot bear higher yields. The two sides are being crushed in the same vice: refinancing rates that destroy deal economics, and deposit competition that erodes the interest-rate cushion banks have left.

The real twist is that industrial and multifamily—the strongest real estate segments—are actually absorbing losses from office. Industrial had a banner 2025 with 940 million square feet of leasing, the second-best year on record, fueled by e-commerce tenants accounting for 56% of retail sales growth and needing 50 to 70 million square feet of warehouse space for every 1% rise in online penetration. Multifamily absorbed 124,600 units in Q2 2026 alone and drove 39.5% year-over-year growth in investor transaction volume, powered by a 3.4-million-unit housing shortage and a 105% premium to buy rather than rent. But both segments are refinancing into the same higher-rate environment. The difference is they earn enough to service the debt. Offices do not. This is creating a bifurcated market where strong asset classes are paying more to fund weak ones, and the debt wall is forcing a capital reallocation that looks less like recovery and more like triage.

The evidence

  • Commercial Real Estate: $957 billion in CRE loans matured in 2025, with $2.8 trillion more through 2028, all refinancing at 6.2% versus original 4.3% rates (2025-2026)
  • Commercial Real Estate: CMBS delinquencies reached 7.29% in 2025, the highest distress signal in the market (2025)
  • Commercial Real Estate: Chapter 11 bankruptcies hit a 10-year high in 2025, and office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025 before modest absorption (2025)
  • Commercial Banking: $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure held by banks; $1.26 trillion matures by 2027, many refinancing at 190-basis-point spreads (2026)
  • Commercial Banking: Uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 as deposit costs remained sticky and competition intensified (Q4 2025)

Who rides it

Industrial landlords and multifamily operators are riding this force because their tenants have pricing power and lease growth resilience. Industrial absorbed 940 million square feet in 2025, the second-best year on record, because e-commerce tenants need 50 to 70 million square feet of warehouse space for every 1% increase in online penetration—a structural requirement they will pay for. Multifamily absorbed 124,600 units in Q2 2026 and drove 39.5% year-over-year growth in investor transaction volume, lifted by a 3.4-million-unit housing shortage and a 105% premium to buy versus rent. Both asset classes can refinance at 6.2% and still maintain positive cash flow, which means they can absorb rate increases while office buildings cannot. Real estate investors with logistics and residential portfolios are consolidating and buying at distressed valuations from borrowers forced to sell. Banks lending to these strong segments are actually more profitable because yield is higher and credit losses are lower.

Who's squeezed

Office building owners, especially those holding Class B and C properties, are getting crushed. The sector sits in structural crisis: office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025 and has only begun to decline as 127 million square feet was absorbed, but the underlying demand is gone. Refinancing that building at 6.2% often destroys the debt service coverage ratio. Owners are forced to refinance into the same higher-rate environment, accept losses on resale, or default. Community and regional banks holding concentrated CRE portfolios face margin compression from deposit competition and credit losses from office defaults. The $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure on bank balance sheets is not diversified enough in smaller banks to absorb losses on the weak segment while rates remain higher. Developers and building managers face obsolescence: office-to-apartment conversions reached 90,300 units in 2026, a 28% year-over-year jump, signaling a wholesale rewrite of the use case for millions of square feet that will never be profitable offices again.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The single biggest risk is a cascading default spiral in office and secondary properties. When one major owner defaults on a $500 million or $1 billion property, it forces a mark-to-market loss on comparable collateral across the banking system, which triggers more defaults and more mark-downs in a feedback loop. The $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure sits concentrated in smaller banks that do not have the capital buffers or diversification to absorb a 10% or 20% loss on their portfolio. A wave of bank failures in 2026 or 2027, timed to coincide with the peak refinancing wall, could trigger a credit crunch that starves even strong borrowers (industrial, multifamily) of capital to expand or refinance. The broader economy would suffer not because the real estate problem is new, but because the debt maturity cliff is concentrated in time and overlaps with rising labor costs and energy prices.

The commercial-debt wall in a nutshell

Commercial real estate borrowers are staring down a refinancing crisis: nearly $1 trillion in loans came due in 2025 alone, and $2.8 trillion more mature through 2028, all refinancing at rates 190 basis points higher than their originals.

D · The tensions

Building Costs Bite

Tariffs, labor, and rates raise the cost to build anything new.

The construction industry is caught in a vise. Labor shortages, tariff shocks, and elevated borrowing costs have made new buildings more expensive to build and harder to finance. The split is brutal: data centers (the only growth story) are surging while traditional offices, retail, and housing are stalling.

What changed

The commercial construction market in the US is $315.5 billion in 2026, growing just 1.1%—a reflection of a deep, two-tier split. Data center construction is the only engine: starts reached $77.7 billion in 2025, a stunning 190% jump from 2024, as Amazon commits $23 billion to an Ohio facility and Microsoft deploys what it calls the world's most powerful data center in Wisconsin, both coming online in 2026. The Stargate Project, a $500 billion four-year AI infrastructure investment by OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle, and MGX announced in January 2025, anchors long-term pipelines. But office construction hit a wall. Hybrid work hollowed out office demand by 41% since 2019; new office deliveries dropped 26% in 2025, and vacancy concentrates in older Class-B and Class-C towers while Class-A trophy buildings stay full at premium rents. Retail, warehouse, and hospitality remain soft but stable—no recovery in sight.

The binding constraint is labor scarcity, which now costs the industry $10.8 billion annually. A 500,000-worker shortage has pushed wage inflation to 4% per year and forced mid-market contractors to turn away work. Material costs are surging from tariff shocks: effective tariff rates on construction goods hit 25–30% in 2025 (the highest in 40 years), raising the typical home cost by $10,900 per unit. December 2025 saw monthly spending on data center construction average $6.5 billion—up from just $500 million in mid-2021. Elevated mortgage rates at 5.7–6.6% in August 2026 have frozen financing for traditional commercial deals, squeezing both developers and lenders.

The home builders industry reflects this pain even more sharply. At $166.2 billion in 2026, the market is flat (0.0% growth in 2026, 1.1% CAGR from 2021–2026) and margins are compressed to 6–8% net, down from 6.1% in 2022. Housing starts crashed 15.4% month-over-month in May 2026 to 1.177 million (seasonally adjusted annual rate), the lowest since May 2020, as buyers confronted the combined shock of tariff-driven costs and persistent high rates near 6%. Builders have cut prices by an average of 5% and are offering mortgage rate buydowns to move inventory, hollowing out profits. Sixty percent of builders report tariff-driven cost increases; smaller builders are hit hardest because they cannot absorb the margin squeeze. M&A activity among home builders doubled between August 2025 and June 2026: 18% of builders report acquisition approaches (up from 9%), signaling that scale and capital strength now separate winners from sellers. Major deals include Taylor Morrison acquired by Berkshire Hathaway, Tri Pointe Homes acquired by Sumitomo Forestry, and United Homes Group and Holiday Builders acquired by Stanley Martin Homes. Construction M&A deals as a whole surged 18.2% to 562 transactions in 2025 as firms consolidated to offset labor shortages and rising input costs.

This is a structural reckoning, not a cycle. Tariff regimes are sticky, labor shortages reflect demographic collapse, and rates will not reset to 3% overnight. The data center boom is real and capital-intensive, but it does not employ construction workers at the same scale as mid-market office and retail projects. Smaller builders, independent contractors, and traditional commercial developers face a narrowing window: either consolidate, pivot to niche markets (or niche markets), or exit.

The evidence

  • Commercial Building Construction in the US: $315.5 billion market (2026) with 1.1% growth; data center starts surged 190% to $77.7 billion in 2025, but office deliveries fell 26% in 2025 as hybrid work reduced demand by 41% since 2019; labor shortage costs $10.8 billion annually.
  • Home Builders in the US: $166.2 billion market (2026) with flat 0.0% growth; housing starts crashed 15.4% month-over-month in May 2026 to 1.177 million annualized (lowest since May 2020); tariffs added $10,900 per unit cost; M&A activity doubled (18% of builders acquired or approached by June 2026 vs. 9% in August 2025).
  • Tariff Impact (2025-2026): Effective tariff rates on construction goods hit 25-30% in 2025 (40-year high); 60% of builders report tariff-driven cost increases; construction M&A surged 18.2% to 562 transactions in 2025 as firms consolidated.
  • Data Center Boom (2025-2026): Stargate Project announced ($500 billion over four years); Amazon committed $23 billion to Ohio expansion; Microsoft deployed mega-facility in Wisconsin; both due live in 2026; monthly data center spending reached $6.5 billion in December 2025.
  • Labor and Rates (2025-2026): 500,000-worker shortage drives 4% annual wage growth; mortgage rates 5.7-6.6% in August 2026; margin compression to 6-8% net for builders (down from 6.1% in 2022).

Who rides it

Large-cap builders with scale and capital (D.R. Horton, Lennar, PulteGroup, Berkshire Hathaway, Sumitomo Forestry) are consolidating smaller rivals and can absorb tariff shocks and margin compression. Data center developers and capital-intensive infrastructure firms tied to AI booms (Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, SoftBank) are winning massive project pipelines and long-term contracts. Established commercial real estate players with Class-A trophy assets in tight markets command premiums while older Class-B and Class-C buildings struggle.

Who's squeezed

Smaller home builders, independent contractors, and mid-market commercial developers are squeezed on both price and cost. Labor shortages force them to turn away jobs or pay premiums they cannot pass through. Tariffs bite hardest on smaller firms with thin margins and limited purchasing power. Retail and hospitality developers are stuck in soft markets with no end in sight. Regional construction firms without scale or diversification into data centers face consolidation pressure or exit.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The labor shortage is structural, not cyclical. Demographic decline, immigration politics, and decades of underinvestment in construction training mean the 500,000-worker gap will not close soon. Tariff regimes, whether 25-30% or higher, look sticky given political commitments and reshoring ideology. If mortgage rates stay above 5.5%, housing starts will remain depressed, which means fewer new units, which means rents stay high, which means first-time buyers stay locked out. The debt wall in commercial real estate (maturing office mortgages, refinancing risk) could trigger a cascade of distressed sales and further consolidation.

E · The big picture

The Real-Estate Reckoning

Hybrid work and higher rates have shattered the old real-estate math; capital now rotates away from offices toward logistics, data centers, and housing.

The math broke in two directions at once. Hybrid work hollowed out downtown offices—office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025 and only fell to 17.7% by mid-2026 after 127 million square feet of absorption, revealing that Class B and C office buildings are now economically obsolete. At the same time, interest-rate hikes destroyed the leverage game that built modern real estate: $957 billion in commercial real estate loans matured in 2025 alone, with another $2.8 trillion due through 2028, and refinancing at higher rates is simply unaffordable. Capital that once chased office towers and debt-fueled deals now hunts for hard assets with real cash flow: warehouses for e-commerce, data centers for AI compute, and housing stock for a shortage that sits at 3.4 million homes.

What changed

The office sector entered structural crisis. National office vacancy climbed steadily, then got stuck at an artificially low 17.7% by mid-2026 only because developers were forced to accept conversions to apartments—90,300 office-to-apartment conversion units in 2026 alone, a 28% year-over-year jump, now representing 47% of the entire 193,900-unit adaptive reuse pipeline. The tenants willing to stay in class A trophy assets in major CBDs paid premium rates, but everyone else either left or never showed up. Class B and C buildings became insolvent: landlords couldn't raise rents, refinancing windows slammed shut, and Chapter 11 bankruptcies among commercial real estate owners hit a 10-year high in 2025 with 694 corporate bankruptcies (the highest in 14 years). CMBS delinquencies reached 7.29% in 2025, the highest distress signal in the market, and multifamily loan delinquencies hit 1.37% in Q3 2025—a 3.4× increase over two years and the worst level since 2008.

Industrial real estate and data centers captured all the growth. Logistics operators leased 940 million square feet in 2025, the second-best year on record, driven by e-commerce tenants accounting for 56% of retail goods sales growth and requiring 50-70 million square feet of warehouse space for every 1% increase in online share. Colocation facilities for AI exploded: the US market jumped from $46.84 billion in 2025 to $72.37 billion in 2026, a 55% spike in one year, with growth driven by AI infrastructure demand—training workloads burning 30-100+ kW per rack, inference pulling 10-20 kW, all requiring liquid cooling and direct power ties. North American colocation occupancy hit 1% vacancy by 2026 (nearly full), forcing operators to treat power access and regulatory tariffs as the new competitive moats rather than square footage. Grid interconnection queues now exceed 1,400 GW of stuck requests with four-to-five-year lead times in saturated markets like Northern Virginia, Dallas, and Phoenix. Federal regulators issued data-center-specific transmission tariffs in December 2025, and states rushed their own: Oregon's POWER Act (August 2025) mandated 10-year power-purchase agreements for facilities larger than 20 MW.

Multifamily housing absorbed capital and buyers because the shortage is real. Apartment rents stopped climbing in 2025-2026 after years of double-digit growth, with luxury vacancy jumping to 11.4%, but the underlying squeeze remains: 3.4 million homes short, and buying costs 105% more than renting on an equivalent basis. Multifamily net absorption hit 124,600 units in Q2 2026, and investor transaction volume surged 39.5% year-over-year, signaling capital rotating into housing despite modest rental growth forecasted at 1.2% for 2026. The apartment market is consolidating at brutal scale: AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential announced a $69 billion merger in late 2025 (closing in 2026) to create the nation's largest apartment REIT with 180,000+ units and expected $175 million in cost cuts within 18 months. Pinnacle filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in May 2025 over $500 million in mortgage debt, and its 5,100 rent-stabilized NYC apartments were auctioned off. Sonder Holdings, the coliving platform, filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in 2025 after its Marriott licensing deal collapsed due to poor financial performance. Smaller multifamily operators and leveraged owners are bleeding out.

Home builders are trapped in a flat, high-friction equilibrium where tariffs and elevated rates have compressed margins while consolidating power to the top tier. Tariffs on construction goods hit 25-30% effective rates by 2025—the highest in 40 years—adding $10,900 per home on average, while skilled labor shortages cost the industry $10.8 billion annually with 4% annual wage growth. Builders responded by cutting prices 5% and offering mortgage rate buydowns, hollowing out margins to 6-8% net in 2026. Housing starts crashed 15.4% month-over-month to 1.177 million annualized by May 2026 (the lowest since May 2020) as buyers faced combined shocks of tariff-driven costs and rates stuck near 6%. M&A activity among builders doubled between August 2025 and June 2026; 18% of builders reported acquisition approaches, up from 9% in August 2025, with major deals like Taylor Morrison acquired by Berkshire Hathaway, Tri Pointe Homes acquired by Sumitomo Forestry, and United Homes Group acquired by Stanley Martin Homes signaling that capital strength and scale now separate winners from sellers. Smaller builders lack the balance sheets to absorb tariff shocks or the refinancing capacity to survive rate cycles.

The evidence

  • Commercial Real Estate: Office vacancy stuck at 17.7% mid-2026 despite 127M sq ft absorption; CMBS delinquencies 7.29% in 2025 (distress peak), but $2.8T maturity wall through 2028 and 694 Chapter 11 bankruptcies in 2025 (10-year high) signal ongoing crisis.
  • Apartment Rental: Multifamily delinquencies hit 1.37% in Q3 2025 (3.4× over two years, worst since 2008); AvalonBay-Equity Residential $69B merger (late 2025) creates 180,000+ unit mega-REIT with $175M cost cuts planned; Pinnacle bankruptcy (May 2025) liquidates 5,100 NYC units.
  • Colocation Facilities: Market exploded from $46.84B (2025) to $72.37B (2026); North American occupancy 1% vacant; grid interconnection queues >1,400 GW stuck 4-5 years; December 2025 FERC tariff rules + August 2025 Oregon POWER Act mandate power contracts for 20+ MW facilities.
  • Home Builders: Tariff rates 25-30% effective (40-year high), +$10,900 per home; housing starts crashed 15.4% to 1.177M annualized by May 2026; M&A doubled (18% acquisition approaches vs 9% in August 2025); Taylor Morrison (Berkshire Hathaway), Tri Pointe (Sumitomo), United Homes (Stanley Martin) signal consolidation.
  • Multifamily Housing: 3.4M home shortage nationwide; buying costs 105% premium vs renting; 124,600 net absorption Q2 2026 + 39.5% investor transaction surge YoY; rental growth forecast 1.2% for 2026 (from 1.4% in 2025), flat after years of double-digit gains.

Who rides it

Logistics operators and data-center companies win outright. Warehouse leasing hit 940 million square feet in 2025 (second-best year on record) as e-commerce captured 56% of retail goods sales growth and demanded 50-70 million square feet per 1% online penetration bump. Colocation jumped 55% in revenue in a single year; Equinix and Digital Realty control ~10% each of the US market in a consolidating industry, and they now hold pricing power because power access and regulatory tariff expertise have become the rare assets. Large multifamily consolidators—AvalonBay and Equity Residential post-merger, Summit Properties acquiring Pinnacle's distressed NYC portfolio, and the tier-1 home builders with balance sheets to absorb tariff shocks and capital to refinance at any rate—capture scale, negotiate supply deals, and convert market chaos into margin. Top-tier builders like Berkshire Hathaway (Taylor Morrison), Sumitomo Forestry (Tri Pointe), and Stanley Martin (United Homes) now have pricing power and the scale to weather tariff volatility.

Who's squeezed

Class B and C office landlords got crushed. Small to mid-market multifamily operators face 1.37% delinquency rates (highest since 2008), and rent-controlled markets like New York and California squeeze owners between frozen pricing and surging costs (labor, insurance, maintenance all up). Mid-market home builders now face acquisition pressure as tariffs erode margins and smaller operators lack capital to absorb $10,900-per-home cost shocks. Office building owners in secondary markets watch their Class B stock become worthless; refinancing at 2025-2026 rates is unaffordable, and there are no buyers for marginal properties. Tenants in rent-stabilized apartments in New York and California get cheaper housing but watch their buildings deteriorate as landlords defer maintenance and insurance costs balloon. Commercial real estate agents and lenders tied to office transactions have seen deal flow evaporate as defaults and restructurings replace new leases.

The main worry

The single biggest risk

The hidden crisis is the refinancing wall and the political fault line it creates. $2.8 trillion in commercial real estate maturities through 2028, following $957 billion in 2025, means that owners are either accepting distressed sales, converting assets to lower-use classes, or defaulting. CMBS delinquencies at 7.29% in 2025 and multifamily delinquencies at 1.37% in Q3 2025 signal that stress is accelerating, not stabilizing. At the same time, the housing shortage (3.4 million homes) and the tariff shock ($10,900 per home) are pinching renters and buyers simultaneously: rents are flat, homebuilding is crashing, and the capital that would normally bridge the gap is tied up in logistics and data-center plays. Political pressure to regulate data-center power tariffs (Oregon's POWER Act, FERC's December 2025 rules) could flip the cost advantage for data centers if states decide to tax hyperscale facilities to protect grid equity, and any hint of rate cuts or real-estate stimulus could swiftly redirect capital away from e-commerce logistics back to office conversion schemes that destroy value.

In one sentence

The real-estate reckoning in a nutshell

Hybrid work and higher rates broke the old real-estate leverage game, forcing capital to rotate from offices toward logistics warehouses, data centers, and housing—and a $2.8-trillion debt wall through 2028 is forcing the reckoning.

By the numbers
19.6%
Office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025, then fell to 17.7% by mid-2026 after 127 million square feet of absorption.
$2.8T
Commercial real estate loans totaling $2.8 trillion are due to mature through 2028, following $957 billion that matured in 2025, forcing a refinancing reckoning at higher rates.
90,300
Office-to-apartment conversions reached 90,300 units in 2026, a 28% year-over-year jump, now representing 47% of the 193,900-unit adaptive reuse pipeline.
$72.37B
US colocation facilities market jumped to $72.37 billion in 2026, up from $46.84 billion in 2025 (55% spike) as AI infrastructure demand exploded.
1%
North American colocation occupancy fell to 1% vacancy by 2026, making power access and regulatory tariffs the new competitive moats rather than square footage.
1.37%
Multifamily loan delinquencies hit 1.37% in Q3 2025, a 3.4× increase over two years and the highest level since the 2008 financial crisis.
25-30%
Effective tariff rates on construction goods hit 25-30% in 2025 (40-year high), adding $10,900 to the typical home cost and forcing builders to cut prices 5% while absorbing margin loss.
1.177M
US housing starts crashed to 1.177 million annualized in May 2026 (seasonally adjusted), the lowest since May 2020, as buyers recoiled from combined tariff and rate shocks.

The synthesis · The Real-Estate Reckoning

The patterns

Hybrid work broke the office and higher rates broke the math — capital rotates from offices to logistics, data centers, and housing, and a debt wall forces the reckoning.
The through-line

Hybrid work and higher rates broke the old real-estate leverage game, forcing capital to rotate from offices toward logistics warehouses, data centers, and housing—and a $2.8-trillion debt wall through 2028 is forcing the reckoning.

Where it shows up

A

The office crisis

Office vacancy broke the revenue model for real estate and architecture, forcing a decade-long reckoning on distressed towers and refinance cliffs.

A

Adaptive reuse & conversion

Hybrid work and higher rates created a $39.8 billion adaptive-reuse opportunity, but tariffs and labor shortages are crushing the margins of the fragmented contractors supposed to build it—pushing capital upmarket to PE rollups and away from the small firms that do most of the actual work.

B

The housing squeeze

Higher rates and tariffs trapped homebuilders in a margin crunch while rent controls left apartment owners unable to cover surging costs, forcing both sides to consolidate around winners with scale and capital strength.

B

Logistics & data centers

Capital flowed from office real estate to logistics and data centers because they move goods and compute—but now the constraint is electricity, not space, and power access has become the only moat that matters.

B

Owning the land

As office towers empty and traditional housing becomes unaffordable, capital quietly rotates into land leasing, RV parks, and manufactured housing—where occupancy stays near 95% and pricing power grows because supply is stuck.

C

Hotels as real estate

Higher rates and labor scarcity bifurcated the hotel market into high-margin luxury and extended-stay winners and contracting economy properties, while large chains and asset financiers consolidated control by franchising brands and acquiring distressed real estate as collateral.

C

Retail's property fallout

Tariffs and e-commerce broke department stores; now their real estate is flooding the market with no clear next tenant, forcing landlords to either discount massively, hold vacant space, or accept redevelopment losses.

D

The commercial-debt wall

Commercial real estate borrowers are staring down a refinancing crisis: nearly $1 trillion in loans came due in 2025 alone, and $2.8 trillion more mature through 2028, all refinancing at rates 190 basis points higher than their originals.

D

Building costs bite

Tariffs, labor shortages, and high rates have split construction into two economies: data centers booming at $77.7 billion starts in 2025 while homes, offices, and retail stall, squeezing smaller builders and forcing consolidation.

Who wins across the board

Logistics operators and data-center companies win outright. Warehouse leasing hit 940 million square feet in 2025 (second-best year on record) as e-commerce captured 56% of retail goods sales growth and demanded 50-70 million square feet per 1% online penetration bump. Colocation jumped 55% in revenue in a single year; Equinix and Digital Realty control ~10% each of the US market in a consolidating industry, and they now hold pricing power because power access and regulatory tariff expertise have become the rare assets. Large multifamily consolidators—AvalonBay and Equity Residential post-merger, Summit Properties acquiring Pinnacle's distressed NYC portfolio, and the tier-1 home builders with balance sheets to absorb tariff shocks and capital to refinance at any rate—capture scale, negotiate supply deals, and convert market chaos into margin. Top-tier builders like Berkshire Hathaway (Taylor Morrison), Sumitomo Forestry (Tri Pointe), and Stanley Martin (United Homes) now have pricing power and the scale to weather tariff volatility.

Who's squeezed across the board

Class B and C office landlords got crushed. Small to mid-market multifamily operators face 1.37% delinquency rates (highest since 2008), and rent-controlled markets like New York and California squeeze owners between frozen pricing and surging costs (labor, insurance, maintenance all up). Mid-market home builders now face acquisition pressure as tariffs erode margins and smaller operators lack capital to absorb $10,900-per-home cost shocks. Office building owners in secondary markets watch their Class B stock become worthless; refinancing at 2025-2026 rates is unaffordable, and there are no buyers for marginal properties. Tenants in rent-stabilized apartments in New York and California get cheaper housing but watch their buildings deteriorate as landlords defer maintenance and insurance costs balloon. Commercial real estate agents and lenders tied to office transactions have seen deal flow evaporate as defaults and restructurings replace new leases.
